# Images of the Russian Empire
### Colorizing the Prokudin-Gorskii photo collection

## Overview
Imagine seeing history in full color: glass-plate negatives from the early 1900s, each photographed by Sergei Prokudin-Gorskii through red, green, and blue filters as silent, incomplete layers waiting to be aligned and merged. In this project, I'll breathe life back into these photos using nothing more than math, geometry, and intuition.

>[!note] Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
>For a data matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_1 & \dots & \vec{x}_n\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$ with SVD $A=U\Sigma V^T$,
>
>1. $$U_\mathscr{l} \in \sum^{n}_{i=1}\underset{W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times \mathscr{l}}}{\mathrm{argmin}}||\vec{x}_i-W^TW\vec{x}_i||^2,$$
> where  $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times \mathscr{l}}$ is an [[2.9c Matrix Orthonormality|orthonormal matrix]] such that $W^TW=I_\mathscr{l}$, and $U_\mathscr{l}$ consists of the first $\mathscr{l}$ columns of the matrix of principal components $U$.
>
>2. $$S_{\text{PCA}} \in \sum^{n}_{i=1}\underset{S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d}{\mathrm{argmin}}||\vec{x}_i-\mathrm{proj}_S(\vec{x}_i)\vec{x}_i||^2,$$
>where $\mathrm{dim}(S) \leq \mathscr{l}$, and $S_{\text{PCA}}=\mathrm{Span}(\vec{u}_1,\dots,\vec{u}_\mathscr{l})$ is the span of the first $\mathscr{l}$ columns of the matrix of principal components $U$.
>
>3. 
# Intuition
We can compute the PCA of a data matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$  by first centering $A$ around the mean of its datapoints ($\frac{1}{n}A\vec{1}_n$) s.t. $D = A(I_n - \frac{1}{n}\vec{1}_n\vec{1}_n^T)$. Then, $\mathrm{rank}(D)=r \leq \mathrm{min}\{m, n\}$. Suppose that the *ground truth* data matrix (containing the noiseless data) in reality spans an $\mathscr{l}$-dimensional subspace $S_{gt} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, such that $\mathscr{l} \leq r$. Then, the remaining $r-\mathscr{l}$ dimensions of $D$ are due to noise. The goal of PCA is to extract the "best" $\mathscr{l}$-dimensional subspace from the noisy data such that it minimizes the distance between the real subspace and our approximation. 13.title: 4.2c.3 MLR + Batch Gradient Descent
13.path: Statistics & Data Science/6. Machine Learning/6.1 Supervised Learning/6.1b Regression/4.2c Multiple Linear Regression/4.2c.3 MLR + Batch Gradient Descent.md
13.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2c.3 MLR + Batch Gradient Descent]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/05/08 23:46:02","modified":"2024/05/22 03:21:59"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Gradient Descent and The Gradient Vector
>We may use an iterative algorithm, known as gradient descent, to numerically compute the optimal value of $\theta$ where the loss of a [[4.2c.1 Multiple Linear Regression|linear regression]] model is minimized by guesstimating the minimum until we converge to the real minimum value such that
>$$\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t - \alpha\frac{d}{d\theta}L(\theta_t),$$
>where $\alpha$ is the learning rate (or the magnitude of the steps).
>
>
>In doing so for multivariate models, we may generalize the gradient descent process for $n$ minimum theta values $\vec{\theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\theta}_0 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{\theta}_n\end{bmatrix}$ as
>$$\vec{\theta}_{t+1}=\vec{\theta}_t-\nabla_\vec{\theta}L(\theta_t),$$
>where $\nabla_\vec{\theta}L(\theta_t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_0} \\ \dots \\ \partial\theta_n\end{bmatrix}$ is the gradient vector.
>>[!warning] Convexity of the Loss Function
>>If our loss function is not convex (has more than one local minimum), choosing the wrong $\theta_G$ may lead to convergence to the wrong minimum.

# Intuition
Suppose we start at an optimal value of $\theta_G=\theta_0$. Since our guess $\theta_0 \neq \hat{\theta}$, we can split our guess into two cases:
1. The guess $\theta_0$ "undershoots" $\hat{\theta}$ ($\theta_G < \hat{\theta}$).
	- The derivative of our loss function will be **negative**, so we must **increase** our guess by moving in the positive direction of $\theta$ until $\theta_G \to \hat{\theta}$.
2. The guess $\theta_0$ "overshoots" $\hat{\theta}$ ($\theta_G > \hat{\theta}$).
	- The derivative of our loss function will be **positive**, so we must **decrease** our guess until $\theta_G \to \hat{\theta}$.

14.path: Statistics & Data Science/6. Machine Learning/6.1 Supervised Learning/6.1b Regression/4.2c Multiple Linear Regression/4.2c.1 Multiple Linear Regression.md
14.content:

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/07 00:27:05","modified":"2024/03/07 01:05:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Multiple Linear Regression (SLR)
>The multiple regression line is the unique straight line that minimizes the mean squared error across a dataset using multiple features given by the equation
>$$
>\hat{\mathbb{Y}} = \mathbb{X}\theta \iff
>\begin{bmatrix} \hat{y}_1 \\ \hat{y}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_n \end{bmatrix} =
>\begin{bmatrix}
>1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_1p \\
>1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_2p \\
>\vdots &   & \ddots &   & \vdots \\
>1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_np \\
>\end{bmatrix}
>\begin{bmatrix} \theta_0 \\ \theta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta_p \end{bmatrix}
>$$
>where $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the prediction vector, $\mathbb{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (p+1)}$ is the design matrix containing $x_{ij}$ for the $i$th observation and $j$th feature, and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+1)}$ is the parameter vector.

15.title: 4.2c.2 MLR + MSE
15.path: Statistics & Data Science/6. Machine Learning/6.1 Supervised Learning/6.1b Regression/4.2c Multiple Linear Regression/4.2c.2 MLR + MSE.md
15.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2c.2 MLR + MSE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/07 00:45:05","modified":"2025/01/21 17:38:28"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Estimate
>When fitted using [[6.6a.2 MSE (L2 Loss)|L2 loss]], the general solution to [[4.2c.1 Multiple Linear Regression|multiple linear regression]] is of the form
>$$\hat{\theta} = (\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{Y}$$
>for an invertible $\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X}$ only possible when $\mathbb{X}$ is in full column rank.
# Proof
We first take the original definition of MSE and massage it into vector form using the L2 norm:
$$MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2=\frac{1}{n}(||\mathbb{Y} - \hat{\mathbb{Y}}||_2)^2=\frac{1}{n}(||\mathbb{Y} - \mathbb{X}\theta||_2)^2$$
Since $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} = \mathbb{X}\theta$ is a linear combination of $\mathbb{X}$, $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} \in \mathrm{span}(\mathbb{X})$. To minimize the MSE we need that $\hat{\mathbb{Y}}$ which is closest to $\mathbb{Y}$. It turns out that the closest vector to $\mathbb{Y}$ in $\mathrm{span}(\mathbb{X})$ is the one right below $\mathbb{Y}$. Therefore, $\hat{\mathbb{Y}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{Y}$ onto $Span(\mathbb{X})$. However, the formula for orthogonality (perpendicularity) requires the dot product of two vectors to be equal to zero, or similarly $M^T \vec{v}=\vec{0}$. We can substitute $M$ with the design matrix, and $\vec{v}$ with the residual vector $\vec{e}$ to find $\theta$:
$$\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbb{Y}-\hat{\mathbb{Y}})=\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbb{Y}-\mathbb{X}\theta)=\vec{0} \iff \mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{Y}=\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X}\theta$$
Therefore,
$$\theta=(\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{Y}.$$
Note that $\vec{e} \perp Span(\mathbb{X})$, which includes $\mathbb{X}, \hat{\mathbb{Y}}$, their columns and any other vector/matrix $\in Span(\mathbb{X)}$.

17.title: 4.3b.3 Constant + MAE
17.path: Statistics & Data Science/6. Machine Learning/6.1 Supervised Learning/6.1b Regression/4.2b Constant Model/4.3b.3 Constant + MAE.md
17.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3b.3 Constant + MAE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/06 23:35:43","modified":"2025/01/21 17:38:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Constant + MAE Solution
>The solution to the [[4.2b.1 Constant Model|constant model]] fitted with [[6.6a.1 MAE (L1 Loss)|L1 Loss]] is
>$$\hat{\theta}_0 = median(y).$$
# Proof
We cannot go straight to differentiation since absolute values are undefined at 0 (or when $y_i=\theta_0$). Therefore, we need to separate the loss function into piecewise cases:
$$
|y_i-\theta_0|=
\begin{cases}
y_i - \theta_0 & \text{if } \theta_0<y_i \\
\theta_0 - y_i & \text{if } \theta_0>y_i
\end{cases}
$$

Then we differentiate the loss function with respect to $\theta_0$:
$$\frac{d}{d \theta_0}|y_i-\theta_0|=
\begin{cases}
-1 & \text{if } \theta_0<y_i \\
1 & \text{if } \theta_0>y_i
\end{cases}
$$
We can summarize this piecewise case as
$$\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MAE=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{d}{d \theta_0}|y_i-\theta_0|=\frac{1}{n}\left[\sum^{}_{\theta_0<y_i}(-1)+\sum^{}_{\theta_0>y_i}(1)\right]$$

Then, we set $\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MAE=0$:
$$0=\frac{1}{n}\left[\sum^{}_{\theta_0<y_i}(-1)+\sum^{}_{\theta_0>y_i}(1)\right] \iff\sum^{}_{\theta_0<y_i}(1)=\sum^{}_{\theta_0>y_i}(1)$$
Which means that the amount of observations greater than $\theta_0$ must be equal to the amount of observations less than $\theta_0$, or, in other words,
$$\hat{\theta}_0 = median(y).$$

18.title: 4.2b.2 Constant + MSE
18.path: Statistics & Data Science/6. Machine Learning/6.1 Supervised Learning/6.1b Regression/4.2b Constant Model/4.2b.2 Constant + MSE.md
18.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2b.2 Constant + MSE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/06 23:10:30","modified":"2025/01/21 17:38:28"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Constant + MSE Solution
>The solution to the [[4.2b.1 Constant Model|constant model]] fitted with [[6.6a.2 MSE (L2 Loss)|L2 Loss]] is
>$$\hat{\theta}_0 = \bar{y}.$$
# Proof
First we differentiate MSE with respect to $\theta_0$:
$$\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MSE=\frac{-2}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\theta_0)$$
Then, we set $\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MSE=0$:
$$0 =\frac{-2}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\hat{\theta}_0) \iff \sum^{n}_{i=1}y_i=n \hat{\theta}_0$$
Therefore, we find that
$$\hat{\theta}_0=\frac{1}{n}\sum y_i=\bar{y}.$$

>[!note] Sampling Error (Variability)
>Sampling variability refers to the inherent variation that occurs between drawn samples due to the impracticability of utilizing the whole population.

>[!example] Measuring Height
>Again, we want to measure the average height of Berkeley students. However, we can't measure the whole student body (>40,000), since that would take a lot of time and effort. We decide to measure a sample of 50 students 3 times after choosing 5 locations on campus at random. In the first sample, the average height is 5'6. In the second, 5'5. In the third, 5'8. The variance between the 3 sample medians is due to sampling error.

31.content:

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 05:22:23","modified":"2023/12/13 06:15:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

> [!note] Measurement Bias
> Measurement bias occurs when there is something systematically (consistently) wrong with our measured recordings as compared to their true values.

>[!example]  Measuring Height
>We want to perform a study of the average height of a Berkeley student. Therefore the population mean will go down by 2 inches.

36.title: 2.2a Kernel Density Estimate
36.path: Statistics & Data Science/1. EDA/1.2 Data Visualization/2.2 KDE Theory/2.2a Kernel Density Estimate.md
36.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2a Kernel Density Estimate]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/07 11:25:04","modified":"2024/03/07 11:50:51"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] KDE Formula
>A kernel density estimate is a smooth, continuous function that approximates the underlying probability distribution of a dataset. Mathematically,
>$$f_a(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}K_\alpha(x, x_i),$$
>where $K_\alpha(x, x_i)$ is the kernel centered at observation $x_i$, $x$ represents a vector of all values in the dataset (or on the number line), and $\alpha$ is the bandwidth/smoothing parameter. Note that we divide the sum by $\frac{1}{n}$ to normalize the area under the curve.

# Examples
>[!example] Gaussian Kernel
> The Gaussian kernel can be expressed as
> $$K_\alpha(x, x_i)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \alpha^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-x_i)^2}{2\alpha^2}},$$
> where the bandwidth $\alpha$ acts as a standard deviation and $x_i$ acts as the mean (since the curve is centered around it).

>[!example] Boxcar Kernel
>The Boxcar kernel can be expressed as the piecewise
>$$K_\alpha(x,x_i)=
>\begin{cases}
>\frac{1}{\alpha} & \text{if } |x-x_i| \leq \frac{\alpha}{2} \\
>0 & \text{if else}
>\end{cases}.
>$$

46.title: 4.1b Least Squares
46.path: STAT 20/4. Prediction/4.1 Evaluating Predictions/4.1b Least Squares.md
46.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.1b Least Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/14 03:06:47","modified":"2023/12/14 04:26:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Optimization
>The least (minimized) squares equations for $b_0$ and $b_1$ are:
>- $$\text{Slope: } b_1=\frac{s_y}{s_x}r$$
>Where $s_i$ is the standard deviation for variable $i$, and $r$ is the correlation coefficient of the variables.
>- $$\text{Intercept: } b_0=\bar{y}-b_1\bar{x}$$
>Where $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ is the mean (mid) point in the scatter plot since the least squares line has to pass through it.

### Intuition
We can express the RSS formula as a function of the slope ($b_1$) and the y-intercept ($b_0$) of the linear model using $\hat{y}_i = b_0+b_1x_i$:
$${RSS}(b_0,b_1)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}[y_i-(b_0+b_1x_i)]^2$$
We must minimize this model for $b_0$ and $b_1$ in order to find the linear model. Two ways to do this is using the newer **Gradient Descent** (which also fits deep-learning models), or the older **Nelder-Mead Algorithm** which works by taking the smallest midpoint on a n-dimensional simplex (a 2D triangle or a 3D pyramid), and transforming it to the most optimal (downhill) point. When optimized, we get the least squares solution.

47.title: 4.1c Explanatory Power
47.path: STAT 20/4. Prediction/4.1 Evaluating Predictions/4.1c Explanatory Power.md
47.content: NOTE TITLE: [[4.1c Explanatory Power]] METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/20 04:50:14","modified":"2023/12/14 05:18:58"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!Theorem] >We can define explanatory power as >$$R^2=\frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}.$$ >$0 \leq R^2 \leq 1$: a lower $R^2$ means predictions are less accurate. ### Intuition Before we construct a linear prediction model, we need to make a naive prediction using another type of summary. Usually this is the mean, denoted by $\bar{y}$. We then must measure the degree to which this naive prediction $\bar{y}$ explains away variability in $y_i$. We must first define two more expressions, the **Sum of Squares Due to Regression**, and the **Total Sum of Squares**. $$SSR=\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2$$ The s**um of squares due to regression** explains how much variance was removed due to the regression model. It makes sense: it is the squared sum of residual between each of the points on the linear model and the mean. $$TSS = \sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2$$ The total sum of squares represents the total variability of the data from the mean. It is basically variance without the normalization (division by $\frac{1}{n-1}$). Here is a chart representing all 3 of the statistics (the third one is the Residual Sum of Squares). Because $TSS$ is the total sum, and $SSR$ is the sum due to regression, we can find $SSR$ as a proportion of $TSS$: $$R^2= \frac{SSR}{TSS}=\frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$$ ["Of all the variability in your y-variables, what proportion is explained using the linear model?"] Since SSR is the opposite of the RSS, and SSR+RSS make up TSS, we can find $R^2$ using RSS: $$R^2=1-\frac{RSS}{TSS} = \frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$$

48.title: 4.1a Residual Sum of Squares
48.path: STAT 20/4. Prediction/4.1 Evaluating Predictions/4.1a Residual Sum of Squares.md
48.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.1a Residual Sum of Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/20 03:45:21","modified":"2023/12/14 04:15:11"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] RSS & Least Squares
>The residual sum of squares formula is,
$${RSS} = \sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2,$$
>for a value $y_i$ and its fitted value on a regression line $\hat{y}_i = b_1x_i + b_0$, in a set of $n$ observations
### Intuition
The residual sum of squares formula calculates all the squared residuals within $n$ between the actual y-value ($y_i$) and the y-value predicted by the linear model ($\hat{y}_i$). It essentially is a measure of the model error, since the larger the residuals between each $i \to n$, the larger the RSS.

53.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.5a Formulating Hypotheses]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/06 10:34:08","modified":"2023/12/14 01:33:28"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Hypotheses
>There are two hypotheses in hypothesis testing:
>- **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** A description of the chance process for generating data. Usually states that nothing out of the ordinary is happening, and has to be refuted with data.
>- **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_A$)**: The assertion that a mechanism other than the null hypothesis generated the data.

>[!Info]
>There are two types of hypothesis testing:
>1. **Independence Hypothesis:** Has an explanatory and a response variable.
>2. **Point Hypothesis:** Compares 

>[!EXAMPLE] USA vs. Kristen Gilbert
>- $H_0 =$ Gilbert being on shift was independent from the increased number of deaths.
>-  $H_A =$ The occurrence of a death is _dependent_ on the presence of Gilbert.

54.title: 3.5b Null Distribution
54.path: STAT 20/3. Generalization/3.5 Hypothesis Testing/3.5b Null Distribution.md
54.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.5b Null Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/14 01:17:42","modified":"2023/12/14 02:40:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Null Distribution
>The null distribution is the sampling distribution of a null hypothesis, and is made up of a test statistic. Test statistics may include finding the mean, a difference in proportions, the chi-squared statistic, and others.

>[!example] US v. Gilbert
>In the US v. Gilbert case, it is important to find whether there was any evidence of foul play on Gilbert's side. In order to create our null distribution, we will use a difference in the proportions of deaths when Gilbert was on shift, and when she was not. However, we need to make sure that the data is fully random. In order to do that, we must permute the data set so that any possible dependence between Gilbert being on shift and deaths is removed:
>```R
># Load the Data Frame
>code_blue <- read_csv("https://www.dropbox.com/s/yj3grtilupyj9pv/code_blue.csv?dl=1") %>% slice_sample(prop = 1)
>
># Shuffle the response and explanatory variables 5000 times and calculate the null distribution of the difference in proportions between deaths on and off Gilbert's shift 
>null <- code_blue %>% specify(explanatory = staff, response = death, success = "yes") %>% hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% generate(reps = 5000, type = "permute") %>% calculate(stat = "diff in props")
>
># Plot!
>plot(null %>% ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + geom_histogram())
>```

55.title: 3.5c The P-Value
55.path: STAT 20/3. Generalization/3.5 Hypothesis Testing/3.5c The P-Value.md
55.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.5c The P-Value]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/14 01:17:28","modified":"2023/12/14 07:31:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] P-Value
>The p-value is the probability of a test statistic as extreme (or more extreme) than the one observed under the null hypothesis. If the p-value is high, it is consistent with the null hypothesis. If it is very low, it is very unlikely in a real-world scenario, so the null hypothesis can be rejected.

>[!example] USA v. Gilbert
>Before we shuffled the data, the difference in proportion of deaths was $p_{Gilbert} - p_{\text{No Gilbert}} = \frac{40}{257}-\frac{34}{1384}=0.131$. This is a pretty big discrepancy, but we still need to compare it to the null distribution:
>```R
># Load the Data Frame
>code_blue <- read_csv("https://www.dropbox.com/s/yj3grtilupyj9pv/code_blue.csv?dl=1") %>% slice_sample(prop = 1)
>
># Shuffle the response and explanatory variables 5000 times and calculate the null distribution of the difference in proportions between deaths on and off Gilbert's shift 
>null <- code_blue %>% specify(explanatory = staff, response = death, success = "yes") %>% hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% generate(reps = 5000, type = "permute") %>% calculate(stat = "diff in props")
>
># Plot!
>plot(null %>% ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + geom_histogram(bins = 23) + annotate("segment", x = .131, xend = .131, y = 0, yend = 600, color = "tomato"))
>```
>The difference, highlighted in red on the plot, is nowhere near the null distribution. This means that the p-value is 0, since there are no values larger than 0.131.

58.title: 3.4c Bootstrapping
58.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.4c Bootstrapping]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 23:29:17","modified":"2023/12/20 04:30:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bootstrapping
>Bootstrapping is a method of estimating a sampling distribution using an empirical distribution by (1) turning it into the **Bootstrap population**, (2) sampling the same number of rows from it with replacement, and (3) calculating a sample statistic until enough statistics (usually 10,000 reps) are gathered to form the **Bootstrap sampling distribution**.
2
>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's go through the process of Bootstrapping step by step. Let's say Yelp is down and we only remember 100 restaurants' 5-star ratings. We want to devise an average rating for all SF restaurants on Yelp. We can write down the ratings we do remember, randomly resample them with replacement and calculate the average rating of each sample. Then, we plot the Bootstrap sampling distribution:
>```R
># Create population (usually we won't be able to do this)
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) 
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows) 
>
># Sample from population to create empirical distribution (usually your data set, in this case the 100 restaurants you remember)
>sampl <- data.frame(sample_n(df, size = 100, rep = T))
>
># Utilize the Bootstrapping pipeline (resample and record the average rating of restaurants for each sample)
>bs <- sampl %>% specify(response = stars) %>% generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") %>% calculate(stat = "mean")
>
># Plot!
>bs_sd <- bs %>% ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + geom_histogram()
>plot(bs_sd)
>```

59.title: 3.4b Confidence Intervals
59.path: STAT 20/3. Generalization/3.4 Making Inferences/3.4b Confidence Intervals.md
59.content: NOTE TITLE: [[3.4b Confidence Intervals]] METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 19:30:05","modified":"2023/12/14 04:18:42"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!note] Confidence Interval >A confidence interval with z-score $z$ is a range of values, >$$[\bar{x} - z \times SE, \bar{x} + z \times SE],$$ > derived from the sampling distribution and believed to contain the true value of the population parameter recorded by the sampling distribution with a certain confidence. ### Intuition Suppose we have a standard normal distribution $X \space \textasciitilde \space N(0, 1)$. We can calculate the probability of a number or interval as a part of the whole distribution by looking at the area under the curve: We can see that instead of the observed values, the x-axis records the number of standard deviations each point is from the mean. For example, it turns out that 68% of data falls within -1 and 1 standard deviations from the mean. We see all major intervals below: - $[-\upsigma, \upsigma] = 0.68$ - $[-1.96\upsigma, 1.96\upsigma] = 0.95$ - $[-2.58\upsigma, 2.58\upsigma] = 0.99$ The multiplicative constant before the standard deviation is known as the z-score. We have already implicitly defined the confidence interval; it is simply a generalization of the intervals above. We can finally denote for any z-score $z$, $\bar{x}$ standard error $SE(\bar{x})$ of a sampling distribution, $[\bar{x}-z \times SE, \bar{x}+z \times SE]$. #### Example >[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco >Consider our sampling distribution of the average rating of restaurants in San Francisco when sampling 100 restaurants per sample. We can now plot a confidence interval on our plot! >```R ># Ignore this. Basically creating the population and drawing a sample. >set.seed(123) >rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) >df <- data.frame(stars = rows) >df %>% specify(response = stars) %>% generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") %>% calculate(stat = "mean") %>% get_ci(level = .95) >``` >Running the example above, we can say with 95% confidence that the population parameter falls between 3.22 and 3.35. This means that 5% of the time a sample from the population will generate a confidence interval which does not contain the population parameter, not that 95% of the time the population parameter falls in that range: think about the population parameter as a constant, and the confidence interval as a variable. Therefore, 5% of all generated confidence intervals from all samples of the population do not contain the population parameter.

60.title: 3.4a Standard Error
60.path: STAT 20/3. Generalization/3.4 Making Inferences/3.4a Standard Error.md
60.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Standard Error]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 10:04:18","modified":"2023/12/14 04:18:36"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

> [!note] Standard Error of the Mean
> For a population distribution with a standard deviation $\upsigma$ or an empirical distribution with a standard deviation $s$, and a sample size $n$,
> $$SE(\bar{x}) \approx \frac{\upsigma}{\sqrt{n}} \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
> is the standard error of the sampling distribution.
> 
> When $\frac{n}{N}$ (sampling fraction) is big,
> $$SE(\bar{x}) \approx \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\frac{\upsigma}{\sqrt{n}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
> is the standard error of the sampling distribution, where $\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$ is the finite population correction (FPC) factor.
### Intuition
Standard error suggests how much the values of a sampling distribution deviate from the population parameter. When we don't have access to the population distribution, an estimate can be made using an empirical distribution. From the equation above, we can see that as $n$ increases, $SE(\bar{x})$ decreases. This is because as we increase the number of samples $n$, the distribution becomes more condensed around the mean (check [[3.3c Sampling Distribution|3.3c]] for an example of this.

62.title: 3.3c Sampling Distribution
62.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.3c Sampling Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:56:57","modified":"2023/12/13 23:17:54"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Sampling Distribution
>The sampling distribution is a probability distribution of a statistic (a mean or a median) based on many samples of equal size from the population .

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's say we sample 100 restaurants at a time, calculate their average rating, and repeat the process 500 times (in STAT 20 this is usually the standard repetition number). We can then make a good inference about the whole population based on our sample. Check this out:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) 
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows) 
sampl_1 <- data.frame(avg_stars = replicate(500, mean(sample_n(df, size = 10, rep = T)$stars)))
sampl_2 <- data.frame(avg_stars = replicate(500, mean(sample_n(df, size = 100, rep = T)$stars)))
s_1 <- ggplot(sampl_1, aes(x = avg_stars)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "Sampling Distribution 1 \n (n = 10 per sample)") 
s_2 <- ggplot(sampl_2, aes(x = avg_stars)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "Sampling Distribution 2 \n (n = 100 per sample)") 
>plot(s_1 + s_2)
>```
>All sampling distributions become more normal ($X \enspace \textasciitilde \enspace N(\upmu, \upsigma$) as we increase sample size. This is seen in the second plot, which also has a mean closer to the population distribution ($\upmu=3.3$) than the first plot. Therefore, as we increase sample size, our accuracy increases and our distribution becomes more normal.

63.title: 3.3b Empirical Distribution
63.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.3b Empirical Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:53:11","modified":"2023/12/13 19:10:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Empirical Distribution
>The empirical distribution is a distribution derived from a single sample of the population that is significantly smaller than the population distribution.

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's say we look at the Yelp pages of 100 restaurants and sample them by recording their 5-star ratings. Then the count of the 100 samples filtered by their number of stars is the empirical distribution:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15))
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows)
>sampl_1 <- sample_n(df, size = 10, rep = T)
>sampl_2 <- sample_n(df, size = 50, rep = T)
>p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Population \n Distribution")
>s_1 <- ggplot(sampl_1, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Empirical Distribution 1 \n (n = 10)")
>s_2 <- ggplot(sampl_2, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = paste("Empirical Distribution 2 \n (n = 50)"))
>plot(p + s_1 + s_2)
>```
>As we can see after running the code above, the bigger the sample size, the more the empirical distribution resembles the population distribution. After some calculations we find out that sample one (with n = 10) has a mean and standard deviation of $\bar{x}_1 = 3.90$, $s_1 = 1.29$, whereas sample two (with n = 50) has the statistics $\bar{x}_2 = 3.06$, $s_2 = 1.08$. Therefore sample two comes closer to the population mean and s.d. of $\upmu = 3.28$ and $\upsigma = 1.08$.

64.title: 3.3a Population Distribution
64.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.3a Population Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:47:25","modified":"2023/12/13 09:56:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Population Distribution
>The population distribution consists of all the members in a population. It is tough to collect data for every member of the population (called a census), so other methods are needed to summarize data.

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>If we want to eat somewhere in San Francisco, but we want to look at the restaurants' Yelp ratings first, then the ratings of each of all the restaurants in the city will make up the population distribution. Let's say restaurants are rated on a 5-star basis. Then the count of all restaurants in San Francisco on Yelp, separated by the number of stars they have, will make up the population distribution:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15))
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows)
>p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar()
>plot(p)
>```
>From the plot above, we can conclude that the mean and standard deviation of the distribution are $\upmu = 3.3$ and $\upsigma = 1.1$.

>[!note] Angular Momentum
>In rotational motion, the angular equivalent of linear momentum is called **angular momentum**, and measures the quantity of rotation a rigid body has about a given axis. It is defined as
>$$L = I\omega,$$
>where I is the rotational inertia of the body about the axis of rotation, and $\omega$ is the [[1.5a Rotational Kinematics|angular velocity]]. Angular momentum is a vector quantity, with a direction given by the right-hand rule, and can be positive or negative depending on the sense of rotation.
>
>Just as linear momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$ is conserved in the absence of net external forces, angular momentum is conserved in the absence of net external torques.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Screw This!
>You apply a force $F$ at an angle $\phi$ with respect to the handle of the wrench at a point with a distance $r$ away from the screw:
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 21.11.46.png|250]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the torque $\tau$ applied by the force. Express it first using $r, F, \phi$, and then using $d, F$.
>>The torque can be expressed as $\tau = rF \sin \phi$, since the perpendicular component of force is the one pointing counterclockwise, indicating a positive movement. Similarly, using $d, F$, torque can be expressed as $\tau = dF$, since $d=r\sin \phi$, as shown in the diagram.


>[!example] (Easy) Seesaw
>A seesaw with length $L/2$ on each side of the pivot makes a $30\degree$ angle with respect to the horizontal. Three forces $F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}$ act on the seesaw.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 20.14.22.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the net torque applied by these forces.
>>The component perpendicular to the seesaw for each force is:
>>- $-F_{1}\cos 30\degree$ (negative since it is clockwise)
>>- $F_{2}\sin 30\degree$
>>- $F_{3}\sin 30\degree$
>>
>As such, the net torque is 
>$$\begin{align}\tau &= -\frac{L}{2}F_{1}\cos 30\degree + \frac{L}{4}F_{1}\sin 30\degree + \frac{L}{2}F_{3}\sin 30\degree \\ &= -\frac{\sqrt{ 3 }}{4}LF_{1} + \frac{1}{8}LF_{2} + \frac{1}{4}LF_{3}. \end{align}$$

>[!example] (Easy) Boom!
>As shown in the figure, a small sphere of mass $m$ is attached to a boom of length $L$ (assumed to have negligible mass) and is released from rest with an initial angle $\theta_{0}$.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 21.29.04.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the torque exerted by gravity on the small sphere with respect to the hinge when it was released.
>>The answer is pretty straightforward, $\tau = Lmg \cos \theta_{0}$.
>
>>[!example]- Show that the kinetic energy of the small sphere due to its translational motion is the same as its rotational kinetic energy with respect to the hinge.
>>We have that $K=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2=\dfrac{1}{2}mL^2 \omega^2=\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2=K_{\text{rot}}$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the speed of the small sphere right before it hits the ground.
>>From conservation of energy, we know that $E_{i}=E_{f}$, such that $mgL \theta_{0} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Therefore, $v=\sqrt{ 2gL \theta_{0} }$.
>
>


>[!example] (Medium) Co-Axial Structure w/ Two Forces
>Consider an object with an co-axial structure, where the inner axis has a radius $R_{1}$ and the outer radius is $R_2$ as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-13 at 0.15.49.png|300]]
>
>Suppose a force $F_{1}$ is applied to the inner axis at a point shown in the figure and has a direction with an angle $\theta_{1}$ with respect to the horizontal line.
>
>Another force $F_{2}$ is applied on the outer radius at a point and direction shown in the figure with angle $\theta_{2}$ with respect to the horizontal line.
>
>The object is fixed so that it cannot move translationally, but is allowed to rotate about its central axis that is perpendicular to the radii. Suppose the object has a rotational inertia $I$ with respect to the central axis.
>
>>[!example]- Find the angular acceleration of the object.
>>For your ease, please draw a diagram of this setup in 2D.
>>
>>The equation for the torque becomes $I \alpha = R_{1}F_{1} \sin \theta_{1}+R_{2}F_{2}\cos \theta_{2}$ since both forces are clockwise, and we take the component that's tangential to the surface (and equivalently, perpendicular to the radius). Therefore, $\alpha = \dfrac{1}{I}(R_{1}F_{1} \sin \theta_{1}+R_{2}F_{2}\cos \theta_{2})$.

>[!example] (Medium) Co-Axial Pulley
>Shown in the figure is a “co-axial” pulley with an inner core of radius $R_{1}$ protruding from a larger disk of radius $R_{2}$. Two blocks of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ with $m_{2} > m_{1}$ are hung by two ropes that are wound on $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ respectively. The rotational inertia of the pulley is $I$.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 21.52.56.png|150]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the block $m_{1}$.
>>We have that $T_{1}-m_{1}g=m_{1}a_{1}$ and $T_{2}-m_{2}g=-m_{2}a_{2}$. The boxes have different accelerations because they are not on the same disk. We also have that $a_{1}=\alpha R_{1}$ and $a_{2}=\alpha R_{2}$. 
>>
>>Now look at the torque equation. Since the smaller pulley is being pulled counterclockwise by $T_{1}$ and the bigger pulley is being pulled clockwise by $T_{2}$, it follows that 
>>$$-I \alpha = T_{1}R_{1} - T_{2}R_{2} \iff I \alpha = T_{2}R_{2} - T_{1}R_{1}.$$
>>
>>Plugging for $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, as well as $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$, we obtain
>>$$I \alpha = m_{2}R_{2}(-\alpha R_{2} + g) - m_{1}R_{1}(\alpha R_{1} + g),$$
>>such that $\alpha = \dfrac{m_{2}R_{2}-m_{1}R_{1}}{I+m_{1}R_{1}^2+m_{2}R_{2}^2}g$, and therefore $a_{1} = \alpha R_{1}=\dfrac{R_{1}(m_{2}R_{2}-m_{1}R_{1})}{I+m_{1}R_{1}^2+m_{2}R_{2}^2}g$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the tension of the rope.
>>Since $T_{1}=m_{1}(a_{1}+g)$, and we found $a_{1}$ in the last part, then
>>$$T_{1}=\frac{m_{1}m_{2}R_{1}R_{2})+Im_{1}}{I+m_{1}R_{1}^2+m_{2}R_{2}^2}g$$

72.title: 1.5b Rotational Inertia
72.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.5 Rotational Dynamics/1.5b Rotational Inertia.md
72.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.5b Rotational Inertia]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/11 19:28:33","modified":"2025/08/13 03:17:42"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rotational Inertia
>**Rotational inertia** (also called the **moment of inertia**) is the rotational analogue of mass. While mass $m$ in translational motion measures resistance to changes in linear velocity, rotational inertia measures a rigid body’s resistance to changes in angular velocity. It depends on both the distribution of mass and the distance of each mass element from the axis of rotation, such that
>$$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2,$$
>where $m_{i}$ is the mass of each object in the system, and $r_{i}$ is its distance from the axis of rotation.

# Derivation
Given the definition of rotational inertia, we can redefine kinetic energy $K=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ as rotational kinetic energy $K_{\text{rot}}=\dfrac{1}{2}I \omega^2$. Now imagine a circle, and draw its radius as a line. Given two points on the same line, one will have traveled more distance than the other. As such, we can say that **the rotational kinetic energy of a rotating object is the sum of translational kinetic energy of the points that make up the object**, such that
$$K=\sum_{i} \frac{1}{2}m_{i}v_{i}^2.$$
This is shown in the following graph, given a 2D disk:

```tikz
\begin{document}
\begin{tikzpicture}[line width=0.8pt, scale=0.95, rotate=60]
  % Disk outline (no fill)
  \draw (0,0) circle [radius=3cm];

  % Axis (pivot)
  \fill (0,0) circle (2pt);
  \node[below left] at (0,0) {axis};

  % Dotted radius (instead of the red rod)
  \draw[dotted] (0,0) -- (3,0);

  % Rotation arrow and label
  \draw[->] (1.1,0.7) arc[start angle=35, end angle=155, radius=1.2cm];
  \node at (0,1.5) {$\omega$};

  % Mass points along the radius
  \def\rone{2.7}  % r1
  \def\rtwo{1.7}  % r2
  \fill (\rone,0) circle (2pt);
  \fill (\rtwo,0) circle (2pt);

  % Velocity vectors (perpendicular to radius)
  \draw[->] (\rone,0) -- ++(0,0.9);
  \draw[->] (\rtwo,0) -- ++(0,0.6);

  % Labels
  \node[below] at (\rone,-0.15) {$m_1$};
  \node[below] at (\rtwo,-0.15) {$m_2$};
  \node[right] at (\rone,0.85) {$v_1$};
  \node[right] at (\rtwo,0.55) {$v_2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{document}
```

As such, given $v_{i}=\omega r_{i}$, this becomes
$$K=\sum_{i} \frac{1}{2}m_{i}r_{i}^2\omega^2,$$
which leads us to the definition of the moment of inertia, $I=\sum_{i}m_{i}r_{i}^2$.

# Examples
>[!example] Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Frame with Point Masses
>Consider very light rectangular frame with negligible mass with length $a$ and width $a/2$. At the vertices are four small spheres each with mass $M$. 
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 19.44.23.png|650]]

>>

73.title: 1.5e Rolling Motion
73.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.5 Rotational Dynamics/1.5e Rolling Motion.md
73.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.5e Rolling Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/11 20:42:42","modified":"2025/08/13 05:39:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rolling Motion
>**Rolling motion** is the combination of translational motion of a rigid body’s center of mass and rotational motion about its center of mass. 
>
>A common example is a wheel rolling on a surface. In this motion, the center of mass translates with velocity $v_{\text{C.M.}}$ while every point on the body also rotates with angular velocity $\omega$:
>
>
>If the wheel **rolls without slipping**, experiencing static friction, then the translational and rotational speeds are related by
>$$v_{\text{C.M.}} = R\omega \iff a_{\text{C.M.}}=R\alpha,$$
>where $R$ is the radius of the wheel. The point of contact with the ground has zero instantaneous velocity relative to the surface.
>
>If **slipping occurs**, $v_{\text{C.M.}} \neq R\omega$, and the point of contact moves relative to the ground. Rolling without slipping is a key condition in problems involving rotational dynamics, energy conservation, and torque analysis.

# Derivation
# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Rolling Cylinder I
>A cylinder of uniform mass $M$ and radius $R$ is placed on a frictional surface. The rotational inertia of the cylinder with respect to its central axis is $I$. A constant force of magnitude $F$ is applied to the top of the cylinder in the horizontal direction as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-13 at 0.32.16.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the cylinder, assuming that it does not skid or slide on the surface.
>>Since we have static friction in the backward direction, it holds that $F-f_{s}=Ma$ in the horizontal. We also calculate torque as $I \alpha = R(F + f_{s})=R(2F-Ma)$. Since $a = R\alpha$, then
>>$$\frac{Ia}{R}=R(2F-Ma) \iff a=\frac{2FR^2}{I+R^2M}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the minimal value of the coefficient of static friction $\mu_{s,\min}$ needed in order for the perfect rolling condition (no skidding, no sliding) to hold?
>>Since $f_{s}=F - Ma$ as found before, we substitute for $a$ and solve:
>>$$f_{s}=\frac{I-R^2M}{I+R^2M}F \le \mu_{s, \min}Mg \iff \mu_{s} \geq \frac{I-R^2M}{I+R^2M} \frac{F}{Mg},$$
>>where the equality is the value of $\mu_{s, \min}$.

>[!example] (Medium) Rolling Cylinder II
>A cylinder of uniform mass $M$ and radius $R$ is placed on a frictional surface. The rotational inertia of the cylinder with respect to its central axis is $I$. A constant force of magnitude $F$ is applied to the bottom right of the cylinder, at a point that is $45\degree$ to the vertical line, and with a direction that is $45\degree$ above the horizontal, as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-13 at 1.57.59.png|300]]
>
> Assume the cylinder does not skid nor slide on the surface, and that the force is not large enough to lift the cylinder. 
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the cylinder, including the magnitude and direction.
>>We have that $I\alpha=R(F-f_{s})$ This is because the movement is to the left, but the force of friction that assists the rolling motion is clockwise as opposed to the force. Then, we also have $-Ma=F\cos 45\degree$

74.title: 1.5a Rotational Kinematics
74.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.5 Rotational Dynamics/1.5a Rotational Kinematics.md
74.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.5a Rotational Kinematics]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/04 11:43:15","modified":"2025/08/11 20:45:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rotational Motion
>To describe an object's rotational motion, we track its angular displacement $\Delta\theta$, where
>$$\Delta \theta = \theta - \theta_{0},$$
>such that if $\Delta \theta > 0$, the rotation is counter-clockwise, and vice-versa.
>
>Then, **angular velocity** can be defined as the overall rate of change of the object's rotation, where
>$$\omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}, \enspace \text{and} \enspace \omega = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}=\frac{d \theta}{dt}.$$
>
>Just like in translational kinematics, **angular acceleration** denotes the rate of change in angular velocity over time, such that 
>$$\alpha_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\omega - \omega_{0}}{t - t_{0}} = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t}, \enspace \text{and} \enspace \alpha = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\omega}{dt}.$$
>
>Similarly, the equations for motion at constant acceleration still hold, such that
>$$
>\begin{align}
>\omega &= \omega_0 + \alpha t && \enspace \text{(Angular Velocity)}, \\
>\theta &= \theta_0+\omega_0t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 && \enspace \text{(Angular Displacement)}, \\
\omega^2 &= \omega_0^2+2\alpha(\theta-\theta_0) && \enspace \text{(Angular Velocity-Displacement)}.
>\end{align}
>$$
>
>In addition, angular motion can be used to describe an object's translational motion. Let $r$ be the distance of a point from the rotational axis. Then, one can express the distance traveled as $d=r\Delta \theta$. As such, $v=rd\theta=\omega r$, and $a=\alpha r$.

75.title: 1.4b Center of Mass
75.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.4 Linear Momentum/1.4b Center of Mass.md
75.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4b Center of Mass]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 23:54:23","modified":"2025/08/13 05:37:31"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Center of Mass
>The **center of mass** (CoM) is the average position of mass in a system, weighted by how much mass is at each point. It denotes where the “balance point” of the system is. For a system of particles with masses $m_i$ at positions $\vec{r}_i$, the center of mass is defined as
>$$\vec{r}_{\text{C.M.}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i \vec{r}_i,$$
>where $M = \sum_i m_i$ is the total mass of the system.
>
>For continuous systems, the center of mass is defined as
>
>The center of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated at that point and all external forces were applied there. If **no external force** acts on a system, then the **center of mass moves at constant velocity**, regardless of internal motion or deformation.
>
>As such, the **momentum of the center of mass** equals the **total momentum** of the system, where
>$$\vec{P} = M \vec{v}_{\text{C.M.}}.$$

# Derivation


# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Two Rods in 1D
>Consider an $L$-shaped bracket as shown. The bottom end of the bracket is aligned on the $x$-axis with a nonuniform mass density $\lambda(x) = \lambda_{0} \dfrac{x^2}{L^2}$ while the vertical end is aligned on the $y$-axis with a uniform mass density $\lambda_{0}$. The constant $\lambda_{0}$ has a dimension of mass per unit length. 
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 15.58.23.png|200]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the center of mass of the $L$-shaped bracket.
>>The rods are continuous, so we find that the two masses in this system are $m_{0} = \lambda_{0}L$ and $m_{1} = \frac{\lambda_{0}}{L^2} \int_{0}^{L}x^2dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\lambda L$. As such, $M=\frac{4}{3}\lambda_{0}L$ is the total mass of the system.
>>
>>Then, we calculate the first moments of both masses,
>>$$M_{x}=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{L^2} \int_{0}^{L} x^3 =\frac{1}{4}\lambda_{0}L^2,$$
>>and
>>$$M_{y} = \lambda_{0}\int_{0}^{L} x dx = \frac{1}{2}\lambda_{0}L^2$$
>>
>>Finally, we obtain $x_{\text{C.M.}} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\lambda_{0}L^2}{\frac{4}{3}\lambda_{0}L}= \dfrac{3}{16}L$, and $y_{\text{C.M.}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{0}L^2}{\frac{4}{3}\lambda_{0}L}=\dfrac{3}{8}L$.

>[!example] (Medium) Equilateral Triangle in 2D
>Consider an equilateral triangle whose sides have a common length $L$.
>>[!example]- Assuming the mass is uniformly distributed, find the center of mass of the equilateral triangle.
>>We place the midpoint of the base of the equilateral triangle at the origin. Then we have two symmetrical right-angled triangles with $h=\sqrt{ 3 }L / 2$ and base $L / 2$. The part of the triangle on the positive $x$-axis forms the equation $h(x)=-\sqrt{ 3 }x + \sqrt{ 3 }L / 2$. As such, we have the double integral for mass (given $\sigma = 1$ WLOG):
>>$$M=2 \int^{L / 2}_{0} \int^{h(x)}_{0}dydx = 2\int^{L / 2}_{0} [-\sqrt{ 3 }x + \sqrt{ 3 }L / 2 ]dx = -\sqrt{ 3 }x^2 + \sqrt{ 3 }Lx \Big|^{L / 2}_{0}=\frac{\sqrt{ 3 }}{4}L^2.$$
>>
>>Given this, we have that 
>>$$y_{\text{C.M.}}= \frac{1}{M} 2\int^{L / 2}_{0} \int^{h(x)}_{0} y dydx = $$
>>

>[!example] (Medium) CoM of an Arc in 2D
>Consider an arc that spans an angle of $120\degree$ with a radius $R$. Assume the arc has a uniform linear mass density and the center of curvature is located at the origin of the coordinate system.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-11 at 16.43.25.png|200]]
>
>>[!example] Find the center of mass of this arc.
>>
>

76.title: 1.4a Linear Momentum
76.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.4 Linear Momentum/1.4a Linear Momentum.md
76.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4a Linear Momentum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 23:54:15","modified":"2025/08/04 19:05:18"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Momentum
>**Linear momentum** (SI: $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}$) is a vector quantity that measures how difficult it is to stop an object in motion. For a particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$, its momentum is defined as
>$$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}.$$
>Linear momentum is also the integral of [[1.2a Newton's Laws|net force]] with respect to time, such that $\frac{d}{dt}\vec{p}=m\vec{a}$. This implies that **if no external force** acts on objects in a system, then the total momentum of said objects is **conserved**, such that $\vec{P}_{i}=\vec{P}_{f}$, where $\vec{P}$ represents the total momentum of the system.
>
>This conservation law is especially useful when analyzing **collisions**, where two or more objects transfer momentum over short timescales:
>- In an **elastic collision**, both **momentum and mechanical energy** are conserved.
>
>- In an **inelastic collision**, **momentum is conserved**, but **mechanical energy is not**. Some of the energy is converted to other forms (e.g., thermal energy or sound).
>	- Furthermore, a **perfectly inelastic collision** is one where the objects stick together after impact, maximizing energy loss from the system’s mechanical energy..


# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Understanding Momentum
>A bead is moving on a frictionless surface heading toward a vertical semi-circular loop of radius $R$ with a speed $v$. Suppose the bead has an initial speed that is fast enough to reach the top of the loop.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-04 at 13.43.50.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- If the system includes the bead, Earth, and the gravitational interaction between them, is the energy of this system conserved?
>>Although the normal force between the bead and the loop is external, $N=0$. Then energy is conserved, although some of the kinetic energy becomes potential energy because of gravity.
>
>>[!example]- If the system includes the bead, Earth, and the gravitational interaction between them, is the momentum of this system conserved?
>>The momentum is not conserved, as some of the speed of the ball converts to gravitational potential energy. 

>[!example] (Easy) Colliding Particles
>Two particles of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ travel at an initial speed $v_{0}$, but with different angles as shown in the right figure. After the two particles collide, they both fly out with an angle $45\degree$ with respect to the horizontal.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-04 at 14.58.18.png|225]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the final speeds $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ of each particle.
>>Considering the $x$ and $y$ components of the speed of the particles, one obtains the following momentum conservation system:
>>$$\begin{dcases} \frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{0}+\frac{\sqrt{ 3 }}{2}m_{2}v_{0} = \frac{\sqrt{ 2 }}{2}m_{1}v_{1}+\frac{\sqrt{ 2 }}{2}m_{2}v_{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{ 3 }}{2}m_{1}v_{0}+\frac{1}{2}m_{2}v_{0} = \frac{\sqrt{ 2 }}{2}m_{1}v_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{ 2 }}{2}m_{2}v_{2}, \end{dcases}$$
>> yielding $v_1 = \dfrac{m_1(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{6}) + m_2(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6})}{4 m_1}v_{0}$ and $v_2 = \dfrac{m_1(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}) + m_2(-\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6})}{4 m_2}v_{0}$.

>[!example] (Medium)
>Two blocks of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ respectively are placed on a frictionless surface. The block $m_{2}$ is initially at rest, and attached with a spring of spring constant $k$ on its back. The block $m_{1}$ is then given an initial speed $v_{0}$ and collides head onto the block $m_{2}$.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-04 at 15.35.51.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- What is the maximum compression of the spring throughout the entire collision process?
>>Maximum compression occurs when both objects have the same instantaneous speed. Since the collision contains an elastic spring, both momentum and kinetic energy are preserved: 
>>- For energy, $E_{i}=\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{0}^2$ is purely kinetic energy, whereas $E_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{1}+\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ is both elastic potential and the kinetic energy of both objects moving together at the same speed $v_{1}$.
>>- For momentum, $P_{i}=m_{1}v_{0}$, whereas $P_{f}=(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{1}$.
>>
>>As such, we obtain the following system of equations:
>>$$\begin{dcases} \frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{0} = \frac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{1}^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \\ m_{1}v_{0}=(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{1}, \end{dcases}$$
>>solve for the displacement to obtain $x=\sqrt{ \dfrac{m_{1}m_{2}}{k(m_{1}+m_{2})} }v_{0}$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the velocity of the two blocks after the collision process.
>>In this elastic collision, both energy and momentum are preserved. After the collision, the objects go their separate ways. Therefore,
>>$$\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{0}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{1}^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_{2}v_{2}^2 \\ m_{1}v_{0} = m_{1}v_{1} + m_{2}v_{2}, \end{cases}$$
>>which yields $v_{1}=\dfrac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}v_{0}$ and $v_{2}=\dfrac{2m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}v_{0}$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the condition on $m_{1}$ and $m_2$, such that block $m_{1}$ will move backwards after the collision?
>>It must hold that $v_{1} = \dfrac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}v_{0} < 0$ from the last part. As such, $m_{1} < m_{2}$ in order for block $m_{1}$ to move backwards after the collision.


>[!example]
>A rectangular block has its upper right corner carved out. The carved out portion is a quarter of a cylinder, yielding a circular slope of radius $R$. The remaining block has a mass $M$. A small bead of mass $m$ is placed at the top of the slope. All contact surfaces are frictionless. Both the small bead and the block are initially at rest, and the bead slides down from the top of the circular slope.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-04 at 17.34.24.png|250]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the displacement of the block when the small bead slides to the bottom of the circular slope and is just about to leave the block.

77.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3e Power.md
77.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.3e Power]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/02 15:37:42","modified":"2025/08/02 15:50:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Power
>Power (SI: Watt / $\text{W} \equiv \text{J} / \text{s}$) quantifies how rapidly energy is transferred or transformed. It measures the rate at which a system does work or converts energy, providing insight into how fast a physical process occurs.
>
>More particularly, **average power** denotes the total amount of energy transferred, divided by the total time it takes, such that
>$$\bar{P} = \frac{E}{\Delta t} = \frac{W}{\Delta t},$$
>where $W$ is the net work done and $E$ is the energy transferred over some time frame $\Delta t = t_{f}-t_{i}$.
>
>Similarly, **instantaneous power** describes the rate of energy transfer at a specific infinitesimal point in time, such that
>$$P = \frac{dE}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}.$$

78.title: 1.3c Work-Energy Principle
78.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3c Work-Energy Principle.md
78.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.3c Work-Energy Principle]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/01 16:10:12","modified":"2025/08/02 15:33:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Work-Energy Principle
>The **Work–Energy Principle** states that when a net force acts on an object and changes its speed, the total work done by the force equals the change in the object’s kinetic energy.
>
>If an object of mass $m$ is subject to a net force that causes it to speed up or slow down from an initial speed $v_i$ to a final speed $v_f$, then the net work $W$ done on the object is
>$$\sum W = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2.$$

# Proof
Proceed using Newton's Second Law, such that $F_{\text{net}}=m\vec{a}=m\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$. Work is then defined as
$$\begin{align}
W&=\int_{\mathcal{P}} F_{\text{net}} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&=m\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&=m \int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \vec{v} \cdot d\vec{v} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}^2\Big|_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}_{f}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}_{i}^{2} \\
&= \Delta K.
\end{align}$$
# Examples

>[!example] Hemisphere Pulling Problem
>A small sphere of mass $m$ is attached to a string being pulled from the bottom of a hemisphere $\theta=0$ to the top $\theta = \pi / 2$. It is pulled slowly, such that at every moment the sphere is nearly in equilibrium. Throughout the entire process, the string is tangent to the hemisphere.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-01 at 21.19.51.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- When the sphere is at an angle $\theta$, what is magnitude of the string’s tension?
>>In the $x$ direction of the tangent, there is tension $T$, which is opposed by gravity with an $x$ component of $mg\cos\theta$. Given that the sphere is "nearly" at equilibrium, $a=0$, then $T-mg\cos\theta=0 \iff T=mg\cos \theta$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by the string on the sphere throughout the process?
>>It holds that $W = \int |\vec{F}| \cdot |d\vec{r}|$. From the previous part, $|\vec{F}|=T=mg\cos\theta$. Here, $|d\vec{r}|=Rd\theta$ since $|\vec{r}|=R\theta$, which is the arc length. Since both $T$ and $d\vec{r}$ are in the same direction, the angle between them is $0$, and therefore $\cos0 = 1$:
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{T} &=\int T \cdot dr \cdot \cos0 \\
>>&= \int mg \cos\theta \cdot R \cdot d\theta \\
>>&= mgR \sin\theta \Big |^{\pi / 2}_{0} \\
>>&= mgR.
>>\end{align}$$
>> A quicker way to derive this would be to label the positive axis as the axis of direction, As such, $W_{T}=$
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by the normal force throughout the process?
>>The normal force exerted on the ball by the hemisphere is upward, whereas the vertical component of gravity in terms of the ball's reference frame is $mg \sin\theta$. Once again, because the sphere is in quasi-equilibrium, then $N-mg\sin\theta=0 \iff N=mg\sin\theta$. However, because the angle between $N$ and $dr$ is $90 \degree$, it turns out that
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{N} &=\int N \cdot dr \cdot \cos \pi / 2 \\
>>&= \int mg \sin\theta \cdot R \cdot d\theta \cdot 0 \\
>>&= 0
>>\end{align}$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by gravity throughout the process?
>>Opposite to the direction of displacement, the horizontal component relative to the ball's reference frame is $F_{G}=mg\cos\theta$. Then, 
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{G} &=\int F_{G} \cdot dr \cdot \cos \pi \\
>>&= -mgR\int \cos\theta \; d\theta \\
>>&= -mgR \sin\theta \Big|^{\pi / 2}_{0} \\
>>&= -mgR.
>>\end{align}$$
>
>>[!example]- Is there a relationship between parts 2 and 4?
>>Since the sphere moves slowly and remains in quasi-equilibrium, its speed does not change, so $\Delta K = 0$. By the work–energy principle:
>>$W_{\text{net}} = W_T + W_G = \Delta K = 0$
>>
>>As such, the work done by tension exactly cancels the work done by gravity ($W_T = -W_G$).
>>

79.title: 1.3b Kinetic Energy
79.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3b Kinetic Energy.md

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/01 16:09:47","modified":"2025/08/03 20:30:42"}

>[!note] Kinetic Energy
>**Kinetic energy** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) quantifies the motion of an object in terms of how difficult it would be to stop it. The faster and more massive an object, the harder it is to stop, and the more kinetic energy it has.
>
>Mathematically, the kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving with speed v is given by the equation
>$$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2.$$

80.title: 1.3d.3 Elastic Potential Energy
80.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3d Potential Energy/1.3d.3 Elastic Potential Energy.md
80.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.3 Elastic Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 18:29:27","modified":"2025/08/03 23:50:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Elastic Potential Energy
>**Elastic potential energy** $U_s$ is the scalar quantity stored in a system when it is deformed from its equilibrium configuration by an internal restoring force, assuming it obeys [[1.2b.4 Spring Force|Hooke's Law]].
>
>Mathematically, the elastic potential energy given a displacement $x$ from equilibrium is
>$$U(x) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2,$$
>where $k$ is the spring constant (a measure of stiffness), and $x$ is the displacement from the system’s equilibrium length. 
>
>This energy is always non-negative and reaches zero when the system is at rest in its natural, undeformed configuration.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Spring-Loop Track Energy Transfer
>A block of mass $m$ is first pushed against a spring of force constant $k$ by a length $R$ and released from rest. After the release it moves toward a vertical circular track of radius $R$, as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-03 at 20.35.22.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Assuming the block gains enough speed to reach to the top of the vertical track, what is the kinetic energy of the block when it reaches the top?
>>The elastic potential energy before release is $U=\dfrac{1}{2}kR^2$. The potential energy is transformed to kinetic energy and as such, the total energy before the loop is $E_i=\dfrac{1}{2}kR^2+0$. After the loop, the box is displaced by $2R$ in the $y$ direction. This means that the total energy $E_{f}=K_{f}+U_{f}$, where $U_{f}=2mgR$ is the gravitational potential energy, as it is conservative, and therefore relies only on the initial and final displacement of $0$ and $2R$ respectively. Since the system is conserved (i.e., there are no other outside forces to consider since we assume the surface is frictionless and there is no drag), $E_{f}-E_{i}=0$. Therefore, 
>>$$K_{f}+2mgR-\frac{1}{2}kR^2=0 \iff K_{f}=\frac{1}{2}kR^2-2mgR.$$
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force between the track and the block when the block reaches the top of the track.
>>The block pushes on the loop, and therefore the loop pushes black at the block. Since the two vertical forces in play here are the normal force and the force of gravity $mg$, and both are downward, then $\dfrac{mv^2}{R}=N+mg$ per circular motion. Given the answer for $K_{f}$ in the previous step,
>>$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{1}{2}kR^2-2mgR = \frac{1}{2}(RN+mgR),$$
>>
>>which when solved yields $N=kR-5mg$.

>[!example] (Medium) Critical Friction in a Coupled Spring-Pulley System
>A block of mass $m_2$ is placed on a frictionless table with another block $m_3$ placed on top of it. The surface between $m_2$ and $m_3$ has a coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$. 
>
>The block $m_2$ is connected with another block $m_1$ by a massless rope which wraps around a massless pulley as shown in the figure. The rope does NOT slip over the pulley when moving. 
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-03 at 21.18.12.png|300]]
>
>The block $m_1$ is connected with a spring of force constant $k$ whose other end is fixed to the ground. The spring is stretched with an amount $h$ away from its equilibrium point and the whole system is released from rest.
>
>
>>[!example]- Find the minimum value of $\mu_{s}$ such that the block $m_{3}$ can remain on block $m_{2}$ without falling off.
>>For block $m_{3}$, static friction is what accelerates the block rightward. Therefore, $f_{s}=m_{3}a$. 
>>
>>For block $m_{2}$, tension opposes static friction, such that $T-f_{s}=m_{2}a \iff T=(m_{2}+m_{3})a$. 
>>
>>For block $m_{1}$, tension opposes gravity and the spring force, such that $T-F_{s}-m_{1}g=-m_{1}a$, as block $m_{1}$ accelerates downward, in the negative direction. Additionally, since the displacement of the spring force from equilibrium is in the positive direction, $F_{s}=-kh$. Solving for tension, one obtains
>>$$(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})a=m_{1}g-kh \iff a=\frac{m_{1}g-kh}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}.$$
>>
>>From the definition of static friction force, it is known that $F_{\text{s}} \leq\mu_{s}N$, where $N-m_{3}g=0$. As such,
>>$$m_{3}\frac{m_{1}g-kh}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}} \leq \mu_{s} m_{3}g,$$
>>and therefore $\mu_{s} \geq \dfrac{m_{1}g-kh}{g(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})}$.
>
>>[!example]- After we release the system, what is the speed of $m_{1}$ when the spring returns to its equilibrium position?
>>Before release, $E_{i}=0+\dfrac{1}{2}kh^2+m_{1}gh$. However, because the whole system moves, $E_{f}=\dfrac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})v^2$. Per conservation of energy, $E_{i}=E_{f}$, and therefore,
>>$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2m_{1}gh+kh^2}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}}.$$

81.title: 1.3d.1 Potential Energy
81.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3d Potential Energy/1.3d.1 Potential Energy.md
81.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.1 Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/02 16:21:42","modified":"2025/08/04 11:53:09"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Potential Energy
>**Potential energy** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) is a scalar quantity that denotes how much work a system can release or absorb due to the relative positions of its parts. 
>
>It is defined for systems where internal forces do work that depends only on the initial and final positions–and not on the path taken–called **conservative forces**, for which it holds that
>$$\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0.$$
>
>Mathematically, the change in potential energy is defined as the negative of the work done by conservative forces, where
>$$\Delta U = -W_{\text{ext}}.$$
# Intuition
Potential energy is introduced a configuration-based quantity that depends on the relative position of interacting objects. Consider the gravitational interaction between two objects, say Earth and an apple. There are **two perspectives**:
1. **External Force View (apple only)**
	- Gravity is an external force.
    - The work done by gravity leads to a change in kinetic energy, such that $\Delta K = W_{\text{ext}}$.
2. **System View (apple + Earth)**
    - Gravity is internal to the system.
    - No external work is done, so the total mechanical energy stays constant, such that $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0 \implies \Delta K = -\Delta U$.

From both, we conclude that $\Delta U = -W_{\text{ext}}$.

# Examples

82.title: 1.3d.2 Gravitational Potential Energy
82.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.3 Work and Mechanical Energy/1.3d Potential Energy/1.3d.2 Gravitational Potential Energy.md
82.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.2 Gravitational Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 15:44:29","modified":"2025/08/03 20:29:11"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Gravitational Potential Energy
>**Gravitational [[1.3d.1 Potential Energy|potential energy]]** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) describes the interaction between two objects with mass based on how far apart they are. It is defined for systems where gravity is the internal conservative force.
>
>If two spherical objects of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are separated by a center-to-center distance $r$, the gravitational potential energy of the system is given by
>$$U(r) = -G\frac{ m_{1} m_{2}}{r},$$
>where $G$ is the [[1.2b.6 Law of Universal Gravitation|gravitational constant]].
>
>For **objects near Earth's surface**, it holds that for $r=R+h$ such that $R$ is Earth's radius and $h$ is the height of the object between sea level and the Kármán line (i.e., $h_{max} \approx 100 \; \text{km}$),
>$$U(r) \approx U(R)+mgh = mgh,$$
>where $m$ is the object's mass, $g=G \dfrac{M}{R^2}$ is the gravitational field strength near Earth's surface, and $h$ is the height of the object from Earth's surface. Note that $U(R) = 0$ since the baseline is defined as Earth's surface.
>
>>[!warning] Infinity as the Potential Energy Baseline
>The general formula assumes that $U(\infty) \equiv 0$, meaning the potential energy is zero when the two objects are infinitely far apart and $U(0) \equiv -\infty$ if they are at a singularity. The negative sign indicates that energy must be added to the system (i.e., work must be done) to separate the objects and overcome gravity.
# Intuition
Observe the gravitational force on $m_{2}$ an external force. Define $\hat{r}$ as the positive unit vector, and $\vec{r}$ as the displacement vector from $m_{1}$ to $m_2$. Then, the work done by the gravity of the left object with mass $m_1$ on the right object with mass $m_{2}$ between center-to-center distances $r_{i}$ and $r_{f}$ can be defined as
$$\begin{align}
W_{G} &= \int^{\vec{r}_{f}}_{\vec{r}_{i}} F_{G} \cdot d\vec{r}  \\
&= \int^{\vec{r}_{f}}_{\vec{r}_{i}} -G \frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^2}\hat{r} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&= -Gm_{1}m_{2} \int^{r_{f}}_{r_{i}} \frac{1}{r^2}dr \\
&= G \frac{Mm}{r_{f}} - G \frac{Mm}{r_{i}}.
\end{align}$$
Because $W_G$ has been regarded as an external force, it follows that the change in potential energy between $r_{i}$ and $r_{f}$ is equal to $\Delta U = -W_{G}=G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{i}} - G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{f}}$.

Here is where the reference point of $U(\infty) \equiv 0$ comes in. Given this reference point, it follows that the potential energy at a center-to-center distance of $r$ is equal to the potential energy at an infinite distance away, plus the change from infinity to $r$, such that
$$\begin{align}
U(r) &= U(\infty) + \Delta_{\infty \to r}U \\
&=0+G \dfrac{Mm}{\infty} - G \dfrac{Mm}{r} \\
&= -G \frac{Mm}{r}.
\end{align}$$

### GPE at Earth's Surface
Now we proceed to our definition for potential energy near Earth's surface. here, the reference point is sea level, such that $U(R) = 0$. Let an object be $h$ meters above sea level (or more generally, Earth's surface). Then,
$$\begin{align}
U(R+h) &= -G \frac{Mm}{R+h} \\
&= -G \frac{Mm}{R} + G \frac{Mm}{R^2}h+\ldots \\
&\approx -G \frac{Mm}{R}+m \frac{GM}{R^2}h \\
&= U(R)+mgh \\
&= mgh
\end{align}$$
using Taylor Series decomposition with the fact that $h \ll R$ near Earth's surface, thereby making all but the first two components irrelevant.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Diverting an Asteroid
>An asteroid of mass $m$ is flying toward Earth. When it is a distance $r_{0}$ away from Earth’s center, it has a speed $v_{0}$. Superman tries to intercept the asteroid and push it away, so that it will not be attracted by earth again.
>
>>[!example]- What is the minimal work Superman needs to apply on the asteroid?
>>The total mechanical energy of the asteroid is $E_{i}=K+U=\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^2-G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{0}}$. Since Superman must oppose that energy, $E_{f}=0$. As such, the work that Superman must exert on the asteroid to divert its course is 
>>$$W_{S}=E_{f}-E_{i}=0+G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{0}}-\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^2.$$

>[!example] Satellite Orbit
>A satellite of mass $m$ is orbiting around Earth with a circular orbit of radius $R_{1}$, as shown below.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-03 at 18.35.53.png|200]]
>
>>[!example]- What is the total mechanical energy of the satellite?
>>
>
>>[!example]- What is the least amount of energy required to boost the satellite to the higher orbit with radius $R_{2}$?

85.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b.5 Drag Force]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 21:12:22","modified":"2025/08/01 14:00:48"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Drag Force
>**Drag force** is the resistive force experienced by an object moving through a fluid (such as air or water). It always acts in the direction **opposite** to the object’s velocity relative to the fluid and depends on the **speed**, **shape**, and **surface properties** of the object, as well as the **viscosity** of the fluid.
>
>When the relative speed is small and the fluid flow is smooth (laminar), the drag force is approximately **proportional** to the object’s speed, such that
>$$\vec{F}_{\text{drag}} = -b \vec{v},$$
>where $b$ is a positive constant depending on the fluid’s viscosity and the object’s geometry. The negative sign indicates that drag opposes motion.
>
>When the object moves faster and the flow becomes more **turbulent**, the drag force becomes roughly **proportional to the square of the speed**, such that $\vec{F}_{\text{drag}} \propto -v^2$.

>[!note] Spring Force
>**Spring force** is the restoring force exerted by a spring when it is compressed or stretched from its equilibrium position. It acts in the direction opposite to the displacement and is given by **Hooke’s Law**, such that
>$$\vec{F}_s = -k\vec{x},$$
>where $\vec{F}_s$ is the spring force, $\vec{x}$ is the displacement from equilibrium, and $k$ is the spring constant (in N/m), which quantifies the stiffness of the spring. The negative sign indicates that the force always acts to restore the spring to equilibrium.

87.title: 1.2b.3 Friction
87.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.2 Dynamics/1.2b Macroscopic Forces/1.2b.3 Friction.md
87.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b.3 Friction]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:55:57","modified":"2025/08/01 13:50:40"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Friction
>**Friction** is a resistive force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact, and it always **acts parallel to the contact surface**:
>1. **Static friction** acts when two surfaces are in contact but not moving relative to each other. It prevents motion from starting and adjusts its magnitude up to a maximum limit, such that
>$$|\vec{F}_{\text{fr}}| \leq \mu_s |\vec{F}_N|,$$
>where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction, and $\vec{F}_N$ is the normal force.
>‎ 
>2. **Kinetic friction** (or sliding friction) acts when two surfaces slide against each other. It has a constant magnitude given by
>$$|\vec{F}_{\text{fr}}| = \mu_k |\vec{F}_N|,$$
>where $\mu_k$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction. Kinetic friction is typically smaller than the maximum static friction.

# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Pushing a Box on a Bigger Box on a Frictionless Surface
>A smaller block of mass $m$ is placed on a larger block of mass $M$: 
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-01 at 12.57.27.png|250]]
>
>The surface between the larger block and the horizontal surface is frictionless. On the other hand, there is friction between the two blocks and the coefficient of static friction is $\mu_{s}$. A horizontal force $F$ is applied on the smaller block.
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the blocks.
>>In the horizontal direction, the smaller block $m$ has a resistive backward static friction force $F_{s}$, as well as the pushing force applied forward $F$. Similarly, since the blocks move together, there is a forward static friction force $F_{s}$ applied to the larger box $M$. As such, per Newton's Second Law,
>>$$\begin{cases}F-F_{s}=ma \\ F_{s}=Ma\end{cases}$$
>>which when solved for accleration leads to $a=\dfrac{F}{M+m}$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force $N$ between the two blocks.
>>In the vertical direction of mass $m$, an upward normal force is exerted on it and a downward force of gravity $mg$ too. As such, it holds that $N-mg=0$, since the blocks do not move vertically. Therefore, $N=mg$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the maximal value of the force $F$, denoted as $F_{max}$, such that the smaller block can remain on the larger block without sliding on it?
>>As seen before, it holds that $F-F_{s}=ma$. Given the acceleration from part 1, one obtains$F_{s} = F-ma \leq \mu_{s}mg$, and therefore
>>$$F\left( 1-\frac{m}{M+m} \right) \leq \mu_{s}mg \iff F \leq \frac{\mu_{s}(M+m)m}{M}g=F_{\text{max}}.$$

>

>

>
>For the first part, suppose that all three blocks move at a constant speed $v$ when $F$ is applied.
>>[!example]- What is the frictional force between (1) blocks $A$ and $B$ and (2) the surface and block $C$?

Similarly, for block $C$, it holds that $F_{s}^{(B)}-F_{k}=m_{C}a_{C}$. Since velocity is constant, it follows that $a=0$, and as such, one must solve for
>>$$\begin{cases}F_{s}^{(A)}=0 \\ F-0-F_{s}^{(B)}=0 \\ F_{s}^{B}-F_{k}=0\end{cases}$$
>>This yields a solution of $F_{s}^{(A)}=0$, $F_{s}^{(B)}=F$, and $F_{k}=F$.
>>
>>Consider why $F_{s}^{(A)}=0$. When a block is already moving at constant speed, it doesn't need extra force to accelerate horizontally. However,

>Now, suppose the surface is frictionless, and the three blocks still move together.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:55:44","modified":"2025/07/31 21:23:21"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] The Normal Force
>**Normal force** is the contact force that acts **perpendicular** to the surface between two objects. It arises when two surfaces are pressed together and prevents them from passing through each other.
>
>When an object rests on a surface, the normal force balances the component of the object’s weight perpendicular to that surface. For an object of mass m resting on a horizontal surface:
>$$\vec{N} + \vec{F}_g = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad N = mg,$$
>as shown in the following figure:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>    % Draw the table
>    \draw[thick] (-2,0) -- (2,0); % table surface
>
>    % Draw the box
>    \draw[thick, fill=black, fill opacity=0.1] (-0.5,0) rectangle (0.5,1);
>
>    % Label the box
>    \node at (0, 0.5) {m};
>
>    % Draw the force of gravity (downward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,0) -- (0,-1) node[below] {$\vec{F}_G$};
>
>    % Draw the normal force (upward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,1) -- (0,2) node[above] {$\vec{F}_N$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>If multiple surfaces are in contact, the normal force splits, such that $N_1 + N_2 = mg$.

(cont'd) ##### Hidden

>**Gravity** is the **attractive force** exerted by a massive body on another object with mass. Near Earth’s surface, this force causes all objects to accelerate downward at approximately $9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2$, regardless of their mass.
>
>The gravitational force on an object is given by the equation
>$$\vec{F}_G = m \vec{g},$$
>where $m$ is the object’s **mass**, $\vec{g}$ is the **acceleration due to gravity** (typically $\vec{g} = -9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2$), and $\vec{F}_G$ is the **weight** of the object, directed downward toward the center of the Earth.
>
>When an object is in contact with a surface, the surface resists compression by exerting a **normal force**, per [[1.2a Newton's Laws|Newton's Third Law]]. Normal Force is denoted as $\vec{F}_N=-\vec{F}_G$, and **always acts perpendicular** to the surface, even on slopes:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>    % Draw the table
>    \draw[thick] (-2,0) -- (2,0); % table surface
>
>    % Draw the box
>    \draw[thick, fill=black, fill opacity=0.1] (-0.5,0) rectangle (0.5,1);
>
>    % Label the box

>
>    % Draw the force of gravity (downward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,0) -- (0,-1) node[below] {$\vec{F}_G$};
>
>    % Draw the normal force (upward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,1) -- (0,2) node[above] {$\vec{F}_N$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>>[!warning] Mass vs. Weight
>>Note that mass is a scalar and does not change with location. Weight is a **force** and depends on the gravitational field strength at a given place.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:49:03","modified":"2025/07/31 19:13:35"}
