>[!note] Tension Force
>**Tension**, denoted $\vec{F}_{T}$ or $\vec{T}$, is the contact force transmitted through a string, rope, cable, or any other flexible connector when it is pulled tight by forces acting from opposite ends. It arises from Newton’s Third Law–the object pulls on the rope, and the rope pulls back on the object with equal and opposite force:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{amsmath}
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.2, line cap=round, line join=round, >=stealth]
>  % Axes
>  \draw[->] (-0.5,0) -- (5,0) node[right] {$x$};
>  \draw[->] (0,-0.5) -- (0,2.5) node[above] {$y$};
>
>  % Block
>  \draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (1.2,1.2) node[midway] {$m$};
>
>  % Rope
>  \draw[thick] (1.2,0.6) -- (3.5,0.6);
>
>  % Hand (point)
>  \filldraw[black] (3.5,0.6) circle (2pt) node[right] {Hand Pulling};
>
>  % Tension Vectors
>  \draw[->,thick] (1.2,1) -- +(0.7,0) node[midway, above] {$\vec{T}$};
>  \draw[->,thick] (3.5,1) -- +(-0.7,0) node[midway, above] {$\vec{T}$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>
>
>For a massless and inextensible string, the tension is **uniform** throughout its length.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Simple Pulley
>A window washer pulls themselves upward using the following Atwood machine:
>![[Screenshot 2025-07-31 at 13.31.33.png|100]]
>The window washer and the triangular frame have masses of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ respectively. The window washer lifts themself up slowly with a constant acceleration $a$.
>>[!example]- Find the force at which the window washer pulls the rope.
>>Since two vertical segments of rope support the same object, $$(m_{1}+m_{2})a=2T-(m_{1}+m_{2})g \iff T=\dfrac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})(a+g).$$
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force between the frame and the window washer.
>>Now consider only the triangular frame. Gravity pulls down on it with a force of $m_{2}g$, and the window washer exerts a downward force of $N$ on the frame. However, the frame is also pulled up by $T$. As such,
>>$$m_{2}a=T-N-m_{2}g \iff N=\dfrac{1}{2}(m_{1}-m_{2})(a+g).$$

>[!example] (Medium) Double Pulley
>A window washer pulls themselves upward using the following double Atwood machine:
>![[Screenshot 2025-07-31 at 13.35.34.png|150]]
>The window washer and the triangular frame have masses of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ respectively. The window washer lifts themself up slowly with a constant acceleration $a$.
>>[!example]- If the washer pulls down the rope by an amount $|\Delta y|$, how much will the washer and the frame go up?
>>Let $L=\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}+\ell_{3}$ represent the initial length of the rope based on the length from the ceiling to the first pulley, the length from the first pulley to the second, and from the second to the window washer's hand. Then, if the window washer pulls down $\ell_{3}$, this means that both $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ are shortened by some $x$. As such, $L=(\ell_{1}-x)+(\ell_{2}-x)+(\ell_{3}+|\Delta y|)$, which simplifies to $2x=|\Delta y|$ or $x=\dfrac{1}{2}|\Delta y|$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the system.
>>By Newton's Third Law, the rope segment pulled by the window washer has a tension of $T$. 
>>
>>Additionally, the frame and the window washer are pulled up by two tensions, which means that the total tension on the pulley is $2T$.
>>
>>As such, in the $y$-direction one can conclude that $(m_{1}+m_{2})a=3T-(m_{1}+m_{2})g$, which yields an acceleration of $a=\dfrac{3T}{m_{1}+m_{2}}-g$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force between the frame and the window washer.
>>Observe the window washer. An upward tension force of $T$ is exerted on them by the rope, as well as the downward force of gravity by Earth. Then, $N$ is the upward normal force exerted on the washer by the frame. As such,
>>$$m_{1}a=N+T-m_{1}g,$$
>>which simplifies to $N=\dfrac{T(2m_{1}-m_{2})}{m_{1}+m_{2}}$.


>[!example] (Hard) Accelerating Pulley
>A block of mass $m_{2}$ is placed on a table and attached to a rope. The rope wraps around a light pulley whose mass is negligible and hangs another block $m_{1}$ as shown in the following figure:
>![[Screenshot 2025-07-31 at 14.03.47.png|150]]
>>[!example]- Suppose we move up the pulley with an acceleration $a_{0}$ while the block $m_{2}$ remains at rest. Find the acceleration of block 1.
>>Let $L=\ell_{1} + \ell_{2}$. Suppose the pulley moves by some $|\Delta y|$. Then, the left side of the rope $\ell_{1}$ increases by $|\Delta y|$, while block 1 is lifted by $|\Delta y|$ without decreasing $\ell_{2}$. 
>>
>>However, since $L$ is constant, $\ell_{2}$ also decreases by $|\Delta y|$ for a total displacement of $\Delta x=2|\Delta y|$ on the block. 
>>
>>Take the second derivative of displacement and obtain $a_{1}=2a_{0}$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the tension of the rope when the pulley moves up with an acceleration $a_{0}$.
>>Consider mass $m_{1}$. It is pulled down by gravity $m_{1}g$, and pulled up by tension $T$. As such,
>>$$2m_{1}a_{0}=T-m_{1}g \iff T=m_{1}(2a_{0}+g).$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the minimum $a_{0}$ in order to lift up $m_{2}$?
>>a

>>Now, examine the lower Atwood. For blocks $A$ and $B$, one obtains the following system of equations. Note that the second equation has a negative sign to denote that block $B$ is moving downward:
>>$$\begin{cases}\hphantom{-}m_{A}a = T_{1}-m_{A}g \\ -m_{B}a = T_{1}-m_{B}g \end{cases}.$$
>>Solving this system leads to $T_{1} = \dfrac{2m_{A}m_{B}}{m_{A}+m_{B}}g = \dfrac{4}{3}mg$.

>>Note that $T_{2}=2T_{1}$ still holds.

>>
>>Now proceed as follows. It holds that $T_{2}-m_{C}g=-m_{C}a$. It is known from the last problem that the weights of a pulley accelerate at $a_{w}=2a$. As such, one obtains the following system:
>>$$\begin{cases}T_{1}-m_{A}g=2m_{A}a \\ T_{1}-m_{B}g=-2m_{B}a \\ 2T_{1}-m_{C}g=-m_{C}a.\end{cases}$$

92.title: 1.2a Newton's Laws
92.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.2 Dynamics/1.2a Newton's Laws.md
92.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Newton's Laws]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:14:49","modified":"2025/08/11 20:01:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Newton's Laws
>**Newton’s Laws** describe the relationship between force, motion, and interaction: how objects behave when forces act on them or when they interact with other objects:
>1. **Newton’s First Law** states that ***an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force***. This only holds in inertial reference frames, where motion is not observed to spontaneously accelerate or decelerate.
>‎ 
>2. **Newton’s Second Law** defines the precise relationship between force and motion: the net force **exerted** on an object is equal to the product of its mass and [[1.1b Acceleration|acceleration]], such that
>$$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}.$$
>The First Law is a special case of the Second Law, where $\sum \vec{F} = 0$.
>‎ 
>3. **Newton’s Third Law** states that if object $A$ exerts a force on object $B$, then $B$ simultaneously exerts a force of ***equal magnitude*** and ***opposite direction*** on $A$. These action–reaction pairs act on different objects and therefore do not cancel.
>
>>[!warning] Fictitious Forces
# Derivation


# Examples
>[!example] Newton's Second Law
>The figure below shows the result of an experiment on Newton’s Second law, where we apply forces on three objects of mass $M_{1}$, $M_{2}$ and $M_{3}$, and measure the acceleration:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usepackage{amsmath}
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, thick]
>
>  % Axes
>  \draw[->] (0,0) -- (4.5,0) node[right] {$F$};
>  \draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,4.5) node[above] {$a$};
>
>  % Lines for different masses
>  \draw[green, opacity=0.75, thick] (0,0) -- (2,4) node[above right] {$M_1$};
>  \draw[red, thick] (0,0) -- (2.5,3.5) node[above right] {$M_2$};
>  \draw[orange, thick] (0,0) -- (3.5,2.5) node[above right] {$M_3$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>>[!example]- What is the relation between the inertial masses of these three objects?
>>Let $a=\dfrac{1}{M_{i}}F$. Then, we see that there is an inverse relation between mass and acceleration: given the same force, a lighter object will be accelerated more than a heavier object. As such,
>>$$M_{1} < M_{2} < M_{3}.$$


>[!example] Two Masses
>Consider two objects $A$ and $B$. When we apply a force $F$ on object $A$, it obtains an acceleration of $3 m/s^2$. The ratio of the two objects’ masses is $m_{A}$ : $m_{B} = 3 : 2$. The two objects are placed together, and $F$ is applied to them such that the two move together.
>>[!example]- What is the acceleration of the combined system?
>>Since $\dfrac{m_{A}}{m_{B}}=\dfrac{3}{2}$, then $m_{B}=\dfrac{2}{3}m_{A}$. If the same force is applied on both objects, then $3m_{A}=a(m_{A}+m_{B})$, so $a=\frac{3m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}}=9/5 \; \text{m/s}^2$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/29 14:29:26","modified":"2025/07/29 16:48:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Speed and Velocity
>To describe motion, we track how an object’s position changes over time using quantities like displacement, velocity, speed.
>
>The change in position of an object over a time interval is called **displacement**, defined as the difference between the final and initial position vectors, such that
>$$\Delta x = x - x_{0},$$
>where $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the initial $n$-dimensional position of the object at time $t_0$, and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is its final position at another point in time $t$.
>
>Then, **average velocity** can be defined as the overall rate of change of position,
>$$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t},$$
>whereas **instantaneous velocity** captures the object's average velocity over an infinitesimal time interval:
>$$v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta r}{\Delta t}=\frac{d x}{dt}.$$
>
>**Speed** is the scalar magnitude of instantaneous velocity, such that $s = \|v\|_{2}$. However, **average speed** is defined as the scalar that measures how much ground was covered regardless of direction, expressed as
>$$s_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{\Delta t},$$
>where $d$ is the total distance that the object traveled.

96.title: 1.1b Acceleration
96.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1b Acceleration]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/29 14:29:38","modified":"2025/07/30 20:49:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Acceleration
>**Average acceleration** is the rate at which an object’s [[1.1a Speed and Velocity|velocity]] changes over a time interval. It is a vector that points in the direction of the velocity change, defined as
>$$\vec{a}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\vec{v} - \vec{v_{0}}}{t - t_{0}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t},$$
>where $\vec{v}_0$ is the initial velocity and $\vec{v}$ is the final velocity at time $t$.
>
>On the other hand, **instantaneous acceleration** is the object’s acceleration at a specific moment in time. It is defined as the derivative of velocity with respect to time, such that
>$$\vec{a} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}.$$
>
>If acceleration stays **constant** during a time interval, we can use the following equations to describe motion:
>$$
>\begin{align}
>v &= v_0 + at && \enspace \text{(Velocity)} \\
>x &= x_0+v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2 && \enspace \text{(Displacement)} \\
>v^2 &= v_0^2+2a(x-x_0) && \enspace \text{(Velocity-Displacement)}
>\end{align}
>$$

# Derivation
Let's derive the equations for motion at constant acceleration:
1. Per the definition of instantaneous acceleration, $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$.  By integrating, we get $v=\large\int adt=at+C$. The constant $C=v_{0}$ only works if $a$ is constant and can be pulled out of the integral.
2. We start with $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v_{0}+at$ and integrate to obtain $x = \large\int (v_{0}+at) dt=v_{0}t+\frac{1}{2}at^2+C$.
3. This equation combines the above and eliminates time.

# Examples
>[!example] Colliding Balls
>Thelma stands on top of a building whose height is $H$ and throws a ball upward. The speed of the ball when it leaves her hand is $v_{T}$ . Bob is standing at the bottom of the building and at the same instant throws another ball upwards with speed $v_{B}$. 
>>[!example]- What is the slowest that $v_{B}$ can be if Bob’s ball hits Thelma’s ball when still on the way up?
>>Since Bob and Thelma are trying to collide the two balls that are strictly moving in the $y$ direction, then there must be a point where $x_{B}(t)=x_{T}(t)$, such that $v_{T}-gt > 0$. 
>>
>>We solve the equality:
>>$$H+v_{T}t-\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2=v_{B}t-\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \iff t=\dfrac{H}{v_{B}-v_{T}}.$$
>>
>>Then, we satisfy the constraint, such that $v_{T}-g\dfrac{H}{v_{B}-v_{T}}>0 \iff v_{B} > \dfrac{gH+v_{T}^2}{v_{T}}.$
>>
>>So Bob's ball needs to have a starting speed of at least $\dfrac{gH+v_{T}^2}{v_{T}}$.

>[!example] Sliding Balls
>An object $A$ slides down from a frictionless ramp of angle $\theta$ and height $h$ from rest, while another object $B$ is launched from the bottom of the ramp with some initial speed and slides up along the ramp. The two objects collide at the middle point of the ramp.
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usepackage{amsmath}
>\usetikzlibrary{angles,quotes}
>
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>  % Points
>  \coordinate (B) at (0,0);
>  \coordinate (C) at (4,0);
>  \coordinate (A) at (4,3);
>
>  % Triangle
>  \draw[thick] (B) -- (C) -- (A) -- cycle;
>
>  % Right angle mark
>  \draw (C) -- ++(-0.3,0) -- ++(0,0.3);
>
>  % Angle theta at B
>  \draw pic["$\theta$", draw=black, angle eccentricity=1.3, angle radius=0.8cm] {angle=C--B--A};
>
>  % Labels
>  \filldraw[green] (B) circle (2pt) node[below left] {\textbf{B}};
>  \filldraw[orange] (A) circle (2pt) node[above right] {\textbf{A}};
>  \node at (4.3,1.5) {\textit{h}};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>>[!example]- Find the initial speed of the object $B$.
>>Since object $B$ is moving up the ramp, it has an acceleration in its $x$-direction of $g\sin\theta$ (and therefore an acceleration in its $y$-direction of $g\cos\theta$, however we only need the $x$-direction here). Draw a plot with $g$, $x$ and $y$ to convince yourself
>>
>>Object $A$ has the exact same acceleration, and starts from rest. In order for them to meet in the middle, we deduce that the time of the collision is $v_{B_{0}}-(g\sin\theta)t=0 \iff t=\dfrac{v_{B_{0}}}{g\sin\theta}$. 
>>
>>Then, we equate the two positions, such that
>>$$x_{A_{0}}-\left(\frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\right)t^2=v_{B_{0}}t-\left(\frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\right)t^2 \iff x_{A_{0}}=v_{B_{0}}t.$$
>>
>>Notice that we can express the starting displacement of $A$ as $x_{A_{0}}=\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$ if we assume that $B$ starts at the origin. Plugging the values for $t$ and $x_{A_{0}}$ into our equation, we obtain $v_{B}=\sqrt{ gh }$.
>
>>[!example]- What are the speeds of $A$ and $B$ when they meet?
>>Given that $A$ and $B$ meet in the center of the hypotenuse with length $\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$, their ending position will be $x=\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$.
>>
>>As such, the final speed of object $A$ right before the collision is 
>>$$\begin{align}v_{A}&=\sqrt{ 0-2g\sin\theta\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta} \right) }\\&=\sqrt{gh}.\end{align}$$
>>
>>Meanwhile, object $B$ will have a speed of 
>>$$\begin{align}v_{B}&=\sqrt{ gh - 2g\sin\theta \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta} } \\ &= \sqrt{ gh - gh } \\ &= 0.\end{align}$$

>[!note] Doppler Effect
>The **Doppler Effect** is the apparent change in the frequency (or wavelength) of a wave as observed by an observer moving relative to the source of the wave. This effect occurs for all types of waves, including sound, light, and water waves. For a sound wave, the observed frequency $f{\prime}$ is given by:
>$$f\prime = \frac{v \pm v_{O}}{v \pm v_{S}}f_{S},$$
>where $\pm v_{O}$ is the speed of the observer (positive if moving toward the source), while $\pm v_{s}$ is the speed of the source (positive if moving toward the observer). The frequency $f_{S}$ is the source frequency.

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/02 17:12:15","modified":"2024/12/05 11:47:05"}

>[!note] Longitudinal Wave
>A **longitudinal wave** is a wave in which particles of the medium move parallel to the direction of wave propagation (e.g., sound waves, movement of a slinky). A series of compressions and expansions travel along a longitudinal wave. 
>1. **Compressions** are those areas where the coils are momentarily close together. 
>2. **Expansions** (sometimes called rarefactions) are regions where the coils are momentarily far apart. 
>
>Compressions and expansions correspond to the crests and troughs of a transverse wave. As such, a longitudinal wave can be graphically represented by plotting density versus position, resembling a transverse wave and visually clarifying the wave’s behavior.
>
>Moreover, the speed of a longitudinal wave over a solid is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}},$$
>whereas its speed over a fluid is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}},$$
>where $E$ is the elastic modulus of the material, $B$ is the bulk modulus of the liquid, and $\rho$ is the material's density.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>Since longitudinal waves can be represented as transverse, we can use the equation $v=\lambda f$ to find the wave's wavelength, frequency and period.

>[!note] Scattering
>**Scattering** refers to the interaction of waves with a boundary or medium, resulting in portions of the wave being reflected, transmitted, or absorbed. There are two types of general scattering:
>1. **Reflection** occurs when a wave hits a new medium (such as a fixed support), and by Newton's third law, the support invokes an equal and opposite in magnitude reaction, thereby causing the wave to invert and proceed to travel in the opposite direction.
>2. Transmission occurs when a wave passes through a medium or boundary and continues to propagate in the new medium.

>[!note] Transverse Wave
>A **transverse wave** is a wave in which particles of the medium move perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation (e.g. light waves, water waves). A series of crests and troughs travel along a transverse wave:
>1. The **crests** of a transverse wave represent the ***positive*** peaks of its oscillation.
>2. The **troughs** of a transverse wave represent the ***negative*** peaks of its oscillation.
>
>A transverse wave's vertical displacement at distance $x$ and time $t$ can be modeled as a function, 
>$$D(x, t)=A\sin(kx \pm  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$$
>where $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ is the wave's wavenumber ($\lambda$ is the wave's wavelength), $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ is the wave's natural frequency ($T$ is its period), and $A$ is its peak $y$-axis displacement (amplitude). The $\pm$ sign is negative as the wave is moving towards the ***right*** of the x-axis.
>
>Furthermore, the speed of a transverse wave is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{F_{T}}{\mu}} = \lambda f,$$
>where $F_{T}$ is the tension on the cord, and $\mu = \frac{m}{\ell}$ is the mass per unit length of the cord, whereas $\lambda$ and $f$ are the sinusoidal wavelength and frequency respectively.

103.title: 1.1v.3 Standing Waves
103.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.1 Dynamics/1.1v Wave Motion/1.1v.3 Standing Waves.md
103.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1v.3 Standing Waves]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/18 20:00:57","modified":"2024/12/18 22:08:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Standing Wave
>A standing wave is a wave pattern that results from the constructive interference (superposition) of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude traveling in opposite directions. Unlike traveling waves, standing waves appear stationary, with certain points (called nodes) remaining at rest, while other points (called antinodes) oscillate with maximum amplitude. The vertical displacement of a standing wave at distance $x$ and time $t$ is represented by the function
>$$D(x, t) = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega_{n}t),$$
>where $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ is the wave's wavenumber ($\lambda$ is the wave's wavelength), $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ is the wave's natural frequency ($T$ is its period), and $A$ is its peak $y$-axis displacement (amplitude).
>
>A standing wave contains two types of points:
>1. **Nodes**, where the wave displacement is always $0$ due to destructive interference.
>2. Antinodes, where the wave displacement is always $D$ due to constructive interference.
>
>Furthermore, a standing wave can occur at multiple frequencies $f_{n}$, known as **resonant frequences**. More specifically,
>$$f_{n} = \frac{v}{2\ell}n = nf_{1}$$
>where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, guides the frequencies at which a standing wave occurs. Here, $f_{1}=\frac{v}{2\ell}$ represents the **first harmonic** of the wave, whereas frequencies of $n>1$ are known as $n$-th **harmonics**, or $(n-1)$-th **overtones**.
# Intuition
Since the only thing that distinguishes the two waves from one another is their direction, and we have
$$D(x, t)=A\sin(kx \pm  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$$
by the definition of the transverse wave, we have the superimposed wave
$$D_{3}(x, t)=D_{1}(x, t)+D_{2}(x,t),$$
where $D_{1}(x,t)=A\sin(kx -  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$ is the wave traveling to the right of the $x$-axis, and $D_{2}(x,t)=A\sin(kx +  \omega_{n} t + \phi)$ is the wave traveling to the left. Then,
$$\begin{align}
D_{3}(x, t) &= A\sin(kx -  \omega_{n} t + \phi) + A\sin(kx + \omega_{n} t + \phi) \\
&= 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega_{n}t).
\end{align}$$

105.title: 1.1u.2 Simple Pendulum
105.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.1 Dynamics/1.1u Oscillatory Motion/1.1u.2 Simple Pendulum.md
105.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1u.2 Simple Pendulum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/18 18:40:42","modified":"2024/12/18 19:22:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Simple Pendulum
>A simple pendulum is a [[1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion|simple harmonic oscillator]] consisting of a small, massive objet (called the **bob**) suspended from the end of a lightweight cord, which swings back and forth under the influence of gravity. Its angular displacement follows the formula,
>$$\theta(t)=\theta_{\text{max}}\cos(\omega_{n}t+\phi),$$
>where $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{g}{\ell } }$ is the natural frequency of the pendulum with $\ell$ being the length of the string, and $\theta_{\text{max}}$ is its peak angle of displacement.

# Intuition
The restoring force exerted on a pendulum when it is displaced from its equilibrium (resting) position can be modeled as
$$F=-mg\sin\theta,$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between the pendulum's equilibrium position and current position. For small angles, the following holds:
$$\sin \theta \approx \theta \enspace \text{ (for } \theta < 15\degree\text{)}.$$
Therefore, 
$$F=-mg\theta \enspace \text{ (for } \theta < 15\degree\text{)}.$$
A swinging pendulum always makes an arc with its equilibrium position. Therefore, $s=\theta \ell,$ where $\ell$ is the length of the pendulum's string (and the radius if hypothetically the pendulum makes a circle). We get:
$$F=-\frac{mg}{\ell}s.$$
This formula roughly resembles $-kx$. Therefore, we can approximate $k=\frac{mg}{\ell}$. Since a simple pendulum follows SHM, we get $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{mg}{\ell m} }=\sqrt{ \frac{g}{\ell} }$. This means that the equation for angular displacement becomes
$$\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}+\frac{g}{\ell}\theta=0 \iff \theta(t)=\theta_{\text{max}}\cos(\omega_{n}t+\phi).$$
The amplitude equals $\theta_{\text{max}}$ since it is assumed that SHM starts when the pendulum is at $\theta_{\text{max}}$ before being released for the first time.

106.title: 1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion
106.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.1 Dynamics/1.1u Oscillatory Motion/1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion.md
106.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/21 01:09:59","modified":"2024/12/18 18:56:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
>Any oscillating system for which the net restoring force is directly proportional to the negative of the displacement is said to exhibit **simple harmonic motion (SHM)**, as it is sinusoidal with a single frequency. Such a system is often called a **simple harmonic oscillator (SHO)**. Due to its sinusoidal nature, the displacement of any system in simple harmonic motion can be modeled as
>$$x = x_{0}\cos(\omega t + \phi),$$
>where $x_{0}$ is the waveform's amplitude, representing the initial displacement of the oscillator from its equilibrium position), $\omega = 2\pi f = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ is its natural frequency, and $\phi$ is its phase.
>
>The total energy of the simple harmonic oscillator is then given by
>$$E=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_{0}^2\sin^2(\omega t+\phi)+\frac{1}{2}kx_{0}^2\cos^2(\omega t + \phi).$$

# Intuition
We start with Newton's second law: $\sum F=ma$. Since $a=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, and the total force exerted by a spring is given as $\sum  F =-kx$. Therefore,
$$m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-kx \iff \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+\frac{k}{m}x=0.$$
This is an un(der)damped ($\zeta = \frac{\alpha}{\omega_{0}}=0$) second order differential equation with natural frequency $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{k}{m} }.$ Solving for it by definition, we get
$$\begin{align}
x(t)&=K_{1}\cos(\omega_{n}t)+K_{2}\sin(\omega_{n}t).
\end{align}$$
At $t=0$, $x(0)=K_{1}\cos(\omega_{n}0)=K_{1}=x_{0}$. Therefore, $K_{1}=x_{0}$.

If we take the derivative of $x(t)$, we get:
$$\dot{x}(t)=-\omega_{n}x_{0}\sin(\omega_{n}t)+\omega_{n}K_{2}\cos(\omega_{n}t).$$
Setting $t=0$, we get 
$\dot{x}(0)=\omega_{n}K_{2}=\dot{x_{0}}=v_{0}$. Therefore, $K_{2}=\frac{v_{0}}{\omega_{n}}$. We find that the general solution to the simple harmonic model is
$$x(t)=x_{0}\cos(\omega_{n} t)+\frac{v_{0}}{\omega_{n}}\sin(\omega_{n} t),$$
where $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$. If we assume that $v_{0}=0$ (i.e. the SHO starts motion after $t=0$), we get the final form,
$$x(t)=x_{0}\cos(\sqrt{ \frac{k}{m} }t).$$

109.title: 1.1p.2 Elastic Collisions
109.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.1 Dynamics/1.1q Linear Momentum/1.1p.2 Elastic Collisions.md
109.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1p.2 Elastic Collisions]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/25 17:07:35","modified":"2024/12/19 01:21:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Elastic Collision
>An **elastic collision** is a type of collision in which the total **kinetic energy** and the total **momentum** of the system are conserved. In an elastic collision, ***no energy is lost*** to heat, sound, or deformation; instead, the ***kinetic energy is fully retained*** in the system, such that
>$$\begin{alignat}{0}
>\underbrace{m_A\vec{v}_A + m_B\vec{v}_B}_\text{Momentum before collision} = \underbrace{m_A\vec{v}'_A + m_B\vec{v}'_B}_\text{Momentum after collision} \\
>\text{and} \\
>\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}m_A\vec{v}_A^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_B\vec{v}_B^2}_\text{KE before collision} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}m_A\vec{v}'^2_A + 
>\frac{1}{2} m_B\vec{v}'^2_B}_\text{KE after collision}
\end{alignat}.$$
> This implies that in $1$-dimensional calculations, the relative speed of the two objects before the collision equals their speed of separation after the collision, such that
> $$v_{A}+v_{A}'=V_{B}+V_{B}'.$$
> A consequence of this means that in an elastic collision, the colliding objects ***change their direction after the collision***.

# Examples
>[!example] Two Blocks, One Spring
>A 3.0-kg block slides along a frictionless tabletop at 8.0 m/s toward a second block (at rest) of mass 4.5 kg. A coil spring, which obeys Hooke's law and has spring constant $k = 760 \text{ N/m}$, is attached to the second block in such a way that it will be compressed when struck by the moving block. 
>
>A collision involving a spring will lead to the blocks sticking together first. Therefore, we can say that
>$$m_{A}v_{A}+m_{B}v_{B}=(m_{A}+m_{B})v_{f} \iff v_{f}=\frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}}v_{A}$$
>Since block $B$ is at rest, $m_{B}v_{B}=0$. Since the system is elastic, $v_{f}=v_{A}$, as all energy is conserved. We can then apply the law of conservation of energy in the same way, such that
>$$\frac{1}{2}m_{A}v_{A}^2=\frac{1}{2}(m_{A}+m_{B})v_{f}^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \iff kx^2 = m_{A}v_{A}^2-(m_{A}+m_{B})\left(\frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}} \right)^2v_{A}^2$$
>This yields $x \approx 0.39$.

110.title: 1.1p.1 Linear Momentum
110.path: Physics/1. Classical Mechanics/1.1 Dynamics/1.1q Linear Momentum/1.1p.1 Linear Momentum.md
110.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1p.1 Linear Momentum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/25 15:52:31","modified":"2025/08/04 13:29:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Momentum
>**Linear momentum** ($\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}$) is a measure of an object’s tendency to stay in motion and is conserved in isolated systems. Mathematically, the momentum of an object is defined as the product of its mass and its velocity, such that
>$$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}.$$
>Alternatively, since a force is required to change the momentum of an object, [[1.2a Newton's Laws|net force]] can be defined as the derivative of momentum with respect to time, such that
>$$\sum\vec{F} = \frac{d}{dt}\vec{p} = \frac{d}{dt}(m\vec{v})=m\vec{a}.$$
>The equation above implies that if no external forces act on an object, then the total momentum of that object is said to be conserved. 
>
>More generally, the sum of the momenta of $n$ colliding objects is conserved when
>$$\underbrace{m_A\vec{v}_A + m_B\vec{v}_B}_\text{momentum before collision} = \underbrace{m_A\vec{v}'_A + m_B\vec{v}'_B}_\text{momentum after collision}.$$

# Intuition
Although the law of conservation of linear momentum was discovered experimentally, we can prove it using Newton's laws of motion. Consider a large number of objects colliding, such that their linear momentum is equal to $\vec{P}=\vec{p}_1+\vec{p}_2+\ldots=\sum\vec{p}_i$. Consider also that there are external forces acting on the objects, such as friction, drag, gravity, etc. Momentum is conserved if we measure it immediately before the collision, and immediately after.

Differentiating $\vec{P}$, we find that
$$\frac{d}{dt}\vec{P}=\sum\frac{d}{dt}\vec{p}_i=\sum\vec{F}_i.$$

For any object $i$, $\vec{F}_i$ represents its net force. The forces are either external (exerted by objects outside of the system) or internal (exerted by objects inside the system). Since by Newton's third law internal forces occur in pairs, they cancel each other out. Therefore, $\vec{F}_i$ consists only of external forces. If $\vec{F}_i=0$, then the linear momentum of object $i$ is conserved.

111.title: 1.1k.2 Nonuniform Circular Motion

111.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.1k.2 Nonuniform Circular Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/28 23:49:53","modified":"2024/09/30 12:57:07"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nonuniform Circular Motion
>Nonuniform circular motion occurs when an object moves along a circular path with a changing speed. Unlike [[1.1k.1 Uniform Circular Motion|uniform circular motion]], where the speed remains constant, nonuniform circular motion involves variations in the magnitude of the velocity, though the direction of motion is still continuously changing as the object follows the circular path:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{amsmath}
>
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>    % First graph: Forces (left side)
>    \begin{scope}[shift={(-2.5,0)}, rotate=90]
>        % Circle & Radius
>        \draw[dashed,thick] (0,0) circle (2);
>        
>        % Force vectors
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(0,-1) node[right] {$\vec{F}_{\text{tan}}$}; % Tangential force
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(-0.925,-0.925) node[below] {$\vec{F}$}; % Radial force
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(-1,0) node[below right] {$\vec{F}_R$}; % Total force
>        
>        % Labels
>        \node at (2,0) [circle,fill,inner sep=1.5pt] {}; % point on the circle
>    \end{scope}
>    
>    % Second graph: Accelerations (right side)
>    \begin{scope}[shift={(2.5,0)}, rotate=90]
>        % Circle
>        \draw[dashed,thick] (0,0) circle (2);
>        
>        % Acceleration vectors
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(0,-1) node[right] {$\vec{a}_{\text{tan}}$}; % Tangential acceleration
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(-0.925,-0.925) node[below] {$\vec{a}$}; % Total acceleration
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(-1,0) node[below right] {$\vec{a}_R$}; % Radial acceleration
>        
>        % Labels
>        \node at (2,0) [circle,fill,inner sep=1.5pt] {}; % point on the circle
>    \end{scope}
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Since acceleration has more than one direction, so does force. Therefore,
>$$\vec{a} = \vec{a}_R + \vec{a}_{\tan} \implies |\vec{a}| = \sqrt{|\vec{a}_R|^2 + |\vec{a}_{\tan}|^2}$$
>where $a_R = \frac{|\vec{v}^2|}{r}$ and $a_{\tan} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$.

112.content:

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/28 20:11:07","modified":"2024/09/28 23:53:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Uniform Circular Motion
>An object that moves in a circle at constant speed $\vec{v}$ is said to experience **uniform circular motion**. The *magnitude* of the velocity remains constant in this case, but the *direction* of the velocity continuously changes as the object moves around the circle. Thus, an object revolving in a circle is continuously accelerating, even when the speed remains constant: 
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=3, rotate=60]
>
>    % Draw the circle (part of it)
>    \draw[thick] (1.5,1.25) arc (42:-3:2cm);
>
>    % Points A and B on the circle
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above right:{B}] at (2,0) {};
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above:{A}] at ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) {};
>
>    % Center of the circle C
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=below:C] at (0,0) {};
>
>    % Draw radii
>    \draw[thick] (0,0) -- (2,0) node[midway,right] {$r$}; % Radius to A
>    \draw[thick] (0,0) -- ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) node[midway, left] {$r$}; % Radius to B
>
>    % Arc and angle
>    \draw[->] (1,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=30,radius=1] node[midway, below]{$\Delta \theta$};
>
>    % Tangential displacement arc (delta l)
>    \draw[dashed,thick] (2,0) -- ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) node[pos=0.25, below] {$\Delta \ell$};
>
>    % Velocity vectors
>    \draw[->,thick,green] (1.55,1.25) -- +(0.35,-0.5) node[right] {$\vec{v}_1$}; % Velocity at A
>    \draw[->,thick,green] (2.025, 0.25) -- +(0.025, -0.65) node[right] {$\vec{v}_2$}; % Velocity at B
>
>	% Downward acceleration
>	\draw[->,thick,orange] (1.925,0.5) -- +(-0.45,-0.125) node[below] {$\vec{a} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Mathematically, the acceleration of an object in uniform circular motion is expressed as
>$$a_R = \frac{v^2}{r},$$
>where $r$ is the radius of curvature of the curve.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>1. In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant, but the acceleration is not zero.
>>2. Since $a_R$ is directed towards the center of the circle at all times, its **centripetal force** $\sum F_R = ma_R$ must also be directed towards the center of the circle.

115.title: 1. Standard Form Optimization
115.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/1. Standard Form Optimization.md
115.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1. Standard Form Optimization]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/10 15:25:10","modified":"2025/03/10 16:58:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Standard Form 
>A standard  optimization problem is typically stated as follows:
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & f_{0}(x) \\ \text{subject to:} \quad & f_{i}(x) \leq 0, \quad i=1,\ldots,m, \end{aligned}$$
>where $p^*$ is the **optimal value**, $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the **decision variable**, $f_{0}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is the **objective function** (or cost), and $f_{i}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \space i = 1,\ldots,k$ are the $k$ optimization **constraints**.
>
>Other than inequality constraints, an optimization problem may have equality constraints $h_{i} = 0$ (equivalently represented via a pair of inequalities $h_{i} \geq 0$ and $h_{i} \le 0$), and set constraints $x \in \mathcal{X}$.
>
>Furthermore, maximization problems can be readily recast as minimization problems, such that
>$$p^* = \max\limits_{x}f_{0}(x) = -\min\limits_{x}-f_{0}(x).$$
>>[!warning] "Subject To" Notation
>>In the above, the term “$\text{subject to:}$” is sometimes replaced with the shorthand “$\text{s.t.:}$,” or simply by colon notation “$\text{:}$”.

# Properties
#### (*Feasible Set*) $\mathcal{X} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : f_{i}(x) \leq 0 \enspace \forall i = 1,\ldots,k \}$.
The feasible set is the set of points that satisfy the constraints of an optimization problem. If $\mathcal{X} = \emptyset$, the problem is said to be **infeasible**, such that $p^* = \begin{dcases}+\infty & \text{if }p^*=\min\limits_{x}f_{0}(x), \\ -\infty & \text{if }p^*=\max\limits_{x}f_{0}(x).\end{dcases}$
#### (*Optimal Set*) $\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=\{ x \in \mathcal{X} :  f_{0}(x)=p^*\}=\arg\min\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}f_{0}(x)$.
If $\mathcal{X}=\emptyset$, then, naturally $\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=\emptyset$. However, the converse isn't true. There may be feasible solutions to an optimization problem, but the optimal set is empty because:
1. The optimal solution is at a limit (i.e., $f_{0}$ diverges at $x^*$).
2. The constraints of the optimization problem are not satisfied.
#### (*Sub-optimality*) If $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $p^* < f_{0}(x) \le p^* + \epsilon$, then $x$ is $\epsilon$-suboptimal.

116.title: 1.2a Least Squares
116.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/9. Least Squares/1.2a Least Squares.md
116.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Least Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/10 00:16:22","modified":"2025/03/10 20:28:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Optimization
>**Least squares** optimization is a method for finding an approximate solution to a system of equations $A\vec{x}=\vec{y}$ for which $\nexists\vec{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$. Formally, given a real matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and a vector $\vec{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the least squares problem finds (at least one) vector $\vec{x}^* \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $A\vec{x}^*$ is the [[10. Projection Theorem|orthogonal projection]] of $\vec{y}$ onto $\mathcal{R}(A)$,
>$$\vec{x}^* \in \arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|A\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|_{2}^2,$$
>where $\vec{x}^*$ is always an optimal solution to the system of normal equations $A^TA\vec{x}=A^T\vec{y}$.
>
>Particularly, if $A$ is in full column rank (i.e., $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n$), and therefore $Ax=y$ is *overdetermined*, then the least squares solution is given as
>$$\vec{x}^* = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T\vec{y}.$$
>
>Moreover, if $A$ is in full row rank (i.e., $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$), and therefore $A\vec{x}=\vec{y}$ is *undetermined* with infinite solutions, then the least squares solution is defined as the solution of the system with the smallest Euclidean norm, such that
>$$\vec{x}^* = \arg\min\limits_{\vec{x}:A\vec{x}=\vec{y}}\|\vec{x}\|_{2} = A^T(AA^T)^{-1}\vec{y}.$$
>>[!warning] LS and the Pseudoinverse
>>Note that the set of optimal solutions to the least squares problem can be expressed as
>>$$\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=A^\dagger \vec{y} + \mathcal{N}(A),$$
>>where $A^\dagger \vec{y}$ is the minimum-norm point in the optimal set. This means that if $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = \min(m, n)$ (i.e., $A$ is full rank), then the optimal solution $x^* = A^{\dagger}\vec{y}$.
# Proofs
### 1. General Solution
Per the Projection Theorem, we know that given any $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, there exists some $\bar{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$ at minimal distance from $\vec{y}$. We also know that $(y-\bar{y}) \perp \mathcal{R}(A) \equiv (y-\bar{y}) \in \mathcal{N}(A^T)$. As such, for all $y$,
$$A^T(y-\bar{y}) = 0.$$
Furthermore, since $\bar{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$, there certainly exists some $x$, such that $Ax = \bar{y}$. Combining the two equations,
$$A^Ty-A^TAx=0 \iff A^TAx=A^Ty.$$
### 2. Full Col. Rank Solution
Since $A^TA$ is invertible for wide matrices of full column rank, we have $x^*=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Ty$.
### 3. Full Row Rank Solution
When a tall matrix $A$ has full row rank $m \leq n$, the rank-nullity theorem implies that the nullspace of $A$ is nontrivial, such that $\text{Nullity}(A) = n-m \geq 1$. 

### 4. Pseudoinverse Solution


# Variants
#### (*Weighted LS*) For $W = \operatorname{diag}(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{m})$, $\exists\vec{x}^*_{w}=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|W(A\vec{x}-\vec{y})\|_{2}^2$, such that $A^TW^TWA\vec{x}_{w}^* = A^TW^TW\vec{y}$.
The proof is simple. We know from the proof of general LS that $x^*$ is the optimal solution to $A^TAx=A^Ty$. We then take $A_{w}=WA$, $y_{w} = Wy$, and substitute for the solution, such that
$$A_{w}^TA_{w}\vec{x}=A_{w}^Ty_{w} \iff A^TW^TWAx=A^TW^TWy.$$
#### (*Linearly Constrained LS*) For $\begin{aligned} \min_\limits{x} \quad & c^T x \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b\end{aligned}$

#### (*$\ell^2$-Regularized LS*) For $\lambda > 0$, $x^*=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|A\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|_{2}^2+\lambda\|\vec{x}\|_{2}^2$ is the optimal solution to $(A^T A + \lambda L^T L)\vec{x} = A^T \vec{y}$.

117.title: 4.1 Duality
117.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.1 Duality]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/15 17:13:17","modified":"2025/04/23 13:23:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Duality
>**Duality** in optimization is the framework that associates every optimization problem, known as the **primal problem**, with another similar problem on the dual space called the **dual problem**. Let $F: X \times Y \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{ +\infty \}$ be a **perturbation function** (i.e., $F(x, 0) = f(x)$), and $p^*$ be the solution to the primal problem
>$$p^* = \inf_{x \in X} f(x).$$
>Then, $p^*$ can be associated with an **always convex** dual optimization problem on the dual space $Y^*$, such that
>$$d^* = \sup_{y^* \in Y^*} \{ -F^*(0, y^*) \}.$$
>The values between these problems are always related via the **weak duality principle**, such that $$p^* \geq d^*.$$
>Moreover, **strong duality** holds (i.e., $p^* = d^*$) if certain constraint qualifications are met.

# Example
>[!example] Sion's Minimax Theorem

>[!note] Fenchel Duality
>**Fenchel duality** is a framework in convex analysis that creates a [[4.1 Duality|dual optimization problem]] using the concept of [[2.3 Convex Conjugates|convex (Fenchel) conjugates]]. >$$p^* = \inf_{x \in X} \{ f(x)+g(Ax) \}.$$
>Then, the **Fenchel dual** is given as 
>$$d^* = \sup_{y^* \in Y^*}\{ -f^*(A^Ty^*)-g^*(-y^*) \}.$$
>If $f$ and $g$ are convex and $\exists x_{0} \in \operatorname{dom} f \cap \operatorname{dom} (g $

# Proof
Consider the perturbation function $F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Ax-y)$. Then, the primal problem is given on the function $F(x,0)$. Taking the convex conjugate of $F(x,0)$, we get:
$$F^*(x^*, 0)=\sup_{x \in X}\{ \langle x^*, x \rangle - F(x^*, x) \}$$

119.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/4. Duality/4.3 Lagrangian Duality/4.3a Lagrangian Duality.md
119.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3a Lagrangian Duality]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/15 17:24:21","modified":"2025/04/23 14:17:20"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Lagrangian Duality
>A **Lagrangian dual** is a type of duality for primal optimization problems problems of the form
>$$\begin{align*} p^* = \min\limits_{x \in X} \quad & f_{0}(x) \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & f_{i}(x) \le 0, \quad i=1,\ldots,m, \\ \quad & h_{j}(x) = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, k, \end{align*}$$
>such that the constraints are embedded into the objective via the multipliers $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^k$: 
>$$\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda,\mu)=f_{0}(x)+\sum^{m}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}f_{i}(x)+\sum^{k}_{j=1}\mu_{i}h_{i}(x).$$
>Then, the Lagrangian dual problem is given as
>$$d^*=\sup_{\lambda \geq 0}\inf_{x \in X}\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda,\mu).$$

120.title: 4.3b.2 KKT Conditions
120.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/4. Duality/4.3 Lagrangian Duality/4.3b Constraint Qualifications/4.3b.2 KKT Conditions.md
120.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3b.2 KKT Conditions]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/15 17:25:02","modified":"2025/04/30 17:37:49"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Conditions
>A triple of primal and [[4.3a Lagrangian Duality|Lagrange dual]] variables $(x, \lambda, \mu) \in X \times \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is said to satisfy the **Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT)** conditions if it satisfies the following three conditions:
>1. (*Feasibility*) The vector $x$ is primal-feasible, and the pair $(\lambda, \mu)$ is dual feasible, such that $f_{i}(x) \leq 0$ for all $i=1, \ldots, m$, $h_{i}(x)=0$ for all $i=1, \ldots, k$, and $\lambda \geq 0$.
>2. (*Stationarity*) The gradient of the Lagrangian with respect to $x$ vanishes, such that 
>$$\nabla f_{0}​(x)+\sum\limits_{i=1}^m​\lambda_{i}​\nabla f_{i}​(x)+\sum\limits_{j=1}^k​\mu_{j}​\nabla h_{j}​(x)=0.$$
>3. (*Complementary Slackness*) Each inequality constraint is either “active” or its multiplier is zero, such that 
>$$\lambda_{i}f_{i}(x)=0, \quad i=1,\ldots,m.$$
>Given that all $f_{i}$ are convex, and all $h_{j}$ are affine, the KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient for optimality (i.e., strong duality holds if and only if the KKT conditions are satisfied).

121.title: 4.3b.1 Slater's Condition
121.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/4. Duality/4.3 Lagrangian Duality/4.3b Constraint Qualifications/4.3b.1 Slater's Condition.md
121.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3b.1 Slater's Condition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/15 17:24:56","modified":"2025/04/30 16:55:52"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Slater's Condition
>**Slater’s condition** ensures that the feasible region has “room” inside its boundary by requiring at least one point to lie strictly within all inequality constraints. Let the domain of an optimization problem be
>$$\mathcal{D} = \bigcap\limits_{i=0}^n\operatorname{dom}f_{i}.$$
>Then, strong duality holds (i.e., $p^* = d^*$) if both of the following conditions hold:
>1. Each $f_{i}: X \to \mathbb{R} \cap \{ +\infty \}$ is convex. 
>2. There exists some $x_{0}$, such that $f_{i}(x_{0}) < 0$ for all constraints $i = 1,\ldots,n$.

>[!note] Quadratic Program
>A **Quadratic Program (QP)** is an [[1. Standard Form Optimization|optimization problem]] where the objective function is quadratic, and the constraints are affine. Its **standard form** is given as
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & \frac{1}{2}x^THx+c^Tx \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b, \end{aligned}$$
>where $f_{0}(x)=\langle c, x \rangle$ for some decision variable $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constants $H \in \mathbb{S}^n$ (and $H \in \mathbb{S}^n_{+}$ for the QP to be convex), $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

123.title: 2.1 Linear Programing
123.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/3. Conic Optimization/2.1 Linear Programing.md
123.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1 Linear Programing]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/05 02:54:56","modified":"2025/03/11 04:21:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Program
>A **Linear Program (LP)** is an [[1. Standard Form Optimization|optimization problem]] where the objective function and constraints are all affine. Its **standard form** is given as
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & c^T x \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b, \\ & x \geq 0\end{aligned}$$
>where $f_{0}(x)=\langle c, x \rangle$ for some decision variable $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constants $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $d \in \mathbb{R}$.
>
>The feasible set of an LP is a *polyhedron* (or a *polytope* if fully bounded). 
# Intuition
Intuitively, in linear programming:
- You have a collection of variables $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.
- You form a linear expression $c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 + \dots + c_n x_n$ (the “objective”) that you want to make as large (maximize) or as small (minimize) as possible.

At the same time, each variable combination must satisfy a series of linear constraints, such as:
- $a_{1,1} x_1 + a_{1,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{1,n} x_n \;\le\; b_1,$
- $a_{2,1} x_1 + a_{2,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{2,n} x_n \;\le\; b_2,$
and possibly some equalities, like
- $a_{3,1} x_1 + a_{3,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{3,n} x_n \;=\; b_3.$

Each constraint chops off a portion of the space of all possible $x$. Because the constraints are linear, the feasible region (the set of all allowable solutions) is a **convex polytope** (think of a polygon in 2D, a polyhedron in 3D, etc.).
# Properties

# Examples
>[!example] Revenue Maximization

>[!example] Slack Variables
>Express the following problems as LPs:
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \left[\max\limits_{i=1,\ldots,n} x_{i} - \min\limits_{j=1,\ldots,n}x_{j} \right] \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b\end{aligned}$$
>>[!example]- Solution
>>**Solution:** We can introduce *slack variables* that form a high and low bound on the elements of $x$, such that
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x, u, t} \quad & u-t \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b, \\ & u \geq x_{i}, \space i=1,\ldots,n, \\ & t \leq x_{i}, \space i=1,\ldots,n. \end{aligned}$$
>
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \sum^{n}_{i=1}|x_{i}| \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b\end{aligned}$$
>>[!example]- Solution
>>We introduce a single bounded slack variable $t$, such that
>>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \sum^{n}_{i=1}t \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b, \\ \quad & t \geq x_{i}, \space i = 1,\ldots,n \\ \quad & t \geq -x_{i}, \space i = 1, \ldots, n, \end{aligned}$$
>>to cover both positive and negative elements of $x$.

124.title: 2.3 Convex Conjugates
124.path: Mathematics/9. Mathematical Optimization/2. Convex Analysis/2.3 Convex Conjugates.md
124.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.3 Convex Conjugates]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/29 22:36:19","modified":"2025/05/15 13:51:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Convex Conjugate
>The **convex (Fenchel) conjugate** $f^*: X^* \to \mathbb{R}$ of a function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ is used to represent $f$ as a set of supporting hyperplanes with slopes $x^*$, such that the parameters of each $x^*$ are encoded in $f^*$. Then, $f^*(x^*)$ is the intercept at which the line $\langle x^*, x \rangle$ becomes a tangent of $f$.  Formally,
>$$f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x \in X} \{ \langle x^*, x \rangle - f(x)\},$$
>such that $t(x) = \langle x^*, x \rangle - f^*(x^*)$.
>
>>[!warning] Preservation of Convexity
>>The convex conjugate of any function is always a convex function.

# Properties
#### (*Fenchel's Inequality*) Any conjugate pair $f, f^*$ satisfies $\langle x^*, x \rangle \leq f(x) + f^*(x^*)$.
#### (*Weak Duality of Biconjugation*) For any $f$, it follows that $f^{* *} \leq f$, such that $f^{**}=f$ if and only if $f$ is convex and l.s.c.
#### (*Affine Conjugate*) Any $a(x)=\langle x^*_{a}, x \rangle + b$ has $a^*(x^*)=\begin{dcases}-b & x^*=x_{a}^* \\ + \infty & x^* \neq x_{a}^*\end{dcases}$, and $a^{**}(x)=a(x)$.


# Examples
>[!example] Economic Interpretation
>Let $x$ be the quantity of some goods you are trying to sell (i.e., laptops, tablets, phones, etc.). Then $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ can be defined as the total cost of producing the goods (i.e., the dot product between $x$ and the respective cost of producing 1 unit of each good). Take the Fenchel conjugate of $f(x)$:
>$$\underbrace{f^*(x^*)}_{\text{Profit}}=\sup_{x \in X}\{ \underbrace{\langle x^*, x \rangle}_{\text{Revenue}} - \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{Cost}} \}.$$
>Then, $f^*: X^* \to \mathbb{R}$ represents the optimal profit given the goods are sold at some prices $x^*$ per 1 unit of goods.

>A set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **open** if for any $x \in \mathcal{X}$, there exists an Euclidean ball $B_{\epsilon}(x)=\{ y \in \mathbb{R}^n : \| y-x \|_{2} \}$ with some radius $\epsilon > 0$, such that $B_{\epsilon}(x) \subseteq \mathcal{X}$. Similarly, $\mathcal{X}$ is said to be **closed** if its complement $\mathbb{R}^n \backslash \mathcal{X}$ is open. An example of an open set is any interval $(a,b)$.

131.title: 10. Projection Theorem
131.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[10. Projection Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 16:55:35","modified":"2025/05/14 03:30:20"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Projection Theorem
>For any vector $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a subspace $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the projection of $\vec{x}$ onto $\mathcal{S}$ is the unique linear operator in $\mathcal{S}$ that minimizes the distance between $\vec{x}$ and $\mathcal{S}$, defined as
>$$\Pi_\mathcal{S}(\vec{x})=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{y} \in \mathcal{S}} ||\vec{x}-\vec{y}||,$$
>such that $\Pi_\mathcal{S}(\vec{x}) \in \mathcal{S}$ and the residual vector $\vec{x}-\Pi_S(\vec{x}) \perp \mathcal{S}$.
>
>Then, the general solution of $\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x})$, given a matrix $S \in \mathcal{S}^n$, such that $\operatorname{rank}(S)=n$ (i.e., $S$ is full-rank),
>$$\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = S(S^TS)^{-1}S^T\vec{x},$$
>where $P = S(S^TS)^{-1}S^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is called the **projection matrix**.
>
>If $S$ is not full rank (i.e., $\operatorname{rank}(S)<n$), given an orthonormal basis matrix $B_{S}$ of $\mathcal{S}$, the orthonormal projection of $\vec{x}$ onto $\mathcal{S}$ can be expressed as
>$$\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = B_{S}^TB_{S}\vec{x} = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\langle \vec{(B_{S})}_{i}, \vec{x} \rangle \vec{(B_{S})}_{i},$$
>which can be equivalently written as $\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\langle \vec{s}_{i}, \vec{x} \rangle}{\|\vec{s}_{i}\|^2} \vec{s}_{i}$ if the basis vectors $s_{i}$ are orthogonal rather than orthonormal.
# Proof
# Properties
#### (*Linearity*) 

#### (*Orthogonal Decomp.*) If $S^\perp=\{ x \in \mathcal{X} : \langle x, s \rangle=0 \enspace \forall s \in S \}$, then $\mathcal{X}=S \oplus S^\perp$.

# Examples
>[!example] Projection Onto a Hyperplane
>**Conditions:** Let $y = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$, and let $\mathcal{H} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : c^Tx = 0 \}$ be a hyperplane<sup>[[3.4f Hyperplanes|3.4c]]</sup> in $\mathbb{R^2}$, such that $c=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$. 
>
>**Task:** Compute the minimum distance from $y$ to $\mathcal{H}$.
>
>**Solution:** Since $c$ is the normal direction of the hyperplane, it follows that $y - p^* \parallel c$ (since the error term of a projection is always perpendicular to the space of the projection). This, in turn, implies that the error term is some scaling of $c$, such that 
>$$y-p^* = \alpha c.$$
>
>Since $p^* \in \mathcal{H} \perp c$, it also follows that $c^Tp^*=0$.  As such, 
>$$c^T(y-p^*) = \langle c, y \rangle - 0 = \alpha \|c\|^2_{2} \iff \alpha = \frac{\langle c, y \rangle}{\|c\|^2_{2}}.$$
>
>Therefore, $\alpha = \frac{2}{2} = 1$, meaning that the distance $\|y-p^*\|_{2}=\|c\|_{2}=\sqrt{ 2 }$.

135.title: 2.9b Set Orthonormality
135.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/9. Orthogonality/2.9b Set Orthonormality.md
135.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9b Set Orthonormality]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 04:46:32","modified":"2024/04/25 17:00:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Orthonormality of Sets
>A set of vectors $S$ is an orthonormal set if and only if for all $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in S$
>$$
>\left<\vec{x},\vec{y}\right>=
>\begin{cases}
>1 & \text{if } \vec{x}=\vec{y} \\
>0 & \text{if } \vec{x} \neq \vec{y}
\end{cases}
$$

# Intuition
The above equation is equivalent to saying that:
1. All $n^2$ pairs of vectors $\vec{x},\vec{y} \in S \in \vec{R}^n$ are [[2.9 Orthogonality|orthogonal]].
2. All $n$ vectors in $S$ are in unit norm ($\left<\vec{x},\vec{y}\right>=||\vec{x}||^2=||\vec{y}||^2=1$).
Essentially, a set is orthonormal if it is orthogonal AND all of its vectors are normalized. This goes one step further and is useful for

136.title: 2.9c Matrix Orthonormality
136.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/9. Orthogonality/2.9c Matrix Orthonormality.md
136.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9c Matrix Orthonormality]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 16:42:33","modified":"2025/03/09 23:12:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Orthonormal Matrices
>If a [[4.1 Matrix|matrix]] $Q$...
>- is a tall matrix ($Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ for $m > n$), then it has **orthonormal columns** if and only if $$Q^TQ=I_n.$$
>- is a wide matrix ($Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ for $m < n$), then it has **orthonormal rows** if and only if $$QQ^T=I_m.$$
>- is a square matrix ($Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$), then it is **orthonormal** if and only if $$Q^T=Q^{-1}.$$
 

# Intuition
Essentially, the above theorem may be translated into [[2.9b Set Orthonormality|set orthonormality]]:
- A tall matrix has orthonormal columns $\iff$ its column vectors form an orthonormal set.
- A wide matrix has orthonormal rows $\iff$ its row vectors form an orthonormal set.
- A square matrix is orthonormal $\iff$ both its row and column vectors form orthonormal sets.

As such, the product of the matrix and its transpose is equal to the identity matrix $I$ since the pairwise dot product of its columns/rows is 0 when two different columns/rows are multiplied and 1 when the same column/row is multiplied. This leads to an identity matrix.

The last equality simply shows that both of the above hold, since $QQ^{-1}=Q^{-1}Q=I_n$.

# Properties

#### (*Preservation of Length and Angle*) $\|Qx\|_{2} = \|x\|_{2}$.

#### (*Projection Onto Range*) If $Q^TQ=I_{n}$, then $QQ^T$ is a projection onto $\text{Col}(A)$.

137.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/9. Orthogonality/2.9a Orthogonal Vectors.md
137.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9a Orthogonal Vectors]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 04:26:43","modified":"2025/03/06 02:40:49"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Orthogonality
>A set of vectors $S \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is **pairwise orthogonal** if and only if every *distinct* pair of vectors  $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in S$ is pairwise orthogonal, such that
>$$\left<\vec{x},\vec{y}\right>=0.$$
>If $S$ is orthogonal, then it is linearly independent and contains at most $n$ vectors.
>
>Two sets of vectors $S_1$ and $S_2$ are **mutually orthogonal** if:
>- All $\vec{x} \in S_1$ and $\vec{y} \in S_2$ are pairwise orthogonal.
>- The bases $B_1$ and $B_2$ of $S_1$ and $S_2$ are orthogonal to each other.
>
>>[!warning] Orthogonality in Euclidean Space
>>Two nonzero vectors $\vec{x}$ and $\vec{y}$ are orthogonal if they are perpendicular in Euclidean space, such that they make an angle of $\theta=90\degree$ between them. This is critical in order to meet the dot product criterion $|\vec{x}||\vec{y}|\cos\theta=0$.

139.title: 2.8a Basis
139.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.8a Basis]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 15:30:23","modified":"2025/05/14 01:01:55"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Basis
>A set of vectors $B = \{ \vec{v}_1,\vec{v}_2,\dots,\vec{v}_n \} \in \mathcal{V}$ is a **basis** of the [[vector spaces|vector space]] $\mathcal{V}$ if:
>1. The vectors $\vec{v}_1,\vec{v}_2,\dots,\vec{v}_n$ are [[2. Linear Equations|linearly independent]].
>2. The span of $B$ equals $\mathcal{V}$ (i.e., any vector $v \in \mathcal{V}$ can be built as a linear combination of $B$).
# Intuition
A basis is not unique.

# Example
>[!example] Basis of Vector Space $\mathbb{R}^3$
>Any vector in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be built using the equation
>$$
>\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=
>a \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+
>b \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+
>c \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=
>a \vec{e}_1 + b \vec{e}_2 + c \vec{e}_3,
>$$
>where $\vec{e}_n$ is the standard unit vector at position $n$. 
>
>Therefore, a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the set of vectors $\left\{
>\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
>\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
>\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \right\}.$

140.title: 2.8b Change of Basis
140.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/8. Bases/2.8b Change of Basis.md
140.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.8b Change of Basis]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 15:28:01","modified":"2024/04/11 05:37:48"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Change of Basis
>Let $\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, \dots, \vec{v}_n \}$ be a V-[[2.8a Basis|basis]] (nonstandard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Let $\vec{x}$ be a vector given in the standard basis. The representation of $\vec{x}$ in the V-basis is
>$$\vec{z} = V^{-1}\vec{x},$$
>where $V := \begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \vec{v}_2 & \dots & \vec{v}_n\end{bmatrix}$ is an invertible square basis matrix.

# Intuition
Think of it this way: we can translate a vector $\vec{z}$ in V-basis to $\vec{x}$ in our basis using a matrix $V$ that contains the representation in our basis of what V-basis members see as their standard basis ($\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right\}$). Suppose V-basis unit vectors $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$ can be translated into standard basis using our unit vectors as $\vec{v}_1=2\vec{e}_1+3\vec{e}_2$  and $\vec{v}_2=\vec{e}_1-2\vec{e}_2$. Therefore, the V-basis matrix representation in our (standard) basis is $V=\begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \vec{v}_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}$. Algebraically, we can convert a V-basis vector $\vec{z}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=3\vec{v}_1+2\vec{v}_2$ to our basis as $\vec{x}=3(2\vec{e}_1+3\vec{e}_2)+2(\vec{e}_1-2\vec{e}_2)=8\vec{e}_1+5\vec{e}_2=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.$ We can quickly verify this by equivalently solving $\vec{x}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}$. Then, in order to reverse the process, we redo it backwards (by taking the inverse). 

### Why do we take the inverse to translate to V-basis?
Think of it in the following way: the way people using V-basis see our basis is $V^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{7} & \frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7} & -\frac{2}{7}\end{bmatrix}$. For them, $\vec{e}_1 = \frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_1 + \frac{3}{7}\vec{v}_2=$ and $\vec{e}_2 = \frac{1}{7}\vec{v}_1 -\frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_2$. We can quickly verify this by running our representations of the V-basis vectors $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$ to find out that $\vec{e}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\vec{e}_2=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$. Therefore, our vector $\vec{x}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}=8\vec{e}_1+5\vec{e}_2$ can be written in V-basis as $\vec{z}=8\left(\frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_1+\frac{3}{7}\vec{v}_2\right)+5\left(\frac{1}{7}\vec{v}_1+-\frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_2\right)=\frac{16}{7}\vec{v}_1+\frac{24}{7}\vec{v}_2+\frac{5}{7}\vec{v}_1-\frac{10}{7}\vec{v}_2=3\vec{v}_1+2\vec{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$. This can also be verified by solving $\vec{z}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{7} & \frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7} & -\frac{2}{7}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}=8\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7}\end{bmatrix}+5\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{7} \\ -\frac{2}{7}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$.

### How can we find the inverse coefficients algebraically?
Consider our main example where $\vec{v}_1=2\vec{e}_1+3\vec{e}_2$  and $\vec{v}_2=\vec{e}_1-2\vec{e}_2$. We can solve for the representations of $\vec{e}_1$ and $\vec{e}_2$ in V-basis such that 
$$
\begin{dcases}
	\vec{e}_1=\vec{v}_2+2\vec{e}_2 \\
	\vec{e}_1=\frac{1}{2}\vec{v}_1-\frac{3}{2}\vec{e}_2
\end{dcases}
\iff
\frac{7}{2}\vec{e}_2=\frac{1}{2}\vec{v}_1-\vec{v}_2
\iff
\begin{dcases}
\vec{e}_1 = \frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_1+\frac{3}{7}\vec{v}_2\\
\vec{e}_2 = \frac{1}{7}\vec{v}_1-\frac{2}{7}\vec{v}_2
\end{dcases}.
$$
We can verify that this is true by substituting for the respective values of $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$. As such, our standard basis vectors are represented in V-basis as $\left\{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{7}\\ \frac{3}{7}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{7} \\ -\frac{2}{7}\end{bmatrix}\right\}$. 

Why does this equal $V^{-1}$?

142.title: 5.1 Eigenvectors
142.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/5. Spectral Theory/5.1 Eigenvectors.md
142.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[5.1 Eigenvectors]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 16:52:25","modified":"2025/05/14 23:04:15"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Eigenvector
>An **eigenvector** of a square [[4.1 Matrix|matrix]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a nonzero vector $\vec{v} \in \mathbb{R^n}$ that does not change direction when $A$ is applied to it. Instead of being rotated or distorted, it is simply stretched or shrunk by both $A$ and the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\operatorname{\det}(A-\lambda I)$, called the **eigenvalues** of $A$. Formally,
>$$A \vec{v}=\lambda \vec{v},$$
>where $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.
>>[!warning] Eigenvector Triviality
>>Eigenvector equations always have infinitely many solutions (or none). The trick is to find free variables in the system.
# Intuition
Suppose we applied a linear transformation $A$ to a known vector $\vec{x}$. However, even with the transformation, the resulting vector $\vec{z}=A \vec{x}$ is just a linear combination of $\vec{x}$ ($\mathrm{Span}(\vec{x})=\mathrm{Span}(\vec{z})$), scaled by the factor $\lambda$. Therefore, $\vec{z}=\lambda \vec{x}$ too! Such a vector $\vec{x}$ that ==remains on its span after a linear transformation== is an eigenvector of $A$, whereas $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue is the scaling factor of that eigenvector when $A$ is applied. However, we are usually tasked with finding the eigenvectors of $A$.

To find such an eigenvector $\vec{x}$, we must solve for $A \vec{x}-\lambda \vec{x} = (A-\lambda I)\vec{x}=\vec{0}$. We do this by calculating $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, or the **characteristic polynomial** of $A$. This is because the determinant of a matrix is 0 when the matrix is not in full rank, and therefore squishes the possibilities of the span on a single line with area 0. We can say that the eigenvalues of $A$ "throw it off" from linear independence (if it was ever in such) in order to ==squish it into the lower-dimensional subspace== $\text{span}(\vec{x})$.

Thus, formally, an eigenvector of $A$ is any nonzero vector that is a scalar multiple of itself ($\text{span}(\vec{x})=\text{span}(A\vec{x})$) when multiplied by $A$.

Then, the resulting eigenvalue when $A$ is applied to an eigenvector $\vec{x}$ is essentially ==the scaling factor== of the transformation We simply use eigenvalues to make our lives much easier when applying transformations.

Eigenvalues also ==do not have to be real or unique==. Check out the examples below to see examples of nonstandard eigenvalue cases.

# Properties
#### (*Rayleigh Quotient*) For some real symmetric matrix $A$, $R(A)=\dfrac{x^TAx}{\|x\|^2}$, such that $\lambda_{\max}^{(A)}=\max\limits_{\|x\|=1}R(A)$, and $\lambda_{\min}^{(A)}=\min\limits_{\|x\|=1}R(A)$.

# Examples
>[!example] Repeated Eigenvalues
>Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. Since the diagonal entries of $A$ are equal and the far entries have a product of 0, this matrix will yield a single eigenvalue $\lambda=2$. There are no eigenvectors associated with this matrix.

144.title: 4.8 Trace
144.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.8 Trace]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/15 17:49:24","modified":"2025/03/06 17:30:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Trace of Matrix
>The trace of a [[4.1 Matrix|matrix]] is the sum of its diagonal entries. Formally, for a general matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$,
>$$\mathrm{Tr}(A)=\sum^{\mathrm{min}\{m, n\}}_{i=1}A_{ii}.$$

# Properties
##### $\mathrm{tr}(ABC)=\mathrm{tr}(BCA)=\dots=\mathrm{tr}(CAB)$
Trace is invariant under cyclic permutations.
##### $\mathrm{tr}(\vec{b}\vec{a}^T)=\vec{a}^T\vec{b}$
The trace (sum of products) of the outer product of two matrices is equal to the dot product of those two matrices.

##### $|A|_F=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(A^TA)}$

$$
\begin{align}
\mathrm{tr}(A^TA)&=\sum^{r}_{i=1}(A^TA)_{ii} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}A_{ii}^TA_{ii} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}A_{ii}^2
\end{align}
$$
for $r=\mathrm{min}\{m,n\}$.
##### $\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_i$

145.title: 4.7 Inversion of a Square Matrix
145.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/4. Matrices/4.7 Inversion of a Square Matrix .md
145.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.7 Inversion of a Square Matrix ]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 16:47:40","modified":"2025/05/14 03:09:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Matrix Inverse
>A [[4.2c Square Matrix|square matrix]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is said to be **invertible** if it is nonsingular (i.e. $\operatorname{det}(A) \neq 0$), such that there exists a matrix $A^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ for which
>$$AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I_n.$$
>If only one of the above conditions hold, we say that matrix $A$ is left-invertible (such that $A^{-1}A=I$), or right-invertible (such that $AA^{-1}=I$).
>
>We can find the inverse of a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$ by dividing its transpose by its [[4.6 Determinant of a Square Matrix|determinant]] so that
>$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{det}(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -c \\ -b & a\end{bmatrix}.$$
>
>Furthermore, if two square matrices $A,B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ are invertible, it holds that $(AB)^{-1} = A^{-1}B^{-1}$.
# Intuition
The matrix inversion formula just says that given a linear transformation of the n-space $A$, its inverse will reverse that transformation so when $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$ is applied, there is no net change for any vector in the space by yielding the[[4.2a Identity Matrix| identity matrix]] $I_n$.

146.title: 4.5 Rank
146.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.5 Rank]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/06 17:34:53","modified":"2025/05/14 03:04:46"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rank
>The **rank** of a matrix is the dimension of its [[4.4 Matrix Spaces|range]] (or equivalently, its column space). It tells us how many linearly independent columns (or rows) exist in the matrix. Formally, for a general matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$,
>$$\operatorname{Rank}(A) \leq \min(m, n),$$
>where if $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = \min(m, n)$, then $A$ is said to be in **full rank**.
>
>Conversely, the **nullity** of a matrix $A$, denoted as $\operatorname{Nullity}(A)$ is the dimension of its [[4.4b Null Space|null space]] It represents the number of independent solutions to the homogeneous equation $Ax = 0$. Per the **rank-nullity theorem**, 
>$$\operatorname{Rank}(A) + \operatorname{Nullity}(A) = n.$$

# Properties
#### (*Determinant Relation*) $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = \min(m, n)$ if and only if $\operatorname{\det}(A) \neq 0$.

147.title: 4.9b Operator Norm
147.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/4. Matrices/4.9 Matrix Norms/4.9b Operator Norm.md
147.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.9b Operator Norm]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/08 16:44:59","modified":"2025/05/14 03:38:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Operator Norm
>The $\ell^p$-induced **operator norm** of a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, given a [[3.5b p-Norm|vector p-norm]],  is the maximum normalized amount by which $A$ can stretch any nonzero vector, such that
>$$\|A\|_{p} = \max\limits_{\vec{x} \neq 0}\frac{\|A\vec{x}\|_{p}}{\|\vec{x}\|_{p}} = \max\limits_{\|\vec{x}\|_{p} \leq 1}\|A\vec{x}\|_{p},$$
>where the latter comes from the fact that the operator norm measures the magnitude relative to the unit norm (it is normalized). Then:
>- The $\ell^1$-induced norm is the largest absolute column sum, $\|A\|_{1}=\max\limits_{j=1,\ldots,n}\sum\limits^{m}_{i=1}|A_{ij}|$.
>- The $\ell^\infty$-induced  norm is the largest absolute row sum, $\|A\|_{\infty}=\max\limits_{i=1,\ldots,m}\sum\limits^{n}_{j=1}|A_{ij}|$.
>- The $\ell^2$-induced (spectral) norm corresponds to the square root of the largest eigenvalue of $A^TA$, such that $\|A\|_{2}=\sqrt{ \max\limits_{i=1,\ldots,n}\lambda_{i} }$.

# Properties
#### (*Submultiplication*) $\|AB\|_{p} \leq \|A\|_{p}\|B\|_{p}$

150.title: 4.4 Matrix Spaces
150.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/4. Matrices/4.4 Matrix Spaces.md
150.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.4 Matrix Spaces]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/14 02:18:51","modified":"2025/05/14 03:03:21"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Matrix Spaces
>Given a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, the **range** of $A$ (also referred to as the column space) is a [[3.4a Vector Spaces|vector subspace]] in $\mathbb{R}^m$ the represents the [[3.4b Span|span]] of its columns, defined as
>$$\mathcal{R}(A)=\operatorname{span}(\vec{a}_1, \vec{a}_2, …, \vec{a}_n)=\left\{\sum^{n}_{i=1}\alpha_i \vec{a}_i : \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^m,$$
>where $\alpha_{i}$ is the scaling factor (or weight) of the $i$-th column vector of $A$. 
>
>Similarly, the **row space** of $A$, denoted $\operatorname{Row}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, is the span of its rows. The row space of $A$ is related to the column space of $A^T$, such that $\operatorname{Row}(A)=\mathcal{R}(A^T)$ (and vice-versa).
>
>Conversely, the **null space** (or kernel) of $A \in \mathbb{R}$  is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that includes all vectors that output the zero vector when multiplied by $A$, such that
>$$\mathcal{N}(A) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid A x = 0 \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n.$$
>
>Per the **Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra**, every matrix $A$ naturally splits the domain ($\mathbb{R}^n$) and codomain into two complementary parts each. Namely,
>$$\begin{alignat}{0}\mathbb{R}^n = \mathcal{R}(A^T) \oplus \mathcal{N}(A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{R}^m = \mathcal{R}(A) \oplus \mathcal{N}(A^T).\end{alignat}$$

# Proof
We start by observing that every $x \in \mathcal{R}(A^T)$ in the row space of $A$ is orthogonal to every $z \in \mathcal{N}(A)$. This follows from the fact that for some $x=A^Ty$, it can be said that
$$x^Tz=y^TAz = y^T 0 = 0.$$
Thus, $\mathcal{R}(A^T) \perp \mathcal{N}(A)$, or equivalently, $\mathcal{N}(A)=\mathcal{R}(A^T)^\perp$. We know that a direct sum of a subspace and its orthogonal complement equals the whole subspace, and thus,
$$\mathcal{R}(A^T) \oplus \mathcal{R}(A^T)^\perp = \mathcal{R}(A^T) \oplus \mathcal{N}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.$$
By the same reasoning, we can prove the fact for $\mathbb{R}^m$.

>[!note] Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
>Two [[4.3 Matrix Multiplication|matrices]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ can be multiplied to create a matrix $A \times B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$, such that
>$$
>AB=
>\begin{bmatrix}  
>----\vec{a}_1^T---- \\  
>----\vec{a}_2^T---- \\
>\vdots \\  
>----\vec{a}_m^T----
>\end{bmatrix}
>\begin{bmatrix}  
>| & | &  & | \\  
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & | \\
>\vec{b}_1 & \vec{b}_2 & \cdots & \vec{b}_p \\ 
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & |
>\end{bmatrix}
>=
>\begin{bmatrix}
>\vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_p\\
>\vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_p\\
>\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
>\vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_p
>\end{bmatrix},
>$$
>where each element of the resulting matrix $D_{ij} = \vec{a}_i^T\vec{b}_j$ equals the [[3.9a Dot Product|inner product]] of the left ($A$) matrix's $i$th row vector and the right ($B$) matrix's $j$th column vector.
>
>>[!warning] Non-Commutativity
>>The matrix product is non-commutative, meaning that, in general, $AB \neq BA$.

# Properties

>[!note] p-Norm
>For a vector $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the $\ell^p$  [[3.5a Vector Norm|norm]] is expressed as
>$$||\vec{x}||_{p}=\left(\sum^{n}_{i=1}|x_{i}|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.$$
>Special cases of the $p$-norm include $p=1$ (the Manhattan norm), $p=2$ (the Euclidean norm), and $p=\infty$ (the Chebyshev norm), such that $||\vec{x}||_{\infty}=\max(\vec{x})$ is the largest element of $\vec{x}$.
>
>Then, the $\ell^{p}$ **unit norm ball** is defined as the set of all vectors with $\ell^p$ less than or equal to one,
>$$\mathcal{B}^p = \{ \vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : \|\vec{x}\|_{p} \leq 1 \},$$
>and are useful for describing the geometry of the space under the $\ell^p$  norm. Given are illustrations for the respective spaces of the $\ell^1$, $\ell^2$ and $\ell^\infty$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$:

# Properties
#### (Euclidean Norm) For a real vector $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $\|\vec{x}\|_{2}=\sqrt{ \langle \vec{x}, \vec{x} \rangle }$.

>[!note] Vector Norm
>A **vector norm** is a function $\|\cdot\|: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ that provides a way to measure the magnitude of [[3.1 Vector|vectors]] in a vector space. It satisfies the following three properties for all vectors $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in \mathcal{X}$ and scalars $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$:
>1. (*Positive-Definiteness*) $\|\vec{x}\| \geq 0$, where $\|\vec{x}\|=0 \iff \vec{x}=\vec{0}$.
>2. (*Triangle Inequality*) $\|\vec{x}+\vec{y}\|\leq\|\vec{x}\|+\|\vec{y}\|$.
>3. (Positive Homogeneity) $\|\alpha \cdot \vec{x}\|=|\alpha|\cdot\|\vec{x}\|$.

169.title: 3.4a Vector Spaces
169.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/3. Vectors/3.4 Vector Spaces/3.4a Vector Spaces.md
169.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Vector Spaces]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 15:29:07","modified":"2025/05/14 00:44:39"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Vector Spaces
>A **vector space** $\mathcal{X}$ is a set of [[3.1 Vector|vectors]] that is **closed under addition** and **scalar multiplication**, such that it remains unchanged when those operations are performed. Formally, for any $u,v \in \mathcal{X}$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$, 
>$$\alpha u+ \beta v \in \mathcal{X}.$$
>
>A nonempty subset $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ of the vector space is called a **subspace** of $\mathcal{X}$ if it is also closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
>
>An **affine subspace** is a subspace shifted away from the origin) $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{V}$, where every elements satisfies
>$$\mathcal{A}=\{ \alpha \vec{x} + (1-\alpha)\vec{y} : \vec{x},\vec{y} \in \mathcal{V}, \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \}.$$
>
>>[!warning] Zero Vector
>>Both vector spaces and subspaces **always contain the zero vector** (confirmed by setting $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 0$).

# Properties
#### (*Sum of Subspaces*) For all subspaces $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, their sum $\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{W}$ is also a subspace.

#### (*Direct Sum*) For all subspaces $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, if $\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}=\{ 0 \}$, then $\mathcal{U} \oplus \mathcal{V}=\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{W}$ and every vector in $\mathcal{W}$ can be uniquely represented as $w=u+v$.

#### (Dimension of Direct Sum) For any $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, $\dim(\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V})=\dim\mathcal{U}+\dim\mathcal{V}$.

170.title: 3.4b Span
170.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/3. Vectors/3.4 Vector Spaces/3.4b Span.md
170.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.4b Span]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/04 00:30:56","modified":"2025/05/14 00:35:21"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Span
>The **span** of a set of vectors $\mathcal{P}=\left\{\vec{v}_1, \dots, \vec{v}_n\right\} \subseteq \mathcal{R}^n$ is the set of all vectors that can be built using the vectors in $\mathcal{P}$ by scaling and adding them together (i.e., the linear combinations of vectors in $\mathcal{P}$). Formally,
>$$\mathrm{span}(\mathcal{P})=\left\{\sum^{n}_{i=1}\alpha_i \vec{v}_i : \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}\right\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n,$$
>where $\alpha_{i}$ is the scaling factor (or weight) of each vector in $\mathcal{P}$.
>
>If $\mathcal{P}$ contains $k$ linearly independent vectors, then the dimension $d$ of its span is $n \geq d \geq k$. Note that the maximum amount of linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $n$.
>>[!warning] Infinite Property
>>All nonzero vectors in an infinite vector space have an infinitely extending span.

# Intuition
The span is not too hard of a concept.
