173.title: 3.4a Inner Product
173.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/3. Vectors/3.3 Vector Multiplication/3.4a Inner Product.md
173.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Inner Product]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/28 15:27:05","modified":"2025/03/08 00:59:18"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Inner Product
>The **inner product** is a function that takes two vectors and returns a real scalar quantifying how much the vectors align in direction. 
>
>For a vector space on $\mathbb{R}$, the inner product of vectors $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\vec{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is also called the **dot product**:
>$$\langle \vec{x}, \vec{y} \rangle = \vec{x} \cdot \vec{y} = \vec{x}^T\vec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i.$$
>Furthermore, the dot product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be given by the geometric definition,
>$$\vec{x}^T\vec{y} = \|\vec{x}\|\|\vec{y}\|\cos\theta,$$
>where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors.
>
>However, for vector spaces on $\mathbb{C}$, the inner product introduces the [[7.3 Complex Conjugate|complex conjugate]], which keeps the output scalar on the real line. Therefore, for two complex vectors  $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n$  and  $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the inner product is defined as
>$$\langle \vec{x}, \vec{y} \rangle = \vec{x}^T\vec{y}\textasteriskcentered =\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i\textasteriskcentered.$$


# Properties
#### (*Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality*) $|\vec{x}^T\vec{y}| \leq \|\vec{x}\|\|\vec{y}\|$.
This follows from the fact that $\cos\theta \leq 1$.

178.title: 2.12d.2 Compact SVD
178.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/13. Singular-Value Decomposition/2.12d.2 Compact SVD.md
178.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.12d.2 Compact SVD]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/15 18:10:01","modified":"2025/03/09 23:57:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compact SVD
>A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \min\{m,n\}$ can be decomposed using the compact form of the SVD as
>$$A = U_r\Upsigma_rV_r^T$$
>where $U_r \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $V_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$ are matrices with orthogonal columns known respectively as the ***left singular vectors*** and ***right singular vectors*** of $A$, whereas $\Upsigma_r \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$ is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries  are positive ordered scalars known as the ***singular values*** of $A$.

# Intuition
The compact SVD is connected to the outer product SVD as follows:
$$
\begin{align}
\begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & \sigma_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \dots & \vec{v}_r\end{bmatrix}^T &= \begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & \sigma_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1^T \\ \vdots \\ \vec{v}_r^T\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1\vec{v}_1^T \\ \vdots \\ \sigma_r\vec{v}_r^T\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T
\end{align}
$$
Additionally, the compact SVD has a square and invertible $\Upsigma_r$ and is easier than the full SVD to construct by hand, but $U_r$ and $V_r$ aren't square and do not have an inverse, and there is no characterization of null spaces like in the full SVD.
# Properties
We can see that our properties are simply the properties of the outer product SVD in matrix form.
##### $\mathrm{Col}(U_r)=\mathrm{Col}(A).$
Same as outer product SVD.
##### $\mathrm{Col}(V_r)=\mathrm{Row}(A)=\mathrm{Col}(A^T).$
Same as outer product SVD.

179.title: 2.12d.1 Outer Product SVD
179.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/13. Singular-Value Decomposition/2.12d.1 Outer Product SVD.md
179.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.12d.1 Outer Product SVD]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/15 15:55:51","modified":"2025/03/09 23:57:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Outer Product Form of the SVD
>A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \min\{m,n\}$ can be decomposed using the outer product form of the SVD as
>$$A = \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T$$
>where $\{\vec{u}_1, \vec{u}_2, \dots, \vec{u}_r\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, \dots, \vec{v}_r\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ are sets of orthonormal vectors known respectively as the ***left singular vectors*** and ***right singular vectors*** of $A$, whereas $\sigma_1 > \dots > \sigma_r > 0$ are positive ordered scalars known as the ***singular values*** of $A$.

# Intuition
Essentially, we can algorithmically compute the SVD as follows:
1. Find and sort $(\lambda_1, \vec{v}_1),...,(\lambda_r, \vec{v}_r)$, the orthogonal eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs of $A^TA$.
2. For each pair, find:
	1. $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$
	2. $\vec{u}_i=\frac{1}{\sigma_i}A\vec{v}_i$
We can prove the second step using $\frac{1}{\sigma_k}A\vec{v}_k=\frac{1}{\sigma_k}\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k$. Then $\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k=\left<\vec{v}_k, \vec{v}_i\right>$ will be 0 for $i \neq k$ and 1 for $i = k$ since the right singular vectors are orthonormal. As such, $\frac{1}{\sigma_k}\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k=\vec{u}_k$.

Alternatively, we can find and sort $(\lambda_1, \vec{u}_1),...,(\lambda_r, \vec{u}_r)$, which are the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs of $AA^T$. Then, $\vec{v}_i=\frac{1}{\sigma_i}A^T\vec{u}_i$ or $\vec{v}_i^T=\frac{1}{\upsigma_i}A\vec{u}_i^T$.

This SVD form is messy, albeit the most efficient to compute since it decomposes $A$ into $r$ rank-1 matrices.

# Properties
##### $\{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{Col}(A)$
Since $\{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$, we only need to prove that it spans $\mathrm{Col}(A)$:
$$
\begin{align}
A\vec{x} &= \left(\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\right)\vec{x} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\left(\vec{v}_i^T\vec{x}\right) \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\left<\vec{x},\vec{v}_i\right>\vec{u}_i.
\end{align}
$$
The result is a linear combination of $\vec{u}_i$. Therefore, $\mathrm{Col}(A) \subseteq \mathrm{Span}(\vec{u}_1,\dots,\vec{u}_r)$. Since both $\mathrm{Col}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Span}(\vec{u}_1,\dots,\vec{u}_r)$ have the same dimension $r$, they are equal.

#### $\{\vec{v}_1, \dots, \vec{v}_r\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{Row}(A)=\mathrm{Col}(A^T)$
Since $A^T=\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{v}_i\vec{u}_i^T$, we can proceed using the same reasoning as above.



#### $(\sigma_i^2,\vec{u}_i)$ is an eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of $AA^T$
For any $\vec{u}_k \in \{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$:
$$
\begin{align}
AA^T\vec{u}_k
&=
\left(\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\right)\left(\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_j\vec{v}_j\vec{u}_j^T\right)\vec{u}_k \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_i\sigma_j\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_j\vec{u}_j^T\vec{u}_k \\
&=
 \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_i\sigma_j\vec{u}_i\left<\vec{v}_j,\vec{v}_i\right>\left<\vec{u}_k,\vec{u}_j\right> \\
&=
\sigma^2_k\vec{u}_k.
\end{align}
$$
We obtain this from the fact that $\left<\vec{v}_j,\vec{v}_i\right>=\begin{cases}0 & \text{ } i \neq j \\ 1 & \text{   } i = j\end{cases}$  and $\left<\vec{u}_k,\vec{u}_j\right>=\begin{cases}0 & \text{ } k \neq j \\ 1 & \text{   } k = j\end{cases}$ since all elements of both sets are orthonormal to each other by set orthonormality. Therefore the equation is non-zero if and only if $k=i=j$.
#### $(\sigma_i^2,\vec{v}_i)$ is an eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of $A^TA$
Proceed by same reasoning as above.
#### $A\vec{v}_i=\sigma_i\vec{u}_i \iff A^T\vec{u}_i=\sigma_i\vec{v}_i$
$$
\begin{align}
A\vec{v}_k&=\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k \\
&= \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\left<\vec{v}_k,\vec{v}_i\right>\vec{u}_i \\
&=\sigma_i\vec{u}
_i\end{align}
$$
Since due to orthonormality the equation is non-zero only when $k=i$.




# Application

180.title: 13.3 Low-Rank Approximation
180.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/13. Singular-Value Decomposition/13.3 Low-Rank Approximation.md
180.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[13.3 Low-Rank Approximation]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/26 18:45:48","modified":"2025/03/09 23:54:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Eckart-Young-Minsky Theorem
>A general matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \mathrm{min}\{m, n\}$ can be approximated by a lower-rank matrix $A_k$ with rank $1 \leq k \leq r$, such that $A_k$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation to $A$,
>$$A_k = \arg\min\limits_{A_{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}} \|A-A_{k}\|_F^2.$$
>We may then approximate our matrix $A$ using [[13. Singular-Value Decomposition|singular value decomposition]] as
>$$A_{k}=\sum^{k}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=U_{k}\Sigma_{k}V_{k}^{T}.$$
# Intuition
Essentially, the above definition states that $A_\mathscr{l}$ is found inside the set of matrices $B$ that minimize the square of the [[4.9a Frobenius Norm|Frobenius norm]] of $A-B$ (in other words $A \approx B$). This holds mostly if the data is real, and therefore has some linear, low-rank structure with some singular values being large, and some very small. Then, we can equivalently say that the first $\mathscr{l}$ ordered singular values are large, and the remaining $r-\mathscr{l}$ are small:
$$\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=\sum^{\mathscr{l}}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T+\sum^{r}_{i=\mathscr{l}+1}\underbrace{\sigma_i}_{\approx 0}\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=\sum^{\mathscr{l}}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T.$$

181.title: 13.2 Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
181.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/13. Singular-Value Decomposition/13.2 Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse.md
181.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[13.2 Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/25 15:58:44","modified":"2025/03/09 23:42:38"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
>Any matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \mathrm{min}(m, n)$ and [[13. Singular-Value Decomposition|SVD]] $A=U\Sigma V^T$ has a **Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse**, defined as 
>$$
>A^\dagger = V\Sigma^\dagger U^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m},
>$$
>where $\Sigma^\dagger = \begin{bmatrix}\Upsigma_r^{-1} & 0_{r \times (m-r)} \\ 0_{(n-r) \times r} & 0_{(n-r) \times (m-r)}\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$, with $\Upsigma^{-1}_{r} = \operatorname{diag}(\dfrac{1}{\sigma_{1},}, \ldots, \dfrac{1}{\sigma_{r}}) \in \mathbb{S}^r_{++}$.

# Properties
#### (*Left Inverse*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n \leq m$ (full col. rank), $A^{\dagger}A = V_{r}V_{r}^T=VV^T=I_{n}$.

#### (*Right Inverse*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$ (full row rank), $AA^{\dagger} = U_{r}U_{r}^T = UU^T=I_{m}$.

#### (*Left Decomposition*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n \leq m$, then $A^{\dagger} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T$.
#### (*Right Decomposition*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$, then $A^{\dagger} = A^T(AA^T)^{-1}$.
#### (*Reflexivity*) $AA^{\dagger}A = A$ and $A^{\dagger}AA^{\dagger} = A^{\dagger}$.
#### (Invertibility Equality) If $A$ is invertible, $A^{\dagger} = A^{-1}$.
#### (*Orthogonal Projectors*) $P_{\mathcal{R}(A)}=AA^{\dagger} = U_{r}U_{r}^T$ and $P_{}A^{\dagger}A = V_{r}V_{r}^T$.

184.title: 12.2 Eigendecomposition
184.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/12. Matrix Decomposition/12.2 Eigendecomposition.md
184.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[12.2 Eigendecomposition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 16:23:15","modified":"2025/05/14 22:42:13"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Eigendecomposition
>A [[4.2c Square Matrix|square matrix]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is diagonalizable if it admits $n$ linearly independent [[5.1 Eigenvectors|eigenvectors]], allowing it to be decomposed as
>$$A = V \Uplambda V^{-1},$$
>where $V = \begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \vec{v}_2 & \dots & \vec{v}_n\end{bmatrix}$ forms the eigenbasis of $A$, and $\Uplambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n})$ is a diagonal square matrix that holds the *strictly real* eigenvalues of $A$. 
>
>The **Spectral Theorem** extends this result to symmetric matrices ($A = A^T$), ensuring that they can be diagonalized as 
>$$A= \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}q_{i}q_{i}^T = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}\Pi_{\operatorname{span}(u_{i})} = Q\Lambda Q^T,$$ where $Q$'s columns form an *orthonormal* eigenbasis of $A$, and  $\Uplambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n})$.

# Intuition
We use diagonalization to make linear transformations between matrices easier. We do so by changing the basis of a matrix $A$ so that it is strictly diagonal. We then perform our necessary calculations and change it back to our initial basis.
### Why eigenvectors and eigenvalues?
Essentially, 

# Properties
#### $A^n=V \Uplambda^n V^{-1}$
$$
\begin{align}
A^n &= (V\Uplambda V^{-1})(V\Uplambda V^{-1})...(V\Uplambda V^{-1}) \\ 
&=
V\Uplambda (V^{-1}V)\Uplambda(V^{-1}V)...\Uplambda V^{-1}\\
&=
V\Uplambda^nV^{-1}
\end{align}
$$
# Example
>[!example] Computing Powers of Matrices
>We want to compute the 5th power of $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}$. This is hard, since we will have to perform matrix-matrix multiplication 4 times. Instead, we will find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$, change its basis, perform the calculation and change it back into standard basis. Using simple calculation we find the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2}=5,4$. The corresponding eigenvectors are therefore $\vec{x}_{\lambda_1}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\vec{x}_{\lambda_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$. As such, the eigenbasis of $A$ is $V=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Its inverse is $V^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and the diagonal matrix of eigenvectors is $\Uplambda=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$. We can then perform the computation extremely easily:
>$$\Uplambda^{5}=\begin{bmatrix}5^5 & 0 \\ 0 & 4^5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 3125\end{bmatrix}.$$
>A quick change of basis to reverse the diagonalization will yield:
>$$V \Uplambda^5 V^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}3125 & 6303 \\ 0 & 1024\end{bmatrix}=A^5.$$

185.title: 12.1 QR Decomposition
185.path: Mathematics/5. Linear Algebra/12. Matrix Decomposition/12.1 QR Decomposition.md
185.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[12.1 QR Decomposition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 04:40:40","modified":"2025/05/14 04:05:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] QR Decomposition
>The QR decomposition of a general matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is its factorization into the product of a matrix with [[2.9c Matrix Orthonormality|orthonormal columns]] $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, and an upper triangular matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, for which
>$$A = QR,$$
>
>where $Q=\begin{bmatrix}\vec{q}_1 & \vec{q}_2 & \dots & \vec{q}_\mathscr{l}\end{bmatrix}$, and $R=\begin{bmatrix}\left<\vec{a}_1, \vec{q}_1\right> & \left<\vec{a}_2, \vec{q}_1\right> & \dots & \left<\vec{a}_\mathscr{l}, \vec{q}_1\right> \\ 0 & \left<\vec{a}_2, \vec{q}_2\right> & \dots & \left<\vec{a}_\mathscr{l}, \vec{q}_2\right> \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \ldots & \left<\vec{a}_\mathscr{l}, \vec{q}_\mathscr{l}\right>\end{bmatrix}.$

# Intuition
We can interpret the QR decomposition of $A$ as a change of basis, where an upper-triangular matrix can be transformed into any matrix using an orthonormal basis. More particularly, 
- $A$ is originally expressed in some arbitrary coordinate system (its column vectors may not be orthogonal).

	- $Q$ contains the **orthonormal basis**, computed using Gram-Schmidt.

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/11 16:19:35","modified":"2025/06/06 15:52:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

> [!note] Linear Function 
> A function $f$ with constant $\alpha$, where
> $$f(\alpha x)=\alpha f(x)$$
> is called a [[5. Linear Algebra|linear]] function.

# Explanation
This is pretty simple if we regard the formula above as an equation of two linear functions $f_i$ and $g_i$, where
$$f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)+...+f_n(x_n)+b_f=g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)+...+g_n(x_n)+b_g$$
Over each term of $x$ is applied a certain (linear) transformation, usually a constant. We can expand this equation even further by equating $f_i(x_i)=\alpha_i x_i$. and $g_i(x_i)=\beta_ix_i$. We then have:$$\alpha_1x_1+\alpha_2x_2+...+\alpha_nx_n+b_f=\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+...+\beta_nx_n+b_g$$This suggests that a linear equation (1) is equal to two linear combinations (in this case the LHS and RHS of the 2nd equation).

188.title: 3. Typical Sets
188.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3. Typical Sets]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/27 20:01:58","modified":"2025/03/03 20:26:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Typical Sets
>A **typical set** is an exponentially smaller subset of the space of all $n$-length sequences $\mathcal{X}^n$ (where $|\mathcal{X}^n|=2^{n\log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|}$), which captures most of the probability mass of the source as $n$ grows large. Formally, the $\epsilon$-typical set $A_{\epsilon}^{(n)} \subset \mathcal{X}^n$ is the set of $n$-length sequences $X^{n} = X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$, such that each sequence has a uniform probability of approximately $2^{\mathbb{E}[\log_{2}p_{X}(X^n)]}=2^{-nH(x)}$:
>$$A_{\epsilon}^{(n)} = \{ X^{n} \in \mathcal{X}^n : 2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)} \leq p_{X^n}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) \leq 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)} \},$$
>where $|A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}| \approx 2^{nH(X)}$.
>
>As $n$ grows large, sequences in the (much smaller) typical set $A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}$ contain virtually all the probability mass of $\mathcal{X}^n$. Mathematically, this means that $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}(A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}) = 1$. This property of typical sets is known as **asymptotic equipartition**, and is the LLN-equivalent analogue in information theory. Mathematically,
>$$-\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}p_{X^n}(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) \to H(X) \quad \text{in probability},$$
>meaning that the per-symbol self-information of a sequence converges to the entropy.
# Properties



# Examples

>[!example] Biased Coin Flips
>You flip $100$ coins with probability $1/4$ of coming up heads.
>>[!example]-  What is the size of the sample space? 
>>We know that each coin can either land on $H$ or $T$. For 100 coins, this becomes $|\Omega| = 2^{100}$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the size of the typical set, and how do the two sizes compare?
>>We can calculate the entropy of each coin as $$H(X) = 0.25 \log 4+0.75\log\frac{4}{3}=0.811 \text{ bits per coinflip.}$$
>>Therefore, the size of the typical set is $\approx 2^{81}$, or $\frac{2^{81}}{2^{100}} = \frac{1}{2^{19}}$ of the size of the sample space.

189.title: 6.5a Binary Channel Coding
189.path: Mathematics/4. Information Theory/5. Communication Systems/6.5a Binary Channel Coding.md
189.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[6.5a Binary Channel Coding]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/06 17:10:14","modified":"2025/05/11 17:26:18"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Binary Channels
>The **Binary Erasure Channel (BEC)** is a discrete channel with an **input alphabet** $\mathcal{X}=\{ 0,1 \}$ and an **output alphabet** $\mathcal{Y}=\{ 0,1,e \}$, where $e$ represents an **erasure symbol**, indicating that the transmitted bit was lost with probability $p \in [0,1]$:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75]
>  % Draw Input nodes
>  \draw[->, thick] (0,3) -- (3,3) node[left, at start]{$0$} node[right]{$0$} node[above, midway]{$1-p$};
>  \draw[->, thick] (0,2.9) -- (3, 1.55) node[midway, below]{$p$};
>  \draw[->, thick] (0,0.1) -- (3, 1.45) node[midway, above]{$p$};
>  \draw[->, thick] (0, 0) -- (3, 0) node[left, at start]{$1$} node[right]{$1$} node[below, midway]{$1-p$};
>  \node at (3.3, 1.5) {$e$};
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>In an abstract communications system, the pipeline can be outlined as follows:
>$$M^{(L)} \xrightarrow[f_n: \mathcal{M}^{L} \to \mathcal{X}^{n}]{\text{Encoder}} X^{(n)} \xrightarrow{\text{(Noisy) Channel}} Y^{(n)} \xrightarrow[g_{n}: \mathcal{Y}^{n} \to \mathcal{M}^{L}]{\text{Decoder}} \hat{M}^{(L)}$$
>1. A message $M^{(L)}$ of binary length $L$ goes through an encoder $f_{n}: \mathcal{M}^L \to \mathcal{X}^n$, and is transformed into a codeword $X^{(n)}$ of length $n$ in channel symbols (i.e., in bits if the channel is binary). 
>2. It then goes through the channel, which outputs the random map $Y$ (also of length $n$). 
>3. Finally, the output is ran through a decoder $g_{n}: \mathcal{Y}^{n} \to \mathcal{M}^{L}$, which yields the output $\hat{M}$ of length $L$.
>
>The rate at which the message is conveyed through the channel is given as $R = L/n$ bits per channel symbols (i.e, decoded bits per encoded bits). In binary channels, $R \in [0,1]$. The capacity of a channel is the maximum asymptotic rate at which it can reliably communicate a symbol, given as
>$$C=\max_{p_{X}} I(X;Y) \text{ bits/symbol},$$
>where $C_{\text{BEC}}=1-p$, and $C_{\text{BSC}}=1-H_{b}(p)$. In other words, the channel is stable if $R < C$.
>
>For a BEC, the **maximum probability of erasure** is given as the worst-case probability that the decoder fails to recover the original message:
>$$P_{e}(n)=\mathbb{P}(\hat{M} \neq M)=\max_{x \in \mathcal{X}^L}\mathbb{P}(g(Y^n) \neq x^n \mid X^n = f_{n}(x^n)).$$
>
>Together, these quantities yield the **Shannon Channel Coding Theorem,** which states that as $n \to \infty$, there exists a rate-$R$ communication scheme that achieves 
>$$P_{e}(n) \to\begin{cases}0 & R<C, \\ c \in (0,1) & R=C \\ 1 & R>C.\end{cases}$$
# Proof


# Examples
>[!example] I. Sending a Message
>Consider a binary erasure channel (BEC), which erases channel input with probability $p \in (0,1)$. We wish to send a message of length $L$ bits, and we encode to a codeword of length $n$, where $n,L$ are positive integers and $n>L$. Define $R = L/n$ (in bits per symbol) as the rate of the channel.
>
>Now, recall Shannon’s random codebook argument: we flip $n2^L$ fair coins independently, and populate a $2L \times n$ codebook accordingly ($2L$ codewords, each with length $n$). Suppose that the first codeword is sent through the BEC.
>
>**A)** Give a tight upper bound on the number of bits that can be sent reliably over the channel.
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Since we are considering a BEC, the tight upper bound is $C=1-p$ per symbol. Using the channel $n$ times, the **most** information that can be conveyed  is therefore $n(1-p)$.

>[!note] Shannon's Source Coding Theorem
>**Source coding** is the process of encoding *purely random* information from the symbols $x \in \mathcal{X}$ into a bit string representation that uses the most compressed sequence of bits for which it is possible to recover the symbols.
>
>Source coding is governed by the **Source Coding Theorem**, which states that any source coding scheme must use, on average, at least as many bits per symbol as the [[1. Shannon Entropy|entropy]] of the source, ensuring that the encoded message retains all the original information. 
>
>Mathematically, for a sequence of symbols $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}$ with a random binary length $l(X)$, and an arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0$, there is a source coding scheme from which the sequence can be recovered with high probability (i.e. $p > 1-\epsilon$), such that
>$$H(X) \leq \lim_{ n \to \infty }\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{l(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})}{n} \right] \leq H(X) + \epsilon,$$
>where $\frac{l(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})}{n}$ represents the average bits per symbol of the sequence.
# Intuition

192.title: 2. Mutual Information
192.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2. Mutual Information]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/07 14:50:45","modified":"2025/06/06 15:56:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Mutual Information
>The **mutual information** between two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is a non-negative measure of the reduction in [[1. Shannon Entropy|entropy]] of one variable given knowledge of the other. For discrete variables, it is defined as
>$$\begin{align}
I(X;Y)&=\mathbb{E}\left( \log_{2}\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)} \right) \\
&= \sum_{x,y \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log_{2}\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)} \\
&=H(X)-H(X \mid Y) \\
&= H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y) 
\end{align}$$
>>[!warning] Independence
>>Note that for independent variables, $I(X;Y)=0$.


# Rationale
We begin by rationalizing about the definition of mutual information. Per the definition, mutual information quantifies the reduction in entropy given two variables $X$ and $Y$, compared to just $X$ or $Y$. It is only logical that $I(X;Y)=0$ if $X$ and $Y$ are independent; one will gain no information by observing $X$ (resp. $Y$) given $Y$ (resp. $X$). However, we must reason about the key equation here: $$p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)}.$$



# Properties
#### (Data )

193.title: 1. Shannon Entropy
193.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1. Shannon Entropy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/27 17:56:22","modified":"2025/06/06 15:56:31"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Entropy
>**Entropy** quantifies the [[2.5a Expectation|average number]] of bits (uncertainty) required to convey the information in a random variable. For a discrete random variable $X$, its entropy $H(X)$ is defined as
>$$H(X)=\mathbb{E}\left[ \log_{2} \frac{1}{p_{X}(X)} \right],$$
>where $f(x)=\log_{2}\frac{1}{p_{X}(x)} \geq 0$ is a *concave* function, serving as a quantifier of the uncertainty associated with observing each $x$.

# Intuition
Given $f(x)=\log_{2}\frac{1}{p_{X}(x)}$, we can quickly see that $\lim_{ p_{X}(x) \to 1 }f(x)=0$. This implies that the larger the probability of some $x$ is, the smaller the uncertainty associated with it. The addition of the base 2 logarithm to the function captures the exact amount of bits of information yielded by the value $x$. While any base could be used, base 2 is preferred due to the binary nature of modern computers.

Now, take $X$ and find $f(x)$ for all values. multiplied by the probability of each of those values occurring. You get entropy.

# Properties
#### (*Concavity*) 

#### (*Joint Entropy*) $H(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}\left[ \dfrac{1}{p_{X,Y}(x,y)} \right]$.
#### (*Cond. Entropy*) $H(X \mid Y) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \dfrac{1}{p_{X \mid Y}(X \mid Y)} \right] = \large\sum_\limits{x}p_{X}(x)H(Y \mid X=x)$.
#### (*Chain Rule*) $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y \mid X)$.
By definition, we know that $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y \mid x)$. As such,
$$\begin{align*} 
    H(X, Y) &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x,y)\log_2p(x,y) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x,y)\log_2p(x)p(y \mid x) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x, y)(\log_2p(x) +\log_2p(y \mid x)) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p(x)\log_2p(x)-\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x)p(y \mid x)\log_2p(y \mid x) \\ 
    &= H(X) + H(Y \mid X),
\end{align*}$$
where marginal probability dictates that $-\sum\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum\limits_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x, y) = -\sum\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p(x)$. Essentially, the chain rule states that the joint entropy of $X,Y$ is equivalent to the information that $X$ provides on its own, as well as the extra information provided by $Y$ given $X$.
#### (*Independence*) If $X, Y$ are independent, $H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y)$, and $H(X \mid Y) = H(X)$.
#### (Entropy Bounds) $H(X \mid Y) \leq H(X)$ and $H(X,Y) \leq H(X) + X(Y)$.
#### (*Uniform Dist.*) $H(X) \leq \log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|$. where $H(X)=\log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|$ if $X \sim U(a,b)$.


# Examples

>[!example] Text Compression
>Suppose you want to transmit a message with the letters Y and N, where Y appears 95% of the time. With naive encoding, each symbol takes 1 bit on average. However, entropy tells us that the theoretical limit for compression is
>$$H(X) = 0.95 \log_{2}\frac{1}{0.95} + 0.05 \log_{2}\frac{1}{0.05} \approx 0.286 \text{ bits per symbol.}$$

>[!example] Compression of a Markov Chain
>Consider an irreducible Markov chain $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as shown below:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usetikzlibrary{automata, positioning}
>
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[->, semithick, node distance=3cm]
>    \tikzstyle{every state}=[thick, minimum size=35pt]
>
>    \node[state] (A) {0};
>    \node[state] (B) [right of=A] {1};
>
>    % Loops
>    \path (A) edge [loop left] node {\(1 - p\)} (A);
>    \path (B) edge [loop right] node {\(1 - p\)} (B);
>
>    % Arrows between states
>    \path (A) edge [bend left] node[above] {\(p\)} (B);
>    \path (B) edge [bend left] node[below] {\(p\)} (A);
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Suppose $X_{0} \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)$ and $p \neq 1/2$. Propose a scheme to represent $(X_0,\ldots,X_{n})$ in at most $n$ bits in expectation as $n \to \infty$, and state how many bits that would take.
>
>**SOLUTION:**
>We quickly find that the stationary distribution is $\pi^*=\begin{bmatrix}1/2 & 1/2\end{bmatrix}$, given the transition matrix $P$. We also find that $H(X_{0})=1$ as $X_{0} \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)$. Assuming that the chain has ran for a long time given the stationary distribution above, we find that 
>$$\begin{align} H(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})&=\sum_{x_{n} \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X_{n}}(x_{n})\sum_{x_{n+1} \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}}(x_{n+1} \mid x_{n})\log_{2}\left( \frac{1}{p_{X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}}(x_{n+1} \mid x_{n})} \right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}\right] + \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}\right] \\ &= (1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}.\end{align}$$
>
>This is a crucial result. Since $H(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}) \leq 1$ (where the result equals $1$ if $p=1/2$), this means that if we know $X_{0}$, we will need $nH(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})$ bits of information to determine the rest of the sequence. Recall that $H(X_{0})=1$. Putting this together, we find that we can recover, on average, the Markov Chain with $H(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})=nH(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})+1 < n+1$ bits of information (strict inequality since $p \neq 1/2$.

>[!note] Belief Updating
> Belief updating in [[5.1  Bayesian Game|Bayesian games]] involves players revising their beliefs about other players’ types as the game progresses and new information becomes available. If a player $i \in N$ wants to know the probability of player $j \in N$ playing some type $t_j \in T_j$, then
> - The **prior distribution** over the types of player $j$ from the perspective of $i$ is a probability distribution $P_j: t_j \to [0, 1]$ that represents $i$’s initial beliefs about the types of $j$ before any actions are observed or any information is revealed.
> - The **[[1.6 Bayes' Rule|posterior distribution]]** over the types of player $j$ from the perspective of $i$ is a probability distribution $P_j(\cdot|t_i): t_j \to [0,1]$ that represents $i$’s updated beliefs about $j$'s after observing actions or receiving information.

# Properties
#### *(Independence)* If $P_j(t_j | t_i) = P_j(t_j)$, then $t_i$ gives no information about $t_j$.

202.title: 5.1a Bayes-Nash Equilibrium
202.path: Mathematics/3. Game Theory/5. Incomplete Information/5.2 Static Bayesian Games/5.1a Bayes-Nash Equilibrium.md
202.content:

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/28 10:43:14","modified":"2024/08/09 09:23:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bayes-Nash Equilibrium
>A Bayes-Nash Equilibrium of a [[2.1 Strategic Form Game|static]] [[5.1  Bayesian Game|Bayesian game]] is a strategy profile in which each type $t_i \in T_i$ of every player $i \in N$ uses their [[2.2a Best Response|best response]] to the strategies of all other players given $i$'s beliefs $t_i$ about $t_{-i}$.

# Intuition
#### *(Harsanyi's Theorem)* If the Bayesian game is finite, then a BNE must exist.

# Examples
>[!example] Contributions Game
>Consider our standard contributions game of two players who have two choices: contribute or not contribute. They also have two types: a high contributions cost type $c_H=\frac{3}{4}$, and a low contributions cost type $c_L=\frac{1}{4}$. Note that these types are independent of one another, and therefore there is no posterior belief updating.
>
>To find the BNE, we must use our intuition. There is no definitive method like in other equilibria. Intuitively, suppose there is a BNE if $c_L$ types contribute, and $c_H$ types do not. Then, from the perspective of player $i$:
>- If $P_i$ contributes, their utility is $U_i(\text{C})=1-t_i$.
>- If $P_i$ does not contribute, then $U_i(\text{NC})=1 \times P_j(\text{C}) + 0 \times P_j(\text{NC})=P_j(\text{C}),$ where $P_j(\text{C})$ is the probability of player $j$ contributing (or of $t_j=c_L$, since players contribute only when their type is low cost).
>
>From $P_i$'s perspective, if:
>- $P_i$'s type is $t_i=c_H$, then $P_i$ will prefer to not contribute if $P_j(\text{C}) \geq 1-\frac{3}{4}.$
>	- This is because $P_i$ will choose $\text{NC}$ only if $U_i(\text{NC}) \geq U_i(\text{C})$.
>- $P_i$'s type is $t_i=c_L$, then $P_i$ will prefer to contribute if $1-\frac{1}{4} \geq P_j(\text{C}).$
>	- This is because $P_i$ will choose $\text{C}$ only if $U_i(\text{C}) \geq U_i(\text{NC})$.
>
>Combining the two inequalities, we see that a BNE where $i$ contributes appears to happen only between $\frac{1}{4} \leq P_j(\text{C}) \leq \frac{3}{4}$.
>
>Since the BNE above does not cover all $p \in [0, 1]$, there are more equilibria!

>[!note] Folk Theorem
>The folk theorem states that for an infinitely repeated stage game $G$ with a uniform discount factor $\delta \in (0, 1)$, such that $\delta \to 1$. Then, if all players' payoffs $u_i$ are:
>1. **Feasible**, meaning that they can be achieved arithmetically using some strategy
>2. **Individually rational**, meaning that $u_i > u_i^*$, where $u_i^*$ is player $i$'s worst Nash equilibrium payoff
>
>Then, there exists an SPNE of the repeated game such that each player $i$ receives $u_i$ on average.

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discounting
>Discounting is the process of reducing the value of payoffs in future stages of an [[4.1 Infinitely Repeated Game|infinitely repeated game]] to account for the preference for immediate rewards over delayed ones. This is represented by a discount factor $\delta \in (0,1)$, applied to future payoffs to compute their present value. A player $i$'s discounted payoff, provided that $i$ plays a strategy $s_i \in S_i$, is then given as
>$$\sum^{}_{i=1}\delta^{i-1}u_i(s_i)=\frac{u_i(s_i)}{1-\delta},$$
>where $u_i$ is the payoff function of player $i$.

210.title: 4.2a History
210.path: Mathematics/3. Game Theory/4. Infinite Repetition/4.2 Strategies/4.2a History.md
210.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2a History]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/21 04:57:12","modified":"2024/07/21 07:57:52"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] History
>The history $h_t$ of a [[4.1 Infinitely Repeated Game|repeated game]] at period $t$ is the set of all possible actions taken by all players at times $\tau < t$. Formally, the history of a repeated game at time $t$ given the strategy profile of every stage game at $\tau < t$ can be expressed as
>$$h_t = s_2 \times s_3 \times \ldots \times s_{t-1}$$
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The history of period $1$ is simply $h_1=\emptyset$, since there is nothing occurring before stage $1$ of the game.
# Properties
##### At period $t \geq 2$, the set $h_t$  specifies $n^{t-1}$ actions.

# Example
>[!example] Infinitely Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
>Consider again the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma of two players. At $t=1$, there is no history, so $h_1=\emptyset$. However, at $t=1$, players can play the strategies $s_i=\{D, C\}$. As such, the history at $t=2$ is $h_2=\{(D, D), (D, C), (C, D), (C, C)\}$. Then, at $t=3$, players can again play the strategies $s_i\{D, C\}$. This leads to 
>$$h_3=\{\{(D, D), (D, D)\}, \{(D, D), (D, C)\}, \ldots, \{(C, C), (C, D)\}, \{(C, C), (C, C)\}\},$$
>specifying a complete history of all possible paths of play up to $t-1$.

220.title: 3.2b Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium
220.path: Mathematics/3. Game Theory/3. Dynamic Interaction/3.3 SPNE/3.2b Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium.md
220.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.2b Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/11 12:09:24","modified":"2024/08/09 00:30:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium
>A strategy profile $s^*$ constitutes a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium if for every [[3.2a Subgame|subgame]] $G_E^d$ with root note $d$  in $G_E$, $s^*$ constitutes a [[2.2c Nash Equilibrium|Nash equilibrium]] within $G_E^d$.
>
>Equivalently, a strategy profile $s^*$ constitutes an SPNE if $\forall s_i \in s^*$, every $s_i$ is [[3.2 Sequential Rationality|sequentially rational]] at the root node.
>
>The path of play in a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium is known as the **equilibrium path**.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The SPNE can never involve mixing in extensive form games of perfect information, since every player's action is observable.
# Intuition
What is the difference between NE and SPNE? Well:
- Nash equilibrium requires rational behavior (best response) only on the path of play.
- SPNE requires rational behavior **ON AND OFF** the path of play.
	- Done to add credibility to threats; if a strategy is not rational, then threatening with it will be irrational.

How do we find SPNEs? Using backward induction. Start at the last non-terminal node. Check the best response of the player at that node. Do so for all nodes on that level. Go back one level, and do the same for the other player. More on this in the future!

# Properties
#### *(Existence)* At least one SPNE exists in any finite extensive form game.
#### (*Uniqueness)* If no players are indifferent between terminal nodes, there is a unique SPNE.

# Examples

>In [[2.1 Strategic Form Game|startegic form theory]], a **Nash demand game** is one of infinite strategies where each player $i \in N$ has a demand $d_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for an aggregate quantity of a good $Q$, such that

232.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c Nash Equilibrium]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/30 07:44:09","modified":"2024/07/01 07:36:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nash Equilibrium
>The **Nash equilibrium** of a game is the strategy profile $s^* = (s_i^*, s_{-i}^*)$ which illustrates all players in a game using their [[2.2a Best Response|best response]], such that for all strategies $s_i \in S_i$ of *all* players $i \in N$,
>$$u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \geq u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*).$$
>The payoff that occurs when each player adheres to $s^*$ is the **Nash equilibrium outcome**. 
# Intuition
In a Nash equilibrium outcome, all players know (and expect) the strategy of every other player in the game. In a way, a Nash equilibrium is a stable prescription for play where a single player does not have a positive *unilateral* incentive to deviate from the equilibrium, although they might have an *indifferent* incentive (since we use greater than or equal to '$\geq$' instead of strictly greater than '$>$'). By deviating from the Nash equilibrium, a single player would simply lower their own payoffs if they think the other players will not deviate from their respective strategies, and this is inconsistent with rational play.

Something else to consider is the Nash equilibrium as a *focal point* for players. Since a Nash equilibrium utilizes each player's most rational response, a player could ask themselves what they expect as the outcome of the game by accounting for unreasonable plays (mistakes) by other players. If they expect everyone to play rationally (or coordinate on a Nash equilibrium by pre-play communication), then they are expecting a Nash equilibrium. If mistakes do happen from players, they could be corrected by changes in strategy with trial and error until a Nash equilibrium is reached.

Finally, we can find a Nash equilibrium by identifying the best response $s_i^*$ of player $i$ $S_{-i}$ of $-i$. Then, if $i$'s best response to $-i$ is the best response of $-i$ to $i$, this is a Nash equilibrium. Note that there may be more than one Nash equilibria in a game.

Essentially, when looking for Nash equilibria, ask yourself whether any of the players $i \in N$ have an incentive to deviate from the current strategy profile (change their choice). 
# Properties
##### *(Nash's Theorem)* In a *finite* strategic form game, there is always at least one Nash equilibrium.
We can prove this using [[2.5a Mixed Strategies|mixed strategies]].

##### *(Dominance Subsumption)* Any game with a dominant strategy also has a unique Nash equilibrium.

234.title: 2.2b Strategic Dominance
234.path: Mathematics/3. Game Theory/2. One-Shot Interaction/2.2 Best Responses/2.2b Strategic Dominance.md
234.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b Strategic Dominance]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/30 07:44:09","modified":"2024/06/30 07:46:58"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Strategic Dominance
>**Strategic dominance** in game theory occurs when there is a certain single strategy $s_i' \in S_i$ for a player $i \in N$ that is the [[2.2a Best Response|best response]] for any combination of other players' strategies $s_{-i}$. There are two cases in which this happens:
>- Strategy $s_i'$ **strongly dominates** all other strategies $s_i$ of player $i$ if the payoff of $s_i'$ is *strictly greater* than all of $i$'s other strategies $s_i$ for some strategies of other players $s_{-i}$, such that
>$$u_i(s_i', s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i}).$$
>- Strategy $s_i'$ **weakly dominates** another strategy $s_i^\# \in S_i$ if it does at least as well as $s_i^\#$ for all possible strategies of other players $s_{-i}$, and does better than $s_i^\#$ for certain strategies $\hat{s}_{-i}$ of the other players, such that
>$$\begin{equation}\begin{aligned}u_i(s_i', s_{-i}) &\geq u_i(s_i^\#, s_{-i}) && \text{for all $s_{-i}$}  \\ u_i(s_i', \hat{s}_{-i}) &> u_i(s_i', \hat{s}_{-i}) && \text{for some } \hat{s}_{-i}\end{aligned}\end{equation}$$
>
>A strategy profile to a game in which each player is using their dominant strategy is said to be a **dominant strategy solution**.

# Intuition
Strategic dominance follows the principle of rational choice. Obviously, considering the other players' strategies, one will choose that strategy which puts them at the best position possible. 
- Strongly dominant strategies can be interpreted as strategies that are the only rational response of a player $i$ in a game.
- Weakly dominant strategies can be interpreted as a set of rational strategies that can be used as a best response depending on the other players' strategies.
Here, it is important to note that ==not all games have dominant strategies==.

Let's now look at the solvability of dominance. pg 69-71 (Optional?)

# Examples
>[!example] EASY: Dominant Strategy in Auctions
>Suppose you want to buy a painting of Renoir. You value it at $300,000, meaning this is the true valuation that you give the painting. Then, the rules of game theory dictate that actively bidding until $300,000 and either giving up or winning the auction is the dominant strategy. Consider the other two cases:
>- Suppose you set yourself a lowball limit of $250,000. Then, bidding either continues above your true price of $300,000, or somebody wins the auction with a bid of $270,000. In that case, you're bummed, since you could've gotten a sweet painting for less than it's worth to you.
>- Suppose now you overextended yourself and decide to bid until $350,000. Then, either somebody saves you by bidding higher, or you win the auction. However, you're still bummed, since you are now stuck with a painting that you paid more for than you think is worth.

>See pg. 68

>[!note] Erdos-Renyi Random Graph
>Given a positive integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}$ and a probability value $p \in [0,1]$, an **Erdos-Renyi random graph** $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is an [[3.1 Graph|undirected graph]] on $n$ vertices, such that each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ edges is present independently based on some [[2.2b.3 Bernoulli Distribution|Bernoulli random variable]] $P \sim \text{Ber}(p(n))$. Let $\lambda > 0$ be some constant for which
>$$p(n)=\lambda \frac{\ln n}{n}.$$
>If $\lambda < 1$, then $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}(n,p) \text{ is connected}) \to 0$. However, if $\lambda > 1$, then $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}(n,p) \text{ is connected}) \to 1$.

# Properties

# Examples
>[!example] II. Random Bipartite Graph
>Consider a random bipartite graph with $K$ left nodes and $M$ right nodes. Each of the $K \cdot M$ possible edges of this graph is present independently with probability $p$.
>
>**A)** Find the distribution of the degree of a particular right node.
>>[!example]- A) Solution.

>
>**B)** Now fix a left node $u$ and right node $v$. Conditioned on the event that the edge $(u,v)$ is present, find the distribution of the degree of $v$.
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>Let $D_{v} \sim \operatorname{Ber}(K, p)$ be the random variable representing the degree of vertex $v$, and let $E \sim \operatorname{Ber}(p)$ be the indicator of whether $(u, v)$ exists. Then,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}(D_{v}=d_{v} \mid E=1)&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(E=1 \mid D_{v}=d_{v})\mathbb{P}(D_{v}=d_{v})}{\mathbb{P}(E=1)} \\
&= \frac{1}{p}\mathbb{P}(E=1 \mid D_{v}=d_{v})\mathbb{P}(D_{v}=d_{v}) \\
&= \frac{d_{v}}{pK}\binom{K}{d_{v}}p^{d_{v}}(1-p)
^{K-d_{v}} \\
&= \binom{K-1}{d_{v}-1}p^{d_{v}-1}(1-p)^{K-d_{v}},
\end{align}$$
>>so $D_{v} \sim \operatorname{Bin}(K-1, p)+1$.
>
>**C)** Call a right node with degree one a **singleton**. What is the expected number of singletons in a random bipartite graph?
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>Fix a a right node $v$, and let $D_{v} \sim \operatorname{Bin}(K, p)$ represent its degree. Then, 
>>$$\mathbb{P}(D_{v} = 1)= K \cdot p(1-p)^{K-1}.$$
>>Since there are $M$ right nodes, the expected number is $\mathbb{E}[S]=M \cdot \mathbb{P}(D_{v}=1)$ by the theoretical definition of expectation. For a more rigorous definition, use $S=\sum^{K}_{i=1}1_{\{D_{i}=1\}}$.
>
>**D)** Find the expected number of left nodes connected to at least one singleton.
>>[!example]- D) Solution.

Let $C_{i,j}$ be the indicator of whether the $i$-th left node and the $j$-th right node are connected. We need to calculate
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}(C_{i,j}=1 \mid D_{j}=1)&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(D_{j}=1 \mid C_{i,j}=1)\mathbb{P}(C_{i,j}=1)}{\mathbb{P}(D_{j}=1)} \\
&= \frac{p}{Kp(1-p)^{K-1}}\mathbb{P}(D_{j}=1 \mid C_{i,j}=1), \\
\end{align}$$
where $\mathbb{P}(D_{j}=1 \mid C_{i,j}=1)$ is 


>[!example] III. Connected Random Graph
>We start with the empty graph on $n$ vertices. Iteratively, we add an undirected edge, chosen uniformly at random from the edges that are not yet present in the graph, until the graph is connected.
>
>**A)** Suppose that there are currently $k$ connected components in the graph. Let $X_{k}$ be the number of edges we need to add until there are $k−1$ connected components. Show that $\mathbb{E}(X_{k}) \leq \frac{n-1}{k-1}$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/09 17:41:15","modified":"2025/05/10 19:50:56"}

>[!note] Jointly Gaussian Random Variables
>**Joint Gaussians** are random variables whose joint behavior is completely characterized by a mean vector and covariance matrix. Let $X = \begin{bmatrix}X_{1} & \ldots & X_{n}\end{bmatrix}^T$ be a random vector, and let $Z \in\mathbb{R}^\ell$ be the standard normal vector (i.e., $Z_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for $i=1,\ldots,\ell$ i.i.d.). Then, $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are **jointly Gaussian** if and only if:
>1. There exist some mean $\mu=\mathbb{E}[X] \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and real matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times \ell}$, s. t. $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, AA^T)$, and
>$$X=AZ+\mu.$$
>2. All elements of the affine hull of $X$ (i.e., all affine combinations $u \in \operatorname{aff}(X_1, \ldots, X_{n})$) follow a normal distribution, and therefore $\operatorname{aff}(X_1, \ldots, X_{n})$ is a **Gaussian subspace**.
>
>The PDF of joint Gaussians is defined by a positive definite covariance matrix $\Sigma = AA^T \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^n$ with entries $\Sigma_{i,j}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}, X_{j})$, such that
>$$f_{X}(x_{1},\ldots, x_{n})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ (2\pi)^n \det(\Sigma) }}\exp\left( -\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)  \right).$$
# Properties
#### (*Independence*) Joint Gaussians $X_{1},\ldots, X_{n}$ are indep. iff $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2_{1}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{n})$.
Without loss of generality, we will consider the case of two jointly Gaussian random variables. Let $X_{1},X_{2}$ be uncorrelated joint Gaussians. Therefore,
$$\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{1}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{2}^2\end{bmatrix}.$$
Substituting $\Sigma^{-1}$ into the joint PDF, we have
$$\begin{align}
f_{X}(x_{1},x_{2})&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ (2\pi)^2 }\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}\exp\left( -\frac{1}{2}\left[ \frac{(x_{1}-\mu_{1})^2}{\sigma_{1}^2}+\frac{(x_{2}-\mu_{2})^2}{\sigma_{2}^2} \right] \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }\sigma_{1}}\exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{(x_{1}-\mu_{1})^2}{\sigma_{1}^2} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }\sigma_{2}}\exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{(x_{2}-\mu_{2})^2}{\sigma_{2}^2} \right) \\
&= f_{X_{1}}(x_{1}) \cdot f_{X_{2}}(x_{2}).
\end{align}$$

#### (*Linear Combinations*) Any $U$ s.t. $U_{i} \in \operatorname{aff}(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$ is jointly Gaussian.
Let $U$ be a random vector, such that each $U_{i}=\gamma_{i}^TX+\beta_{i}$ is a linear combination of $X=[X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}]^T$ for some vector of coefficients $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^n$. We also know that 
$$X_{i}=a_{i}^TZ+\mu_{i},$$
and therefore, 
$$\begin{align}
U_{i}&=\gamma_{1}(a_{1}^TZ+\mu_{1})+\gamma_{n}(a_{n}^TZ+\mu_{n})+\beta_{1} \\
&= \gamma^T(AZ+\mu)+\beta_{1}  \\
&= \gamma^TAZ+\gamma^T\mu+\beta_{1},
\end{align}$$
which is simply an affine combination of $\gamma_{i}X_{i}+\beta_{1}$. As such,
$$
U=\begin{bmatrix} U_{1} \\ \vdots \\ U_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \Gamma AZ+(\Gamma \mu+\beta)=BZ+\lambda,
$$
which satisfies definition 1 with coefficients $B=\Gamma A$ and mean $\lambda=\Gamma\mu+\beta$, and therefore $U \sim \mathcal{N}(\Gamma \mu+\beta, \Gamma AA^T\Gamma^T)$

#### (*Covariance*) For $X=AZ+\mu$, it follows that $\Sigma=AA^T$.
Let $\Sigma_{i,j}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}, X_{j})$. This means that
$$\begin{align}
\Sigma_{i,j}&=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{j}]-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\mathbb{E}[X_{j}] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[(a_{i}^TZ+\mu_{i})(a_{j}^TZ+\mu_{j})]-(a_{i}^T\mathbb{E}[Z]+\mu_{i})(a_{j}^T\mathbb{E}[Z]+\mu_{j}) \\
&= \mathbb{E}[a_{i}^TZa^T_{j}Z+a_{j}^TZ\mu_{i}+a_{i}^TZ\mu_{j}+\mu_{i}\mu_{j}]-\mu_{i}\mu_{j} \\
&= a_{i}^T\mathbb{E}[ZZ^T]a_{j} \\
&= a_{i}^Ta_{j}
\end{align}$$
#### (*Covariance Partition*) For random vectors $X,Y$, $\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}\Sigma_{X} & \Sigma_{XY} \\ \Sigma_{YX} & \Sigma_{Y}\end{bmatrix}$.
#### (*Covariance LLSE*) For any joint Gaussians, $\mathbb{L}(Y \mid X)=\mu_{Y}+\Sigma_{YX}\Sigma^{-1}_{X}(X-\mu_{X})$.

(cont'd) #### (*Covariance LLSE*) For any joint Gaussians, $\mathbb{L}(Y \mid X)=\mu_{Y}+\Sigma_{YX}\Sigma^{-1}_{X}(X-\mu_{X})$.
#### (LLSE/MMSE Equivalence) For any joint Gaussians, $\mathbb{L}(Y \mid X)=\mathbb{M}(Y \mid X)$.

# Example
>[!example] I. MMSE for Joint Gaussians
>Find $\mathbb{E}(X \mid Y,Z)$ for the jointly Gaussian random vector
>
>$$
\begin{bmatrix}
X\\
Y\\
Z
\end{bmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal{N}\left(
\mu = \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},
\Sigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 3 & 1\\
3 & 9 & 3\\
1 & 3 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
\right).
>$$
>
>>[!example]- Solution.
>>We proceed by acknowledging that $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=3$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=1$, as well as that $\operatorname{Var}(X)=5$. Since LLSE is equal to the MMSE, we use the formula for general partition of the LLSE:
>>
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}[X \mid Y,Z]&=\mathbb{L}[X \mid Y]+\mathbb{L}[X \mid Z-\mathbb{L}[Z \mid Y]] \\
&= \mathbb{L}[X \mid Y]+\mathbb{L}\left[ X \mid Z-\frac{1}{3}Y \right].
\end{align}$$
>>The variable $Z-\frac{1}{3}Y$ has a mean of 0 (since both $Y,Z$ are zero-mean), and a variance of $\operatorname{Var}(Z)-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2-1=1$. We also have by bilinearity that $\operatorname{Cov}\left( X,Z-\frac{1}{3}Y \right)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1-1=0$. Since the variables are jointly Gaussian, this implies that $X$ and $Z-\frac{1}{3}Y$ are independent, and therefore,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}\left[X \mid Z-\frac{1}{3}Y\right]=0.
\end{align}$$
>>Finally, we have that
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}[X \mid Y,Z]&=\mathbb{L}[X,Y] \\
&= \boxed{\frac{1}{3}Y}.
\end{align}$$

>[!example] II. Joint Gaussians As Linear Transformations of IID Gaussians
>Let $X=\begin{bmatrix}X_{1} & X_{2}\end{bmatrix}^T$ be a jointly Gaussian random vector with mean $\mu=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0\end{bmatrix}^T$ and covariance
>$$
\Sigma_X = 
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1\\
1 & 2
>\end{bmatrix}
=
>\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}\\[6pt]
\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}\\[6pt]
\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2}
>\end{bmatrix}^T
= A A^T.$$
>
>**A)** Express $X_{1},X_{2}$ as linear combinations of i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Let $Z$ be a random vector, such that $Z_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Since $\mu=0$, we have
>>$$\begin{bmatrix}
X_{1} \\ X_2
>>\end{bmatrix}
=
>>A\begin{bmatrix}
Z_{1} \\ Z_{2}
>>\end{bmatrix}
=
>>\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }+1}{2}Z_{1}+\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }-1}{2}Z_{2} \\
\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }-1}{2}Z_{1}+\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }+1}{2}Z_{2}
>>\end{bmatrix}.$$
>
>**B)** Find a matrix $B$ such that the components of $BX$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>We need to find some $B$, such that $BX=Z$. We observe that $X=AZ$. Since $A$ is invertible (i.e., it has a nonzero determinant), $A^{-1}X=Z$, and therefore $B=A^{-1}$. We proceed by finding $\det A=\sqrt{3}$, and therefore,
>>$$B=A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ 3 }}\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }+1}{2} & \dfrac{1-\sqrt{ 3 }}{2} \\
\dfrac{1-\sqrt{ 3 }}{2} &\dfrac{\sqrt{ 3 }+1}{2}
\end{bmatrix}$$

>Consider the Gaussian random vector

242.title: 6.1 Estimator
242.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[6.1 Estimator]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/07 01:09:42","modified":"2025/05/07 19:08:09"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Estimators
>An **estimator** is a function that maps observed data to an estimate of an unknown quantity of the underlying data‑generating process, called a **parameter**. Formally, given an observation sample $X=(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$, an estimator for a parameter $\theta$ is a statistic $\hat\Theta_{n}=g(X)$ for some function $g$ that produces a single “best guess” of $\theta$ based on the observations.
>
>In Bayesian inference,
>
>In classical inference, the estimator is perceived as a statistic that “plugs in” the value of the parameter maximizing the likelihood. Given that the estimation is based on a brittle model, it may not always yield the most suitable estimate. 
>
>The misalignment between the parameter $\theta$ and the estimator $\hat\Theta_{n}$ is known as the **estimation error**, and is given as
>$$\tilde\Theta_{n}=\hat\Theta_{n}-\theta.$$
>
>The **bias** of the estimator is the expected value of the estimation error, and is denoted as
>$$b_{\theta}(\hat\Theta_{n}) = \mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\hat\Theta_{n}]-\theta.$$
>The estimator $\hat\Theta_{n}$ is **unbiased** if $\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\hat\Theta_{n}]=\theta$, and **asymptotically unbiased** if $\lim_{ n \to \infty }\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\hat\Theta_{n}]=\theta$. Furthermore, $\hat\Theta_{n}$ is **consistent** if it converges to the true value of $\theta$, in probability, for every possible value of $\theta$.

243.title: 6.4b Point Testing
243.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/6. Statistical Inference/6.4 Hypothesis Testing/6.4b Point Testing.md
243.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[6.4b Point Testing]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/08 01:42:12","modified":"2025/05/12 03:14:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Point Testing
>A **point test** is a [[6.4 Hypothesis Testing|hypothesis test]] in which the null hypothesis fully specifies the distribution by fixing the parameter to a single value.
>
>For binary hypothesis testing, the **Neyman-Pearson Test** is the point test which maximizes power subject to a constraint on the significance level $\alpha$. Define the **Likelihood Ratio** to be 
>$$L(x)=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{H_{1}}(x)}{\mathbb{P}_{H_{0}}(x)} \quad \text{or} \quad L(x)=\frac{f_{H_{1}}(x)}{f_{H_{2}}(x)}.$$ 
>Then, for some critical threshold $\lambda > 0$ and an observation $x$:
>1. Accept $H_{0}$ if $L(x) < \lambda$.
>2. Reject $H_{0}$ with probability $\gamma \in [0,1]$ if $L(x) = \lambda$.
>3. Reject $H_{0}$ if $L(x) > \lambda$.
>
>This guarantees that the test yields the smallest possible $\beta$ among all tests that do not exceed $\alpha$.

# Intuition
We first begin by expressing the Neyman-Pearson Test as an optimization problem, where
$$\hat{X}$$

# Examples
>[!example] Exponential Hypothesis Testing
>Let $X \sim \operatorname{Exp}(1)$. Given $X$, let $Y \sim \operatorname{Exp}(X)$. Let $c>1$. Suppose that
>- The null hypothesis is $X = 1: Y \sim \operatorname{Exp}(1)$, and
>- The alternative hypothesis is $X= c: Y \sim \operatorname{Exp}(c)$.
>
>Find the decision rule $\hat{X}$ (a function of $Y$) that maximizes $\mathbb{P}(\hat{X}=1 \mid X=1)$ subject to $\mathbb{P}(\hat{X}=1 \mid X=c) \leq 5\%$.
>>[!example]- Solution.
>>We utilize the Neyman-Pearson test with $\alpha \leq 0.05$. We find that
>>$$L(y)=\frac{f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid c)}{f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid 1)}=\frac{ce^{-cy}}{e^{-y}}=ce^{-y(c-1)},$$
>>which is decreasing in $y$ since $c>1$. Since $L(x) \leq \lambda$ is our criterion for accepting the null (we use a $\leq$ instead of a strict inequality since we are working with continuous variables) , we have
>>$$L(y)=ce^{-y(c-1)}\leq\lambda \iff y\leq\frac{\ln(\lambda/c)}{1-c}=t.$$
>>Given $\alpha \leq 0.05$, we also have
>>$$\begin{align}
\alpha &= \mathbb{P}(\hat{X}=1 \mid X = c) \\
&=\mathbb{P}(L(Y) \leq \zeta \mid X=c) \\
&= \mathbb{P}(Y \leq t \mid X=c) \\
&= 1-e^{-ct} \\
&= 0.05 \iff t=-\frac{\ln 0.95}{c}
\end{align}$$
>>Therefore, we equate the two values of $t$ to solve for the threshold $\lambda$, so that
>>$$-\frac{\ln 0.95}{c}=\frac{\ln(\lambda/c)}{1-c} \iff \lambda=c \cdot \exp\left( \frac{-\ln 0.95}{c}(1-c) \right).$$
>>Our rule is then
>>$$\begin{align}
\hat{X}=\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } L(Y) \leq \lambda \equiv Y \leq t \\
c & \text{if } L(Y) > \lambda \equiv Y > t. 
\end{cases}
\end{align}$$


>[!example] Bernoulli Hypothesis Testing
>Suppose that
>- The null hypothesis is $X = 0: Y \sim \operatorname{Ber}\left( 1/4 \right)$, and
>- The alternative hypothesis is $X = 1: Y \sim \operatorname{Ber}\left( 3/4 \right)$.
>
>Using the Neyman–Pearson formulation of hypothesis testing, find the optimal randomized decision rule $\hat{X}$ with respect to the criterion
>$$\begin{align}
\min &\enspace \mathbb{P}(\hat{X}=0 \mid X=1) \\
\text{s.t.} &\enspace \mathbb{P}(\hat{X}=1 \mid X=0) \le \beta,
\end{align}$$
>where $\beta \in [0,1]$ is a given upper bound on the false positive probability.
>>[!example]- Solution.

This question requires us to find the test that minimizes the false negative probability while keeping the false positive probability below $\beta$. We start by computing the likelihood ratio,
$$L(y)=\frac{p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid 1)}{p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid 0)},$$
such that $L(0)=\frac{1/4}{3/4}=1/3$ and $L(1)=\frac{3/4}{1/4}=3$, or
$$\begin{align}
L(y)=\begin{cases}
1/3 & \text{if } y=0  \\
3 & \text{if } y=1.
\end{cases}
\end{align}$$
Since $L(1) = 3 \geq 1/3=L(0)$, $L(1)$, observing $y=1$ is stronger evidence for $X=1$. Recall that with the Neyman-Pearson test,
- If $\lambda \in (1/3, 3)$, then we always accept $H_{0}:X=0$ on $y=0$, since $L(0) < \lambda$, and conversely, we always reject $H_{0}$ on $y=1$, since $L(1)>\lambda$ for all $\lambda$. Therefore, $\gamma=0$, and
$$\begin{align}
\beta&=\mathbb{P}(Y=1 \mid X=0)+\gamma \mathbb{P}(Y=0 \mid X=0) \\
&=1/4+0 \cdot \mathbb{P}(Y=0 \mid X=0) \\
&=1/4.
\end{align}$$
- If $\lambda=1/3$, then we randomize on $y=0$, and always reject on $y=1$ (since $L(1)=3 > 1/3$). Therefore,
$$\begin{align}
\beta &= \mathbb{P}(Y=1 \mid X=0)+\gamma \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid X=0) \\
&= 1/4+\gamma(3/4) \iff \gamma=\frac{4\beta-1}{3}.
\end{align}$$
- If $\lambda =3$, then we always reject $H_{0}$ on $y=0$, since $L(0)=1/3 \cancel{<}3$, and randomize on $y=1$, since $L(1)=3=\lambda$. Therefore,
$$\begin{align}
\beta &= \gamma\mathbb{P}(Y=1 \mid X=0)+\mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid X=0) \\
&= \gamma(1/4)+0 \iff \gamma=4\beta.
\end{align}$$
Then, $\gamma=4\beta$ has a domain of $\beta \in [0, 1/4]$, and $\gamma=\frac{4\beta-1}{3}$ has a domain of $\beta \in [1/4, 1]$. This creates the following rule for the two cases (i.e., where $\beta < 1/4$ and $\beta > \frac{1}{4}$):
$$\begin{align}
\hat{X}_{\beta < \frac{1}{4}}=\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } Y=0 \\
\operatorname{Ber}(\gamma=4\beta) & \text{if }Y=1,
\end{cases}
\end{align}$$
and
$$\hat{X}_{\beta > \frac{1}{4}} = \begin{cases}
\operatorname{Ber}\left( \gamma=\frac{4\beta-1}{3} \right) & \text{if } Y=0 \\
1 & \text{if } Y=1.
\end{cases}$$
For $\beta=1/4$, we have a standard $\hat{X}=1_{Y=1}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[6.4a Hypothesis Testing]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/08 02:21:04","modified":"2025/05/08 16:00:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Hypothesis Testing
>A **hypothesis test** is a formal decision procedure for choosing between two competing statements about a data‑generating distribution:
>- **Null Hypothesis ($H_{0}$):** An explanation of how randomness generates the data. States that nothing out of the ordinary is happening.
>- **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_{1}$)**: The assertion that a mechanism other than the null hypothesis is generating the data.
>
>However, hypothesis tests can be prone to errors. Let $\hat{X}: x \to \{ H_{0}, H_{1}\}$ be some binary hypothesis test, and let $X \in \{ H_{0}, H_{1} \}$ be the ground truth. Then:
>- A **Type-I Error** (i.e., a false negative) occurs with probability $\alpha$ (known as the **significance level**) if the null is rejected even though it is in fact true. Formally,
>$$\alpha=\mathbb{P}(\hat{X} = H_{0} \mid X = H_{1}).$$
>- A **Type-II Error** (i.e., a false positive) occurs with probability $\beta$ if one fails to reject the null when the alternative is true. Formally,
>$$\beta=\mathbb{P}(\hat{X} = H_{1} \mid X = H_{0}).$$
>The probability $1-\beta$ of the test to correctly reject the null is called the **power** of the test.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/01 18:55:17","modified":"2025/05/08 20:30:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) Estimate 
>The **maximum‑a posteriori (MAP) estimate** chooses the [[6.1 Estimator|estimator]] under which the parameter $\theta$ is most probable _after_ observing the data, by maximizing the posterior distribution. Let $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be observed data with likelihood $p_X(x \mid \theta)$, and assume a prior distribution $p_{\Theta}(\theta)$ on the random parameter $\Theta$. Then, the **MAP estimate** of $\theta$ is the value that maximizes the posterior $p_{\Theta}(\theta\mid X)$, such that
>$$\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}(x)=\arg\max_{\theta} p_{\Theta \mid X}(\theta \mid x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})=\arg\max_{\theta} \{ p_{X \mid \Theta}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \mid \theta) \cdot p_{\Theta}(\theta) \}.$$

# Examples
>[!example] I. Poisson Process MAP
>Customers arrive to a store according to a Poisson process with rate $\lambda=1$. The store manager learns of a rumor that one of the employees is sending every other customer to the rival store, so that deterministically, every odd-numbered customer is sent away.
>
>Let $X = 1$ be the hypothesis that the rumor is true and $X = 0$ the rumor is false, assuming that both hypotheses are equally likely. Suppose a customer arrives to the store at time $0$. After that, the manager observes $T_{1}, \ldots,T_{n}$, where $T_{i}$ is the time of the $i$-th subsequent sale, $i = 1, \ldots, n$. Derive the MAP rule to determine whether the rumor was true or not.
>
>>[!example]- Solution.
>>Since both hypotheses are equally likely, MAP is equivalent to MLE. We form the posterior 
>>$$f_{T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n} \mid X}(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n} \mid 1)=\prod^{n}_{i=1}(t_{i}-t_{i-1})e^{-(t_{i}-t_{i-1})}$$

>[!example] II. Laplace Prior and $\ell^1$-Regularization (LASSO)
>Suppose you draw $n$ i.i.d. data points $(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})$, where the true relationship is given by $Y = WX + \epsilon$ for $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$. In other words, $Y$ has a linear dependence on $X$ with additive Gaussian noise. Further suppose that $W$ has a Laplace prior distribution,
>$$f_{W}(w)=\frac{1}{2\beta}e^{-|w|/\beta}.$$
>Show that finding the MAP estimate of $W$ given the data points $\{ x_{i}, y_{i} \}_{i=1}^n$ is equivalent to minimizing the cost function
>$$J(w)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2+\lambda|w|,$$
>and determine $\lambda$.
>>[!example]- Solution.
>>Since we know $f_{W}(w)$, we need to find $f_{X, Y \mid W}(x_{i}, y_{i} \mid w)$, which is equivalent to $\epsilon=Y-WX \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. As such, 
>>$$f_{E \mid W}(\epsilon \mid w)=\prod^{n}_{i=1}f_{E_{i}}(\epsilon_{i})=\prod^{n}_{i=1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }\sigma}e^{-(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$
>>This means that our likelihood function is 
>>$$L(w)=\frac{1}{2\beta}e^{-|w|/\beta}\prod^{n}_{i=1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }\sigma}e^{-(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2/(2\sigma^2)} \propto e^{-|w|/\beta}\prod^{n}_{i=1}e^{-(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$
>>Taking the log-likelihood, we have
>>$$LL(w)=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2-\frac{|w|}{\beta}.$$
>>Since we are maximizing for $LL(w)$, which is concave on $w$ (positive absolute values are convex, and we have a negative absolute value), then we are minimizing for 
>>$$-LL(w)=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-wx_{i})^2+\frac{|w|}{\beta},$$
>>where $J(w)=-2\sigma^2LL(w)$ with $\lambda=2\sigma^2/\beta$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/01 18:55:17","modified":"2025/05/08 20:30:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) >[!example] III. Bayesian Estimation of Exponential Distribution
>Suppose that $X$ is Exponential with unknown rate $\Lambda$. As a Bayesian practitioner, you have a prior belief that the random variable $\Lambda$ is equally likely to be $\lambda_{1}$ or $\lambda_{2}$.
>
>**A)** You collect one sample $X_{1}$ from $X$. Find the posterior distribution $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda = \lambda_{1} \mid X_{1} = x_{1})$.
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>We know by Bayes that 
>>$$\mathbb{P}(\Lambda=\lambda_{1} \mid X_{1} = x_{1}) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(X_{1} = x_{1} \mid \Lambda = \lambda_{1})\mathbb{P}(\Lambda=\lambda_{1})}{\mathbb{P}(X_{1}=x_{1})}$$
>>Here, by definition we have that the prior is $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda = \lambda_{1})=1/2$, and $\mathbb{P}(X_{1}=x_{1} \mid \Lambda = \lambda_{1})=\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x_{1}}$. Then, by total probability, we also have $\mathbb{P}(X_{1}=x_{1})=1/2 \cdot[\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x_{1}}+\lambda_{2}e^{-\lambda_{2}x_{1}}]$. As such,
>>$$\mathbb{P}(\Lambda=\lambda_{1} \mid X_{1}=x_{1})=\frac{\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x_{1}}}{\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x_{1}}+\lambda_{2}e^{-\lambda_{2}x_{1}}}.$$
>
>**B)** Instead of using MAP or MLE and fixing some $\lambda$ of $\Lambda$, we will keep the full information of the posterior distribution of $Λ$. Compute the distribution of $X$ as
>$$f_{X}(x)=\sum_{\lambda \in \{ \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2} \}}f_{X \mid \Lambda}(x \mid \lambda) \cdot \mathbb{P}(\Lambda=\lambda \mid X_{1} = x_{1}).$$
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>We find that $f_{X \mid \Lambda}(x \mid \lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. Using the answer from the previous part, we have
>>$$f_{X}(x)=\frac{\lambda_{1}^2e^{-\lambda_{1}(x_{1}+x)}+\lambda_{2}^2e^{-\lambda_{2}(x_{1}+x)}}{\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x_{1}}+\lambda_{2}e^{-\lambda_{2}x_{1}}} \cdot $$
>
>**C)** The fully Bayesian approach from part **B)** is often computationally intractable, which is one of the main reasons why point estimates are common in practice. Supposing that $\lambda_{1} > \lambda_{2}$, compute the MAP estimate for $\Lambda$, and calculate $f_{X}(x)$ again using the MAP rule.
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>We formulate our MAP/ML (equivalent here, since the prior of $\lambda$ is uniform) estimate as
>>$$\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_{\lambda \in \{ \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2} \}}\mathbb{P}(X=x_{1} \mid \Lambda=\lambda) \cdot \mathbb{P}(\Lambda=\lambda)=\arg\max_{\lambda \in \{ \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2} \}} \mathbb{P}(X=x_{1} \mid \Lambda = \lambda),$$
>>where our likelihood function $\mathbb{P}(X=x_{1} \mid \Lambda=\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x_{1}}$ turns into $\ln \lambda-\lambda x_{1}$ when log-likelihood is applied. Given $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}$, it also follows that $\ln \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}x_{1} > \ln \lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}x_{1}$ only if 
>>$$x_{1} < \frac{\ln(\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{2})}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}=\alpha.$$
>>Since the value of $X_{1}$ determines the parameter $\lambda$ for all subsequent observations, this result implies that 
>>$$\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MAP}}=\begin{cases}
\lambda_{1} & \text{if } x_{1} < \alpha \\
\lambda_{2} & \text{if } x_{1} \geq \alpha.
\end{cases}$$
>>As such, we get that
>>$$f_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}
\lambda_{1}e^{-\lambda_{1}x} & \text{if } x_{1} < \alpha \\
\lambda_{2}e^{-\lambda_{2}x} & \text{if } x_{1} \geq \alpha,
\end{cases}$$
where $\alpha = \dfrac{\ln(\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{2})}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}$ is the intersection of the distributions with parameters $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$.

249.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[6.2c LLSE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/08 21:56:45","modified":"2025/05/11 02:21:51"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Least Squares Estimate (LLSE)
>The **linear least‐squares estimator (LLSE)** of a random variable $Y$ given another random variable $X$ is the best linear predictor of $Y$. Concretely, we seek constants $a$ and $b$ such that the linear function $\hat{Y}=aX+b$ minimizes the squared error $\mathbb{E}[(Y-\hat{Y})^2]$:
>$$\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X] = \min_{a,b}\mathbb{E}[(Y−(aX+b))^2],$$
>which is achieved by the optimal value
>$$\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}(X-\mathbb{E}[X]).$$
>The LLSE is unbiased, meaning that $\mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}_{\text{LLSE}}]=\mathbb{E}[Y]$.

# Intuition
In the geometric sense, things become much simpler to explain. Let the random variables $X,Y$ be equivalent to vectors $x, y \in L^n(\Omega)$ in the Hilbert space of dimension $n$, such that $x,y,u$, are linearly independent, and their span forms the 3-dimensional Hilbert subspace of random variables. Here, $u$ is the unit-norm uniform vector (i.e., $u=\frac{1}{\|1\|_{2}}$). Then:
1. $\mathbb{E}[XY] \equiv \langle x,y\rangle$. 
2. $\mathbb{E}[X^2] \equiv \|x\|^2_{2}$.
3. $\rho=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}[XY]}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] }} \equiv \dfrac{\langle x,y \rangle}{\|x\|_{2}\|y\|_{2}}$.

Now, let $\bar{x}=\dfrac{x-\langle x, u \rangle u}{\|x-\langle x, u \rangle u\|_{2}}$ be the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalized vector of $x$, such that $\{ \bar{x}, u \}$ form a basis in 2-dimensional space. We can project $y$ onto this basis, such that
$$\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X]=\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{Span}(\bar{x}, u)}(x)=\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{Span}(u)}(x)+\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{Span}(\bar{x})}(x).$$
This is equivalent to
$$\mathbb{L}(Y \mid X)=\langle y, u \rangle u+\langle y, \bar{x} \rangle \bar{x}=\mathbb{E}[Y]+\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}Y] \cdot \bar{X}.$$
Here, $\bar{X}=\frac{X-\mathbb{E}[X]}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(X) }}$. Substituting, we get the standard LLSE equation:
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}(Y \mid X)&=\mathbb{E}[Y]+\frac{\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}[X] \cdot \mathbb{E}[Y]}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(X)} } \cdot \frac{X-\mathbb{E}[X]}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(X) }} \\ \\
&= \mathbb{E}[Y] + \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}(X-\mathbb{E}[X]).
\end{align}$$
# Properties
#### (*Orthogonality*) $\operatorname{Cov}(E, Y)=0$, where $E=Y-\hat{Y}_{\text{LLSE}}$.
#### (*Independence Partition*) It holds that $\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X,Z]=\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X]+\mathbb{L}[Y \mid Z]$ if $X, Z$ are independent and $\mu=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}^T$.
Let $x,y,z$ represent $X,Y,Z$ in the Hilbert space. Since $y,z$ are orthogonal, $\left\{  \bar{y}=\frac{y}{\|y\|_{2}}, \bar{z}=\frac{z}{\|z\|_{2}}  \right\}$ form an orthonormal basis. We can decompose the projection into
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}(X \mid Y,Z) &= \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{y},\bar{z})}(x) \\
&= \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{y})}(x)+\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{z})}(x) \\
&= \langle x, \bar{y} \rangle \bar{y} + \langle x, \bar{z} \rangle \bar{z} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X\bar{Y}]\bar{Y}+\mathbb{E}[X\bar{Z}]\bar{Z},
\end{align}$$
where $\bar{Y}=\frac{Y}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[Y^2] }}$ and $\bar{Z}=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[Z^2] }}$. As such,
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}(X \mid Y,Z)&=\frac{\mathbb{E}[XY]}{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}Y+\frac{\mathbb{E}[XZ]}{\mathbb{E}[Z^2]}Z \\
&= \mathbb{L}(X \mid Y) + \mathbb{L}(X \mid Z).
\end{align}$$
#### (Zero-Mean Partition) $\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X,Z]=\mathbb{L}[Y \mid X]+\mathbb{L}[Y \mid Z - \mathbb{L}[Z \mid X]]$ for any $X,Y,Z$ if $\mu=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}^T$.
We proceed in the same manner as above, but with an extra step: Gram-Schmidt.
# Examples
>[!example] Orthogonal LLSE
>Consider zero-mean random variables $X,Y,Z$ with $Y,Z$ orthogonal. 
>
>**A)** Show that
>$$\mathbb{L}(X \mid Y,Z) = \mathbb{L}(X \mid Y) + \mathbb{L}(X \mid Z).$$
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Let $x,y,z$ represent $X,Y,Z$ in the Hilbert space. Since $y,z$ are orthogonal, $\left\{  \bar{y}=\frac{y}{\|y\|_{2}}, \bar{z}=\frac{z}{\|z\|_{2}}  \right\}$ form an orthonormal basis. We can decompose the projection into
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}(X \mid Y,Z) &= \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{y},\bar{z})}(x) \\
&= \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{y})}(x)+\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(\bar{z})}(x) \\
&= \langle x, \bar{y} \rangle \bar{y} + \langle x, \bar{z} \rangle \bar{z} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X\bar{Y}]\bar{Y}+\mathbb{E}[X\bar{Z}]\bar{Z},
\end{align}$$
where $\bar{Y}=\frac{Y}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[Y^2] }}$ and $\bar{Z}=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[Z^2] }}$. As such,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{L}(X \mid Y,Z)&=\frac{\mathbb{E}[XY]}{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}Y+\frac{\mathbb{E}[XZ]}{\mathbb{E}[Z^2]}Z \\
&= \mathbb{L}(X \mid Y) + \mathbb{L}(X \mid Z),
\end{align}$$
given that $X,Y,Z$ are all zero-mean (note that the means are all absent from the expression, which is why there is a mismatch between the general formula and the zero-mean formula).
>
>**B)** Now, for any zero-mean random variables $X,Y,Z$, explain why it holds that
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>We proceed in the same manner as in part **A)**, but with an extra step: Gram-Schmidt.

NOTE TITLE: [[6.2a MLE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/01 18:53:44","modified":"2025/05/08 16:58:31"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Maximum Likelihood (ML) Estimate
>The **maximum-likelihood (ML) estimate**  chooses the [[6.1 Estimator|estimator]] under which the observations are “most probable” by maximizing their likelihood. Let $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be observed data described by the joint PMF $p_{X}(x;\theta)$ whose form depends on the unknown parameter $\theta$, known as the **likelihood function**. Then, the **maximum-likelihood estimate** of $\theta$ is that value which maximizes the likelihood function, such that
>$$\hat{\theta}_{\text{ML}}(x) = \arg \max_{\theta} p_{X \mid \Theta}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \mid \theta).$$
>If the observations in $X$ are independent, the likelihood function can be decomposed as $p_{X \mid \Theta}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \mid \theta)=\prod\limits^{n}_{i=1}p_{X_{i} \mid \Theta}(x_{i} \mid\theta)$. Then, one may employ the **log-likelihood function**, denoted
>$$\ln p_{X \mid \Theta}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \mid \theta)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\ln p_{X_{i} \mid \Theta}(x_{i} \mid \theta).$$
>>[!warning] Working With Continous Data
>>For the case where the observation vector $X$ consists of continuous data, one may simply use the likelihood function $f_{X}(x;\theta)$.

# Properties
#### (*Invariance*) For some function $h$, if $\zeta = h(\theta)$, then $\hat\zeta_{n} \in h(\hat\Theta_{n})$.

#### (*Asymptotic Normality*) If $\theta$ is scalar, $\dfrac{\hat\Theta_{n}-\theta}{\sigma(\hat\Theta_{n})} \to \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$.

# Examples
>[!example] MLE of Uniform Distribution
>Find the MLE of $\theta$ given $X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim_{\text{iid}} \text{Uniform}([0,θ])$.
>>[!example]- Solution
>>Since the distribution is uniform, it follows that $p_{X}(x;\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta} \mathbb{1}_{\{ 0 \leq x \leq \theta \}}$. Given i.i.d. variables, the likelihood function can be written using log-likelihood as 
>>$$p_{X}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n};\theta)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\ln p_{X}(x_{i}; \theta) \mathbb{1}_{\{ 0 \leq x_{i} \leq \theta \}}.$$
>>When $\hat\theta = \max_{i} X_{i}$, 
>>$$p_{X}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n};\theta)=-n\ln \theta.$$
>>Taking the derivative of the log-likelihood on the domain $[\max_{i}X_{i}, +\infty)$, we have
>>$$\frac{\delta}{\delta \theta}(-n\ln \theta)=-\frac{n}{\theta}<0.$$
>>This means that the likelihood is strictly decreasing in $\theta$. As such, $\hat\theta = \max_{i} X_{i}$.

>[!example] Maximum Likelihood Estimation for the Binary Symmetric Channel
>You are testing a digital link that corresponds to a BSC with some error probability $\epsilon \in [0,0.5]$.
>Suppose that you observe an input bit $X$ and an output bit $Y$. Calculate the MLE of $\epsilon$.
>>[!example] Solution.
>>Here, we want to find 
>>$$\hat\epsilon_{\text{MLE}}=\arg\max\limits_{\epsilon \in [0, 0.5]}\mathbb{P}_{\epsilon}(X=x, Y=y),$$
>>i.e., we need to first figure out the joint distribution $\mathbb{P}_{\epsilon}(X=x, Y=y)$.
