252.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/4. Stochastic Processes/4.2 Poisson Processes.md
252.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2 Poisson Processes]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/23 17:56:55","modified":"2025/08/06 12:53:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) #### (*Random Incidence Paradox*) $\mathbb{E}[(T_{n+1}-t^*)+(t^*-T_{n})]=\dfrac{2}{\lambda}$.
Consider some random arrival time $t^*$ dividing the inter-arrival time $S_{n+1}=T_{n+1}-T_{n}$ into two distinct intervals, $L=t^*-T_{n}$ and $M=T_{n+1}-t^*$. Then, because inter-arrival times are memoryless, $L \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $M \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, and $L,M$ are independent of one another. By the linearity of expectation, 
$$\mathbb{E}[L]+\mathbb{E}[M]=1/\lambda+1/\lambda=2/\lambda.$$
This is a paradox for a reason: wouldn't $\mathbb{E}[T_{n+1}-T_{n}]=1/\lambda$? The answer is also yes! We can make the following rationale:
1. $\mathbb{E}[T_{n+1}-T_{n}]=1/\lambda$ is the expected inter-arrival time in a Poisson process.
2. $\mathbb{E}[(T_{n+1}-t^*)+(t^*-T_{n})]=2/\lambda$ is the expected inter-arrival time in the interval which some random $t^*$ falls into.

It turns out that this result leads us to the conclusion that since we are choosing our time $t^*$ randomly, it’s more likely it lands in a longer interval than a short one regardless of its distribution. Longer intervals have a better chance to be chosen, while shorter intervals have a lower chance. Think about that the next time you are trying to catch the next bus!
# Examples
>[!example] Bus Station
>You are waiting for a bus at a bus station. A-line buses arrive at the station according to a Poisson process with an average arrival time of 10 minutes. 
>>[!example]- If the A-line has been running for a long time and you arrive at the bus station at a random time, what is your expected waiting time?
>>The expected time of the Poisson Process $\text{PP}(0.1)$ is $1/0.1=10$ minutes. Therefore, on average, you will have to wait 10 minutes for the next bus.
>
>>[!example]- On average, how many minutes ago did the last A-line bus leave?
>>The memoryless property still applies backwards in time, so on average, the last bus arrived 10 minutes ago as well.
>
>The bus station you are waiting at also services B- and C-line buses, and you can use the C-line to reach your destination. There is a 95% chance that the next C-line bus will arrive within 26 minutes.
>
>>[!example]- You are in a rush to make it to your probability class–what is the chance that the next C-line bus will arrive within 6 minutes?
>>We start by observing that $F_{T}(x=26)=1-e^{-26\lambda}=0.95$. Solving, we obtain $\lambda \approx 0.115$ (i.e., 8.7 minutes on average per bus). We then plug in $F_{T}(x=6)=1-e^{-6 \cdot 0.115} \approx 0.5$.
>
>The B-line buses arrive every 5 minutes on average. However, B-line buses take you on a completely different route, and are not useful.
>>[!example]- What is the chance that an A-line or C-line bus will arrive before a B-line bus?
>>Assume all three lines are independent Poisson processes, so the time until the next bus on each line is exponential with rates $\lambda_{A}=1/10$, $\lambda_{B}=23/200$, $\lambda_{C}=1/5$. We merge these 3 processes and look at the result:
>>$$\mathbb{P}(\min(T_{A}, T_{C}) < T_{B})=\frac{\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}}{\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{B}+\lambda_{C}} \approx 0.52.$$

>[!example] Spam/Ham (Poisson Merging)
>Emails to Bob gets automatically classified, and those considered to be Spam are routed to a Spam folder. Emails not classified as spam are routed to Bob's Inbox. Regular email arrives as a Poisson Process with rate **10 msgs/hr** and Spam arrives at a rate of **20 msgs/hr**. A regular email is classified as **spam with probability 0.05** and a spam email is classified as **regular mail with probability 0.01**. 
>>[!example]- Bob checks his Inbox after a long time and selects the most recent message. What is the probability it is spam?
>>Genuine mails that pass the spam filter arrive at $\lambda_{\text{regular}}=10 \cdot (1-0.05)=9.5$ msgs/hr. Spam mails that pass the spam filter arrive at $\lambda_{\text{spam}}=20 \cdot 0.01=0.2$ msgs/hr.
>>
>>As such, the probability of spam mail in Bob's Inbox is $\dfrac{0.2}{9.5+0.2}=0.0206$.
>
>>[!example]- What’s the probability that the top email in his spam mail is regular mail?
>>We use the logic from the previous problem: genuine mail gets rejected by the spam filter at a rate of $\lambda_{\text{reg, rej}}=10 \cdot 0.05=0.5$ msgs/hr, whereas spam gets rejected at a rate of $\lambda_{\text{spam, rej}}=20 \cdot (1-0.01)=19.8$ msgs/hr.
>>
>>As such, the probability of regular mail in Bob's spam mail is $\dfrac{0.5}{19.8+0.5}=0.0246$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/25 17:33:17","modified":"2025/04/08 14:21:58"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Reversibility of Markov Chains
>An irreducible Markov chain $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with stationary distribution $\pi^*$ some $Y_{N-n}$, such that $X_{n}=Y_{N-n}$ for all $n=1,\ldots,N$. The reverse transition probabilities $\hat{P}(x_{n+1},x_{n})$ of $Y_{N-n}$ are defined via the **detailed balance equation**, such that
>$$\hat{P}(x_{n+1}, x_{n})=\frac{\pi^*(x_{n})P(x_{n}, x_{n+1})}{\pi^*(x_{n+1})},$$
>where the equality $\hat{P}(x_{n+1}, x_{n})=P(x_{n+1}, x_{n})$ must hold for the chain to be reversible. Note that $y_{n}=x_{n+1}$ and $y_{n+1}=x_{n}$ holds for all $n$.
>
>>[!warning] DBE Generality
>>Note that this is the *local* (and stronger) form of the detailed balance equation. The equation above can be applied to any Markov chain in order to get its reversed form (although a Markov chain is only reversible if it is equal to its reverse!).

255.title: 5.3 Distribution of Markov Chains
255.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/4. Stochastic Processes/4.33 Markov Chains/5.3 Distribution of Markov Chains.md
255.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[5.3 Distribution of Markov Chains]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/25 13:44:35","modified":"2025/06/10 18:33:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Markov Chain Distribution
>The probability mass function $\pi_{n}: \mathcal{X} \to [0, 1]$ (or $\pi_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times |\mathcal{X}|}$) of the random variable $X_{n}$ represents the probability of the [[5.1 Markov Chains|Markov chain]] being in each possible state in $\mathcal{X}$ at time $n$. It can be used in tandem with the transition probability matrix $P$ to derive the $n$-th distribution in the sequence, such that $\pi_{n}=\pi_{n-1}P$, or equivalently,
>$$\pi_{n} = \pi_{0}P^n.$$
>
>If $\pi^*=\pi^*P$, then $\pi^*$ is said to be an **invariant distribution**. Per the **Big Theorem**, an irreducible Markov chain has a unique invariant distribution $\pi^*$, such that $\pi^*(x)$ is the long-term fraction of time that $X_{n}$ is equal to $x$, defined as
>$$\pi^*(x) = \lim_{ n \to \infty } \frac{1}{n}\sum^{n-1}_{i=0}\mathbb{1}_{\{ X_{i} = x \}}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = x]}.$$
>
>Furthermore, if the Markov chain is also [[5.2 Markov Chain Periodicity|aperiodic]], then any $\pi_{n}$ converges to $\pi$, such that $$\lim\limits_{n \to \infty}\pi_{n}(x)=\sum^{}_{y \in \mathcal{X}}\lim\limits_{n \to \infty}\pi_{0}(x)P^n(y, x)=\pi^*(x).$$

# Properties
#### (*Balance Equation*) $\pi^*(x)=\sum\limits^{}_{y \in \mathcal{X}}\pi^*(y)P(y, x)$

256.title: 5.1 Markov Chains
256.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/4. Stochastic Processes/4.33 Markov Chains/5.1 Markov Chains.md
256.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[5.1 Markov Chains]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/23 17:56:20","modified":"2025/06/10 18:54:31"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time Markov Chains
>A **discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC)** is a model used to represent systems that move randomly between states in discrete steps, where the future state depends only on the current state. Formally, a sequence of random variables $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a DTMC on the state space $\mathcal{X}$ if it satisfies the **Markov property**,
>$$\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n}, \ldots, X_{0} = x_{0}) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n})=P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}).$$
>When  $\mathcal{X}$ is finite, the set of one-step transition probabilities $\{ P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}) : x_{n},x_{n+1} \in \mathcal{X}\}$ can be organized into a row-stochastic one-step **transition probability matrix** $P \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}| \times |\mathcal{X}|}$, such that its rows sum to one. Then, the $k$-step transition equation is given as $P_{k}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X_{k}=y \mid X_{0} = x) = P^k(x,y)$.
>
>States in $\mathcal{X}$ can be characterized using hitting times. The **hitting time** $T_{x} = \min\{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{+} : X_{n}=x\}$ of a state $x \in \mathcal{X}$ in a Markov chain is a random variable denoting the number of time steps required for the chain to visit $x$ for the first time. Let $\rho_{x,y}=\mathbb{P}(T_{y} < \infty \mid X_{0}=x)$ be the probability of reaching state $y$ when starting at state $x$. Then:
>- State $x$ is **transient** if there's a nonzero chance of never returning after leaving (i.e., $\rho_{x,x} < 1$).
>- State $x$ is **recurrent** if you're guaranteed to return to it eventually (i.e., $\rho_{x,x}=1$). That is:
>	- State $x$ is **null recurrent** if the chain takes an infinite amount of time, on average, to return to $x$ (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = x] = \infty$).
>	- State $x$ is **positive recurrent** if $\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = x] < \infty$.
>		- State $x$ is **absorbing** if you never leave it once you enter it (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = x]=0$).
>
>We say that state $x$ **communicates** with state $y$ (i.e., $x \leftrightarrow y$) if it is possible to reach both state $y$ from state $x$ and state $x$ from state $y$, for which $\rho_{x,y} >0$ and $\rho_{y,x} > 0$. A **communicating class** is a maximal set of states $C \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ which communicate with each other, such that $x \leftrightarrow y, \space \forall x,y \in C$. A Markov chain is **irreducible** if every state can be reached from every other state, such that $C=\mathcal{X}$. More particularly:
>- If a finite Markov chain is irreducible, then it contains exclusively positive recurrent states.
>- If an infinite Markov chain is irreducible, then it contains exclusively positive recurrent, null recurrent, or transient states.
> 


# Properties

#### (*Chapman-Kolmogorov Eq.*) $P^{k+\ell}(x,y)=\sum\limits_{i \in \mathcal{X}}P^k(x, i) P^\ell(i,y) \iff P^{k+\ell}=P^kP^\ell$.
You might be asking why the frick is simple matrix multiplication an equation named after two mathematicians. 
#### (*Mean Hitting Time*) $\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = x_{0}]=\begin{dcases}1+\sum_{i \in \mathcal{X}}P(x_{0},i)\cdot\mathbb{E}[T_{x} \mid X_{0} = i] & \text{if } x \neq x_{0} \\ 0 & \text{if } x = x_{0}\end{dcases}$

#### (*Mean Total Visits*) Let $N_{x} = \sum\limits_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\mathbb{1}_{\{ X_{n} = x \}}$. Then, $\mathbb{E}[N_{x} \mid X_{0} = x]=\dfrac{\rho_{x}}{1-\rho_{x}}$ .
Note that this equation converges only for transient states.

#### (*Mean Prob. of Reachability*) $\mathbb{E}[T_{x}<T_{y}]$

257.title: 5.2 Markov Chain Periodicity
257.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/4. Stochastic Processes/4.33 Markov Chains/5.2 Markov Chain Periodicity.md
257.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[5.2 Markov Chain Periodicity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/24 22:56:02","modified":"2025/06/10 18:33:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Periodicity of MCs
>A positive recurrent [[5.1 Markov Chains|Markov chain]] state $x \in \mathcal{X}$ is **periodic** if it has a period equal to the greatest common divisor of all of the time steps $n > 0$ at which the Markov chain, starting from state $x$, has a positive probability of returning to $x$. Formally,
>$$d(x) = \gcd\{ n \in \mathbb{Z}_{+} : P^n(x, x) > 0\}.$$
>If $d(x)=1$, then $x$ is **aperiodic**.
>
>If all of the states in a Markov chain share a common period $d=d(x), \space \forall x \in \mathcal{X}$, then the Markov chain is periodic with period $d$. If $d=1$, then the Markov chain is aperiodic.

>[!note] Markov Chain
>A **discrete-time Markov chain** is a sequence of random variables $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where the future only depends on the current state. Formally, $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a Markov chain if and only if it satisfies the Markov property,
$$\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n}, \ldots, X_{0} = x_{0}) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n})=P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}).$$
>
>When $\mathcal{X}$ is finite, the set of one-step transition probabilities $\{ P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}) : x_{n},x_{n+1} \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}\}$ can be organized into a **transition probability matrix** $P \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}| \times |\mathcal{X}|}$, such that its rows sum to one. Then, the $k$-step transition equation is given as $$P_{k}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X_{k}=y \mid X_{0} = x) = P^k(x,y).$$
>
>Similarly, a sequence of random variables $(X_{t})_{{t \in \mathbb{R_{+}}}}$ is a **continuous-time Markov chain** on $\mathcal{X}$ if it satisfies the continuous-time Markov property,
>$$\mathbb{P}(X_{t+\delta t} = x_{t+\delta t} \mid X_{t} = x_{t}, \ldots, X_{0} = x_{0}) = \mathbb{P}(X_{t+\delta t} = x_{t+\delta t} \mid X_{t} = x_{t}).$$
>
>Different from DTMCs, CTMCs employ a **rate matrix** 
>
>>[!warning] Dependence on Past States
>>The fact that knowledge of the current state $X_{n}$ fully determines the distribution of the next state $X_{n+1}$ does not imply that $X_{n+1}$ is independent of all $X_{n-k}$ for $k \geq 1$. In general, the random variables in a Markov chain are *not independent*.

260.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/3. Limits and Convergence/3.1 Concentration Inequalities.md
260.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.1 Concentration Inequalities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/07 14:26:17","modified":"2025/08/08 20:52:26"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Concentration Inequalities
>**Concentration inequalities** provide probabilistic bounds on how far a random variable is likely to be from some central value without requiring full knowledge of the distribution:
>- The **Markov inequality** provides a bound on the probability that a nonnegative random variable takes a value significantly larger than its mean. Let $X \ge 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[X] < \infty$. Then for any $c > 0$,
>$$P(X \ge c) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{c}.$$
>
>- The **Chebyshev inequality** strengthens this by incorporating variance, yielding a bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean from above or below by more than a specified amount. For any $X$ with $\mathbb{E}[X] < \infty$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) < \infty$, it follows that
>$$P(|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \ge c) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.$$
>By applying Markov’s Inequality to the nonnegative random variable $(X-\mu)^2$, Chebyshev’s bound follows immediately.
>‎ 
>- Finally, the **Chernoff bound** provides an exponentially decreasing bound on the tail probabilities of a random variable using its [[Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.3 Functions of Random Variables/2.5c Moment Generating Functions.md|moment generating function]]. For any $X$ with $M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] < \infty$, and for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$, it directly follows from the Markov inequality that
>$$\mathbb{P}(X \ge c) \le \inf_{t \ge 0} \left\{ \frac{M_{X}(t)}{e^{tc}} \right\}.$$

# Intuition
The proof for Markov's Inequality is derived directly from the definition of expectation:
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}x \cdot \mathbb{P}(X=x) \\
&\ge \sum^{}_{x \ge c}x \cdot \mathbb{P}(X=x) \\
&\ge \sum^{}_{x \ge c}c \cdot \mathbb{P}(X = x) \\
&= c \sum^{}_{x \ge c} \mathbb{P}(X = x) \\
&= c \cdot \mathbb{P}(X \ge c),
\end{align}$$
where the second line follows from the fact that $X$ is nonnegative.

As previously mentioned, Chebyshev's Inequality is a direct consequence of centering $X$ around its mean. Define $Y=(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2$. Then,
$$\begin{align}
P((X-E[X])^2 \ge c^2)&=P(| X-E[X] | \ge c) \\
&\ge \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]}{c^2} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.
\end{align}$$

261.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/3. Limits and Convergence/3.3 Central Limit Theorem.md
261.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.3 Central Limit Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/21 15:42:11","modified":"2025/08/09 15:00:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Central Limit Theorem
>The **Central Limit Theorem** states that, under certain conditions, the distribution of the **standardized sum** (or average) of a large number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables approaches a [[2.2c.5 Gaussian Distribution|normal distribution]], regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.
>
>Formally, let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and define the sum $S_{n}=\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$. Then, it follows that
>$$\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \frac{S_{n} - \mathbb{E}[S_{n}]}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(S_{n}) }} \leq x \right) = \lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \frac{S_{n} - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{ n }} \leq x \right) = \Phi(x),$$ 
>where $\Phi(x)$ is the CDF of the normal distribution.

# Proof




# Examples
>[!example] Binomial Concentration
>Here, we will prove that the binomial distribution is concentrated about its mean as the number of trials tends to $\infty$. Suppose we have i.i.d. trials, each with a probability of success $1/2$. Let $S_{n}$ be the number of successes in the first $n$ trials.
>>[!example]- Compute the mean and variance of $S_{n}$.
>>Since $S_{n} \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$, it follows that $\mathbb{E}(S_{n}) = n/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_{n})=n/4$.
>
>>[!example]- Define $Z_{n}$ in terms of $S_{n}$ such that $Z_{n}$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$.
>>To normalize the sum, let $Z_{n} = \frac{S_{n} - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{ n }}$. Since $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ should be the mean and variance of a single trial $X_i$, then in terms of $S_{n}$,
>>$$Z_{n} = \frac{S_{n} - \mathbb{E}(S_{n})}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(X) }} = \frac{S_{n} - n/2}{\sqrt{ n } / 2}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the distribution of $Z_{n}$ as $n \to \infty$?
>>Per CLT, we have that $\lim\limits_{ n \to \infty } f_{Z}(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }}e^{-z^2 / 2}$, and therefore $Z_n \to \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ in the discrete realm.
>
>>[!example]- Use the bound $P(Z > z) \le (z\sqrt{ 2\pi })^{-1} e^{−z^2/2}$ (where $Z$ is a standard normal) to approximately bound $P(S_{n}/n > 1/2 + \delta)$, where $\delta > 0$.
>>It follows that
>>$$\begin{align}\mathbb{P}(S_{n} / n > 1 / 2 + \delta) &= \mathbb{P}((\sqrt{ n } / 2) Z_{n}) + n / 2 > n / 2 + \delta n) \\ &= \mathbb{P}(Z_{n} > 2\delta \sqrt{ n })  \leq \frac{1}{2\delta\sqrt{ 2\pi n }}\exp(-2\delta^2n).\end{align}$$

>[!example] Packet Erasures & Inverse CDFs
>Alice is sending $1\;000$ bits to Bob. The probability that a bit gets erased is $p$, and the erasure of each bit is independent of the others.
>
>Alice is using a scheme that can tolerate up to one-fifth of the bits being erased. That is, as long as Bob receives at least 801 of the 1000 bits correctly, he can decode Alice’s message. The probability of more than $1 / 5$ of the bits being erased should be at most $10^{-6}$.
>
>>[!example]- Use Chebyshev’s inequality to upper bound $p$ such that the probability of a communications breakdown is at most $10^{-6}$.
>>Express the number of erased bits as $N \sim \text{Bin}(1000, p)$. Then,
>>$$\begin{align}
P(N \ge 200) &= P(N - 1000p \ge 200-1000p)  \\
&\leq \frac{1000p(1-p)}{(200-1000p)^2} \\
&= \frac{p(1-p)}{40(1-5p)^2} \leq 10^{-6}
\end{align}$$
>>which yields $p \le 3.9986 \times 10^{-5}$.
>
>>[!example]- Use CLT to find an approximate bound for p such that the probability of a communications breakdown is at most $10^{-6}$. Note that $\Phi^{-1}(1-10^{-6}) \approx 4.753$.
>>Let $N \sim \operatorname{Bin}(1000, p)$ be again the number of erasures. Then, $Z=\dfrac{N-1000p}{10\sqrt{ p(1-p) }}$. As such, it holds that
>>$$\begin{alignat}{0}
>>\begin{aligned}
>>P(N \ge 200) &= P\left( Z \ge \frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} \right) \\ &= 1- \Phi\left( \frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} \right) \le 10^{-6} \\
>>\end{aligned} \\ \\
>>\Big\Updownarrow \\ \\
>>\begin{aligned}
>>\frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} &\ge \Phi^{-1}(1-10^{-6}) = 4.753.
>>\end{aligned}
>>\end{alignat}
>>$$
>>This yields $p \le 0.1468$.

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/08 05:55:31","modified":"2025/08/07 15:44:46"}

>[!note] Laws of Large Numbers
>**The Weak Law of Large Numbers** is a direct consequence of [[3.1 Concentration Inequalities|Chebyshev’s inequality]] and describes the convergence of sample averages to the expected value. Formally, if $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$, then for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$P\left(\left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i - \mu\right| \ge \varepsilon\right) \to 0 \quad \text{as} \quad n \to \infty.$$
Since the variance of the sample mean is $\sigma^2/n$, Chebyshev’s inequality shows that the probability of a deviation of size $\varepsilon \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, establishing convergence in probability.

>- **Continuous random variables** can take on any value within a given interval of the [[1.1 Probability Space|continuous sample space]], such that they feature an *uncountable* range $\mathcal{X}=[a, b]$ for some bounds $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$.

267.content:

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/07 11:23:33","modified":"2025/08/09 12:55:13"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Gaussian Distribution
>A continuous random variable $X \in \mathbb{R}$ follows the **Gaussian distribution** $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with parameters $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, defined by the [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|probability density function]]
>$$f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}.$$
>
>The Gaussian distribution is used to model real-valued data that tend to cluster around a central value (mean) $\mu$ with symmetric dispersion $\sigma$.
>
>Moreover, if $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, then $X$ is a **standard normal random variable**. Its probability density function simplifies to $f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$, which leads to its cumulative distribution function,
>$$\Phi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2 \pi }}\int^{x}_{-\infty}e^{-x^2/2}dx.$$
>
>A key characteristic of the normal distribution is the **empirical rule (68-95-99 rule)**, which states that around $68\%$, $95\%$, and $99\%$ of the data falls within $1\sigma$, $2\sigma$, and $3\sigma$ of the mean.
>>[!warning] Standardization
>>Any Gaussian random variable can be standardized into the Normal distribution using the transformation $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)]=\mu$.

#### (*Variance*) $Var[X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)] = \sigma^2$.

#### (*Sum*) If $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_{X}^2)$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\eta, \sigma_{Y}^2)$, then $X+Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu+\eta, \sigma_{X}^2+\sigma_{Y}^2)$.
#### (*Rotational Symmetry*)
#### (Positive Gaussian) $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X>0] = \sigma \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X+Y > 0]$.
Since we know that $f_{X \mid A}(x)=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(X \in A)}$, we proceed as follows:
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}[X \mid X > 0] &= \int^{\infty}_{0} xf_{X \mid X >0}(x)dx \\
&= \frac{\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xf_{X}(x)dx}{\mathbb{P}(X>0)} \\
&= \frac{\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xf_{X}(x)dx}{0.5} \\
&= \frac{2}{\sigma\sqrt{ 2\pi }}\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xe^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}dx \\
&= -\sigma^2\sqrt{ \frac{2}{\pi\sigma^2} } e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} \bigg|^{\infty}_{x=0} \\
&= \sigma \sqrt{ \frac{2}{\pi} }
\end{align}$$


# Examples

269.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/07 19:13:22","modified":"2025/08/06 18:11:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Probability Density Function (PDF)
>The probability [[2.2a Probability Distribution|distribution]] of a continuous random variable $X$ is fully described by a non-negative **probability density function (PDF)** $f_{X}: \mathcal{X} \to [0,\infty)$, which illustrates the density around each value $x \in \mathcal{X}$. In particular, the probability that the value of $X$ falls within an interval $[a, b]$ over the real line is given as
>$$\mathbb{P}(a \leq X \leq b)=\int^{b}_{a}f_{X}(x)dx,$$
>and can be interpreted as the area under the graph of the PDF.
>
>The cumulative probability that $X$ takes on a value less than or equal to $x$ in the PDF is given by the non-decreasing **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** $F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ , formally defined as
>$$F_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}(X \leq x)=\int^{x}_{-\infty}f_{X}(t)dt,$$
>implying that the PDF is the rate of change of the CDF, $f_{X}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}F_{X}(x)$.
>
>>[!warning] PDFs Measure Density
>>For an individual point $x$, $\mathbb{P}(X = x) = \int^{x}_{x}f_{X}(x)dx = 0$. However, an alternative to this is to select the interval $[x, x + \delta]$ for a very small length $\delta$, and compute
>>$$\int^{x+\delta}_{x}f_{X}(x)dx \approx f_{X}(x) \cdot \delta.$$

# Properties
#### (*Event Conditioning*) If $A \in \mathcal{F} \text{ s.t. } \mathbb{P}(X \in A) > 0$, then $f_{X \mid A}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{f_{X}(x)}{\mathbb{P}(X \in A)} & x \in A, \\ 0 & \text{o.w.}\end{cases}$
#### (R.V. Conditioning) $f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=$
#### (*Joint PDFs*) $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{Y}(y)f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)$.
#### (*Marginality*) $f_{X}(x)=\displaystyle\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}f_{Y}(y)f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)dy$.

#### (*Continuous Bayes'*) $f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\displaystyle\frac{f_{X}(x)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)}{f_{Y}(y)}=\frac{f_{X}(x)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)}{\displaystyle\int f_{X}(t)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid t)dt}.$
#### (*Independence*) R.V.'s $X,Y$ are independent iff $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X}(x) \cdot y_{Y}(y)$ $\forall x,y$.

#### (*Joint CDFs*)

#### (*Sum Convolution*) If $W=X+Y$, $f_{W}(w)=\large\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}f_{X}(x)f_{Y}(w-x)dx$.

270.title: 2.2c.3 Exponential Distribution
270.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.2 Probability Distributions/2.6c Continuous Distributions/2.2c.3 Exponential Distribution.md
270.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c.3 Exponential Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/05 12:41:58","modified":"2025/08/09 16:39:45"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Exponential Distribution
>A non-negative continuous random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Exponential distribution** $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ with parameter $\lambda > 0$, defined by the [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|probability density function]]
>$$f_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda x} &\text{if} \enspace  x \geq 0 \\ 0 &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
>The CDF for the Exponential distribution is $F_{X}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$.
>
>The Exponential distribution represents the waiting time until the first occurrence of an event in a process where events occur continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate $\lambda$.
>
>Additionally, akin to the discrete [[2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution|Geometric distribution]], the exponential distribution is the only continuous PDF that has the **memoryless property**, which states that the probability of needing more than $m$ additional trials to get the first success is independent of the $k$ trials that have already been conducted, such that
>$$\mathbb{P}[X > k + m \mid X > k] = \mathbb{P}[X > m],$$
>showing that whether or not you start fresh or you have already had $k$ failures, the chance of needing more than $m$ additional trials remains the same.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}(X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda))= \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}(X \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda))=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}$.
#### (*Discretization*) If $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$, $\lfloor X \rfloor + 1 \sim \operatorname{Geom}(1-e^{-\lambda})$.
We know that the CDF of $W$ is $F_{W}(w)=1-e^{-\lambda w}$. Then, $F_{X}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \in \mathbb{N}$. We are trying to find the probability of W falling in the interval $[x, x+1)$ (since this continuous interval represents the floor of values of $x$). As such,
$$\begin{align}
f_{X}(x)&=F_{X}(x+1)-F_{X}(x) \\
&=1-e^{-\lambda(x+1)}-1+e^{-\lambda x} \\
&=e^{-\lambda x}(1-e^{-\lambda})\\
&=(e^{-\lambda})^x(1-e^{-\lambda}),
\end{align}$$
which represents a geometric distribution with $p=1-e^{-\lambda}$ by definition.

# Examples
>[!example] Exponential Order Statistics
>Let $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n} \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{i})$ be mutually independent. 
>>[!example]- What is the distribution of $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$?
>>Observe that since each variable $X_{i}$ denotes the time at which the $i$-th event occurs, then $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$ denotes the time until an event occurs. As such, the minimum will be much smaller than just a single $X_{i}$.
>>
>>Think about this in survival time terms. The survival time of $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$ is
>>$$\begin{align}
>>P(\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) > t) &= P(X_{1} > t, \ldots, X_{n} > t) \\
>>&= P(X_{1}>t) \times \ldots \times P(X_{n} > t) \\
>>&= \prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\lambda_{i} t} \\
>>&= e^{-t \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}},
>>\end{align}$$
>>and therefore $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) \sim \operatorname{Exp}\left( \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} \right)$.
>>
>>Think of it like $n$ independent phone lines, each getting random calls at their own rate $\lambda_i$. The time until the very first phone rings is faster because all the lines are “competing”–together, they get calls at the combined rate $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_n$.
>
>Now let $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3} \sim_{\text{iid}} \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ be mutually independent.
>>[!example]- Given that $\min(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}) = m$, what is the probability that the difference between the median and the smallest is at least $s$?


$$$$

271.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c.2 Continuous Uniform Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 15:27:36","modified":"2025/06/06 15:31:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Continuous Uniform Distribution
>A continuous random variable $X$ with $a<b$ follows the **Uniform distribution** $X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ if it is equally likely to take any value in the interval $[a,b]$.  Formally, the Uniform distribution of a random variable is given by the PDF
>$$f_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a} & \text{if } x \in [a, b], \\
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}$$
>so that every subinterval of $[a,b]$ of the same length has the same probability.
>
>Then, the CDF of $X$ is given by
>$$F_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}
0 & x \leq a, \\
\dfrac{x-a}{b-a} & x \in (a, b), \\
1 & x \geq b.
\end{cases}$$

# Examples
>[!example] Meeting Probability
>Two bankers each arrive at the station at some uniformly random time between 5:00AM and 6:00AM. They stay exactly 5 minutes, and then leave.
>>[!example]- What is the probability that they meet on a given day?
>>Let $X, Y \sim_\text{iid}\text{Uniform}(0, 60)$ represent the exact time (in minutes) of each banker's arrival. We are trying to solve for the constraint $|X-Y|\leq 5$, such that $p=\mathbb{P}(|X-Y| \leq 5)$. With this inequality, we get $Y \geq X-5$ and $Y \leq X+5$. The following is a visual representation of the area between our two lines:
>>```tikz
>>\usepackage{pgfplots}
>>
>>\begin{document}
>>\begin{tikzpicture}
>>  \begin{axis}[
>>    width=8cm, height=8cm,
>>    xmin=0, xmax=60,
>>    ymin=0, ymax=60,
>>    axis equal image,
>>    xlabel={$X$},
>>    ylabel={$Y$},
>>    ylabel style={rotate=-90},
>>    title={Region $|X-Y| \leq 5$}
>>  ]
>>    % Shade the region |x - y| < 5 by plotting its polygonal boundary:
>>    \addplot [
>>      draw=none,
>>      fill=black,
>>      opacity=0.1,
>>    ] coordinates {
>>      (0,0)   % lower‐left corner of the square
>>      (5,0)   % intersection of y = x - 5 with y=0
>>      (60,55) % intersection of y = x - 5 with x=60
>>      (60,60) % upper‐right corner of the square (still inside |x-y|<5)
>>      (55,60) % intersection of y = x + 5 with y=60
>>      (0,5)   % intersection of y = x + 5 with x=0
>>      (0,0)   % back to (0,0) to close the polygon
>>    };
>>
>>    % Draw the boundary lines y = x + 5 and y = x - 5:
>>    \addplot [
>>      domain=0:60,
>>      samples=2,
>>      thick,
>>    ] {x + 5} node[midway, sloped, above] {$Y = X + 5$};
>>
>>    \addplot [
>>      domain=0:60,
>>      samples=2,
>>      thick,
>>    ] {x - 5} node[midway, sloped, below] {$Y = X - 5$};
>>
>>    % Draw the square [0,60]×[0,60]:
>>    \draw[black] (axis cs:0,0) rectangle (axis cs:60,60);
>>  \end{axis}
>>\end{tikzpicture}
>>\end{document}
>>```
>>To find the area between the curves, we can integrate and remove the extra parts. However, an easier method would be to think of the unshaded area as two triangles, each with area $\frac{1}{2}55^2$, and subtract them from the total area of $60^2$. That area of the inequality is
>>$$60^2-55^2=(60-55)(60+55)=575.$$
>>Since our sample space has an area of $60^2=3600,$
>>$$\mathbb{P}(|X-Y| \leq 5) = \frac{575}{3600}=\frac{23}{144}.$$

273.title: 2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution
273.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.2 Probability Distributions/2.2b Discrete Distributions/2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution.md
273.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:56:00","modified":"2025/08/06 13:17:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Geometric Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 1$ follows the **Geometric distribution** $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$ if it represents the number of trials required to obtain the *first success* in a sequence of independent [[2.2b.3 Bernoulli Distribution|Bernoulli trials]]. Formally, the Geometric distribution of a random variable is given by the PMF,
>$$p_{X}(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p,$$
>where each trial has a probability $p$ of success.
>
>The geometric distribution is the only discrete distribution that is **memoryless**, meaning that the probability of needing more than $m$ additional trials to get the first success is independent of the $k$ trials that have already been conducted. Formally,
>$$\mathbb{P}[X > k + m \mid X > k] = \mathbb{P}[X > m],$$
>showing that whether or not you start fresh or you have already had $k$ failures, the chance of needing more than $m$ additional trials remains the same.

# Intuition
I honestly cannot help you if you don't understand the PMF for the geometric distribution. There is a $p^1$ factor, which indicates that there is only a single success. It is self-descriptive.

However, when I first learned about the memoryless property (i.e. right now), I was confused. So let's get through it together. We have $k$ as the number of initial (failed) trials, and $m$ as the sequential number of trials to get a single success. Then,
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[X > k+m \mid X > k] &= \frac{\mathbb{P}[X > k+m \cap X > k]}{\mathbb{P}[X > k]} \\ 
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}[X > k+m]}{\mathbb{P}[X > k]} \\
&= \frac{(1-p)^{k+m}}{(1-p)^k} \\
&= (1-p)^m \\
&= \mathbb{P}[X > m].
\end{align}$$
where the tail probability of the Geometric random variable is given by $\mathbb{P}[X > x]=(1-p)^x$.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Geom}(p)]=\frac{1}{p}$.
We start by setting up our equation for solving the expectation using the [[2.6b.2 Tail Sum Formula|tail sum formula]] by saying that
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] &= \sum^{\infty}_{j=i}\mathbb{P}[X=j] \\
&=\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}p(1-p)^{j-1} \\
&=\frac{p}{1-p}\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}(1-p)^{j} \\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Using the definition of the infinite geometric sum $S_n=\sum^{\infty}_{i=0}a_ir^i=\frac{a_1}{1-r}$ with $a_1=(1-p)^i$ and $r=1-p$ (a is not $1$ since geometric series start at $j=1$, and it is not $1-p$ since $j=i$, we are led to,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] &= \frac{p}{1-p}\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}(1-p)^{j} \\
&= \frac{p}{1-p}\frac{(1-p)^i}{1-(1-p)} \\
&= (1-p)^{i-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
This means that for large $n$, the probability that we need $i$ trials or more before the first success is determined by $\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] = (1-p)^{i-1}$. Then the probability that we will get a success in less than $i$ trials is $\mathbb{P}[X < i] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[X \geq i]$. 

Let's put this in perspective using a biased coin with a probability of heads $p=\frac{1}{3}$. The probability that we need 1 toss or more before the first success is 1. That we will need 2 or more is $1-p=\frac{2}{3}$. The probability that we will need 3 or more tosses before a success is $(1-p)^2=\frac{4}{9}$. The probability that we will get a successful trial before 3 tosses (so in the first 2 tosses) is $1-\frac{4}{9}=\frac{5}{9}$. Looking at the outcome space for 3 trials or success, we can see why:
$$\Upomega=\set{TTT, TTH, TH, H}$$
Here, $\mathbb{P}[X=3]=\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{3})^2=\frac{4}{27}$. This is confirmed by $\mathbb{P}[X=3]=\mathbb{P}[TTH]$. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[X < 3]=\mathbb{P}[TH]+\mathbb{P}[H]=\frac{1}{3}\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{5}{9}$, which is equal to $1 - (1-p)^2=\frac{5}{9}$.

We now calculate the expectation of the geometric distribution using the [[2.6b.2 Tail Sum Formula|tail sum formula]] and the previously introduced infinite geometric sum as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}(1-p)^{i-1} \\
&= \frac{(1-p)^{1-1}}{1-(1-p)} \\
&= \frac{1}{p}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Therefore, $\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}$ for a geometric distribution.

#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Geom}(x)]=\frac{1-p}{p^2}$
We already know that $\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}$. Therefore, using $Var[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-E[X]^2$, we only need to find $E[X^2]$. We proceed as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X^2] &= \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
# Examples
>[!example] Class Enrollment

>[!example]  Laundry Time
>To avoid doing laundry too often, Marcus creates a system. Each night, he labels one of his shirts as the "dirtiest." In the morning, he randomly picks one of his clean shirts to wear. If he happens to wear the dirtiest one, he throws it in the dirty pile at the end of the day (shirts in the dirty pile aren’t reused). Once all his shirts end up dirty, Marcus does laundry. That night, he again designates one shirt as the dirtiest, and the cycle begins anew.
>
>>[!example]- If Marcus has $n$ shirts, what is the expected number of days that transpire between laundry events?
>>Observe that the cycle can be broken into $n$ phases. During phase $i$:
>>1. Marcus labels one of the remaining $n-i+1$ shirts as the dirtiest.
>>2. In the morning, he picks one of those $n-i+1$ shirts.
>>3. 
>>The number of days it takes for Marcus to throw each shirt in the dirty pile can be expressed as the sum $D=\sum^{n}_{i=1}S_{i}$, where $S_{i} \sim \text{Geom}\left( \dfrac{1}{n-i+1} \right)$. This probability works solely because once Marcus labels a shirt as the "dirtiest," no other shirt can claim this position before the "dirtiest" is thrown in the dirty pile.

274.title: 2.2b.4 Binomial Distribution
274.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.2 Probability Distributions/2.2b Discrete Distributions/2.2b.4 Binomial Distribution.md
274.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.4 Binomial Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 16:48:10","modified":"2025/08/08 19:57:49"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Binomial Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Binomial distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ if it represents the number of **successes** in (i.e., the sum of) $n$ independent [[2.2b.3 Bernoulli Distribution|Bernoulli trials]], where each trial has a probability $p$ of success. Formally, the Binomial distribution of a random variable is given by the PMF,
>$$p_{X}(x)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x},$$
>where $\binom{n}{x}=\frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}$ is the binomial coefficient, $p^{k}$ is the probability of exactly $k$ successes, and $(1-p)^{n-x}$ is the probability of the remaining trials being failures.


# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)]=np.$
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)]=np(1-p)$.
$$\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(X) &= \mathbb{E}(X^2) - \mathbb{E}(X)^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}(I_{i}) + \sum_{i \ne j}^{n}\mathbb{E}(I_{i}I_{j}) - n^2p^2 \\
&= np + n(n-1)p^2 - n^2p^2 \\
&= np + n^2p^2-np^2-n^2p^2 \\
&= np-np^2 \\
&= np(1-p).
\end{align}$$
Since there are exactly $n(n-1)$ ordered distinct pairs of $i, j$ and $I_{i} \sim_{\text{iid}} \text{Ber}(p)$, so $\mathbb{E}(I_{i}I_{j})=\mathbb{E}(I_{i})\mathbb{E}(I_{j})$ for $i \neq j$.

#### (*MGF*) $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=(1-p+pe^t)^n$.
#### (Sum) Let $X=\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$, where $X_{i} \sim_{\text{iid}} \text{Bin}(n_{i}, p)$. Then, $X \sim \text{Bin}\left( \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}n_{i}, \; p \right)$.

# Examples
>[!example] Packet Routing
>Consider a system with $n$ inputs and $n$ outputs. At each input, a packet appears independently with probability $p$. If a packet appears, it is destined for one of the $n$ outputs uniformly randomly, independently of the other packets.
>
>
>>[!example]- Let $X$ denote the number of packets destined for the first output. What is the distribution of $X$?
>>Let $A$ be the event that the packet appears, and let $B_{i}$ be the event that the packet hits the $i$-th output. Then, $\mathbb{P}(A \cap B_{i})=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B_{i})=p\frac{1}{n}=\frac{p}{n}$ by independence. The distribution of $X$ can be modeled as $\operatorname{Bin}(n, \frac{p}{n})$. There are $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, and each trial has the same probability of success $\frac{p}{n}$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the probability of a *collision* (that is, more than one packet heading to the same output)?
>>Let $X=X_{1}+X_{2}+\ldots+X_{n}$ denote the total number of packets, where each $X_{i}$ denotes the number of packets destined for the $i$.-th output. Then, $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, p)$, since every packet is generated by one of the $n$ inputs with probability $p$ and goes to exactly one output with probability $\frac{1}{n}$, so counting the packets at each output and summing them gives the total number of packets generated. We have that:
>>$$$$

275.title: 2.2b.8 Poisson Distribution
275.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.2 Probability Distributions/2.2b Discrete Distributions/2.2b.8 Poisson Distribution.md
275.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.8 Poisson Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:56:26","modified":"2025/06/06 17:15:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Poisson Distribution
>A discrete random variable follows the **Poisson distribution** $X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)$ if it represents the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, given that these events occur independently and at a constant average rate $\lambda$. Formally, the Poisson distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!},$$
>where if $\lambda < 1$, the PMF is monotonically decreasing, and if $\lambda > 1$, the PMF first increases then decreases as $x \to \infty$.
# Intuition
The Poisson distribution is used in "rare" events such as in phone call disconnections, radioactive emissions, crossovers in chromosomes, and calculating the number of cases of a disease. This model is appropriate when some event can be assumed to happen randomly with a constant density in a continuous region (of time or space), such that occurrences in disjoint subregions are independent (each event is considered a separate occurrence). 
# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)]=\lambda$.
We calculate the expectation of a poisson random variable using the Taylor series expansion $e^x=\sum^{\infty}_{n=0}\frac{x^n}{n!}$,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=0}i \times \mathbb{P}[X=i] \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}i\frac{\uplambda^i}{i!}e^{-\uplambda} \\
&= \lambda e^{-\uplambda}\sum^{\infty}_{i=1}\frac{\uplambda^{i-1}}{(i-1)!} \\
&= \lambda e^{-\uplambda}e^\uplambda \\
&= \lambda
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Note that we omit the 0th term due to it being equal to 0.
#### (*Variance*) $Var[X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)]=\lambda$.
We already know that $\mathbb{E}[X]=\uplambda$. Therefore we need to calculate $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]$ (0 is again trivial in the summation, as well as 1 this time):
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=2}i(i-1)\frac{\lambda^i}{i!}e^{-\lambda} \\
&= \lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum^{\infty}_{i=2}\frac{\lambda^{i-2}}{(i-2)!} \\
&= \lambda^2
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Knowing this, we can calculate the variance from the expansion $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]$
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
Var(X)&=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2 \\
&= \uplambda^2+\uplambda-\uplambda^2 \\
&= \uplambda
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
#### (*Sum*) If $X \sim \operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ and $Y \sim \operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$, then $X+Y=\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda + \mu)$.

#### (*Binomial Approximation*)
# Examples
>[!example] Probability of Typos on a Page
>Suppose we are writing an article and make on average 1 typo per page. We can then model a Poisson distribution with $\lambda=1$. So the probability that we make 5 typos on a page is
>$$\mathbb{P}[X=5]=\frac{1^5}{5!}e^{-1}=\frac{1}{120e} \approx 0.003.$$
>Now suppose the article has 200 pages. If the number of typos on each page is independent, then the probability that there is at least one page with exactly 5 typos is
>$$
>\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
>\mathbb{P}[\exists \text{a page with exactly 5 typos}] &= 1 - \mathbb{P}[\text{every page has } \neq 5 \text{ typos}] \\
>&= 1-\prod^{200}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[\text{page i has } \neq 5 \text{ typos}] \\
>&= 1-\prod^{200}_{i=1}(1 - \mathbb{P}[X=5]) \\
>&= 1-\left(1 - \frac{1}{120e}\right)^{200} \approx 0.46
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
>$$

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:50:13","modified":"2025/06/06 17:16:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Hypergeometric Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Hypergeometric distribution** $X \sim \text{Hypergeom}(N, K, n)$ if it represents the number of successes in a sample of size $n$ drawn without replacement from a finite population of $N$ items that contains $K$ successes. Formally, the Hypergeometric distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=\frac{\binom{K}{x}\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}}=\frac{\frac{K!}{(K-x)!}\frac{(N-K)!}{(N-K-(n-x))!}}{\frac{N!}{(N-n)!}},$$
>where $x$ is the number of successes in the sample and satisfies $\max(0, n)-(N-K) \leq x \leq \min(N, k)$.
# Intuition
We want to draw $n$ balls from a box of $N=B+W$ balls without replacement. Consider a case of a sequence $\upomega$ of n draws where the first $k$ balls are black and the next $n-k$ balls are white. Then, the probability of this particular sequence will be:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[\upomega] &= \frac{B}{N} \times \frac{B-1}{N-1} \times...\times \frac{B-k+1}{N-k+1} \times \frac{W}{N-k} \times \frac{W-1}{N-k-1} \times...\times \frac{W-(n-k)+1}{N-n+1} \\ &= \frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{W!}{(W-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}} \\ &= \frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{(N-B)!}{(N-B-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Because of this, each sample point of a Hypergeometric [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|distribution]] can be viewed as binomial without repetition.

Now, in order to find all distinct sequences with $n$ draws of $k$ black balls and $n-k$ white balls, we need to multiply by $\binom{n}{k}$, leading to:
$$\mathbb{P}[X=k]=\binom{n}{k}\frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{(N-B)!}{(N-B-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}}=\frac{\binom{B}{k}\binom{N-B}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}$$
If we had white, black and orange balls, then we need another variable, say $j$, for the number of draws of white balls, and the rest would go to orange.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \operatorname{Hypergeom}(N, K, n)]=\frac{nK}{N}$
#### (*Variance*) $\operatorname{Var}(X \sim \operatorname{Hypergeom}(N, K, n))=\frac{nK(N-K)(N-n)}{N^2(N-1)}.$

> [!note] Bernoulli Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \in \{ 0, 1 \}$ follows the **Bernoulli distribution** $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$ if it represents a **single trial** with binary outcomes. Formally, the Bernoulli distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}p & \text{if } x=1, \\ 1-p & \text{if } x=0, \end{cases}$$
>where $p$ is the probability of a successful outcome.
### Explanation.
The Bernoulli [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|distribution]] is used for probabilities where the event either happens, or does not happen. Following this, the random variable can only take two values (1 or 0).

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)]=p.$
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)]=p(1-p)$.

280.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/04 01:27:20","modified":"2025/06/06 17:15:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Probability Mass Function (PMF)
>The probability [[2.2a Probability Distribution|distribution]] of a discrete random variable $X$ is fully described by a non-negative **probability mass function (PMF)** $p_{X}: \mathcal{X} \to [0,1]$, formally defined as
>$$p_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}[X=x],$$
>where $\set{ X=x } \in \mathcal{F}$ is the event consisting of all outcomes where the random variable $X$ equals the specific value $x \in \mathcal{X}$.
>
>The cumulative probability that $X$ takes on a value less than or equal to $x$ in the PMF is given by the monotonically non-decreasing **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** $F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$, formally defined as
>$$F_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}[X \leq x]=\sum^{}_{k \leq x}p_{X}(k),$$
>implying that the PDF is the rate of change of the CDF, $p_{X}(x)=F_{X}(x)-F_{X}(x-1)$.
>>[!warning] PMFs Sum to One
>>For a PMF to meet the sum-to-one criterion of any probability function,
>>$$\sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X}(x)=1.$$

# Properties
#### (*Joint Distribution*) $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}[X=x \space \cap \space Y=y]$.
#### (*Conditionality*) $p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\cfrac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{Y}(y)}$.
#### (*Marginality*) $p_{X}(x)=\sum\limits_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p_{X,Y}(x,y)$.
#### (*Independence*) If $X,Y$ are independent, then $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{X}(x) \cdot p_{Y}(y)$ and $p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=p_{X}(x)$.

281.title: 2.5b Second-Order Moments
281.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.3 Functions of Random Variables/2.5b Second-Order Moments.md
281.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5b Second-Order Moments]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/08 14:25:48","modified":"2025/08/08 14:28:53"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Variance, Covariance, Correlation (Second-Order Moments)
>The **variance** of a random variable is its second central moment, and measures the spread of values around its [[2.5a Expectation|expected value]], such that
>$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2] - E[X]^2.$$
>
>The square root of variance, $\sigma_{X}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$, is known as the **standard deviation** of $X$.
>
>Given random variables $X, Y$, the variance of their sum can generally be expressed as
>$$\operatorname{Var}(\alpha X + \beta Y + k)=\alpha^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+\beta^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\alpha\beta\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y),$$
>where $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ is the second mixed central moment of $X$ and $Y$, such that
>$$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])]=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y],$$
>and serves as a measure of the linear association between them (i.e., negative correlation indicates inverse relationship and vice-versa). Note that if $X, Y$ are independent, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$ (but not the other way around).
>
>A measure for covariance normalized by the product of their standard deviations is given by the unit-less **correlation coefficient**. Formally,
>$$\rho_{X,Y} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)},$$
>where $-1 \leq \rho_{X,Y} \leq 1$, such that  $\rho_{X,Y}=0$ indicates no relationship between $X$ and $Y$.
>
>>[!warning] Non-Negativity of Variance
>>Since $(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \geq 0$ for all $X$, the variance of any random variable is always non-negative.

# Intuition


# Properties
#### (*Cond. Variance*) Any $X,Y$ satisfy $\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y = y)= \mathbb{E}\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y])^2 \mid Y\right]$

#### (*Total Variance*) Any $X,Y$ satisfy $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])$.
#### (*Linearity of Covariance*).
# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Optimal Hedge Ratio
>You just bought one share of stock $A$ and want to hedge it by shorting stock $B$. A short is an investment strategy where you borrow stock and sell it immediately rather than buy it, in the hopes that you will be able to buy it and return it at a lower price in the future. Assume that the variance of stock $A$'s return is $\sigma_{A}^2$, the variance of stock $B$'s return is $\sigma_{B}^2$, and their correlation coefficient is $\rho$.
>
>>[!example]- How many shares of $B$ should you short to minimize the variance of the hedged position? 
>>Denote $P=A-kB$ as the value of your portfolio. We are trying to solve for $k^*=\arg\min\limits_{k}\operatorname{Var}(P)$. We proceed as follows:
>>$$\begin{align}
\frac{\delta}{\delta k}\operatorname{Var}(P)&= \frac{\delta}{\delta k}[\sigma^2_{A}+k^2\sigma^2_{B}-2k\rho \sigma_{A} \sigma_{B}] \\
&= 2k\sigma^2_{B}-2\rho\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B} \\
&= 0 \iff k^*= \rho\frac{\sigma_{A}}{\sigma_{B}},
\end{align}$$
>>which is known as the Beta coefficient in portfolio management, and is used to evaluate the relative risk of stock $A$ to stock $B$.

>[!example] (Hard) Elevator Variance
>A building has n upper floors numbered $1, 2, \ldots, n$, plus a ground floor $G$. At the ground floor, $m$ people get on the elevator together, and each person gets off at one of the $n$ upper floors uniformly at random and independently of everyone else.
>>[!example]- What is the variance of the number of floors the elevator does not stop at?
>>Let $I_{j}$ be the indicator that nobody gets off at floor $j$. Then, let $N=\sum^{n}_{j=1}I_{j}$ be the number of floors that the elevator does not stop at. The probability that a person exits on each form is uniform with a value of $\dfrac{1}{n}$. Since each person exits independently, then the probability that none of the $m$ people exit on each floor is $\left ( 1-\dfrac{1}{n} \right )^m$. As such,
>>$$\mathbb{E}(N)=\sum^{n}_{j=1}\mathbb{E}(I_{j})=\sum^{n}_{j=1}\left ( 1-\dfrac{1}{n} \right )^m=n\left ( 1-\dfrac{1}{n} \right )^m.$$
>>
>>Then, $\operatorname{Var}(N)=\mathbb{E}(X^2)-E(X)^2=n\left ( 1-\dfrac{1}{n} \right )^m - n^2\left ( 1-\dfrac{1}{n} \right )^{2m}.$$

282.title: 2.5a Expectation
282.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.3 Functions of Random Variables/2.5a Expectation.md
282.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5a Expectation]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/04 16:34:02","modified":"2025/08/08 15:41:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Expectation (LOTUS)
>The **expectation** of a random variable represents its probability-weighted average value. The generalized expectation function can be given by the **Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)**:
>- The expectation of a discrete random variable $X=g(Y)$ with a range $\mathcal{X}$, where $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, is generally defined as,
>$$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}x \cdot p_{X}(x)=\sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}g(y) \cdot p_{X}(g(y)).$$
>
>- Similarly, the expectation of a continuous random variable $X=g(Y)$ is defined as
>$$\mathbb{E}(X)=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x \cdot f_{X}(x)dx=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}g(y) \cdot f_{X}(x)dy.$$
# Intuition
The expectation can be seen as the average or mean of a probability distribution. It is the most expected value given all probabilities.

# Properties
#### (*Linearity*) Any $X,Y$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\alpha X+\beta Y+\gamma]=\alpha \mathbb{E}(X)+\beta \mathbb{E}(Y)+\gamma.$
The linearity of expectation can be proved by taking $\mathbb{P}[X=a]=\sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega}\mathbb{P}[\upomega]$ (sum to one rule). Then taking the definition of a random variable, we get:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{}_{a \in \mathscr{A}}a \times \mathbb{P}[X=a] \\ 
&= \sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega} X(\upomega) \times \mathbb{P}[\upomega]
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Then, for random variables $X$ and $Y$,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X+Y] &= \sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega}(X+Y)(\upomega) \times \mathbb{P}[\upomega] \\ 
&= \sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega} (X(\upomega)+Y(\upomega)) \times \mathbb{P}[\upomega] \\
&= \sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega}X(\upomega) \times \mathbb{P}[\upomega] + \sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega}Y(\upomega) \times \mathbb{P}[\upomega] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X]+\mathbb{E}[Y]
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Why does the probability $\mathbb{P}[\upomega]$ not change with the amount of variables? Well, because we simplify each event $X=a$ into $\upomega \in \Upomega$. All of the above stems from this simple fact, since by the definition of the random variable, $\set{\upomega \in \Upomega : X(\upomega) = a}$ and $\set{(a,\mathbb{P}[X=a]):a \in \mathscr{A}}$. From there, we replace $a$ with $X(\upomega)$, and therefore $\mathbb{P}[X=a]$ with $\mathbb{P}[\upomega]$.
#### (*Tail Formula*) Any $X \geq 0$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X]=\begin{dcases} \sum^{\infty}_{k=1}\mathbb{P}[X \geq k], \\ \int^{\infty}_{0}\mathbb{P}(X \geq k)dk.\end{dcases}$
For a random variable $X$ that takes values $i \in \set{0, 1, 2,...}$, each with probability $p_i$,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= (0 \times p_0)+(1 \times p_1)+(2 \times p_2)+...+((i-1) \times p_{i-1})+(i \times p_i) \\
&= (p_1+p_2+...+p_{i-1}+p_i)+(p_2+...+p_{i-1}+p_i)+...+(p_{i-1}+p_i)+p_i \\
&= \mathbb{P}[X \geq 1]+\mathbb{P}[X \geq 2]+...+\mathbb{P}[X \geq i-1]+\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[X \geq i].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$


#### (*Independence*) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\mathbb{E}[XY]= \mathbb{E}[X]\cdot \mathbb{E}[Y]$.
#### (*Conditionality*) $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y] = \begin{dcases}\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}x \cdot p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), \\ \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x \cdot f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)dx.\end{dcases}$
#### (*Iterated/Total Expectation*)  $\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]]=\begin{dcases}\sum\limits_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p_{Y}(y)\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y], \\ \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}f_{Y}(y)\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]dy.\end{dcases}$

#### (*Wald's Identity*) If $X=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}$, then $\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}] \cdot \mathbb{E}[Y]$.

283.title: 2.5a Expectation
283.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.3 Functions of Random Variables/2.5a Expectation.md
283.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5a Expectation]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/04 16:34:02","modified":"2025/08/08 15:41:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) #### (*Jensen's Inequality*) Any convex $\varphi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $\mathscr{\varphi}(\mathbb{E}[X]) \leq \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]$.

# Examples
>[!example] (Expectation, Indicator Variables) Connecting Ropes
>You have $n$ identical lengths of rope, each with two loose ends. You toss all ropes into a bag, swirl them around, then–without looking–pull out two ends and tie them together.
>>[!example]- What is the probability that the two ends you just tied belong to the _same_ rope?
>>Before grabbing any rope, we have $2n$ possible ends to grab. After grabbing the first end, we grab another one of the $2n-1$ ends. This gives us $2n(2n-1)$ possible outcomes for grabbing two random ends.
>>
>>Consider the possibility of grabbing the same rope. Before grabbing any end, we can blindly pick any one of the $2n$ ropes. However, after we grab our first end, there is exactly $1$ way of grabbing the other end of the same rope. Therefore, there are exactly $2n$ ways of grabbing the same rope. This makes intuitive sense: you can grab either ends of the same rope in the beginning, and then grab the second end. Therefore, we have:
>>$$\mathbb{P}(\text{Same rope in first attempt})=\frac{2n}{2n(2n-1)}=\frac{1}{2n-1}.$$
>
>>[!example]- If you continue this process until all ends are connected, what is the expected total number of times you ever tie the two ends of the same rope together?
>>Consider the following indicator variable:
>>$$I_{i}=\begin{cases}
1 & \text{the two ends of rope } i \text{ are paired}, \\
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}$$
>>where $\mathbb{P}(I_{i}=1)=\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$ for all $i$. Then, $N=\sum^{n}_{i=1}I_{i}$ is the number of self-loops after all ends have been tied. As such,
>>$$\mathbb{E}(N)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{E}(I_{i})=\frac{n}{2n-1}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the expected number of total loops after there are no loose ends left?
>>We start with $2n$ loose ends and immediately tie 2 ends, yielding $2n-1$ loose ends. We proceed until there are no loose ends left. Let $\mathbb{E}[T_{n}]$ represent the number of total loops given $n$ ropes.
>>

>[!example] (Iterated Expectation) Dice Game
>You roll a dice. For each roll, you are paid the face value. If a roll gives 4, 5, or 6, you can roll the dice again. Once you get 1, 2, or 3, the game stops.
>>[!example]- What is the expected payoff of this game?
>>Let $X_{n}$ be your cumulative expected payoff in round $n$, and let $C_{i-1} \sim \text{Ber}(1/2)$ be an indicator variable showing the outcome of your last throw (i.e., whether you rolled 4, 5, 6 or not). Then,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}(X)&=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(X \mid C)) \\
&=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}(X \mid C=0) + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}(X \mid C=1) \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1+2+3}{3}+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(\frac{4+5+6}{3}+\mathbb{E}(X)\right) \\
&= 7.
\end{align}$$
>> We add $\mathbb{E}(X)$ to our payoff on the right hand side, since you continue playing if you roll 4, 5, or 6 for an indefinite amount of time.

>[!example] Ace Hunt
>Ace Hunt is a solo “table game” played with a freshly shuffled 52-card deck placed face-down in the center. You (the dealer) turn over cards one at a time into a single community pile, pausing only when the very first Ace appears; at that moment the hand ends and the total number of cards revealed is recorded. The person whose guess is closest to the recorded number of total cards wins.
>>[!example]- What is the probability that you will need to turn over exactly $k$ cards before revealing the first Ace?
>>Let $X_{n}$ denote the even that the $n$-th card turned over is an Ace. Then, 
>>$$\mathbb{P}\left(X_{k+1} \;\middle|\; \bigcap_{i=1}^{k} X_{i} = 0\right)=\frac{4}{52-k}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the expected number of cards you must expose to see the first Ace?
>>Denote $X$ as the number of cards turned over before the first ace. Then, $X=1+\sum^{48}_{i=1}X_{i}$ (since there are at most 48 non-Ace cards drawn before the first ace, where
>>$$X_{i} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{i-th card is not an Ace} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$


>[!example] Coupon Collector
>Let there be $n$ distinct coupon types, labeled $1,2,\dots,n$.  You collect coupons from cereal boxes one at a time; on each trial you receive exactly one coupon, and each type is always equally likely.
>>[!example]- If you want to collect a complete set of coupons with at least one of each type, how many boxes on average are needed to complete the set?
>>Let $X_{i}$ represent the number of additional (marginal) draws needed to collect the $i$-th coupon type after $i-1$ types have been collected. Then, $X=\sum^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$ is the total number of coupons needed for all $n$ coupon types to be collected.
>>
>>Given that $i-1$ coupons are collected, a new coupon will be a different type with probability $1-\frac{i-1}{n}$. Since each $X_{i}$ is a first-success measure, $X_{i} \sim \text{Geom}\left( \dfrac{n-i+1}{n} \right)$. As such,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}(X) &= \sum^{n}_{i=1} \frac{1}{p} \\
&= \sum^{n}_{i=1} \frac{n}{n-i+1} \\
&= n\left( \frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n-1}+\ldots+\frac{1}{2}+1 \right) \\
&=nH_{n}
\end{align}$$
>
>>[!example]- If you have collected $k$ coupons, what is the expected number of distinct coupon types?
>>Let $X=\sum^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$ represent the present coupon types, such that $X_{i}$ indicates whether the $i$-th coupon type is present. The probability of a coupon type that is NOT the $i$-th type is exactly $\dfrac{n-1}{n}$, and therefore $\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=0)=\left(\dfrac{n-1}{n}\right)^k$ indicates that in the sequence of $k$ draws, the $i$-th coupon does not appear once. We can express $X$ as a sum of $X_{i} \sim \text{Ber}\left(1-\left[\dfrac{n-1}{n}\right]^k\right)$, such that
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}(X) &= \sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{E}(X_{i}) \\
&=\sum^{n}_{i=1} \left(1-\left[\dfrac{n-1}{n}\right]^k\right) \\
&= n\left(1-\left[\dfrac{n-1}{n}\right]^k\right).
\end{align}$$

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/17 01:49:33","modified":"2025/02/23 22:36:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Moment Generating Function (MGF)
>A **moment generating function (MGF)** encodes all of the *moments* $\mathbb{E}[X^n]$ of a [[2.1 Random Variables|random variable]] into a single function, making it easier to study its distributional properties. Formally, the moment-generating function of a random variable $X$ is defined as
>$$M_{X}(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \begin{dcases}\sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}e^{tx}p_{X}(x) & x \text{ discrete}, \\ \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}e^{tx}f_{X}(x)dx & x \text{ continuous}.\end{dcases}$$
>The MGF of $X$ can then be used to compute the $n$-th moment of $X$, such that
>$$\frac{d^n}{dx^n}M_{X}(t) \bigg |_{x=0}=\mathbb{E}[X^n].$$

# Properties
#### (Linearity) If $Y=\alpha\\X+\beta$, then $M_{Y}(t)=e^{t\beta}M_{X}(\alpha x)$.

#### (Independence) If $X,Y$ are independent, then $M_{X+Y}(t)=M_{X}(t)M_{Y}(t)$.

286.title: 1.9 Union Bound
286.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/1. Laws of Probability/1.9 Union Bound.md
286.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.9 Union Bound]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/02 23:06:24","modified":"2025/08/07 19:09:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Union Bound
>For any events $A_1,\ldots,A_N \subseteq \Omega$ in the same probability space, the **union bound** states that the probability of the union of the events is at most the sum of their individual probabilities. Formally,
>$$\mathbb{P}\Big[\bigcup^{N}_{i=1}A_i\Big] \leq \sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[A_i].$$
# Intuition
Let's consider why the union bound is true:
1. In the case of [[1.2 Mutually Exclusive Events|mutually exclusive events]], their union is exactly equal to the sum of their marginal probabilities.
2. In the case of all other events, per the [[1.8 Inclusion-Exclusion Principle|inclusion-exclusion principle]], their union is less than their marginal probabilities.

There are no scenarios where the probability of the union exceeds the sum of the individual probabilities. This would imply the inclusion of probability mass outside the defined events, which violates the basic principles of both the union operation and probability as a whole. If you are still unsure, draw a Venn diagram and think about it!


# Examples
>[!example] Matching Beads
>Sinho has a set of 2n beads (n ≥2) of n different colors, such that there are two beads of each color.

He wants to give out pairs of beads as gifts to all the other n−1 TAs, and plans on keeping the final

pair for himself (since he is, after all, also a TA). To do so, he first chooses two beads at random to

give to the first TA he sees. Then he chooses two beads at random from those remaining to give to

the second TA he sees. He continues giving each TA he sees two beads chosen at random from his

remaining beads until he has seen all n−1 TAs, leaving him with just the two beads he plans to

keep for himself. Prove that the probability that at least one of the other TAs (not including Sinho

himself) gets two beads of the same color is at most 1

2.

>[!note] Independence
>Events $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$ in the same [[1.1 Probability Space|probability space]] are said to be **pairwise independent** if for all $i \neq j$ ,
>$$\mathbb{P}[X_{i} \cap X_{j}] = \mathbb{P}(X_{i}) \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_{j}).$$
>
>Furthermore, the events are **mutually independent** if
>$$\mathbb{P}\left( \bigcap\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} \right) = \prod^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}(X_{i}).$$

288.title: 1.6 Bayes' Rule
288.path: Mathematics/2. Probability/1. Laws of Probability/1.6 Bayes' Rule.md
288.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.6 Bayes' Rule]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/24 16:50:57","modified":"2025/08/07 18:23:15"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bayes' Rule
>For a finite set of [[1.2 Mutually Exclusive Events|mutually exclusive events]] $A_1, \ldots, A_{N} \subseteq \Omega$ ($A_{i} \cap A_{j} = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$) with nonzero probabilities ($\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]>0$ for all $i$) that form a partition of the sample space, **Bayes' rule** states that for any event $B \subseteq \Omega$ with nonzero probability ($\mathbb{P}[B]>0$),
>$$\mathbb{P}[A_i \mid B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\sum^{N}_{j=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_j]\mathbb{P}[A_j]}.$$
# Intuition
In its essence, Bayes' rule is just a substitution. To see why, let's start from the basics. By the [[1.3 Conditional Probability|law of conditional probability]], we have:
$$\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] = \frac{\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}.$$
Then:
1. Again by conditional probability, we have $\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] \mathbb{P}[B] = \mathbb{P}[B \mid A_{i}]\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]$. 
2. By [[1.5 Total Probability Theorem|total probability]], we have $\mathbb{P}[B]=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_{i}]\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]$.

Therefore,
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] &= \frac{\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\mathbb{P}[B]} \\
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\sum^{N}_{j=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_j]\mathbb{P}[A_j]}.
\end{align}$$

However, Bayes' theorem is **crucial for Bayesian inference**; a method of statistical inference with the goal of **belief updating**, or updating the probability of a hypothesis as more information is taken into account. For example, we may estimate the **prior probability** $\mathbb{P}[A]$ of an event $A$, and then update the probability to $\mathbb{P}[A \mid B]$, known as the **posterior probability**, once we know that event $B$ has occurred. Real-world data is often conditional rather than joint or marginal, and Bayes' rule helps bridge the gap between posterior and prior beliefs.
# Examples
>[!example] Pharmaceutical Company
>A pharmaceutical company is marketing a new test for a medical disorder. It has the following probabilities:
>1. When applied to an affected person, the test is positive in 90% of the cases and negative in 10% (**false negatives**).
>2. When applied to a healthy person, the test is negative 80% of the time and positive 20% of the time (**false positive**).
>
>Suppose that the incidence of the disease in the U.S. is 5%; this is our prior knowledge. When a person tests positive, what is the updated probability that they have the disease?
>
>Let A be the event that the person is affected, and let B be the event that the person tests positive. Then,
>$$
>\begin{alignat}{0}
>\mathbb{P}[A]=0.05 \\
>\mathbb{P}[B|A]=0.90 \\
>\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}]=0.20
\end{alignat}
>$$
>Since 90% of affected people test positive, and so do 20% of healthy people ($B|\bar{A}$).
>
>We want to calculate $\mathbb{P}[A|B]$. We proceed as follows:
>$$\mathbb{P}[A|B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}$$
>We only need to find $\mathbb{P}[B]$. How? Well, we can picture $\mathbb{P}[A|B]$ in the following graph of $\Upomega$:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[domain=0:4]
>\draw[] (0, 0) ellipse (4 and 2) node[left]{};
>\draw[] (-1, 0) ellipse (2 and 1) node[below]{$A$};
>\draw[] (1.25, 0) circle (1) node[below]{$B$};
>\draw[->] (0.6,0) -- (0.4,-1.25) node[below]{$A \cap B$};
>\draw[->] (1.25,0) -- (2,-1) node[below]{$\bar{A} \cap B$};
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>This means that $\mathbb{P}[B]=\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]+\mathbb{P}[\bar{A} \cap B]$. Applying the rules of conditional probability, we have:
>$$
>\begin{equation}{}
>\begin{aligned}
>\mathbb{P}[B] &= \mathbb{P}[A \cap B]+\mathbb{P}[\bar{A} \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}]\mathbb{P}[\bar{A}]= \\ &= \mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}](1-\mathbb{P}[A])
>\end{aligned}
>\end{equation}
>$$
>Finally, combining the two equations, we have:
>$$\mathbb{P}[A|B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]}{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}](1-\mathbb{P}[A])}$$
