334.title: 4.1 Modular Arithmetic
334.path: Mathematics/1. Discrete Mathematics/4. Modular Arithmetic/4.1 Modular Arithmetic.md
334.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.1 Modular Arithmetic]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/06 05:53:23","modified":"2025/07/27 20:50:23"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Modular Arithmetic
>For any integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and any positive integer $m \in \mathbb{N}$, known as the **modulus**, the **division algorithm** guarantees that there exist unique integers $q$ (the **quotient**) and $0 \leq r \leq m-1$ (the **remainder**), such that 
>$$x = qm + r.$$
>The remainder, written as $r = x \pmod{m}$, is the **unique value** in the set $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ that is **congruent** to $x$ modulo $m$.
>
>In general, two integers $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$ are said to be **congruent** modulo $m$, written $x \equiv y \pmod{m}$, if they leave the same remainder when divided by $m$. Equivalently, $x \equiv y \pmod{m}$ means that $m \mid (x - y)$ (i.e., the difference $x - y$ is divisible by $m$).
>
>We now define arithmetic operations. Suppose $a \equiv c \pmod{m}$ and $b \equiv d \pmod{m}$: 
>1. **Addition:** $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{m}$.
>2. **Multiplication:** $a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod{m}$.
>3. **Exponentiation:** $a^k \equiv c^k \pmod{m}$ and $b^k \equiv d^k \pmod{m}$. Note that modular arithmetic does not preserve congruence in the exponent.
# Intuition & Proof
Floor division and the modulus are complementary operations: floor division gives the integer part of $x$ divided by $m$, while modulo gives the remainder $r$. Any $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ can be decomposed into these parts using the equation $x=\lfloor \frac{x}{m} \rfloor m+(x \pmod{m})$. Here, $q=\lfloor \frac{x}{m} \rfloor$ is the quotient, and $r=x \pmod{m}$ is the remainder. We now proceed with proving our arithmetic operations.
- **Addition.** We know that $c = a + \alpha m$ and $d = b + \beta m$ for some $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore, $c+d=a+b+m(\alpha+\beta)$. By definition, $q=\alpha + \beta$ and $r=a+b$, so $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{m}$.
- **Multiplication.** Just as above, we substitute for $c,d$ such that $cd=(a+\alpha m)(b+ \beta m)$. This results in $cd=ab+m(\alpha b + \beta a + \alpha \beta m)$. Then, $q=\alpha b + \beta a + \alpha \beta m$ and $r=ab$, so $a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod{m}$.
- **Exponentiation.** We already proved multiplication, so exponentiation is simply an extension of this.

# Properties
#### (*Canonical Representation*) For any modulus $m$, the set of all integers $\mathbb{Z}$ can be divided into exactly $m$ non-overlapping infinite sets, where each set contains all integers that leave the same remainder when divided by $m$.

#### (*Prime Modulus*) For any prime modulus $p$, all numbers in $\{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$ have a modular inverse.
This is trivially true, since $\gcd(i, p)=1$ for all $i=1,\ldots,p-1$.

#### (*Wilson's Theorem*) It holds that $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ if and only if $p$ is prime.
Note that $-1 \equiv p-1 \pmod{p}$. We now prove this theorem.
- Sufficiency ($\implies$): in the previous point, we observed that all numbers in $\{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$ have a modular inverse. Since all prime numbers are odd (for the exception of $2$, which has a single element in the set of nonzero residues), this means that their set of residues are even, and therefore all elements can be matched with their inverse. Since the only two numbers that are their own inverses and cannot be matched are $1$ and $p-1$, this means that
$$(p-1)! \equiv (p-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 1 \equiv p-1 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}.$$
- Necessity ($\impliedby$): consider a composite number $n>3$. Then there exist numbers $k,m \in \{ 1, \ldots, n-1 \}$ for which $km=n$, and therefore $km \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$, which is equivalent to saying that $km \mid (n-1)!$ As such, $$(n-1)! \equiv (n-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot m \cdot \ldots \cdot 1 \equiv (n-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 0 \cdot 1 \equiv 0 \not\equiv -1 \pmod{n}.$$
Therefore Wilson's Theorem only holds if $\gcd(i, n)=1$ for all $i \in \{ 1, \ldots, n-1 \}$, which is only true for prime numbers.

#### (*Fermat's Little Theorem*) For any prime modulus $p$ and any $a \in \{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$, it holds that $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.


# Examples
>[!example] Party Tricks
>You are at a party celebrating your completion of the CS 70 midterm. Show off your modular arithmetic skills and impress your friends by quickly figuring out the last digit(s) of each of the following numbers:
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $11^{3142}$.
>>We find that $11^{3142} \equiv 1^{3142} \pmod{10}$, and so the last digit is $1$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $9^{9999}$.
>We simplify, such that $9^{9999} \equiv 9 \cdot 9^{2(4999)} \equiv 9 \cdot 81^{4999} \equiv 9 \cdot 1^{4999} \equiv 9 \pmod{10}$, so the last digit is $9$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $3^{641}$.
>>We proceed as before, so $3^{641} \equiv 3 \cdot 3^{4(160)} \equiv 3 \cdot 81^{160} \equiv 3 \cdot 1^{160} \equiv 3$, so the last digit is $3$.

>[!note] Graph Representation of a Hypercube
>An $n$-dimensional hypercube can be represented as a graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{0, 1\}^n$ vertices, where $V$ is the set of all $n$-bit strings. Two vertices of a hypercube are connected by an edge if and only if the two vertices differ in exactly one bit position.
>
>Recursively, an $n$-dimensional hypercube is the result of joining two $(n-1)$-dimensional hypercubes with vertices $0x$ and $1x$ where $x \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$.
# Properties
##### (Hypercube Vertices) For an n-dimensional hypercube, $v=2^n$.
1. *Base Case:* A 0-dimensional hypercube has $2^0=1$ vertex by inspection.
2. *Hypothesis:* Assume that the theorem holds for $n$ dimensions.
3. *Inductive Step:* We see that for $n+1$, $v=2(2^n)$, and therefore the theorem holds for all $n$.
##### (Hypercube Edges) For an n-dimensional hypercube, $e=n2^{n-1}$.
We observe that the degree of each vertex of an $n$-dimensional hypercube is exactly $n$. Simultaneously, we observe that each edge is counted twice. Therefore, $e=\frac{n2^n}{2}=n2^{n-1}$.

>[!note] Tree (Connected and Acyclic Graph)
>A tree is a [[3.5b Bipartite Graphs|bipartite graph]] that is both *connected* and *acyclic* (contains no cycles) (i.e., when one node is disconnected, the graph becomes disconnected). A graph that is *not connected* and *acyclic* is called a forest, and consist of more than one tree. Trees consist of a root, internal nodes, and leaf nodes. The following are all equivalent definitions of a tree $G=(V, E)$:
>1. $G$ is connected and contains no cycles.
>2. $G$ is connected and has exactly $|V|-1$ edges.
>3. $G$ is connected and the removal of any edge disconnects $G$.
>4. $G$ is acyclic and the addition of any edge creates a cycle in $G$.

# Properties
#### $G$ has exactly $|V| - 1$ edges.
*Backward direction. Proceed by contradiction.*
- If $G$ is connected and has $n-1$ edges, then it is acyclic.
- However, if $G$ had $n-1$ edges and contained a cycle, then removing one of the cycle's edges does not disconnect the graph. Therefore, we can create a tree with $n-2$ edges. However, a graph that contains less than $n-1$ edges is always disconnected (see 3.1).
#### All trees are [[3.3 Bipartition|bipartite]].

#### For all trees, $f=1$.
Since trees are acyclic by definition, it only follows that the plane will not be subdivided into extra faces.

>[!note] Bipartite Graphs
>A **bipartite graph** is a graph whose vertex set $V = U \cup W$ can be divided into two disjoint subsets $U$ and $W$, such that every edge connects a vertex in $U$ to a vertex in $W$, and vice-versa. That is, *no edge connects two vertices within the same subset*, so that $E \subseteq U \times W$. As such, a graph can only be bipartite if it contains no cycles of odd length.
>
>Complete bipartite graphs are denoted as $K_{|U|, |W|}$.
# Intuition
Although we can't prove bipartition, we can think about as to why the sets $V$ and $E$ can be expressed using the two bipartite sets $L$ and $R$:
- The first fact is simply a union of the two groups of nodes, $L$ and $R$. 
- The second fact states that $E$ is equal to or a subset of all possible combinations of edges between the two groups. **A graph where $E = L \times R$ (every vertex from one group connects to all of the vertices from the other) be expressed as $K_{|L|,|R|}$.

>[!note] Quantifier
>A quantifier of a [[1.1 Propositional Logic|proposition]] is a logical operator that specifies how many elements in a domain satisfy a statement which refers to a variable, known as a *propositional formula*. For the *propositional formula* $P(x)$, we can define the *duals*:
>1. ***Universal Quantifier:*** $\forall x P(x) \iff P(x)\text{ is true for all x.}$
>2. ***Existential Quantifier:*** $\exists x P(x) \iff \text{There exists at least one }x\text{ for which } P(x) \text{is true.}$

# Understanding
We can translate any propositional formula from the duals back to propositional forms. For example, take a variable $x$ such that $x \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. Then,
1. $\forall x P(x) \iff P(1) \land P(2) \land P(3)$.
2. $\exists x P(x) \iff P(1) \lor P(2) \lor P(3)$.

# Properties
##### *(DeMorgan's Laws)* $\neg[\forall x P(x)] \equiv \exists x \neg P(x)$, and $\neg [\exists x P(x)] \equiv \forall x \neg P(x)$.

>[!note] Strong Induction
>Strong induction extends [[2.5a Simple Induction|simple induction]] by using an induction induction hypothesis which makes the stronger assumption that $P(0), P(1), \ldots, P(k)$ are all true.

# Understanding
Between [](2.5a%20Simple%20Induction.md)re or less powerful than the other. Recall that we mentioned that in simple induction, if the $k$-th domino falls, so does the $(k+1)$-th. In strong induction, if dominoes $1$ through $k$ fall, so does the $(k+1)$-th.

However, strong induction can greatly help out in certain cases. 

# Examples
>[!example] Prove that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ where $n \geq 12$, there exist $x,y \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n=4x+5y$
>We proceed by *weak* induction on $n$ first. We must start with a few base cases:
>- $n=12$: $12=4 \cdot 3 + 5 \cdot 0$
>- $n=13$: $13=4 \cdot 2 + 5 \cdot 1$
>- $n=14$: $14=4 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 2$
>- $n=15$: $15=4 \cdot 0 + 5 \cdot 3$.
>
>Since the theorem holds for the first 4 cases, we may proceed by with the inductive step by assuming our hypothesis; that $k=4x+5y$ holds for any $k \geq 15$:
>$$n=k+1=4x+5y+1=4(x-1)+5(y+1).$$
>As such, $k+1=4x'+5y'$ where $x'=x-1$ and $y'=y+1$.
>
>We can also utilize strong induction for our inductive hypothesis. Assume that for some $k \geq 15$, the statement $n=4x+5y$ holds for all $n$ such that $12 \leq n \leq k$. How will we show that the statement holds for $n=k+1$? Since $k \geq 15$, we know that $k+1 \geq 16$ and $(k+1)-4 \geq 12$. By the inductive hypothesis, there exist some $x',y' \in \mathbb{N}$ for which 
>$$(k+1)-4=4x'+5y'.$$
>We see that for the values of

>[!example] Prove that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n > 1$ can be written as a product of one or more primes
>We proceed by induction on $n$:
>- *Base case ($n=2$):* $2$ is a prime number so the base case holds.
>- *Hypothesis:* Assume that the statement holds for naturals $n$ up to $k$, such that $2 \leq n \leq k$.
>- *Step:* We must prove that either $k+1$ is either a prime number, or can be written as a product of primes:
>	1. Since $k+1$ is prime, it is a product of itself, and we're done.
>	2. If $k+1$ is not prime, it can be written as $k+1=a \cdot b$ for some naturals $0 < a,b \leq k + 1$, which are assumed by the inductive hypothesis to be able to be written as a product of primes. *This is because any composite number has at least 3 factors (some perfect squares such as 4)*.
>
>As such, we have proved using strong induction that the theorem holds.

350.title: 2.5a Simple Induction
350.path: Mathematics/1. Discrete Mathematics/1. Logic/2.5 Proof by Induction/2.5a Simple Induction.md
350.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5a Simple Induction]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 05:13:38","modified":"2025/01/22 13:29:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Simple (Weak) Induction
>Simple induction is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given propositional function $P(n)$ for an infinite set of numbers by reasoning about it by finite means. It consists of: 
>1. Proving that the statement holds for a lower limit value $n_0$, *usually* 0 or 1, known as the **base case**.
>2. Assuming that the statement holds for *some* $k \geq n_0$, known as the **inductive hypothesis**.
>3. Proving that since the statement $P(k)$ is assumed to hold, it also holds for $k+1$, known as the **inductive step**.
>
>As a [[1.3 Implication|logical implication]], this can be described as
>$$(n_0, k \in \mathbb{N})(k \geq n_0)(P(n_0) \land (P(k) \implies P(k+1))).$$
>>[!warning] Simple vs. Strong Induction
>>Simple induction only assumes that $P(k)$ holds for some number $k \geq n_0$. It does not assume that the proposition holds for all natural numbers $n_0, n_0 + 1, \ldots, k$. The latter is the inductive hypothesis of strong induction (2.5b).
# Intuition
Suppose we have a line of $n$ dominoes. Then, if we knock the $k$-th domino, the $(k+1)$-th domino will be knocked too. This is essentially what simple induction represents; we only have to prove that if we assume our proposition $P(k)$, then $P(k+1)$ is true. The base case is simply an easy test of whether we should even use our time to prove for $P(k+1)$. We will see in 2.5b that strong induction is a little bit more elaborate than simply $P(k) \implies P(k+1)$.

It is also important that we choose a right statement to prove, since not all statements are strong enough to be proven. Check the last example on this page to see this in action.
# Examples
>[!example] *(Gauss Summation)* Proving that $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \space \sum^{n}_{i=0}i=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$
>We proceed by induction on $n$:
>- *Base case: $(n=0)$*: Since $\sum^{0}_{i=0}i=\frac{0(0+1)}{2}=0$, our base case holds.
>- *Inductive hypothesis:* We assume that our statement holds for some arbitrary $n=k \geq 0$.
>- *Inductive step:* Since our statement $\sum^{k}_{i=0}i=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ holds for $k$, it holds for $k+1$ such that 
>$$\sum^{k+1}_{i=0}i=\left(\sum^{k}_{i=0}i\right)+(k+1)=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1)=\frac{k(k+1)+2(k+1)}{2}=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}.$$
>
>By the principles of mathematical induction, the claim holds for $k+1$, and therefore it holds for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

>[!example] Proving that $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \space 3 \mid n^3 - n$
>We proceed by induction on $n$. Since $3 \mid 0$, it holds. We then assume that $3 \mid k^3 - k$ for some $k \geq 0$, such that $k^3 - k = 3q_1$ for some $q$. Our inductive step needs to prove that $3 \mid (k+1)^3-(k+1)$:
>$$
>\begin{align}
>(k+1)^3-(k+1) &= k^3+3k^2+3k+1-(k+1) \\
>&= (k^3-k)+3(k^2+3k) \\
>&= 3q + 3(k^2+k) \\
>&= 3(k^2+k+q).
>\end{align}
>$$
>As such, we have proved that $3 \mid n^3 - n$ for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

>[!example] *(Two-Color Theorem)* Any box with $n$ lines can be colored using 2 colors such that any two adjacent shapes have different colors.
>The following drawing shows that the two-color theorem holds for $n=2$:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>% Box
>\draw[very thick] (0, 0) -- (5, 0) -- (5, -3) -- (0, -3) -- cycle;
>
>% Lines
>\draw[very thick] (3, -3) -- (0, 0);
>\draw[very thick] (0, -1.5) -- (5, -1.5);
>
>% Fills
>\draw[thin, fill=red, opacity=0.25] (1.5, -1.5) -- (0, 0) -- (0, -1.5) -- (5, -1.5) -- (5, -3) -- (3, -3) -- cycle;
>\draw[thin, fill=blue, opacity=0.25] (5, -1.5) -- (5, 0) -- (0, 0) -- (3, -3) -- (0, -3) -- (0, -1.5) -- cycle;
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>Now that we have a clear picture of the idea, we can proceed by induction on $n$:
>- *Base case:* The theorem surely holds for $n=0$ since it can even be colored using 1 color.
>- *Inductive hypothesis:* We assume that the theorem holds for some $k \geq 0$.
>- *Inductive step:*

>[!example] For all $n \geq 1$, the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is a perfect square
>We proceed by induction on $n$:
>- *Base case:* the first odd number is $n=1$, which is a perfect square.
>- *Hypothesis:* Assume that the sum of the first $k$ odd numbers form a perfect square, $m^2$.
>- *Step:* We have that the sum of the first $k+1$ odd numbers is $m^2+k+1$.
>
>...But now what? This doesn't help us at all! It turns out that our statement is too weak to be proven, since it does not have enough structure to make it meaningful.
>
>Let's now do a check on our statement and see the first few base cases:
>- $n=1$: $1=1^2$
>- $n=2$: $1+3=2^2$
>- $n=3$: $1+3+5=3^2$
>- $n=4$: $1+3+5+7=4^2$
>
>It turns out that not only does our statement hold for the base cases, but the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is exactly $n^2$! As such, we can continue with our proof:
>- *Hypothesis*: The sum of the first $k$ odd numbers is $k^2$.
>- *Step:* The $(k+1)$-st odd number is $2k+1$. As such, the sum of the first $k+1$ odd numbers is $k^2+2k+1=(k+1)^2$. Therefore, the theorem holds.

351.title: 1.4c Proof by Contradiction
351.path: Mathematics/1. Discrete Mathematics/1. Logic/1.4 Proof Methods/1.4c Proof by Contradiction.md
351.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4c Proof by Contradiction]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 05:12:51","modified":"2025/06/02 18:07:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Proof by Contradiction
>A proof by contradiction is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given proposition $P$ by assuming the negation $\neg P$ and demonstrating that this assumption leads to a contradiction of two conclusions, $R$, thereby [[1.3 Implication|implying]] that $P$ must be true, such that
>$$\neg P \implies \neg R \land R.$$

# Examples
>[!example] There are infinitely many prime numbers.
>We proceed by contradiction. Assume there is a finite number of $k$ prime numbers, $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$. Then, there is a numbe[](1.3%20Implication.md)ot be prime since it is larger than any prime number. Since every natural number greater than $1$ is either prime or has a prime divisor (proven in 2.5a), then there is a prime number $p \in \{p_1, \ldots, p_k\}$ such that $p \mid n$, which is our statement $R$.
>
>However, by the same logic $p$ must also divide $r = p_1p_2p_3\ldots p_n$. Then, as proven in 2.1, $p \mid n-r$. But $n-r=1$! Since the only positive number that divides $1$ is $1$, $p=1$ is not prime. This is our statement $\neg R$.
>
>Since we have proven $R \land \neg R$, we have a contradiction!

>[!example] $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
>We proceed by contradiction. Assume that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational. By the definition of rational numbers, there exist some $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with no common factors other than $1$ for which $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$ (this is our $R$). 
>
>It follows that $2 = \frac{a^2}{b^2} \iff a^2 = 2b^2$. Since $2b^2$ is a multiple of $2$, it is even, and so is $a^2$. This means that $a$, too, is even (proven in 2.2). Hence, there is some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ for which $a=2q$. We have that $b^2=2q^2$. Since $q$ is an integer, so is $q^2$, and since $b^2$ is even, so is $b$. As such, both $a$ and $b$ are even. 
>
>However, if $a$ and $b$ are even, then they share a common factor of $2>1$. This is our statement $\neg R$, and we have a contradiction since $\neg R \land R$ holds.

353.title: 1.4b Proof by Contraposition
353.path: Mathematics/1. Discrete Mathematics/1. Logic/1.4 Proof Methods/1.4b Proof by Contraposition.md
353.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4b Proof by Contraposition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 05:12:18","modified":"2025/07/12 17:45:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Proof by Contraposition
>A proof by contraposition is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given [[1.2 Implication|implication]] $P \implies Q$ by assuming the truth of the negation of the conclusion $\neg Q$, and demonstrating that the negation of the hypothesis $\neg P$ necessarily follows, such that
>$$\neg Q \implies \neg P.$$

# Examples
>[!example] Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $d$ divide $n$. If $n$ is odd, then $d$ is odd.
>We proceed by contraposition; it is easier to prove that if $d$ is even, then $n$ is even, since any even number is a multiple of $2$. We proceed by expressing $d$ as $d=2k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Because $d \mid n$, then $n=qd$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$. When we substitute for $d$, $n=2(qk)$, which is definitely even since it is divisible by $2$. Since the contraposition holds, so does the original statement.

>[!example] If $a^2$ is even, then $a$ is even.
>We proceed by contraposition. Since $a$ is odd, it can be expressed as $2q+1$ for some quotient $q$. Then, $a^2$ can be expressed as $a^2=4q^2+4q+1=2(2q^2+2q)+1$. Since $2(2q^2+2q)$ is a multiple of $2$, it is clearly even. However, when we add $1$ to it it clearly becomes odd. Therefore, $a^2$ is also odd.

>[!example] *(Pigeonhole Principle)* Let $n,k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. Place $n$ objects into $k$ boxes. If $n > k$, then at least one box must contain multiple objects.
>We proceed by contraposition. If all boxes contain exactly one object, then the number of objects is at most equal to the number of boxes, such that $n \leq k$.

>[!note] Direct Proof
>A direct proof is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given [[1.2 Implication|hypothesis]] $P$ by assuming its truth and demonstrating that the [[1.2 Implication|conclusion]] $Q$ necessarily follows, such that
>$$P \implies Q.$$

# Examples
>[!example] Prove that for any $a,b,c \in Z$, if $a \mid b$ and $a\mid c$, then $a \mid (b + c)$.
>We can express the n[](1.3%20Implication.md)c=q_2a$ for some quotients $q_1,q_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then, $b+c=a(q_1 + q_2)$, which has a factor of $a$ and therefore can be divided by $a$.
>
>Alternatively, this theorem can be expressed in quantifier form as $(\forall a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z})(P(a,b) \land P(a,c)) \implies P(a, b+c)$.

>[!example] Prove that an integer $0 < n < 1000$ is divisible by 9 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
>We can express $n$ as a number $abc$ such that $n=100a+10b+c$. Then, we can express the sum of its digits as a multiple of 9 as $a+b+c=9q$ for some quotient $q \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting for $c=9q-a-b$, it follows that $n=99a+9b+9q=9(11a+b+q)$. Since $9$ factors out, $n$ is divisible by $9$.
>
>Since we are solving for $P \iff Q$, we must also prove for the converse, $Q \implies P$. Suppose that $n=9q$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ is (clearly) divisible by $9$. Then, it follows that $100a+10b+c=9q$ is also divisible by $9$. We can massage the equation such that $99a+9b+(a+b+c)=9q$. This leads to
>$$a+b+c=9(q-11a-b),$$
>which is clearly divisible by $9$.

359.title: 2.6 Causality
359.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.6 Causality]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/28 16:41:00","modified":"2024/12/13 20:35:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] System Causality
>A system $H$ is **causal** if its behavior does not rely on future inputs. In other words, the output $y(n)$ depends only on inputs $x(k)$ where $k \leq n$. Conversely, if $H$ contains a term where $k > n$  (e.g., $k = n + 1$ s.t. $x(k) = x(n+1)$), the system would rely on future inputs and therefore cannot be considered causal.
>
>Additionally, a discrete-time LTI system is **causal** if and only if $h(n) = 0$ $\forall n < 0$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and a continuous-time LTI system is **causal** if and only if $h(t) = 0$ $\forall t < 0$, where $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
# Proof
We can prove causality for discrete-time LTI systems very quickly below:
1. $h(n) = 0 \enspace (\forall n < 0) \implies \text{System is causal.}$
We can simplify the convolution of a causal system such that its sum begins at 0:
$$y(n) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=0}x(n-k)h(k).$$
Since $k=0$ is the initial value of the convolution, this means that there are no inputs $x(n-k)$ in $y(n)$ for which $-k > 0$.
2. $\text{System is causal.} \implies h(n) = 0 \enspace (\forall n < 0)$
We proceed by taking the contrapositive of the statement above, such that $h(n) \neq 0 \enspace (\forall n < 0) \implies \text{System is not causal}$:

360.title: 2.4a Discrete-Time System Identification
360.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/ZZ99 System Identification/2.4a Discrete-Time System Identification.md
360.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.4a Discrete-Time System Identification]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/08 13:05:13","modified":"2024/12/13 02:16:46"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time System ID Process
>For a [[2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System|discrete-time LTI model]] $\vec{x}_d[i+1]$, the system identification algorithm is as follows:
>1. Let $D := \begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i_1]^T & \vec{u}_d[i_1]^T \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \vec{x}_d[i_\mathscr{l}]^T & \vec{u}_d[i_\mathscr{l}]^T\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{l} \times (n + m)}$ and $S := \begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i_1+1]^T \\ \vdots \\ \vec{x}_d[i_\mathscr{l}+1]^T\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{l \times n}}.$
>2. Compute the [[2.10d.4 Matrix Least Squares|OLS]] $\hat{P} := (D^TD)^{-1}D^TS \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{l} \times n}.$
>3. Extract $\begin{bmatrix}\hat{A}_d^T \\ \hat{B}_d^T\end{bmatrix} := \hat{P}$.
# Intuition
We start with our well-known discrete-time $\vec{x}_d[i+1]=A_d\vec{x}_d[i]+B_d\vec{u}_d[i]$. We can rewrite this equation in matrix-vector form as 
$$\vec{x}_d[i+1]=\begin{bmatrix}A_d & B_d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i] \\ \vec{u}_d[i]\end{bmatrix}.$$
We can make our life easier by transposing the equation to place our data points in rows that are vertically stacked. This yields the inner product
$$\vec{x}_d[i+1]^T=\begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i]^T & \vec{u}_d[i]^T\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_d^T \\ B_d^T\end{bmatrix}.$$
We do this so we do not have to transform our least squares later on. Since the dimensions of $A$ are $n \times n$ and the dimensions of $B$ are $n \times m$, we can ensure that there are exactly $n$ columns and $n+m$ rows in $P$ by taking its transpose.  We now want to define our stacked matrices for timesteps $i_1,\dots,i_\mathscr{l}$. Therefore, $P:=\begin{bmatrix}A_d^T \\ B_d^T\end{bmatrix}$, whereas $D:=\begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i_1]^T & \vec{u}_d[i_1]^T \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \vec{x}_d[i_\mathscr{l}]^T & \vec{u}_d[i_\mathscr{l}]^T\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{l} \times (n+m)}$ and $S := \begin{bmatrix}\vec{x}_d[i_1+1]^T \\ \vdots \\ \vec{x}_d[i_\mathscr{l}+1]^T\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{l \times n}}$. We end up with a very familiar equation in $DP=S$.

So what's up with the dimensionality? Matrix $D$ has the dimensions $\mathscr{l} \times (n+m)$ since there are $\mathscr{l}$ timesteps, representing the $\mathscr{l}$ rows in $D$, and $n+m$ columns since the state vector $\vec{x}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ has $n$ elements, whereas the vector of control inputs $\vec{u}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ has $m$ elements. Therefore, each row in $D$ has a combined of $n+m$ elements. We can use the same reasoning for $S$ since the state vector will always contain $n$ elements.

We can now use least squares optimization to find a matrix $\hat{P}$ that minimizes the coefficient matrices $A_d$ and $B_d$. We do so using
$$\hat{P} := (D^TD)^{-1}D^TS.$$
Note that OLS only works when $D$ is invertible $\iff$ is full column rank $\iff$ $\mathrm{Rank}(D)=n+m$ $\iff$ has $n+m$ linearly independent columns. Here are the two other possibilities:
- If $Rank(D) < n+m$ $\implies$ least squares is not possible since $D$ is not invertible. 
- If $D$ has $>n+m$ columns **AND** is full column rank $\implies$ there is more than one solution for $\hat{P}$.

362.title: 2.9d Fast Fourier Transform
362.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.8 Fourier Analysis/2.9d Fast Fourier Transform.md
362.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9d Fast Fourier Transform]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/29 20:08:20","modified":"2024/11/06 15:26:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
>The **Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)** is an efficient recursive algorithm for computing the **Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)** of a sequence. The DFT itself converts a finite sequence of equally spaced samples (usually from a time-domain signal) into a sequence of complex numbers representing the amplitudes and phases of sinusoidal frequency components. For the DFT equations
>$$$$

# Intuition
The FFT algorithm drops the inverse period multiplication in the standard discrete Fourier calculations, such that
$$X[k]=\cancel{\frac{1}{N}}\sum^{N-1}_{n=0}x[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}.$$
The FFT optimizes computational time by only taking periods in the scope of $N=2^\ell$, where $\ell \in \mathbb{N}.$ This step ensures that the finite signal will always have an even number of elements, and is useful for performing linear algebra on the above equations. 
For simplification, we will take $W_N=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}}$. The FFT also performs *decimation in time*, dividing $x[n]$ into two sets of even and odd multiples of $n$, such that two calculations are performed where
$$X[k]=\sum^{\frac{N}{2}-1}_{n=0}x[2n]W_N^{2kn}+\sum^{\frac{N}{2}-1}_{n=0}x[2n+1]W_N^{(2n+1)k}.$$
This can equivalently be represented using $W_{N/2}=e^{-j\frac{4\pi}{N}}$, such that
$$X[k]=\sum^{\frac{N}{2}-1}_{n=0}x[2n]W_{N/2}^{kn}+W_N^k\sum^{\frac{N}{2}-1}_{n=0}x[2n+1]W_{N/2}^{kn}.$$
We see that the right hand side of the equation above closely resembles two Fourier coefficients, one for $e[n]=x[2n]$ and another for $o[n]=x[2n+1]$. Therefore, we can represent the above as
$$X[k]=E[k]+W_{N}^kO[k].$$
However, this only represents the signal for the first half of the period $N$ ($0 \text{ through } \frac{N}{2}-1$). By shifting $k$ by $\frac{N}{2}$, we can obtain the decomposition for the second half of the signal, such that we get $X\left[k+\frac{N}{2}\right].$ This is very straightforward, since the DFT kernel $W_\frac{N}{2}$ is periodic on $\frac{N}{2}$, and therefore both $E[k]$ and $O[k]$ are periodic on $\frac{N}{2}$. The equation becomes
$$X\left[k+\frac{N}{2}\right] = E[k]+W_N^kW_N^{\frac{N}{2}}O[k]=E[k]+W_N^ke^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}\frac{N}{2}}O[k]=E[k]-W_N^kO[k].$$
Therefore, we get the piecewise equation
$$X[k] =
\begin{cases}
E[k]+e^{-j\omega_0k}O[k] & \text{for } k \in [0,\frac{N}{2}) \\
E[k]-e^{-j\omega_0k}O[k] & \text{for } k \in [\frac{N}{2}, N)
\end{cases}$$
where $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{N}$.

363.title: 2.9a Fourier Analysis
363.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.8 Fourier Analysis/2.9a Fourier Analysis.md
363.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9a Fourier Analysis]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/27 01:39:34","modified":"2024/12/16 20:03:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Fourier Analysis
>Fourier analysis is a mathematical technique that decomposes complex functions or signals into a sum of simpler trigonometric functions, specifically sines and cosines, or complex exponentials. In the realm of linear algebra, Fourier analysis can be interpreted as a simple change of basis that compresses a signal to remove its most irrelevant components. 
>
>Any Fourier analysis method contains a synthesis and an analysis equation:
>1. The **synthesis** equation (inverse Fourier) aims to decompose a signal $x$ into a linear combination of its Fourier coefficients in the frequency domain, $X$.
>2. The analysis equation aims to decompose a signal's Fourier coefficients $X$ into a linear combination of its signal values.
>
>The following chart outlines all four Fourier analysis methods:
>
>|     | **D-T**  | **C-T**  |
| :-: | :--: | :--: |
| **D-F** | DTFS | CTFS |
| **C-F** | DTFT | CTFT |
>where the rows signify whether the Fourier analysis is discrete or continuous in the frequency domain, and the columns signify whether it is discrete or continuous in the time domain.
>>[!warning] Note (Periodicity)
>>While the **Fourier series** works with *periodic* signals in the time domain and produces *discrete* frequency coefficients, the **Fourier transform** deals with *aperiodic* signals in the time domain and produces a *continuous* frequency spectrum. Additionally, the DTFT has a *periodic* frequency response over $2\pi$, whereas the CTFT produces a *non-periodic continuous spectrum*.
>
>>[!warning] Note (Infinite Signals)
>>All of the above methods deal with signals of assumed infinite length (with the Fourier series dealing with periodic signals, therefore limiting itself to a finite interval $p$). For signals of finite length, the ***DFT (discrete Fourier transform)*** and the ***CFT (continuous Fourier transform)*** are methods of Fourier analysis that can be applied. Their formulations are very close to the **DTFS** and **CTFS**.
>

364.title: 2.9e Parseval's Theorem
364.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.8 Fourier Analysis/2.9e Parseval's Theorem.md
364.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.9e Parseval's Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/29 19:46:51","modified":"2024/10/29 20:04:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Parseval's Theorem
>Parseval's Theorem states that the total energy of any $p$-periodic discrete signal $x(n)$ in the *time domain* can be expressed as a linear combination of its period with its Fourier coefficients, such that
>$$\sum^{p-1}_{n=0}|x(n)|^2 = p\sum^{p-1}_{n=0}|X_n|^2,$$
>where the right hand side represents the total energy of $x(n)$ in the *frequency domain*.

# Intuition
For discrete-time, we can take the vector equivalent of $x(n)$ to be $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^p$. We can then express $|x(n)|^2$ as the squared norm of vector $\vec{x}$, such that
$$\begin{align}
||\vec{x}||^2 &= \langle \vec{x}, \vec{x} \rangle \\
&= \vec{x}^T\vec{x}\textasteriskcentered \\
\end{align}$$
Applying the equation $\vec{x} = \Psi X$, we get
$$||\vec{x}||^2=(X^T\Psi^T)(\Psi\textasteriskcentered\\X\textasteriskcentered).$$
Since we already know that $\Psi^T\Psi\textasteriskcentered=pI$,
$$\begin{align}
||\vec{x}||^2 &= X^T(pI)X\textasteriskcentered \\
&= pX^TX\textasteriskcentered \\
&=p\langle X, X \rangle \\
&= p||X||^2.
\end{align}$$
Which is equivalent to $\sum^{p-1}_{n=0}|x(n)|^2 = p\sum^{p-1}_{n=0}|X_n|^2$ in the signal domain.

365.title: 2.9b.1 Discrete-Time Fourier Transform

NOTE TITLE: [[2.9b.1 Discrete-Time Fourier Transform]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/05 20:34:25","modified":"2024/11/19 17:34:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT)
>The Discrete-Time Fourier Transform is a mathematical tool used in signal processing to analyze the frequency content of **non-periodic discrete-time signals** into a **continuous functions of frequency**, providing a complete representation of the signal’s frequency spectrum, such that
>$$x[n]=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int^{\pi}_{-\pi}X(\omega)e^{j\omega n}d\omega \iff X(\omega)=\sum^{\infty}_{n=-\infty}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}.$$


# Intuition
We can easily take the analysis equation of a discrete-time Fourier transform just as
$$X(\omega)=\sum^{\infty}_{n=-\infty}x[n]e^{-j\omega n},$$
since this is simply the frequency response of $x[n]$. The intuition behind this equivalence is that both $X(\omega)$ and $H(\omega)$ identically describe how $x[n]$ behaves in the frequency domain.

However, the question is to find the synthesis equation. To proceed, we can equate each of the basis vectors to $\phi_n(\omega)=e^{-j\omega n}$ and find an orthogonal basis by imagining $X(\omega)$ as a weighted linear combination of the basis vectors. We know that $X(\omega)$ is periodic over $2\pi$ (and therefore the DTFT is periodic in frequency). How do we define an inner product in a periodic frequency space? We proceed by defining an inner product of any two $2\pi$-periodic frequency vectors $F, G$, such that the inner product is integrated over a period of $2\pi$:
$$\langle F,G \rangle = \int^{\pi}_{-\pi} F(\omega) G\textasteriskcentered(\omega) d\omega.$$
Then,
$$\langle H, \phi_k \rangle = \sum^{\infty}_{n=-\infty}x[n]\langle \phi_n, \phi_k \rangle=x[k]\langle \phi_k, \phi_k \rangle \iff x[n]= \frac{\langle H, \phi_k \rangle}{\langle \phi_k, \phi_k \rangle}.$$
Since $\langle \phi_k, \phi_k \rangle = 2\pi$ (the Fourier basis of $X(\omega)$ is $2\pi$-periodic), then
$$x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int^{\pi}_{-\pi}X(\omega)\phi_n\textasteriskcentered(\omega)d\omega = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int^{\pi}_{-\pi}X(\omega)e^{j\omega n}d\omega.$$

# Examples
>[!example] DTFT Analysis of $x[n] = \delta[n]$
>The DTFT of $x[n] = \delta[n]$ can be written as
>$$X(\omega) = \sum^{\infty}_{n=-\infty}\delta[n]e^{-j\omega n} = 1.$$
>Therefore, the Fourier transform $x[n] = \delta[n]$ is $X(\omega) = 1 \enspace \forall \omega$.

>[!example] DTFT Synthesis of $X(\omega) = \delta(\omega)$
>The DTFT synthesis of $X(\omega) = \delta(\omega)$ can be written as
>$$x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\pi}_{-\pi}\delta(\omega)e^{j\omega n}d\omega = \frac{1}{2\pi}.$$
>Therefore, the Fourier synthesis results in $x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \enspace \forall n$.

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/19 18:02:37","modified":"2024/11/26 19:46:45"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT)
>The continuous-time Fourier transform is a mathematical tool used in signal processing to analyze the frequency content of **non-periodic continuous-time signals** into **continuous functions of frequency**, providing a complete representation of the signal’s frequency spectrum, such that
>$$x(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}X(\omega)e^{j\omega t}d\omega \iff X(\omega)=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt.$$
>As in discrete time, the frequency response of $x(t)$ is equivalent to its Fourier transform.

# Intuition

# Properties
#### (*Dirac Input*) $x(t)=\delta(t) \iff X(\omega) = 1$.
#### (Unit Input) $x(t)=1 \iff X(\omega)=2\pi\delta(\omega)$
#### (Sine Input) $x(t)=\frac{A}{\pi t}\sin(Bt) \iff X(\omega)=\begin{cases}A & \text{if } -B \leq \omega \leq B \\ 0 &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$.
#### (*Time Shift*) $x(t-t_0) \iff X(\omega)e^{-j\omega t_0}$.
$$\begin{align}
X(\omega) &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(t-t_0)e^{-j\omega t}dt \\
&= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(u)e^{-j\omega(u+t_0)}du \\
&= e^{-j\omega t_0} \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(u)e^{-j\omega u}du \\
&= e^{-j\omega t_0}X(\omega),
\end{align}$$
where $u=t+t_0$ is a change of variables.

#### (*Frequency Shift*) $X(\omega - \omega_0) \iff x(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t}$.

+the special case $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t} \iff X(\omega)=2\pi \delta(\omega-\omega_{0})$

#### (*Convolution*) $y(t) = (x * h)(t) \iff Y(\omega) = X(\omega) H(\omega)$.
#### (*Modulation*) $y(t) = x(t) \cdot c(t) \iff Y(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi}(X * C)(\omega)$.
$$\begin{align}
Y(\omega) &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}y(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt \\
&=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty} x(t)c(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt \\
&= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}c(t) \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty} X(\lambda)e^{j\lambda t}d\lambda\right) e^{-j\omega t}dt \\
&= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty} X(\lambda)\left(\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}c(t)e^{j(\omega - \lambda) t}dt\right)d\lambda \\
&= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty} X(\lambda)C(\omega - \lambda)d\lambda \\
&= \frac{1}{2\pi} (X * C)(\omega),
\end{align}$$
where the two integrals are swapped in order to isolate the coefficient $C(\omega - \lambda)$.

#### (*Differentiation*) $\frac{d^k}{dt^k}x(t) \iff (j\omega)^kX(\omega )$.
#### (*Integration*) $\int x(t)dt = \frac{1}{j\omega}X(\omega )$
# Examples

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/28 16:51:40","modified":"2024/12/17 03:05:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS)
>The **Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS)** is a mathematical method used to represent a **periodic continuous-time signal** as a sum of sinusoidal components or, equivalently, complex exponentials. The CTFS decomposes an ***uncountably infinite signal into a series of countably infinite harmonics*** $k\omega_0$ that represent the signal’s frequency content. The Fourier series for a $T$-periodic continuous-time signal $x: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is
>$$x(t) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}X_{k}e^{jk\omega_0 t} \iff X_{k} = \frac{1}{T}\int^{\frac{T}{2}}_{-\frac{T}{2}}x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t}dt.$$

# Intuition
By decomposing $x(t)$ into a linear combination of its Fourier coefficients $X[k]$ with its basis vectors $\phi_k(t)=e^{j\omega kt},$ we quickly get our synthesis equation 
$$x(t) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}X[k]e^{j\omega_0 kt},$$
where the right hand side is summed over infinity because although $x(t)$ is $p$-periodic, it is a continuous signal and will hold an infinite number of coefficients $X[k]$ over $k \in [0, p)$.

Since a CTFS Fourier basis $\phi_k$ is periodic on $t$ and aperiodic on $k$ (as shown in the properties section below), the synthesis equation can be thought of decomposing an uncountably infinite signal $x(t)$ into a countably infinite set of frequencies $k\omega_0$.

We must proceed with a continuous-time "projection." We take another basis $\phi_\ell$ and see that
$$\langle x, \phi_\ell \rangle = X[\ell] \langle \phi_\ell, \phi_\ell \rangle \iff X[\ell] = \frac{\langle x, \phi_\ell \rangle}{\langle \phi_\ell, \phi_\ell \rangle}.$$
Since we are working in continuous-time (and therefore both $x(t)$ and $\phi_k(t)$ are continuous and $p$-periodic), we define
$$ \begin{align}
\langle \phi_\ell, \phi_\ell \rangle &= \int^{\frac{p}{2}}_{-\frac{p}{2}}\phi_\ell(t) \phi_\ell\textasteriskcentered(t)dt \\
&= \int^{\frac{p}{2}}_{-\frac{p}{2}}e^{j\omega_0 \ell t} \cdot e^{-j\omega_0 \ell t}dt \\
&= \int^{\frac{p}{2}}_{-\frac{p}{2}}dt \\
&= \frac{p}{2} - \left(-\frac{p}{2} \right) \\
&= p.
\end{align}
$$

Note that we take the interval $[-\frac{p}{2}, \frac{p}{2}]$ in order to avoid the intuitive interval $[0, p]=[0, 0]$. 

Similarly,
$$ \begin{align}
\langle x, \phi_\ell \rangle = \int^{\frac{p}{2}}_{-\frac{p}{2}} x(t) \phi_\ell\textasteriskcentered(t).
\end{align}$$
Therefore, our analysis equation becomes
$$X[k] = \frac{1}{p}\int^{\frac{p}{2}}_{-\frac{p}{2}}x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t}.$$
# Properties
#### (Basis $t$-Periodicity) $\phi_k(t+p)=\phi_k(t)$
We find that
$$\phi_k(t+p)=e^{j\omega kt} \cdot e^{j\omega k p}=e^{j\omega kt} \cdot 1 = \phi_k(t),$$
so $\phi_k$ is periodic on $t$.  Therefore, the continuous spectrum is periodic on time.

#### (No Basis $k$-Periodicity) $\phi_{k+p}(t) \neq \phi_k(t)$
We also look at $\phi_k$'s periodicity on $k$:
$$\phi_{k + p}(t)=e^{j\omega kt} \cdot e^{j\omega pt}=e^{j\omega kt} \cdot e^{j2\pi t},$$
which against intuition is not periodic on $k$, as $e^{j2\pi t}$ can hold any value $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and may not be a multiple of $2\pi$. Therefore, the continuous spectrum is aperiodic on frequency.


#### (*Linearity*)
#### (*Time Shift*)


# Examples
>[!example] A CTFS Puzzle
>Consider a periodic, continuous-time sinusoidal signal $x(t)$ with the following properties:
>1. $x(t)=x(t+4)$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
>2. For $k=1,2,3$, there exists $t \in \mathbb{R}$, such that $x(t) \neq x(t+k)$.
>3. $X_{k}=X\textasteriskcentered_{-k}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
>4. $X_{k}=0$ for $k > 2$.
>5. The average value of $x(t)$ over one period is 4.
>6. $\int^{1}_{-3}|x(t)|^2dt=128$.
>7. $x(t)=x(-t)$.
>8. $x(0)=12$.
>
>We proceed in the following manner:
>1. Tells us that $x(t)$ has a period $p=\frac{4}{\ell}$.
>2. Verifies that $\ell=1$ (i.e. the fundamental period of $x$ is $p=4$).
>3. Tells us that the signal is real, since the coefficients' conjugates are symmetric.
>4. Since $k \in [0, 3]$, this means that $X_{3}=X_{-3}=0$.
>5. This can be translated into $\frac{1}{4}\int^{2}_{-2}x(t)dt=4$, and implies that $X_{0}=4$ (since by definition $X_{0}=\frac{1}{T}\int^{\frac{T}{2}}_{-\frac{T}{2}}x(t)e^{j 0 \omega_{0} t}$.
>6. Using Parseval's theorem, $\frac{1}{4}\int^{1}_{-3}|x(t)|^2dt=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|X_{k}|^2=32$. Since $X_{0}=4$ and $X_{3}=X_{-3}=0$, $|X_{1}|^2+|X_{-1}|^2+|X_{2}|^2+|X_{-2}|^2=16$. Since $X_{1}=X_{-1}$ and $X_{2}=X_{-2}$, $|X_{1}|^2+|X_{2}|^2=8$.
>7. This means that the function is even. Therefore, since it is sinusoidal, it may only contain cosine functions (and perhaps a coefficient).
>8. We can formulate $x(t)=X_{-2}e^{-j\pi t}+X_{-1}e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}t}+X_{0}+X_{1}e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}t}+X_{2}e^{j\pi t}$. For $x(0)$, this formulation equals $x(0)=X_{0}+2X_{1}+2X_{2}=12$. Since $X_{0}=4$, $X_{1}+X_{2}=4$.
>
>We now need to simply find $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$. We compare the two equations $X_{1}+X_{2}=4$ (obtained in 8.) and $|X_{1}|^2+|X_{2}|^2=8$ (obtained in 6.). We find that $X_{1}=X_{2}=2$. Therefore, we get:
>$$\begin{align}
x(t)&=2e^{-j\pi t}+2e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}t}+4+2e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}t}+2e^{j\pi t} \\
&= 4\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}t)+4\cos(\pi t)+4.
\end{align}$$

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/22 12:23:39","modified":"2024/12/17 03:00:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS)
>The discrete-time Fourier series is a Fourier transform method that provides a frequency-domain representation of a discrete-time signal defined over all integers. It results in a continuous frequency spectrum. Any $p$-periodic discrete-time signal $x: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ can be written in the frequency domain, such that  
>$$x(n)=\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_{k}e^{j\omega_0kn} \iff X_{k}=\frac{1}{p}\sum^{p-1}_{n=0}x(n)e^{-j\omega_0kn}.$$
>
>The synthesis (left) equation can be transformed into matrix-vector form, such that the formula for the DTFS of a $p$-periodic discrete signal $x(n)$ with eigenvector components $\psi_{k}(n)=e^{j\omega kn}$ is
>$$
>\vec{x} = \Psi\vec{X} \iff
>\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ x(1) \\ \vdots \\ x(p-1)\end{bmatrix} =
>\begin{bmatrix}
>\psi_0(0) & \ldots & \psi_k(0) & \ldots & \psi_{p-1}(0) \\ 
>\psi_0(1) & \ddots & \psi_k(1) & \ddots & \psi_{p-1}(1) \\
>\vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 
>\psi_0(p-1) & \ldots & \psi_k(p-1) & \ldots & \psi_{p-1}(p-1)
>\end{bmatrix}
>\begin{bmatrix}X_0 \\ \vdots \\ X_k \\ \vdots \\ X_{p-1}\end{bmatrix}
>$$
>where $\Psi \in \mathbb{C}^{p \times p}$ is an orthogonal matrix called the **Fourier kernel** representing a [[2.8b Change of Basis|Fourier basis]] with each of its columns $\Psi_k$ being the basis vectors, $\vec{X} \in \mathbb{C}^p$ is the vector of Fourier coefficients, and $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^p$ is the signal output for each $n \in \set{0, 1, \ldots, (p-1)}$.
>
>Then, the solution to the discrete-time Fourier series for $x(n)$ is the projection
>$$\vec{X}(\omega)=\frac{1}{p}\Psi\textasteriskcentered\vec{x},$$
>where $\frac{1}{p}\Psi\textasteriskcentered = \Psi^{-1}$ is known as the **Fourier matrix**.
# Intuition
We start with a very simple change of basis. Consider two discrete functions $\psi_0(n)=1$ and $\psi_1(n)=\begin{cases}1 && (n \mod{2} \equiv 0) \\ -1 && (n \mod{2} \equiv 1)\end{cases}$. 

The functions can equivalently be written as $\psi_0(n) = e^{i0n}$ and $\psi_1(n)=e^{i \pi n}$, which you can find for yourself by solving the complex exponential for the given frequency with any $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. The two functions can also be written as two vectors $\psi_0 = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\psi_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$.

Since the fundamental period of the function is $p=2$ (you can find this using periodicity of discrete signals), this means that any two-periodic signal $x(n)$ can be decomposed as
$$\begin{align}
x(n) &= X_0\psi_0(n) + X_1\psi_1(n) \\
&= X_0e^{i0n}+X_1e^{i \pi n}.
\end{align}$$
Additionally, since $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{p}=\pi$, only the frequencies $0, \pi$ may contribute to the signal. This can be generalized for a $P$-periodic signal $x(n)$, such that the only frequencies that contribute to that signal are contained in the set $\set{0, \omega_0, 2\omega_0, \ldots, (P-1)\omega_0}$.

Proceeding in the 2-period realm, we can find $X_0$ and $X_1$ by solving for their respective vectors' dot products,
$$\begin{align}
\vec{x} \cdot \psi_0 = X_0(\psi_0 \cdot \psi_0) + X_1 \times 0 \iff X_0=\frac{\vec{x} \cdot \psi_0}{\psi_0 \cdot \psi_0} \\

\vec{x} \cdot \psi_1 = X_0 \times 0 +X_1(\psi_1 \cdot \psi_1) \iff X_1=\frac{\vec{x} \cdot \psi_1}{\psi_1 \cdot \psi_1}
\end{align}$$
where $\psi_0 \cdot \psi_1 = 0$ is automatically omitted since the two vectors are orthogonal, and $x$ is the vector of the signal $x(n)$. Note that this was a very simplified example, since ==a 2-period signal is always real== (the sine component of the complex number is always 0). 

We can now continue our $p$-periodic signal generalization by saying that a $p$-periodic signal can be generalized into a $p$-element vector, such that $\vec{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x(0) & x(1) & \ldots & x(p-1)\end{bmatrix}^T$. We will also define a $p$-dimensional orthogonal basis $\set{\psi_0, \psi_1, \ldots, \psi_{p-1}}$. The vector $\vec{x}$ can then be decomposed using
$$\begin{align}
\vec{x} &= X_0\psi_0+X_1\psi_1+\ldots+X_{p-1}\psi_{p-1} \\
&= \sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_k\psi_k \\
&= \sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_ke^{jk\omega_0n}
\end{align}$$
Then, we can find any $X_n$ by projecting $\vec{x}$ onto the coefficient's respective basis vector $\psi_n$:
$$
\begin{align}
\langle \vec{x}, \psi_n \rangle &= \langle \sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_k\psi_k, \psi_n \rangle  \\
&= \sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_k\langle \psi_k, \psi_n \rangle \\
&= X_n\langle \psi_n, \psi_n \rangle \\
&= X_n \times p.
\end{align}
$$
Here, we use the fact that the inner product of two orthogonal vectors is always $0$, as well as the fact that $\langle \vec{x}, \vec{x} \rangle = p$. The latter comes from the relation of the basis vectors to the periodicity of $x(n)$.

Finally, by dividing both sides by $\langle \psi_n, \psi_n \rangle = p$ we can define any Fourier series coefficient $X_n$ as
$$X_n = \frac{1}{p} \langle \vec{x}, \psi_n \rangle.$$
In the signal realm, we can equivalently state that for $\omega_0 \in \set{0, \omega_0, 2\omega_0, \ldots, (p-1)\omega_0}$,
$$x(n)=\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_k\psi_k(n)=\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_ke^{jk\omega_0n} \iff X_k=\frac{1}{p}\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}x(n)(e^{jk\omega_0n})\textasteriskcentered =\frac{1}{p}\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}x(n)e^{-jk\omega_0n}$$
where in the second equation $(e^{jk\omega_0n})\textasteriskcentered = e^{-jk\omega_0n}$.

Therefore, we get our discrete-time Fourier series for $p$-periodic signals with frequency $\omega_0 \in \set{0, \omega_0, 2\omega_0, \ldots, (p-1)\omega_0}$,
$$x(n)=\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_ke^{jk\omega_0n} \iff X_k=\frac{1}{p}\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}x(n)e^{-jk\omega_0n}.$$

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/22 12:23:39","modified":"2024/12/17 03:00:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) #### *(Orthogonal Bases)* $\langle \psi_k, \psi_\ell \rangle = p\delta(k - \ell)$
#### $\Psi^T\Psi\textasteriskcentered = pI$
#### $\Psi^{-1}=\frac{1}{p}\Psi\textasteriskcentered$


>[!example] Discrete-Time Fourier Series by Inspection
>Consider the $p$-periodic discrete signal
>$$x(n)=1+\sin(\frac{2\pi}{p}n)+3\cos(\frac{2\pi}{p}n)+\cos(\frac{2\pi}{p}n+\frac{\pi}{2}).$$
>As a sum of complex exponentials, we can equivalently express it as
>$$x(n)=e^{j\frac{2\pi}{p}0}+\frac{1}{2j}(e^{j\frac{2\pi}{p}n}-e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{p}n})+\frac{3}{2}(e^{j\frac{2\pi}{p}n} + e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{p}n}) + \frac{1}{2}(e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}}e^{j\frac{4\pi}{p}n} - e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}}e^{-j\frac{4\pi}{p}n}).$$
>Using the Fourier series decomposition $x(n)=\sum^{p-1}_{k=0}X_k\psi_k(n)$, we can reorder the complex exponentials by matching their frequencies, such that
>$$x(n) = 
>\underbrace{(1)}_{X_0}e^{j\frac{2\pi}{p}0} +
>\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2j} + \frac{3}{2} \right)}_{X_1}e^{j\frac{2\pi}{p}n} +
>\underbrace{\left(\frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2j} \right)}_{X_{-1}}e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{p}n} +
>\underbrace{\frac{j}{2}}_{X_2}e^{j\frac{4\pi}{p}n} +
>\underbrace{-\frac{j}{2}}_{X_{-2}}e^{-j\frac{4\pi}{p}n}
>$$
>The coefficients $X_{-1}$ and $X_{-2}$ come from seeing that $-1\omega_0=-\frac{2\pi}{p}$, and $-2\omega_0=-\frac{4\pi}{p}$ for $k\omega_0$. From the above, we can infer that $X_{-1}=X_{p-1}$ and $X_{-2}=X_{p-2}$, since we are trying to keep $k \in \set{0, 1, \ldots, (p-1)}$. Therefore, we have 5 coefficients: $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_{p-2}, X_{p-1}$.

>[!example] A DTFS Puzzle
>Consider a signal $x: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ with the following properties:
>1. $x(n+4\ell)=x(n),$ $\forall\ell,n \in \mathbb{Z}.$
>2. $\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)=4.$
>3. $\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)(-1)^n=8.$
>4. $\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}n)=\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}n)=0.$
>
>==(1)== We begin with the first equation, which implies that $n$ is periodic with period $p=\frac{4}{k}$ and fundamental frequency $\omega_{0} = \frac{2\pi}{p}=\frac{k\pi}{2}$. It also implies that we should be looking for 4 Fourier coefficients: $X_{-1}, X_{0}, X_{1}, \text{ and }X_{2}$.
>
>==(2)== Meanwhile, the second equation can be manipulated into 
>$$\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n) \cdot 1= \sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n) e^{j 0 n} = 4.$$
>Dividing the rightmost side by $p$ (assuming $k=1$ such that $\frac{p}{k}=4$), we get 
>$$\frac{1}{4}\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n) e^{j 0 n} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot 4 = 1.$$
>Therefore, $X_{0} = 1$.
>
>==(3)== To proceed, we observe that equation 3 can also be manipulated, such that
>$$\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)(-1)^n=\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)e^{j\pi n}=8.$$
>This implies that $k\omega_{0}=\pi$, or equivalently, $k=2$. As such,
>$$X_{2} = \frac{1}{4}\sum^{2}_{n=-1}x(n)e^{j\pi n}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot 8.$$
>Therefore, $X_{2}=2$.
>

>$$\frac{1}{4}\sum^{2}_{k=-1}x(n)\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}n) = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\sum^{2}_{k=-1}[x(n)e^{j \frac{\pi}{2} n} + x(n)e^{-j \frac{\pi}{2}n}] = 0.$$
>We observe that the right side can be simplified into $\frac{1}{2}X_{1}+\frac{1}{2}X_{-1}=0$, or equivalently $X_{1}=-X_{-1}$.
>

>
>We found the coefficients to be $X_{-1}=0$, $X_{0}=1$, $X_{1}=0$, $X_{2}=2$. We can now find $x(n)$ accordingly:

>\end{align}$$

378.title: 2.5c BIBO Stability
378.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.5 Stability/2.5c BIBO Stability.md
378.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5c BIBO Stability]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/31 01:36:49","modified":"2024/12/13 20:33:38"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bounded-Input, Bounded-Output (BIBO) Stability
>A system $H$ is **BIBO stable** if for any input $x \in \mathbb{X}$ bounded by a number $B_x \in \mathbb{R}^+$, such that $|x(t)| \leq B_x$ $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists a number $B_y \in \mathbb{R}^+$ for which the output $|y(t)| \leq B_y$ $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$.
>
>In addition to this, any [[2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System|discrete-time LTI system]] is BIBO stable if and only if $h$ is absolutely summable ($h \in \ell^1$), such that for some $B_{y} \in \mathbb{R}$,
>$$\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|h(k)| \leq B_{y}.$$
>
>Equivalently, any continuous-time LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if $h$ is absolutely integrable ($h \in \alpha^1$), such that
>$$\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}|h(\tau)|d\tau \leq B_{y}.$$

# Intuition
The proof for the BIBO stability of discrete-time LTI systems can be easily seen by showing that the triangle inequality holds, such that
$$\begin{align}
|y(n)|=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|x(n-k)h(k)| &\leq \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|x(n-k)||h(k)| \\
&\leq B_{x}\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|h(k)| \\
&\leq B_{y}.
\end{align}$$
However, this is only half of proving the dual relationship. Therefore, we need something else to prove that $\text{H is BIBO stable} \implies \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|\delta(k)|\leq B_{y}$. We cam proceed by taking the contrapositive of this statement, such that $\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|\delta(k)| = \infty \implies \text{H is not BIBO stable.}$ We need to prove that a bounded input can lead to an unbounded output.

To proceed, we must make $y(0)$ to blow up using a bounded input $x(n)$:
$$y(0)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(-k)h(k)$$
We choose $x(-n)$ carefully, such that $x(-n)=\text{sgn}(h(n))$, where $\text{sgn}(\cdot)$ is the sign of each value of $h(n)$. This turns the product $x(-k)h(k)$ into the absolute value of the filter, such that
$$\begin{align}
y(0) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\text{sgn}(h(n))h(k) \\ \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}|h(k)| \\
&= \infty.
\end{align}$$
But what if $h(n)$ is not a real-valued filter? Then, we can set $x(-n) = \frac{h\textasteriskcentered(n)}{|h(n)|}$, which yields the equation
$$\begin{align}
y(0) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)\frac{h\textasteriskcentered(k)}{|h(k)|} \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\frac{|h(k)|^2}{|h(k)|}  \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k) \\
&= \infty.
\end{align}$$

# Properties
#### (*Frequency Response*) If $h \in \ell^1$ is BIBO stable, then $|H(\omega)| < \infty$ $\forall \omega \in \mathbb{R}$ and $H(\omega)$ is continuous in $\omega$.



# Examples
>[!example] Is $x(n) = \frac{x(n) + x(n-1)}{2}$ BIBO stable?
>We prove by the definition of BIBO stability:
>$$|y(n)|=\frac{1}{2}|x(n) + x(n-1)|.$$
>We see by the triangle theorem that 
>$$\begin{align}
\frac{1}{2}|x(n) + x(n-1) &\leq \frac{1}{2}|x(n)| + \frac{1}{2}|x(n-1)| \\
&\leq \frac{1}{2}|B_{x}|+\frac{1}{2}|B_{x}| \\
&\leq B_{x}.
\end{align}$$
>Therefore, in this case, $B_{y}=B_{x}$.

380.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.5a Internal Stability]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/13 03:31:42","modified":"2024/12/17 04:42:55"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Internal (Asymptotic) Stability
>A system is **internally stable** if, in the absence of any input (e.g. with $x(n) = 0$  for all $n$), every state trajectory $q(t)$ converges to the zero vector (i.e. $q(t) \to \vec{0}$) as $t \to \infty$, regardless of the value of its initial state $q(0)$.
>
>Additionally, any discrete-time LTI system is **internally stable** if, for every eigenvalue $\lambda_i \in \{ \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \ldots,\lambda_{N} \} \in \mathbb{C}$ of the state matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ defining the system's [[2.2f LTI State Space|state evolution equation]],
>$$|\lambda_{i}| < 1.$$
>
>Similarly, any continuous-time LTI system is internally stable if
>$$\text{Re}\{\lambda_{i}\} < 0.$$
>>[!warning] Note (Marginal Stability)
>>If one or more eigenvalues meet the border conditions (i.e. $|\lambda_{i}| = 1$ in the discrete-time, and $\text{Re}\{\lambda_{i}\} = 0$ in the continuous-time), the system is said to be **marginally stable**. These are the conditions at which $q(t) = q(0)$ $\forall t$.
# Proof
1. **Discrete-Time Proof**
We will complete the proof by observing that any LTI state trajectory $q(n)$ with input $x(n) = 0$ can be expressed as a product of its initial state $q(0)$, such that
$$q(n) = A^nq(0).$$
This is easily observed when we understand that $q(2) = Aq(1) = A(Aq(0)) = A^2q(0)$. We infer that $q(n) \to 0$ as $n \to 0$ only if $A^n \to 0$. We then observe that any diagonalizable matrix $A$ can be expressed using eigendecomposition as 
$$A^n = V\Lambda^nV^{-1}.$$
Finally, we observe that $q(0)$ can be expressed as a linear combination of any eigenbasis in its dimension, such that
$$q(0)=\alpha_{1}\vec{v}_{1} + \ldots + \alpha_{N}\vec{v}_{N}=V\alpha$$
Substituting the two latter equations into the first one, we get
$$\begin{align}
q(n) &= V\Lambda^n(V^{-1}V)\alpha \\
&=V\Lambda^n\alpha.
\end{align}$$
We see that if $\Lambda^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (every eigenvalue is strictly less than one), then $q(n) \to 0$. Then, all 

2. **Continuous-Time Proof**
We proceed in the same manner by observing that
$$q(t) = e^{At}q(0)$$
which is the matrix solution of the scalar differential equation $\dot{q}(t)=aq(t) \iff q(t) = e^{at}q(0)$. Since by its Taylor series expansion $e^{At} = I + \frac{t}{1!}A + \frac{t^2}{2!}A^2 + \ldots$, then by decomposing $q(0)$ into a linear combination of an eigenbasis and expressing $A^n=V\Lambda^n V^{-1}$ as defined above, we get
$$\begin{align}
q(t)&=e^{At}V\alpha \\
&= V\alpha + \frac{t}{1!}V\Lambda (V^{-1}V)\alpha+\frac{t^2}{2!}V\Lambda^2(V^{-1}V)\alpha+\ldots \\
&= V\alpha+tV\Lambda\alpha + \frac{t^2}{2!}V\Lambda^2\alpha+\ldots  \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=0}\frac{t^k}{k!}V\Lambda^k\alpha \\
&= Ve^{\Lambda t}\alpha
\end{align}$$
This means that as $t \to \infty$, $q(t) \to 0$ only if $e^{\Lambda t} \to 0$. This is only a possibility if for all $\lambda_{i} \in \{ \lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{N} \} \in \mathbb{C}$, $\text{Re}\{\lambda_{i}\} < 0$.
# Examples
>[!example] Stability of an RLC Circuit
>In a previous note (2.2f), we found that the state matrix of a series RLC circuit is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{R}{L} & 1 \\ \frac{1}{LC} & 0\end{bmatrix}$.

>[!note] Cascade of Multiple Systems
>In **signals and systems**, a **cascade** refers to the serial connection of two or more systems, where the output of one system serves as the input to the next system. For example, a cascade $H$ of two systems $F$ and $G$ can be graphically represented as
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.3]
>
>% Input
>\draw[->, thick] (-1,0) -- (0,0) node[at start, left]{$x(t)$};
>
>% First block
>\draw[draw, rectangle, minimum width=1.5cm, minimum height=1cm, thick] (0, -0.5) rectangle (1.5, 0.5);
>\node at (0.75, 0) {$F$};
>
>% Arrow between blocks
>\draw[thick] (1.5,0) -- (2,0);
>
>% Second block
>\draw[draw, rectangle, minimum width=1.5cm, minimum height=1cm, thick] (2, -0.5) rectangle (3.5, 0.5);
>\node at (2.75, 0) {$G$};
>
>% Output
>\draw[->, thick] (3.5,0) -- (4.5,0) node[at end, right]{$y(t)$};
>
>% H
>\draw[thick, dashed] (-0.5, -1) -- (4, -1) -- (4, 1) -- (-0.5, 1) -- cycle;
>\node[thick, scale=1.3] at (-0.3, -0.8) {H};
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>For [[2.2a LTI System|LTI systems]], the impulse response of a cascade is given as
>$$h(t) = (f\textasteriskcentered g)(t),$$
>whereas the cascade's frequency response is given as
>$$H(\omega) = F(\omega)G(\omega).$$
>>[!warning] Note (Zero Cascade)
>>If 

# Proof

# Examples
>[!example] (Discrete-Time) Cascade
>Consider a system $F$, governed by the LCCDE
>$$y(n)-y(n-1) = x(n) - x(n-3).$$
>Suppose we cascade $F$ with a new system $G$ ($F$ comes before $G$ as in the figure above), governed by the LCCDE
>$$y(n)-y(n-3) = x(n) - x(n-1).$$
>By plugging in the eigenfunction input $x(n)=e^{j\omega n}$, we find that the frequency responses of $F$ and $G$ are
>$$F(\omega) = \frac{1 - e^{-j3\omega}}{1-e^{-j\omega}} \enspace \text{and} \enspace G(\omega) = \frac{1-e^{-j\omega}}{1 - e^{-j3\omega}}.$$
>We see here that $F(\omega)$ is undefined for $\omega = 2k\pi$, and $G(\omega)$ is undefined for $\omega = \frac{2k\pi}{3}$. We also know by definition that $H(\omega) = F(\omega)G(\omega)$. Since $F$ comes before $G$, any $\omega_{0}$ such that $F(\omega_{0})=0$ will lead to $H(\omega)=0$. Therefore, we can say that
>$$H(\omega) = 
>\begin{cases}
>\text{Undefined} &\text{for } \omega = 2k\pi \\
>0 &\text{for } \omega = \frac{2k\pi}{3} \cap k \pmod{3} \not\equiv 0 \\
>1 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases},$$
>where $k \pmod{3} \not\equiv 0$ becomes a condition since $H(\omega)$ is still undefined for $2k\pi$.

>[!note] Integrator-Adder-Gain Block Diagram
>An **integrator-adder-gain block diagram** is a graphical representation used to illustrate **continuous-time** systems that involve signal integration, summation (addition), or scaling by a gain factor. IAG structures take the input $x(n)$ and output $y(n)$ of a system, and represent the system's manipulation of the input to obtain the output using
>- Integrator blocks ($\boxed{\tiny\int}$), which delay any signal $g(n)$ by 1 unit of time, such that $g(n) \to \boxed{D} \to g(n-1)$.
>- Adder blocks ($\oplus$), which sum two or more signals $f(n)$ and $g(n)$ to produce $f(n) + g(n)$.
>- Gain blocks ($\rhd^{\alpha}$), which scale a signal by a number $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.

386.title: 2.2d LTI Frequency Response
386.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/2.2d LTI Frequency Response.md
386.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2d LTI Frequency Response]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/07 13:27:37","modified":"2024/12/17 03:10:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Frequency Response
>The $2\pi$-periodic continuous frequency response of a discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] can be expressed by convolving its filter $h(n)$ with an eigenfunction input $x(n) = e^{j\omega n}$, such that
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= e^{j\omega n}\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} h(k)e^{-j\omega k} \\
&=H(\omega)e^{j \omega n},
\end{align}$$
>where $H(\omega) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} h(k)e^{-j\omega k}$ is the frequency response of the system, while $\omega$ ($\text{rad}/\text{sample}$) is the fundamental period of the eigenfunction.
>
>Similarly, in continuous-time, the non-periodic continuous frequency response of an LTI system can be expressed by convolving its filter $h(t)$ with an eigenfunction input $x(t) = e^{j\omega t}$, such that
>$$\begin{align}
>y(t) &= e^{j\omega t}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}h(\tau)e^{-j\omega \tau}d\tau \\
>&= H(\omega)e^{j \omega t},
\end{align}$$
>where $H(\omega) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}h(\tau)e^{-j\omega \tau}d\tau$ is the frequency response of the system.
>>[!warning] Note (New Frequencies)
>>If the output $y$ of a system contains frequencies that are not in its input $x$, then that system cannot be an LTI system; no new frequencies can be created in the output of an LTI system.

# Intuition
9/30 lecture around 40 min to 1:10

# Properties
#### (Standard Conversion) $h(t) = \alpha e^{-\alpha t} \iff H(\omega) = \frac{\beta}{\alpha + j\omega}$.

#### (D-T Eigenfunction Periodicity) $e^{j\omega n}$ is $2\pi$-periodic in $\omega$ and is only periodic in $n$ if $\omega$ is a rational multiple of $\pi$.
We need to decompose this problem into two sub-problems:
1. We begin by equating $e^{j(\omega + W)n}=e^{j\omega n}$, which simplifies into $e^{jWn} = 1$ and into $Wn = 2\pi$. This means that $n=\frac{2\pi}{W} = \omega$.

#### (D-T $2\pi$-periodicity) $H(\omega + 2\pi) = H(\omega)$
We can prove by taking the following:
$$H(\omega + 2\pi)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k}e^{-j2\pi k}.$$
Since for any integer $k$, $e^{j2k\pi}=e^{j2\pi}=1$ due to $2\pi$-periodicity of complex exponentials,
$$\begin{align}
H(\omega + 2\pi) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k}e^{-j2\pi k} \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k} \times 1 \\
&= H(\omega).
\end{align}$$
#### (Real Conjugate) If $h(n)=h\textasteriskcentered(n)$ or $h(t) = h\textasteriskcentered(t)$, then $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$.
Saying that a function is equal to its complex conjugate simply means that it is real. We proceed with a simple proof, where
$$\begin{align}
H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h\textasteriskcentered(k)e^{-j\omega k} \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{j(-\omega) k} \\
&= H(-\omega).
\end{align}$$
#### (Even Magnitude) If $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$, then $|H(\omega)| = |H(-\omega)|$.
The LHS implies that $H$ is real.

387.title: 2.2d LTI Frequency Response
387.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/2.2d LTI Frequency Response.md
387.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2d LTI Frequency Response]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/07 13:27:37","modified":"2024/12/17 03:10:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) #### (Even Magnitude) If $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$, then $|H(\omega)| = |H(-\omega)|$.
The LHS implies that $H$ is real.
#### (Odd Phase) If $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$, then $\angle H(\omega) = -\angle H(-\omega)$.
The LHS implies that $H$ is real.
# Examples
>[!example] Does $1 + e^{j\frac{\pi}{4} n} \xrightarrow{H} 2$ describe an LTI system?
>We can quickly express the input as
>$$x(n) = e^{j0n} + e^{j\frac{\pi}{4}n},$$
>and the output as
>$$y(n) = 2e^{j0n}.$$
>We know that for $x(n)=e^{j \omega n}$ the output will be $y(n) = H(\omega)x(n) = H(\omega)e^{j\omega n}$. Therefore,
>$$y(n) = H(0)e^{j0n} + H(\frac{\pi}{4})e^{j\frac{\pi}{4}n}.$$
>Since $H(\omega)$ only depends on $\omega$ (so we can't set $H(\frac{\pi}{4})=e^{-j \frac{\pi}{4} n}$ as it depends on $n$), there is only one valid solution at
>$$H(0) = 2, \enspace H(\frac{\pi}{4})=0.$$ 
>While this result is consistent with the eigenfunction behavior of a D-T LTI system, it does not mean that $H$ is a discrete-time LTI system. Therefore, we cannot determine the LTI properties of $H$ solely based on the eigenfunction property.

>[!example] Does $1 + e^{j\frac{\pi}{4} n} \xrightarrow{H} (-1)^n$ describe an LTI system?
>Once again, we express the input as
>$$x(n) = e^{j0n} + e^{j\frac{\pi}{4}n},$$
>and this time we express the output as
>$$y(n) = e^{j \pi n}.$$
>We can see that
>$$y(n) = e^{j \pi n} = H(0)e^{j0n} + H(\frac{\pi}{4})e^{j\frac{\pi}{4}n}.$$
>This is not an LTI system, as the output has different resonant frequency $w_0 = \pi$ than the input.

> [!example] Find the frequency response of a $2$-point moving average.
> We know that the $2$-point moving average can be expressed in terms of Kronecker deltas, such that
> $$h(n) = \frac{1}{2}\delta(n) + \frac{1}{2}\delta(n-1).$$
> Therefore,
> $$y(n) = e^{j \omega n}\frac{1}{2}\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}[\delta(k) + \delta(k-1)]e^{-j\omega k}.$$
> By inspection, we see that
> $$\begin{align}
> H(\omega) &= \frac{1}{2}\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}[\delta(k) + \delta(k-1)]e^{-j\omega k} \\ 
> &= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}e^{-j\omega} \\
> &= e^{-j\frac{\omega}{2}}\left(\frac{e^{j\frac{\omega}{2}} + e^{-j\frac{\omega}{2}}}{2} \right) \\
> &= \cos(\frac{\omega}{2})e^{-j\frac{\omega}{2}}.
>\end{align}$$
>Then, the magnitude of $H(\omega)$ can be expressed as
>$$\begin{align}
>|H(\omega)| &= |\cos(\frac{\omega}{2})| \cdot |e^{-j\frac{\omega}{2}}| \\
>&= |\cos(\frac{\omega}{2})| \cdot 1 \\
>&= |\cos(\frac{\omega}{2})|,
>\end{align}$$
>where $|e^{-j\frac{\omega}{2}}| = 1$ by the laws of the unit circle.
>
>Note that we can express $H(\omega)$ as a [[2.2j.2 Phasor|phasor]], such that $H(\omega) = |\cos(\frac{\omega}{2})| \angle -\frac{\omega}{2}$. We can also plot the frequency response on a bode plot, such that it consists of its magnitude and phase plots,

>[!example] Find the output of $x(n)=\cos(\omega_0 n)$.
>We can start by expressing $x(n)$ as a sum of complex exponentials, such that
>$$x(n)=\cos(\omega_0 n) = \frac{1}{2}e^{j\omega_0 n} + \frac{1}{2}e^{-j\omega_0 n}.$$
>With this in mind, we can use the frequency response formula to formulate $y(n)$, such that
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) = \frac{1}{2}H(\omega_0)e^{j\omega_0 n} + \frac{1}{2}H(-\omega_0)e^{-j\omega_0 n}
>\end{align}$$
>The second term on the RHS is $H(-\omega)$, since $h(n)$ is real and therefore by the real conjugate property, $h(n) = h\textasteriskcentered(n)$.
>
>We can do some analysis here. If $h(n)$ was complex valued, then
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= \frac{1}{2}H(\omega_0)e^{j\omega_0 n} + \frac{1}{2}H\textasteriskcentered(\omega_0)e^{-j\omega_0 n} \\
>&= \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{1}{2}x\textasteriskcentered \\
>&= \frac{1}{2}2\textrm{Re}\{x\} \\
>&= \textrm{Re}\{ x\} \\
>\end{align}$$
>where $x \in \mathbb{C}$. Note here that $x = H(\omega_0)e^{j\omega_0 n}$ is different from $x(n)=\cos(\omega_0 n)$.
>
>Here, we remember that the frequency response can be represented as a phasor, such that $H(\omega_0) = |H(\omega_0)|e^{j\angle H(\omega_0)}$. Then,
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= \textrm{Re}\{|H(\omega_0)|e^{j\angle H(\omega_0)}e^{j\omega_0n}\} \\
>&= \textrm{Re}\{|H(\omega_0)|e^{j(\omega_0n + \angle H(\omega_0)}\} \\
>&= |H(\omega_0)|cos(\omega_0n + \angle H(\omega_0)).
>\end{align}$$
>**FOR EXAMPLE**, if we were to use the FIR two-point moving average filter from the example above, our output would simplify to
>$$y(n)=|cos\frac{\omega_0}{2}|cos(\omega_0n - \frac{\omega}{2}).$$
>Given an input $x(n)=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)$, where $\omega_0 = \frac{\pi}{2}$, our output will be equal to
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= |\cos\frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{2}|\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}n - \frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{2}) \\
>&= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}n - \frac{\pi}{4}).
>\end{align}$$
>If, for example, we add a phase to our input, such that $x(n) = \cos(\omega n + \phi)$, then
>$$y(n) = |H(\omega_0)|$$

>[!note] LTI System
>A linear time-invariant (LTI) system $H$ is one that is both:
>1. **Linear**, such that its system response follows the principle of superposition (composed of linearity and additivity):
>	1. Homogeneity: $y(\alpha x)$
>
>1. **Time-invariant**, such that a time shift in its input signal results in a time shift in its output signal:
>$$x(t) \to \boxed{h(n)} \to y(t) \implies x(t-t_0) \to \boxed{h(n)} \to y(t-t_0),$$
>where $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$.



# Examples
>[!example] Linearity & Time Invariance
>Are the following signals linear or time invariant?
>- $y(n) = 7x(n+1)$
>- $y(n) = x(n)x(n-1)$
>- $y(n) = e^{x(n)}$

>[!note] State Trajectory in Scalar Continuous-Time LTI Differential Equation Model
>The solution to the scalar (vector-less) continuous-time LTI model
>$$\frac{d}{dt}x(t)=ax(t)+bu(t)$$
>$$x(0)=x_0$$
>for the state scalar as a function of time $x: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}$, the control input as a function of timestep $u: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}$ and scalar coefficients $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ is
>$$x(t)=e^{at}x_0+\int^{t}_{0}e^{a(t-\tau)}bu(\tau)d \tau.$$
# Proof
Since this is a first-order differential equation, we can solve it using the solution for non-homogeneous first-order differential equations $x(t)=e^{\lambda t}x_0+\int^{t}_{0}e^{\lambda (t-\tau)}u(\tau)d\tau$ (see Note 2).

395.title: 2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System
395.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/99b Discrete-Time LTI System/2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System.md
395.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/30 19:06:05","modified":"2024/12/13 02:11:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] State Trajectory In Discrete-Time LTI Model
>The solution to the discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI model]]
>$$\vec{x}[i+1]=A \vec{x}[i]+B \vec{u}[i]$$
>$$\vec{x}[0]=\vec{x}_0,$$
>for the state vector as a function of timestep $\vec{x}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the control inputs as a function of timestep $\vec{u}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and matrices $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ is
>$$\vec{x}[i]=A^i \vec{x}_0 + \sum^{i-1}_{k=0}A^{i-k-1}B \vec{u}[k].$$

# Proof
The proof to this solution is very straightforward. We will use the principle of mathematical induction to figure it out. We will start with the base case,
$$\vec{x}[0]=\vec{x}_0.$$
Knowing this, we can assume the LTI model is true for timestep $i$:
$$\vec{x}[i]=A \vec{x}[i-1]+B \vec{u}[i-1].$$
We will then prove it for $i+1$ as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
	\begin{aligned}
		\vec{x}[i+1] &= A\vec{x}[i]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= A^2\vec{x}[i-1]+AB\vec{u}[i-1]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= A^3\vec{x}[i-2]+A^2B\vec{u}[i-2]+AB\vec{u}[i-1]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= \text{...} \\
					 &= A^{i+1} \vec{x}_0+\sum^{i}_{k=0}A^{i-k}B\vec{u}[k].
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Therefore, for timestep $i$, the solution is
$$\vec{x}[i]=A^i \vec{x}_0 + \sum^{i-1}_{k=0}A^{i-k-1}B \vec{u}[k].$$

396.title: 2.2e LTI LCCDE
396.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/2.2e LTI LCCDE.md
396.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2e LTI LCCDE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/26 15:06:08","modified":"2024/12/14 23:08:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Linear Constant Coefficient Difference Equation (LCCDE) Representation
>A **linear constant coefficient difference equation** is a mathematical expression that describes the relationship between the input and output of an [[2.2 LTI Systems|LTI system]]. In discrete-time, is defined as the relationship
>$$\sum^{N}_{k = 0}a_{k}y(n-k) = \sum^{M}_{m = 0}b_{m}x(n-m),$$
>where $N$ is the order of the equation, and $M$ is the delay of the input terms.
>
>Similarly, in continuous-time, 

# Properties
#### (Transfer Function) $H(\omega) = \frac{\sum^{M}_{m=0}b_{m}e^{-j\omega m}}{\sum^{N}_{k=0}a_{k}e^{-j\omega k}}.$

# Example
>[!example] (Discrete-Time) Finding the Transfer Function Using the LCCDE
>In 2.2d, we found that the system with a recursive LCCDE $y(n)=\alpha y(n-N) + x(n)$ has a frequency response of $H(\omega) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha e^{-j\omega N}}$. However, there is a simpler way to find this. The LCCDE for an eigenfunction input $x(n)=e^{j\omega n}$ becomes
>$$H(\omega)e^{j\omega n} = \alpha H(\omega)e^{j\omega(n-N)}+e^{j\omega n}.$$
>Dividing both sides by $e^{j\omega n}$ and factoring out $H(\omega)$, we get
>$$H(\omega) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha e^{-j\omega N}}.$$
>It's as simple as that.

397.title: 2.2c LTI Impulse Response
397.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/2.2c LTI Impulse Response.md
397.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c LTI Impulse Response]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/24 15:30:14","modified":"2024/12/14 23:02:06"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Impulse Response
>The response of a discrete-time[[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] to a [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta|unit impulse]] $x(n) = \delta(n)$ is used to find its filter, $h(n)$. Mathematically, the solution $y(n)$ to any input $x(n)$ of the discrete-time LTI can be expressed as the [[2.2b LTI Convolution|convolution]]
>$$y(n) = (\delta * h)(n) = h(n).$$
>
>Similarly, the solution $y(t)$ to any input $x(t)$ of the continuous-time LTI can be expressed as the convolution of its
>$$y(t) = ()$$

# Proof
We proceed by a simple proof, taking $x(n)=\delta(n)$ and a filter $h(n)$:
$$\begin{align}
y(n) &= (x \textasteriskcentered h)(n) \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(k)h(n-k) \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(k)h(n-k) \\
&= h(n),
\end{align}$$
since $\delta(k) \neq 0 \iff k = 0$.

# Examples
>[!example] (Discrete-Time) Impulse Response of a Recursive Filter
>A causal, discrete-time LTI system $H$ is characterized by the recursive difference equation $y(n) = \alpha y(n-N)+x(n)$. We can determine its impulse response by observing that for $x(n)=\delta(n)$,
>$$\begin{align}
>h(n) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(n-k)[\alpha h(n-N)+\delta(n)] \\ \\
>&= \alpha h(n-N) + \delta(n).
>\end{align}$$
>We quickly see that since $H$ is causal, then $h(n) = 0$ for all $n < 0$. Therefore, $h(0) = \delta(0)=1$. By observation, we find $h(N) = \alpha$, $h(2N) = \alpha^2$, and so on. Therefore, we can establish that
>$$h(n) = \begin{cases}\alpha^{\frac{n}{N}} \text{ if } n \mod{N} \equiv 0 \\ 0 \text{ otherwise}\end{cases}.$$
>Using the Kronecker delta, we can get rid of this piecewise nature so that
>$$h(n) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\alpha^n \delta(n - kN).$$
>This is because the delta is nonzero only for $n=kN$, (i.e. a multiple of $N$).

398.title: 2.2b LTI Convolution
398.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.2 LTI Systems/2.2b LTI Convolution.md
398.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b LTI Convolution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 21:55:20","modified":"2024/12/17 00:04:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Convolution Representation
>Given a discrete-time input signal $x(n)$, the output of a discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] $y(n)$ can be represented as a weighted combination of impulse responses $h[n]$, such that
>$$y(n) = x(n) * h(n) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(k)h(n-k)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(n-k)h(k).$$ 
>Similarly, given a continuous-time input signal $x(t)$, the output of a continuous-time LTI system $y(t)$ can be represented as
>$$y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(t - \tau)h(\tau)d\tau.$$

# Intuition

# Properties
#### (*Polynomialization*) If for the polynomials $\hat{y}(z)=\hat{x}(z)\hat{h}(z)$, then $y_k=(h * x)_k$ where $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}y_kz^k$.
We start by expanding with the fact that $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{i=-\infty}\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}(x_iz^i)(h_jz^j)$. We can perform a change of variables for $k=i+j$, such that
$$\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}x_kh_{k-i}z^k.$$
By definition, $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}y_kz^k$, and therefore $y_k=\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}y_kz^kx_kh_{k-i}$.
