(cont'd) >[!example] Cascade
>Suppose we have two FIR filters, $a(n)$ and $b(n)$, such that their impulse response is given by
>$$\begin{align}
>a(n) &= a_0\delta(n) + a_1\delta(n-1)+ \ldots + a_N\delta(n-N) && (\text{where } N \in \mathbb{N}), \\  &\text{and} \\ b(n) &= b_0\delta(n) + b_1\delta(n-1)+ \ldots + b_M\delta(n-M) && (\text{where } M \in \mathbb{N}).
>\end{align}$$
>The two filters are placed in a cascade $C$, such that the final system is
>$$x \rightarrow \boxed{\boxed{A} \rightarrow \boxed{B}}^C \rightarrow y.$$
>We can find the cascade by setting $x(n) = \delta(n)$. Then,
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= [(x * a) * b].
>\end{align}$$
>Since the impulse response of any system is its filter, we can simplify this into
>$$\begin{align}
>c(n) &= (a * b) \\
>&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} a(k)b(n-k) \\
>\end{align}$$
>Here, we can see that $a(k)b(n-k)$ is equal to
>$$a_0b_0\delta(k)\delta(n-k) + a_0b_1\delta(k)\delta(n-k-1) + a_1b_0\delta(k-1)\delta(n-k) + a_1b_1\delta(k-1)\delta(n-k-1) + \ldots,$$
>and therefore
>$$\begin{align}
>c(n) &= a_0b_0\delta(n) + (a_0b_1 + a_1b_0)\delta(n-1) + (a_0b_2 + a_1b_1 + a_2b_0)\delta(n-2) + \ldots
>\end{align}$$
>This means that we can model any coefficient $c_n$ of the cascade ($n \leq N$) as
>$$c_n = \sum^{n}_{k=\max(0, n - M)}a_kb_{n-k},$$
>where $k=\max(0, n-M),$ as the two systems are of different sizes, and we need to account for cases where $M < N$. Finally, we can express $c$ as
>$$c(n) = c_0\delta(n) + c_1\delta(n-1) + \ldots + c_{N+M}\delta(n-N-M).$$

403.title: 2.10a Sampling
403.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.10 Sampling Theory/2.10a Sampling.md
403.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.10a Sampling]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/17 04:34:08","modified":"2024/12/17 15:30:36"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
>**Sampling** is the process of converting a **continuous-time signal** into a **discrete-time signal** by taking measurements (samples) of a continuous-time signal $x_{C}(t)$ at a regular sampling period of $T_{s}$ to create a discrete-time signal $x_{D}[n]$ , such that
>$$x_{D}[n]=\left.x_{C}(t) \right\vert_{t=kT_{S}} \text{ for } k \in \mathbb{N}.$$
>This process is also outlined in the block diagram below, where a spike train $z(t)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(t-kT_{S})$ is multiplied with the input to produce the sampled signal $x_{Z}(t)= x_{C}(t) \times z(t)$, which is then converted to a discrete-time signal, $x_{D}[n]$:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usetikzlibrary{arrows.meta, positioning}
>
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2cm, >=Stealth, thick]
>
>% Nodes
>\node (input1) at (0,0) {};
>\node[draw, circle, minimum size=0.5cm, right=of input1] (adder) {$\times$};
>\node[below=1.5cm of adder] (input2) {};
>\node[draw, rectangle, minimum height=1.2cm, minimum width=1.8cm, right=of adder] (box) {Dirac-to\newline-Kronecker};
>\node[right=of box] (output) {};
>
>% Arrows
>\draw[->] (input1.east) -- (adder.west) node[at start, left] {$x_{C}(t)$};    % Input from the left to adder
>\draw[->] (input2.north) -- (adder.south) node[at start, below] {$z(t)$};  % Input from below to adder
>\draw[->] (adder.east) -- (box.west) node[midway, above]{$x_{Z}(t)$};       % Adder output to box
>\draw[->] (box.east) -- (output.west) node[right] {$x_{D}[n]$};      % Box output to the right
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>
>Sampling theory is primarily governed by the **Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem**, which states that a signal $x_{C}(t)$ that is band-limited (i.e. bounded) to a frequency $B$, such that $X(\omega) = 0 \text{ for all }|\omega| \geq B$, can be fully recovered from its sample $x_{D}[n]$ if
>$$\omega_{S} \geq 2B,$$
>where $\omega_{S}=\frac{2\pi}{T_{S}}$ is the sampling frequency, and $B$ is called the **Nyquist rate**.
>
>>[!warning] Note (Aliasing)
>>If the condition is not met ($\omega_{s} < 2B$), frequency components overlap with one another and cause distortion known as **aliasing**. Aliasing makes it impossible to distinguish higher frequencies from lower ones, leading to an inaccurate representation of the original signal. The effects of aliasing can be mitigated by pre-processing the $x_{D}[n]$ with a low pass (anti-aliasing) filter, as explained below.

406.title: 2.1c Signal Periodicity
406.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.1 Signals/2.1c Signal Periodicity.md
406.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1c Signal Periodicity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/15 00:22:00","modified":"2024/12/17 04:37:15"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Periodicity of Signals
>A ***continuous-time*** signal $x$ is said to be periodic if there is a real number $p > 0$, such that
>$$x(t + p) = x(t) \enspace \text{for all } t.$$
>The smallest $p$ for which the above equation holds is called the fundamental period of $x$. The fundamental frequency of $x$ is denoted by
>$$w_{0}=\frac{2\pi}{p}.$$
>
>Additionally, all periodic ***discrete-time*** signals share a fundamental period $p=1$, as well as a fundamental frequency $\omega_{0} = 2\pi$.
>
>>[!warning] Note 1 (Constant Signals)
>>Constant signals (i.e. DC signals) have an undefined period and a fundamental frequency $\omega_{0} = 0$.
>
>>[!warning] Note 2 (Compound Signals)
>>If a signal  $x$ is formed by combining several periodic signals, its overall period is the least common multiple of their individual periods.

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/13 04:48:19","modified":"2024/12/13 18:52:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Continuous-Time Unit Step
>The continuous-time unit step can be defined as a signal $u$, such that
>$$u(t) = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if } t < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } t \geq 0 \end{cases}.$$
>The unit step can be written as the integral of the [[2.1a.1 Dirac Delta|Dirac delta]], such that
>$$u(t) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\delta(\tau)d\tau.$$

409.title: 2.1a.1 Dirac Delta
409.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.1 Signals/2.1b Continuous-Time Signals/2.1a.1 Dirac Delta.md
409.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Dirac Delta]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/07 12:54:13","modified":"2024/12/17 14:15:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Dirac Delta
>The **Dirac delta function**, denoted as  $\delta(t)$, is a mathematical construct used to model an idealized point impulse. Mathematically, it is defined by the piecewise equation
>$$\delta(t) = 
>\begin{cases}
>\infty & \text{for } t = 0 \\
>0 & \text{for } t \neq 0
>\end{cases}.$$
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The Dirac delta is actually not a function. Rather it is a distribution, or a generalized function.

# Properties
#### (Sampling) $x(t)\delta(t - t_0) = x(t_0)\delta(t-t_{0})$

#### (Sifting) $\int^{B}_{A}x(t)\delta(t-t_0)dt = \begin{cases}x(t_0) & \text{if } A < t_0 < B \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$
#### (Convolution) $y(t) = \alpha\delta(t-t_0) \implies (x \textasteriskcentered y)(t) = \alpha x(t-t_0)$
We can easily prove this using the two previous properties:
$$ \begin{align}
(x \textasteriskcentered y)(t) &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)y(t-\tau)d\tau \\
&= \alpha\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau-t_0)d\tau \\
\end{align}$$
Note here that $\delta(t-\tau-t_0) \neq 0 \iff \tau = t-t_0$, so
$$\alpha\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau-t_0)d\tau = \alpha x(t-t_0).$$
#### (Time-Scaling) $\delta(\alpha t) = \frac{1}{|\alpha|}\delta(t)$
This is a bit harder to prove, but since we know that the

410.title: 2.1a.2 D-T Unit Step
410.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.1 Signals/2.1a Discrete-Time Signals/2.1a.2 D-T Unit Step.md
410.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.2 D-T Unit Step]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 18:01:47","modified":"2024/12/13 04:48:42"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time Unit Step
>The discrete-time unit step can be defined as a signal $u: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$, such that
>$$u[n] = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if } n < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } n \geq 0 \end{cases}.$$
>The unit step can be written in terms of a linear combination of shifted [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta| impulses]] as 
>$$u[n] = \sum^{}_{k=0} \delta[n-k] \iff u[n] = \sum^{n}_{l=-\infty}\delta[l] \impliedby l=n-k.$$

411.title: 2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta
411.path: Electrical Engineering/2. Signals & Systems/2.1 Signals/2.1a Discrete-Time Signals/2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta.md
411.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 18:01:06","modified":"2024/12/13 15:19:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Kronecker Delta (Discrete-Time Unit Impulse)
>The **kronecker delta** (i.e. the discrete-time unit impulse) is defined as
>$$\delta[n]=\begin{cases}0 && \text{if } n=0 \\ 1 && \text{if } n \neq 0\end{cases}.$$
>Any arbitrary discrete-time signal $x(n)$ can be decomposed into a linear combination of discrete-time impulses (Kronecker deltas), such that
>$$x[n] = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x[k]\delta[n-k].$$

# Properties
#### (Step Representation) $\delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]$.
The RHS is $1$ only at $n=0$. Any value $n < 0$ will lead to $0-0=0$, whereas any value $n > 0$ will lead to $1-1=0$.

>[!note] Second-Order Circuits
>Second-order circuits are electrical circuits whose behavior is described by a second-order differential equation. These circuits contain both [[2.1i Inductor|inductors]] and [[2.1g Capacitor|capacitors]]. Second-order circuits follow the general equation
>$$\frac{d^2}{dt^2}x(t) + 2\alpha\frac{d}{dt}x(t) + \omega_0^2x(t) = f(t),$$
>where $\alpha$ is the damping coefficient, and $\omega_0$ is the resonant frequency of the circuit at which the impedance is purely real.
>
>The solutions to the second-order differential circuits can be split into 3 cases:
>1. Overdamped Response ($\alpha > \omega_0$):
>$$x(t) = A_1e^{s_1t}+A_2e^{s_2t}+x(\infty),$$
>where $s=-\alpha \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \omega_0^2}$ and the coefficients $A_k =$
>
>2. Critically Damped Response ($\alpha = \omega_0$)
>3. Underdamped Response ($\alpha < \omega_0$)

420.title: 2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals
420.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.2 Circuit Analysis/2.2k Frequency Domain Analysis/2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals.md
420.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:07:32","modified":"2024/11/06 02:18:39"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Sinusoidal Signals
>A **sinusoidal signal** is a type of continuous wave that oscillates smoothly and periodically over time, following the mathematical form of a sine or cosine function. Sinusoidal signals are the core of AC analysis. A sinusoidal signal can be represented of the form
>$$x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi),$$
>where $A$ is the signal's magnitude, $\omega=2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ is its angular frequency, and $\phi$ is its phase angle (the amount by which it is shifted from the standard cosine waveform).

421.title: 2.2j.5 Bode Plots
421.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.2 Circuit Analysis/2.2k Frequency Domain Analysis/2.2j.5 Bode Plots.md
421.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.5 Bode Plots]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:12:26","modified":"2024/11/30 17:06:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bode Plot
>A **bode plot** are graphical representations of the [[2.2j.4 Transfer Functions|frequency response]] of a system. It consists of two separate plots that display how the system's **magnitude** and **phase** responds to different values of $\omega$ on the logarithmic scale.
>
>The magnitude of a transfer function $H(j\omega)$ in decibels (SI: dB) is given by
>$$20\log_{10}|H(j\omega)|,$$
>and the phase of a transfer function is given by
>$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{Im}\{H(j\omega)\}}{\mathrm{Re}\{H(j\omega)\}}.$$

# Intuition

422.title: 2.2j.4 Transfer Functions
422.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.2 Circuit Analysis/2.2k Frequency Domain Analysis/2.2j.4 Transfer Functions.md
422.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.4 Transfer Functions]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:12:37","modified":"2024/11/20 21:03:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Transfer Function
>A **transfer function** is a mathematical representation that describes the input-output relationship of a system in the frequency domain, providing its frequency response. For a system $X(j\omega)$, 
>$$H(j\omega) = \frac{X_\text{out}(j\omega)}{X_\text{in}(j\omega)} = |H(j\omega)|e^{j\omega \phi},$$
>where by definition $|H(j\omega)|$ is the system's gain (or magnitude), and $\phi(j\omega) = \tan^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{Im}\{H(\omega)\}}{\mathrm{Re}\{H(\omega)\}}$ is the system's phase response.

423.title: 2.2j.2 Phasor
423.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.2 Circuit Analysis/2.2k Frequency Domain Analysis/2.2j.2 Phasor.md
423.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.2 Phasor]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 01:23:33","modified":"2024/11/06 02:12:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Phasor
>A **phasor** is a [[7.2a Complex Exponentials|complex number representation]] of a sinusoidal function that helps simplify the analysis of sinusoidal steady-state behavior in electrical circuits. It represents both the amplitude and the phase of a sinusoidal wave. In mathematical terms, a phasor can be expressed as:
>$$X = |X|e^{j\phi} \iff X = |X| \angle \phi,$$
>where $|X|$ is the phasor's peak amplitude, and $\phi$ is its phase angle.
>
>Using [[7.2b Euler's Theorem|Euler's theorem]], any [[2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals|time-varying sinusoidal signal]] $x(t)$ can be expressed in the form
>$$x(t) = \mathscr{Re}\{X e^{j\omega t} \},$$
>where $x(t) = \mathscr{Re}\{|X|e^{j\phi}e^{j\omega t}\} = \cos(\omega t + \phi).$ Only the real part of its phasor is taken, as its imaginary part does not have any physical-world implications.
>
>To gain some intuition, provided is a table of some standard time-variant functions and their phasor representations:
>
>|                  $x(t)$                  |              $X$               |
| :--------------------------------------: | :----------------------------: |
|            $A \cos (\omega t)$             |              $A$               |
|        $A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$         |          $Ae^{j\phi}$          |
|        $-A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$        |     $Ae^{j(\phi \pm \pi)}$     |
|            $A \sin \omega t$             |      $Ae^{-j\pi/2} = -jA$      |
|        $A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$         |     $Ae^{j(\phi - \pi/2)}$     |
|        $-A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$        |     $Ae^{j(\phi + \pi/2)}$     |
|          $\frac{d}{dt} x(t)$           |          $j\omega X$           |
| $\frac{d}{dt} [A \cos(\omega t + \phi)]$ |      $j\omega Ae^{j\phi}$      |
|            $\int x(t) \, dt$             |     $\frac{1}{j\omega} X$      |
|   $\int A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \, dt$   | $\frac{1}{j\omega} Ae^{j\phi}$ |
>>[!warning] Note!
>>Differentiation of a time function $x(t)$ in the time domain is equivalent to multiplication of its phasor counterpart $X$ by $j\omega$ in the phasor domain. Similarly, integration of $x(t)$ in the time domain is equivalent to dividing its phasor $X$ by $j\omega$ in the phasor domain.

# Intuition
The phasor (frequency) domain is generally used for simplification of mathematical derivations. In the phasor domain, as seen above, operations such as differentiation and integration become straightforward.

>[!note] Mesh-Current Method
>The **Mesh-Current Method** is a technique used to find the current flowing in each loop (or mesh) of a circuit. A **mesh** is defined as a loop that does not enclose any other loops. This method simplifies the process of solving for unknown currents in planar circuits by applying [[2.2c KVL|Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law]] to each independent loop.

```tikz
\usepackage{circuitikz}
\begin{document}

\begin{circuitikz} \draw
    % Mesh 1
    (0,0) to[V, v=$V_1$] (0,3) 
    to[R=$R_1$, i=$I_1$] (3,3)
    to[R=$R_3$, i_=$I_1 - I_2$] (6,3) 
    -- (6,0) to[short] (0,0)
    
    % Mesh 2
    (6,0) to[V, v=$V_2$, invert] (6,-3)
    to[R=$R_2$, i=$I_2$] (3,-3)
    -- (0,-3) to[short] (0,0)
    
    % Closing loop for mesh 2
    (3,-3) to[R=$R_3$, i_=$I_2 - I_1$] (3,0)
    ;
    
    % Labels for the mesh currents
    \node at (1.5, 1.5) {$I_1$};
    \node at (4.5, -1.5) {$I_2$};

    % Loops around each mesh
    \draw[dashed, thick, blue] (1.5,0) circle(2);
    \node[blue] at (1.5,4) {Mesh 1: $V_1 = I_1R_1 + (I_1 - I_2)R_3$};
    
    \draw[dashed, thick, red] (4.5,0) circle(2);
    \node[red] at (7.5,-3) {Mesh 2: $V_2 = I_2R_2 + (I_2 - I_1)R_3$};

\end{circuitikz}

\end{document}
```

440.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1i.2 Stored Energy of Inductors]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/03 22:05:16","modified":"2024/02/20 16:29:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stored Energy of an Inductor
>The stored energy $E_L$ of an [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductor]] can be written as
>$$E_L=\frac{1}{2}LI_L(t)^2.$$

# Proof
Since we already know that $P=IV$ and that power is the time-integral of energy (work), we can substitute $V_L=L \frac{dI_L(t)}{dt}$: $$P_L= LI_L(t) \frac{dI_L(t)}{dt}.$$We then manipulate and integrate:
$$\int P_Ldt= L \int I_L(t) dI_L(t).$$
Completing the integration we get:
$$E=\frac{1}{2}LI_L(t)^2.$$

442.title: 2.1f.3ii Inductor Parallel Equivalence
442.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.1 Circuit Components/2.1i Inductor/2.1i.3 Equivalence/2.1f.3ii Inductor Parallel Equivalence.md
442.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1f.3ii Inductor Parallel Equivalence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/04 05:02:06","modified":"2024/10/04 23:25:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Parallel Equivalence
>Two [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductors]] in parallel are equivalent to
>```tikz
>\usepackage{circuitikz}
>\begin{document}
>\begin{circuitikz}[american]
>\draw (-4.5, 6) to [short] (0, 6)
>to [short, i=$I_{test}(t)$] (0, 5)
>to [short] (1.5, 5)
>to [inductor, l=$L_1$, v=$V_1(t)$, i>^=$I_1(t)$] (1.5, 1)
>to [short] (0,1)
>(0, 5) to [short] (-1.5, 5)
>to [inductor, l=$L_2$, v=$V_2(t)$, i>^=$I_2(t)$] (-1.5, 1)
>to [short] (0, 1)
>to [short] (0, 0)
>to [short] (-4.5, 0)
>to [I, l=$I_{test}$, v=$V_{test}(t)$] (-4.5, 6);
>\draw [->] (3, 3)--(5, 3) node[below=5pt, xshift=-28]{$L_{eq}=\left(\frac{1}{L_1}+\frac{1}{L_2}\right)^{-1}$};
>\draw (9,6) to [inductor, v=$V_{eq}(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_{eq}$] (9,0)
>  to [short] (7, 0)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (7, 6)
>  to [short] (9, 6);
\end{circuitikz}
\end{document}
>```
# Intuition
Using NVA,
$$
\begin{alignat}{0}
V_{test} =V_1=V_2 \\
L_{eq}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=L_1\frac{dI_1}{dt}+L_2\frac{dI_2}{dt}
\end{alignat}
$$
Since by KCL $I_{eq}=I_1+I_2$,
$$\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=\frac{dI_1}{dt}+\frac{dI_2}{dt}.$$
From the first and second equations,
$$\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=\frac{L_{eq}}{L_1}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}+\frac{L_{eq}}{L_2}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}.$$
Simplifying, we get
$$L_{eq}=\left(\frac{1}{L_1}+\frac{1}{L_2}\right)^{-1}.$$

443.title: 2.1f.3i Inductor Series Equivalence
443.path: Electrical Engineering/1. Circuits/2.1 Circuit Components/2.1i Inductor/2.1i.3 Equivalence/2.1f.3i Inductor Series Equivalence.md
443.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1f.3i Inductor Series Equivalence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/04 05:01:22","modified":"2024/02/20 16:29:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Series Equivalence
>Two [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductors]] in series are equivalent to
>```tikz
>\usepackage{circuitikz}
>\begin{document}
>\begin{circuitikz}[american]
>  \draw (3,3) to [inductor, v=$V_1(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_1$] (3,0)
>  to [inductor, v=$V_2(t)$, L=$L_2$] (3, -3)
>  to [short] (0, -3)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (0, 3)
>  to [short] (3, 3);
>  \draw [->] (4, 0)--(6, 0) node[below=5pt, xshift=-28]{$L_{eq}=L_1+L_2$};
>  \draw (10,2) to [inductor, v=$V_{eq}(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_{eq}$] (10,-2)
>  to [short] (8, -2)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (8, 2)
>  to [short] (10, 2);
\end{circuitikz}
\end{document}
>```
# Proof
Using $V_{test} = V_{eq}$ and KVL, we deduce that
$$V_{eq} = V_1 + V_2.$$
We then plug-in the equations of the inductors,
$$V_{eq}=L_1\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}+L_2\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}$$
Which leads to
$$V_{eq}=(L_1+L_2)\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}.$$

465.title: 1.4 Bank runs
465.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4 Bank runs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/29 14:47:08","modified":"2025/03/29 14:47:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bank Run
>A bank run occurs when a large portion of a bank's customers withdraws money in a short period of time driven by fears of bank failure. As bank runs progress, they may become **self-fulfilling prophecies**, as the chance of sudden bankruptcy increases. In case a bank lacks liquidity, it may use lenders of last resort such as the [[6.3b Discount Window|discount window]] to prevent bankruptcy.

# Intuition
In fractional-reserve banking systems, banks only keep part of the money that its customers deposit, and loan out the rest of the money. As such, if enough customers withdraw over a short period of time, the bank may not have enough liquidity to satisfy all of the withdrawals. This could be prevented by suspension of payments, which albeit generally a temporary measure while banks sell loans, may be a potential situation for bankruptcy.

Bank runs may also happen as a result of self-fulfilling prophecies. Customers may believe that the bank is inept in some way and may withdraw their money. Since the bank cannot react on time, a bank run occurs.

We can formulate bank run problems based on the [[Prisoner's Dilemma]]: suppose that two investors deposit a $D$ dollars in a bank. The bank has invested $2D$ into a long-term project, yielding $2R$ upon maturity ($R > D$). If the bank is forced to liquidate the project before completion, it will recover $2r$, where $D > r > \frac{D}{2}$. We can create a table to help us with the cases of this problem:
- Before maturity:
	- One of the investors withdraws: the one that withdraws gets $D$, whereas the other gets $2r - D$.
	- Both investors withdraw: each investor receives $r$.
- After maturity:
	- One of the investors withdraws: the one that withdraws gets $D$, whereas the other gets $2R-D$.
	- Both investors withdraw: each investors receives $D$ and the bank profits $2R-2D$.
	- None of the investors withdraws: both investors get $R$.

Here, there are two Nash equilibria:
1. Both investors withdraw and get $r$ each. 
2. Both investors keep their money in the bank and get $R$ each.

Option 1 leads to a bank run, since the investors did not get the full quantity of their money $D$ back. However, the FDIC insures deposits up to some limit such that the minimum amount of money an investor gets is always $D$. Also, if the bank has some backup money, it may also be able to pay off the original investment.

The FDIC's establishment, although beneficial, greatly downplays the credibility of banks, as depositors have weaker incentives to monitor the quality of banks.

# Example
>[!example] Bank Runs During the Great Depression
>During the Great Depression, different federal banks in Mississippi had different approaches to banking panics:
>- Federal Bank of Atlanta (in the south of MS) believed the FED should serve as a lender of last resort, responding to the panics with large infusions of cash.
>- Federal Bank of St. Louis (in the north of MS) believed in the real bills doctrine, only lending backed money and therefore being tougher on discount.
>
>However, at the end, economic characteristics were similar in both parts of Mississippi, and although quality of bank assets was higher in banks governed by the St. Louis fed, more banks were suspended, and lending and trade declined more.
>
>Since the panic was due to illiquidity, FED's action should've been aggressive on a national scale.

>[!note] Double-Entry Accounting
>Double-entry accounting is an accounting system where every financial transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, ensuring that the accounting equation remains balanced. Each **journal entry** has two equal and opposite effects:
>1. A **debit** (Dr.) – An increase in assets or expenses, or a decrease in liabilities, equity, or revenue.
>2. A **credit** (Cr.) – An increase in liabilities, equity, or revenue, or a decrease in assets or expenses.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/16 18:39:30","modified":"2025/03/17 12:38:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Balance Sheet
>The **balance sheet** is a financial statement that provides a snapshot of a company’s financial position at a specific point in time. It follows the fundamental accounting equation
>$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}.$$
>It provides information about the current financial health of the company, including liquidity, leverage, and asset financing. It contains three general financial groups:
>- **Assets** (for accounting purposes) is any resource that is expected to provide future economic benefits. This includes any resource with quantifiable value, such as cash, inventory, machines, buildings, and even contracts with a monetary value. **Goodwill**, which arises when a company acquires another company for more than the fair market value of the acquired company's equity, is also included as part of assets. Goodwill can include brand reputation, customer loyalty, etc.
>- **Liabilities** are financial obligations. This includes money that the corporation owes to lenders, suppliers, employees, etc.
>- **Equity** is the residual value left for owners of a company after the value of its liabilities is subtracted from the value of its assets. This is referred to as the company’s **Book Value**.
>
>>[!warning] The Balance Sheet is a Snapshot
>>Since the balance sheet reflects a single point in time, it should be analyzed alongside the **income statement** and **cash flow statement** for a full financial picture.

470.path: Economics/1. Finance/5. Corporate Finance/5.1 Business Entities.md
470.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[5.1 Business Entities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/18 01:32:57","modified":"2025/03/18 01:51:23"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Business Entities
>**Business entities** are legal structures through which commercial activities are conducted and organized, each offering distinct liability protections, tax treatments, and ownership rules. They can range from simple, single-owner operations to complex corporations with multiple shareholders, including (but not exhausting):
>- **Sole Proprietorship**: A simple structure owned by one person who is personally liable and reports profits on their personal tax return.
>- **Partnership**: An arrangement where owners share profits, are personally liable, and benefit from pass-through taxation.
>- **LLC (Limited Liability Company)**: A hybrid structure offering limited personal liability, flexible management, and pass-through taxation by default.
>- **C Corporation (C Corp)**: A separate legal entity with limited liability for owners, but subject to double taxation at the corporate and shareholder levels.
>- **S Corporation (S Corp)**: A corporation with limited liability, pass-through taxation, a limit of 100 shareholders, and certain ownership restrictions.
>- **Nonprofit Corporation**: A tax-exempt entity formed for charitable, religious, or public service purposes, where no individual is personally liable.

471.title: 4.1 Portfolio Weighting
471.path: Economics/1. Finance/4. Portfolio Management/4.1 Portfolio Weighting.md
471.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.1 Portfolio Weighting]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 20:55:05","modified":"2025/02/25 12:51:26"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Portfolio Weighting
>Portfolio weighting is the process of determining what percentage of the total portfolio value $V$ that each asset should represent, such that each asset's value is equal to $V_{i}=w_{i}V$. A portfolio of $n$ assets can be
>- **Equal-weighted**: all assets have a uniform weight of $w_{i}=\frac{1}{n}$.
>- **Price-weighted**: the $i$-th asset has a weight of $w_{i}=\dfrac{P_{i}}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}P_{i}}$ for a share price $P_{i}$.
>- **Value-weighted (cap-weighted)**: the $i$-th asset has a weight of $w_{i}=\dfrac{P_{i} \cdot S_{i}}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}P_{i} \cdot S_{i}}$ for a share price $P_{i}$ and $S_{i}$ total outstanding shares.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.3b Modern Portfolio Theory]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/17 18:30:08","modified":"2025/03/17 21:21:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Modern Portfolio Theory
>**Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT)** is a framework for constructing an investment portfolio that maximizes returns for a given level of risk. Developed by Harry Markowitz in 1952, it emphasizes diversification to minimize [[4.3a Risk|idiosyncratic risk]] while optimizing expected returns.
>
>MPT measures risk as the standard deviation of the portfolio's returns. For a weighted portfolio with $n$ assets, the portfolio's volatility is then given by
>$$\sigma_{p} = \sqrt{ \sum^{n}_{i=1}\sum^{n}_{j=1}w_{i}\sigma_{i}w_{j}\sigma_{j}\rho_{i,j} },$$
>where $\rho_{i,j}$ is the correlation between the $i$-th and the $j$-th asset.
>
>When assets are not perfectly correlated, the overall portfolio volatility decreases, allowing investors to construct an efficiently weighted portfolio that offers the best possible return for a given level of risk. The set of optimal portfolios forms the **efficient frontier**, a curve that represents the highest expected return achievable at each level of risk:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75]
>
>    % Axes
>    \draw[->] (0,0) -- (7,0) node[right] {$\sigma_p$};
>    \draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,6) node[above] {$E(R_p)$};
>
>    % Risk-free rate
>    \node[left] at (-0.1,1) {$R_f$};
>    \draw[dashed] (0,1) -- (6,4.2) node[above right] {Capital Mkt. Line};
>
>    % Efficient frontier
>    \draw[thick] (3,0.5) .. controls (-1.25,1.2) and (2,2) .. (6,3.5) node[below right] {Efficient Frontier};
>
>    % Points
>    \filldraw[black] (1,1.2) circle (2pt) node[below left] {M};
>    \filldraw[black] (1.6,1.8) circle (2pt) node[below right] {T};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>
> When a risk-free asset is introduced, the efficient frontier transforms into a straight line, known as the **capital market line**, given by the equation
> $$\mathbb{E}(R_{p}) = R_{f} + \frac{\mathbb{E}(R_{M})-R_{f}}{\sigma_{M}}\sigma_{p},$$
> where $\mathbb{E}(R_{M})-R_{f}$ is the market risk premium (expected market return minus the risk-free rate), and $\sigma_{M}$ is the overall market volatility. The slope of the capital market line is called the **Sharpe ratio**, $S_{a}=\frac{\mathbb{E}(R_{M})-R_{f}}{\sigma_{M}}$, and is a measure of the increase in expected return per $1\%$ increase in volatility.
> 
> The **tangency portfolio** ($T$) is the point where the efficient frontier meets the capital market line (CML), representing the optimal mix of risky assets. Maximizing the Sharpe ratio, it allows investors to tailor their risk exposure by combining it with risk-free lending or borrowing.
> 
>>[!warning] Usage of the Sharpe Ratio
>>The Sharpe ratio can be used to determine the risk-reward of any asset (or combination of assets). However, in terms of the capital market line, the Sharpe ratio is used exclusively in combination with market returns and volatility.



# Examples
>[!example] Two-Stock Portfolio
>Suppose you want to pick the optimal portfolio of two stocks, $\text{ABC}$ and $\text{XYZ}$: 
>- Stock $\text{ABC}$ has a return of $9\%$, and volatility of $27\%$.
>- Stock $\text{XYZ}$ has a return of $15\%$, and volatility of $33\%$.
>- The correlation between $\text{ABC}$ and $\text{XYZ}$ is around $0.2$.
>- The risk-free rate is $4.5\%$, and the risk premium is $5\%$. The market volatility is $12.5\%$.
>
>We proceed with the following code:
>
```run-python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
import statsmodels

sigma_abc = 0.27
sigma_xyz = 0.33
corr = 0.2

er_abc = 0.09
er_xyz = 0.15

w = 1
i = 0.05
r = {}
while w >= 0:
    er = w * er_abc + (1 - w) * er_xyz
    risk = np.sqrt((w  * sigma_abc) ** 2 + ((1 - w) * sigma_xyz) ** 2 + 2 * w * (1 - w) * corr * sigma_abc * sigma_xyz, )
    r[w] = (risk, er)
    w -= i
    w = round(w, 2)

sharpe = [(pf[1] - 0.045) / pf[0] for w, pf in r.items()]
opt_idx = sharpe.index(max(sharpe))

risk = [pf[0] for pf in r.values()]
ret = [pf[1] for pf in r.values()]

opt = (risk[opt_idx], ret[opt_idx])
opt_w = [k for k, v in r.items() if v == opt][0]


print(r)
sns.scatterplot(x = risk, y = ret, hue=r.keys())
plt.scatter(x = risk[opt_idx], y = ret[opt_idx], color = 'green', )
plt.annotate(text=f"{opt_w}:{1-opt_w}, Sharpe = {round(max(sharpe), 3)}", xy = opt)

plt.xlabel("Porfolio Risk")
plt.ylabel("Porfolio Return")
plt.legend(title="Weight on ABC")
plt.title("ABC:XYZ Portfolio Weights Return vs. Risk")
```

473.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3d Efficient Market Hypothesis]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/18 01:16:01","modified":"2025/03/18 01:24:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Fama-French EMH
>Market efficiency refers to the degree to which asset prices fully reflect all available information at any given time. An efficient market implies one in which assets are always fairly priced, implying that investors cannot achieve excess returns using available information. The classic Eugene Fama framework defines three levels:
>1. **Weak-Form Efficiency** - prices reflect all past market data (historical prices and trading volume). 
>	- An outcome of this is that technical analysis cannot generate significant returns.
>2. **Semi-Strong-Form Efficiency** - prices reflect all publicly available information (i.e., financial statements, news), including past market data. 
>	- An outcome of this is that fundamental analysis cannot generate significant returns.
>3. **Strong-Form Efficiency** - prices reflect all information, both public and private (including insider trading). 
>	- An outcome of this is that no investor can generate excess returns.
>
>It has been observed that the market *supports weak-form efficiency*, as there is little evidence that technical analysis works consistently, and partially supports semi-strong efficiency, as markets quickly react to public information, although sometimes behavioral biases get in the way. *Strong-form efficiency is not supported*, as insider trading results in so much excess returns that it is illegal.

474.title: 4.3c Capital Asset Pricing Model
474.path: Economics/1. Finance/4. Portfolio Management/4.3 Risk Management/4.3c Capital Asset Pricing Model.md
474.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.3c Capital Asset Pricing Model]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/17 18:42:04","modified":"2025/03/18 01:32:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Capital Asset Pricing Model
>The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) is a financial framework built on top of [[4.3b Modern Portfolio Theory|Modern Portfolio Theory]] that links the expected return of an asset to its risk. It is based on a few key assumptions:
>- All investors are rational and risk-averse.
>- Only systematic risk matters, because idiosyncratic risk is diversified away.
>- Markets are frictionless (i.e., no transaction costs, borrowing constraints, etc.)
>
>CAPM is a single-factor model, which means it explains an asset’s expected return solely through its sensitivity to market risk through the factor, **beta**:
>$$\mathbb{E}(R_{p})=R_{f}+\beta_{p}[\mathbb{E}(R_{M})-R_{f}],$$
>where $\beta_{p}=\dfrac{\sigma_{p,M}}{\sigma_{M}}=\rho_{p,M} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma_{p}}{\sigma_{M}}$ is a measure of the relative sensitivity of the portfolio to market movements.
>
>This fundamental equation gives rise to the **security market line**, which measures the expected return of a portfolio against its beta.
>
>>[!warning] CAPM for Assets vs. Porfolios
>>CAPM can be used for both quantifying individual assets and whole portfolios.

>[!note] Risk
>Risk refers to the uncertainty (volatility) or potential for financial loss in an investment or business decision. It reflects the variability in returns due to external and internal factors. The risk of an asset can be quantified in a variety of ways, including the standard deviation of its price.
>
>Furthermore, risk can be broadly categorized into **systematic risk** and **idiosyncratic risk**:
>- **Systematic (market) risk** affects the entire market or economy. It cannot be eliminated through diversification.
>- **Idiosyncratic risk** affects a specific company, industry, or asset. It can be reduced through diversification.
>

>[!note] Short Selling
>**Short selling** is an investment strategy where an investor borrows shares of a security, sells them immediately at the current market price, and then later buys back the same number of shares to return to the lender and profit from the decline in share price.
>
>Short calls have a predetermined expiration date specified in the option contract, after which the option becomes void and the lender retains the net return with no further obligations.

477.title: 4.2b.2 Arrow-Debreu Securities
477.path: Economics/1. Finance/4. Portfolio Management/4.2 Investment Strategies/4.2b Arbitrage/4.2b.2 Arrow-Debreu Securities.md
477.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[4.2b.2 Arrow-Debreu Securities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/25 15:55:57","modified":"2025/03/29 02:22:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Arrow-Debreu Securities
>An **Arrow-Debreu security** is a contract that pays exactly one unit of currency *if a specific future state occurs*, and nothing otherwise.
>
>In an [[4.2b Arbitrage|arbitrage-free]] market with $N$ assets and $s$ possible future states, every asset’s price can be expressed as a linear combination of exactly $s$ Arrow-Debreu securities, with *no two securities paying in the same state*. The price of an Arrow–Debreu security is called the **state price** $q_i$ for state $i \in \{ 1, \ldots, N \}$. For a payoff matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times N}$ ($N \geq s$) and a state price vector $q \in \mathbb{R}^s$, the vector of today's asset prices $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is expressed as
>$$p=X^Tq.$$
>
>The existence of a distinct Arrow–Debreu security for every possible state implies that the **market is complete**. In other words, the market is complete if $\operatorname{Rank}(X) = s$. This means the $s$-dimensional space of all possible state payoffs is fully spanned by the assets, so every contingent claim can be replicated as a linear combination of these Arrow–Debreu securities.

# Properties
#### (*State Price Decomposition*) $q=\begin{dcases}(X^T)^{-1}p & \text{if } N=s, \\ (XX^T)^{-1}Xp & \text{if } N \ge s, \\ \varnothing & \text{otherwise.}\end{dcases}$
#### (*Uniqueness of State Price*) If LOOP holds and market is complete, then $q$ exists and is unique.

#### (*Market Completeness*) If $\min(q) > 0$, the market is complete.
# Examples
>[!example] Asset Pricing With Sate Prices
>We can describe a 3-state, 3-asset *complete* market as follows:
>
>|     **State/Asset**    |  $\textbf{AD}_{1}$  |  $\textbf{AD}_{2}$  |  $\textbf{AD}_{3}$  | $\textbf{A}_{1}$ | $\textbf{A}_2$ |
|:-------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------:|:-------:|
| $S_{1}$ |   1   |   0   |   0   |    3    |   $u_{1}$    |
| $S_{2}$ |   0   |   1   |   0   |    2    |   $u_{2}$   |
| $S_{3}$ |   0   |   0   |   1   |    1    |   $u_{3}$    |
| **Price**   |  $q_{1}$   |  $q_{2}$   |  $q_{3}$   |         |         |
>Then, the price of asset 1 can be expressed as the linear combination $q_{\text{A}_{1}}=3q_{1}+2q_{2}+q_{3}$. Similarly, the price of asset 2 is $q_{\text{A}_{2}} = u_{1}q_{1}+u_{2}q_{2}+u_{3}q_{3}$.

>[!example] Mortgage-Backed Securities

>[!note] Arbitrage
>**Arbitrage** is the practice of exploiting instantaneous mispricings for the same asset across different markets to secure a low-risk profit.
>
>Arbitrage is precluded by the **Law of One Price (LOOP)**, which states that *assets with identical payoffs in the next period should trade at the same price during the current period* across all locations or forms. A violation of LOOP becomes the source of arbitrage opportunities.
>
>type 1 vs type 2 arb

>[!note] Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
>The **internal rate of return (IRR)** of a series of cash flows is the discount rate $r^*$ that makes the net present value of those cash flows equal to zero. Mathematically, IRR satisfies:
>$$\text{NPV}=0,$$
>where the solution is given by $r^*$.

480.title: 3.1c Average Return
480.path: Economics/1. Finance/3. Valuation Methods/3.1 Calculating Returns/3.1c Average Return.md
480.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.1c Average Return]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 18:18:28","modified":"2025/02/25 00:10:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Average Return
>**Average return** is a measure of the central tendency of returns over a period of time, representing the typical or mean performance of an investment or asset. For returns $R_{t}, R_{t+1}, \ldots, R_{t+n}$, the ***arithmetic average return*** is given as
>$$\bar{R}_{\text{A}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=0}R_{t+i},$$
>whereas the ***geometric average return*** is given as
>$$\bar{R}_{\text{G}}=\left(1+\prod^{n}_{i=1}R_{t+i}\right)^\frac{1}{n}.$$

481.title: 3.1b CAGR
481.path: Economics/1. Finance/3. Valuation Methods/3.1 Calculating Returns/3.1b CAGR.md
481.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[3.1b CAGR]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 18:18:19","modified":"2025/03/18 12:57:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compound Annual Growth Rate
>**Compound Annual Growth Rate** (also called compound return) is the cumulative growth of an investment over multiple periods, where the net simple return $R_{t}$ from each period $t$ is reinvested and earns returns in subsequent periods. Formally, the CAGR between time $t_0$ and $t$, given $n$-period returns, is given as
>$$1+R_{t_{0}, t}=\left[\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+R_{t_{0}+i})\right]^{\frac{1}{nt}}.$$
>
>The compounded return over $T$ years, paid $n$ times per year and given an APR $r$ can generally be calculated as
>$$1+R_{T} = \left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nT}.$$
>
>Letting $n \to \infty$ yields continuous returns, such that
>$$1+R_{T} = \lim_{ n \to \infty }\left[\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\right]=e^{rT},$$
>which yields the **log return** $\ln(1+R_{T})=rT$.
>
>>[!warning] Compound Return Excludes the Initial Period $t$
>>Period $t$ isn’t included in the compound return formula because it’s the the subsequent returns that measure the growth or changes in value over the previous period, not the initial period itself.

>[!note] Total Return
>**Total return** is the percentage change in an investment’s value without compounding or additional contributions. The net simple return is simply (no pun intended) given as
>$$R_{t+1} = \frac{V_{t+1}}{V_{t}}-1,$$
>where $V_{t}$ is the asset's valuation at time $t$. Then, the gross simple return is equal to $1+R_{t+1}$ and represents the revenue multiplier from time $t$ to $t+1$.

484.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.3c ETFs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:30:14","modified":"2025/05/12 21:00:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Exchange-Traded Funds
>An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** is an investment fund that holds a diversified portfolio of underlying assets, and can be bought and sold on stock exchanges (secondary markets), just like individual equities (stocks).
>
>ETFs can be structured to track anything from the price of a commodity to a large and diverse collection of stocks, which may be done either using passive or active investment strategies. **Leveraged ETFs** seek to deliver multiples of daily index returns by leveraging derivatives and shorting. However, leveraged ETFs typically underperform relative to objectives in the long run.
>
>As with [[2.3b Mutual Funds|mutual funds]], dividends, interest, and capital gains (although rare for ETFs) from the pool are distributed to ETF shareholders. However, since ETFs trade intraday, the supply of shares is regulated through a **creation and redemption** mechanism, which keeps market price close to the **Net Asset Value (NAV)** to prevent inefficiencies that create arbitrage opportunities. It involves a two-step process:
>1. When an ETF manager wants to issue more shares, an authorized participant (AP) buys shares of the assets associated with the ETF.
>2. Then, the AP sells or exchanges the assets to the ETF for new shares of the ETF at equal value. 
>
>In turn, the AP sells the ETF shares in the market for a profit if the selling price is greater than the ETF's NAV, creating an arbitrage opportunity.
>
>The top 3 ETFs based on Assets under Management (AUM) are the **SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY)**, the iShares S&5 500 ETF (IVY), and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO).

>[!note] Hedge Funds
>**Hedge funds** are pooled investment vehicles that employ a wide range of strategies–such as long/short equity, global macro, event-driven, and arbitrage–primarily in public markets.
>
>They aim to generate high absolute returns regardless of market direction, often using debt financing (leverage), derivatives, and short selling to amplify gains and hedge risks. 
>
>Managed by professional investment advisors, hedge funds typically cater to institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals, operating with fewer regulatory constraints than mutual funds.

486.title: 2.3a.1 Private Equity
486.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.3 Pooled Investments/2.3a Institutional Investments/2.3a.1 Private Equity.md

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:32:35","modified":"2025/05/12 22:51:22"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Private Equity
>**Private equity firms** are investment management companies that raise capital from institutional and high-net-worth investors to acquire controlling ownership stakes in established but failing privately held or publicly traded companies. 
>
>The goal of PE is to increase the value of these businesses through operational improvements, strategic guidance, and financial restructuring, often using significant leverage (debt financing), before exiting through a sale or IPO.
>
>As with VCs and hedge funds, private equity firms earn profit based on the **2 and 20 model**, which utilizes a 2% management fee (based on AUM), plus 20% of all profits.

487.title: 7.3a.2ii Startup Financing
487.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.3 Pooled Investments/2.3a Institutional Investments/2.3a.2 Venture Capital/7.3a.2ii Startup Financing.md
487.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[7.3a.2ii Startup Financing]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 21:12:50","modified":"2025/05/13 00:00:40"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Startup Financing Lifecycle
>The startup financing lifecycle can be separated in four stages. Founders’ equity claim and control rights are diluted at each stage:
>1. Startups begin in the **pre-seed** stage, with founders contributing initial capital, known as **sweat equity**. They are issued **common stock**, which has the lowest liquidation priority but full voting rights.
>	- Optionally, startups in the early stages may rely on **incubators**, which offer resources such as workspace and support for idea validation, but do not provide capital. Nonprofits do not take equity, whereas for-profits may request a $1\%-5\%$ stake.
>2. As startups build their product and test market fit, **seed funding** through **angel investors** and **accelerators** is done to obtain a larger initial investment. These agents pre-purchase Series A equity with a built-in discount through [[2.3a.2iii Convertible Securities|convertible securities]] due to the unknown valuation of the company. Employees and prospects are incentivized by [[2.3a.2iv Stock Options|stock options]] (in this and all subsequent stages), and a stock option pool (usually $10\%-20\%$ of equity) is reserved for them.
>	- **Angel investors** are accredited investors who provide mentorship and connections, and invest (usually $\leq \$1\text{M}$) in exchange for equity.
>	- **Accelerators** are organizations that support startups with a viable MVP (minimum viable product) that generates some revenue, providing both a workspace, mentorship and capital ($\$25K-\$150K$) in exchange for $5\%-10\%$ equity.
>3. When startups validate and perfect their business plan, **Series A funding** (usually after $\geq 4\text{M}$ of seed investment) is the first external capital raised from angel investors or VCs. It is often the first priced round, where the company's valuation is formally negotiated and set. Series A investors are provided Series A preferred stock.
>4. Subsequent raises (i.e., Series B, C, ...) may occur given that the startup achieves certain growth milestones and no d**own-rounds** (lower valuation at a subsequent raise).
>
>>[!warning] Financing Only Applicable for Unicorns
>>All of the above investment mediums are on the lookout for **unicorns**, which are extremely high-growth potential startups. Unless a startup is a unicorn, it will not get such treatment and should look at other means of financing, such as
>>- **Bootstrapping**, where the startup relies solely on its own savings for growth.
>>- **Revenue-Based Financing**, where the startup relies on a revenue-based payment model (i.e., a fixed percentage of future revenues over a fixed period of time).
>>- **Traditional Loans**, provided by banks, and often backed by the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA).

488.title: 2.3a.2iv Stock Options
488.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.3 Pooled Investments/2.3a Institutional Investments/2.3a.2 Venture Capital/2.3a.2iv Stock Options.md
488.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2iv Stock Options]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 23:14:01","modified":"2025/05/13 00:04:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stock Options
>**Employee Stock Options** are a form of equity compensation that give employees the right–but not the obligation–to purchase a specified number of company shares at a fixed price (called the **strike price**) after meeting certain conditions, such as vesting. 
>
>The **strike price** is usually set at the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the company at the time the option is granted, as determined by a third-party valuation firm (e.g., through a 409A valuation in the U.S.).
>
>ESOs are typically given with a vesting schedule–typically 4 years with a **1-year cliff** (meaning the first 25% vests after one year, and the rest vests monthly or quarterly thereafter). They can be exercised after they vest and within a **fixed post-termination window** (often 90 days after leaving the company).

489.title: 2.3a.2i Venture Capital
489.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.3 Pooled Investments/2.3a Institutional Investments/2.3a.2 Venture Capital/2.3a.2i Venture Capital.md
489.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2i Venture Capital]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:32:44","modified":"2025/05/12 21:21:54"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Venture Capital
>**Venture capital firms** provide funding to early-stage, high-growth potential startups in exchange for equity ownership. Unlike private equity firms, they typically do not utilize debt financing (leverage), do not hold a majority stake in their investments, and instead take on higher risk in pursuit of outsized returns. 
>
>The goal of VCs is to help startups scale rapidly and eventually exit through an acquisition or IPO, realizing significant gains on their equity stake.

490.title: 2.3a.2iii Convertible Securities
490.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.3 Pooled Investments/2.3a Institutional Investments/2.3a.2 Venture Capital/2.3a.2iii Convertible Securities.md
490.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2iii Convertible Securities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 20:36:19","modified":"2025/05/12 23:29:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!notes] Convertible Securities
>**Convertible securities** are financial instruments commonly used in startup financing that begin as debt or contract-based investments and convert into preferred stock upon a specified future event, such as a valuation cap or discount (i.e., shares are priced lower than for new investors at subsequent raises). They allow early-stage startups to delay valuation negotiations while raising initial capital.
>
>There are two major types of convertible securities:
>- **Simple Agreement for Future Equity (SAFEs)** are contractual agreements created by Y Combinator (the largest accelerator in the world) that provide the right to obtain equity in the future without being a loan or having a maturity date.
>	- SAFEs do not have an interest or a maturity date.
>- **Convertible notes** are a short-term debt instrument that converts into equity in a future financing round.
>	- Since convertible notes are debt, they have an interest (usually $4\% - 8\%$ per year) and a fixed maturity date ($12-24$ months). If no conversion event occurs, the debt is due at maturity. Convertible notes work in favor of the investor, who is protected in case of downturn.

491.title: 2.2c Swaps
491.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c Swaps]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/13 14:52:08","modified":"2025/05/13 17:29:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Swaps
>A swap is an OTC derivative in which two parties agree to exchange a stream of cash flows over multiple future dates. It can be interpreted as a series of [[2.2a Forward Contracts|forward contracts]] for each cash flow leg that are calculated differently and netted,  so that only the difference changes hands on each settlement date.
>
>There are many types of swaps, including uncommon (exotic) swaps. Popular swaps include:
>- **Interest-Rate Swaps,** in which two parties exchange a series of fixed‑rate and floating‑rate interest payments on a notional principal over a specified term.
>- **Credit Default Swaps**, where one party pays a periodic fee in exchange for protection ("insurance") against the default of a specified borrower or bond.
>- **Currency Swaps**, where parties exchange principal and interest payments in different currencies over a set period.
>- **Commodity swaps**, where parties exchange cash flows based on the price of a specified commodity over a set period.
>
>In all swaps, one party typically pays the spot (floating) rate, whereas another pays a rate fixed by the swap contract. However, total floating swaps or fixed swaps are common currency swaps.

# Examples
>[!example] I. Interest Rate Swaps and Comparative Advantage
>Suppose AAACorp and BBBCorp are able to obtain the following borrowing rates for 5-year $100M loans from their respective bankers: 
>
>|      | Fixed Rate |      Floating Rate       |
| :--: | :--------: | :----------------------: |
| AAA  |  $4.00\%$  | $\text{Floating}-0.1\%$ |
| BBBB |  $5.20\%$  | $\text{Floating}+0.6\%$  |
>
>The table above shows that AAA has a comparative advantage in fixed rate borrowing, whereas BBB has a comparative advantage in floating rate borrowing.
>
>Suppose further that AAACorp would prefer to pay a floating rate, whereas BBBCorp would prefer to pay a fixed rate. A banker with relationships with both companies notices this, and contemplates the flowing Interest Rate Swap:
>$$\xleftarrow{4\%}\boxed{\text{AAA}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}^{\xleftarrow{4.35\%}}\boxed{\text{BBB}}\xrightarrow{\text{Floating + 0.6\%}}$$
>
>**A)** What would the net effect of the cash flows be for AAACorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Since AAA borrows at $4\%$ and is paid at $4.35\%$, AAA's net gain is $0.35\%$. It pays BBB the floating rate, which means that it net pays $\text{Floating}-0.35\%$, which is 25 basis points better than the direct-market price.
>
>**B)** What would the net effect of the cash flows be for BBBCorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for fixed-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>Since BBB directly borrows at $\text{Floating}+0.6\%$ and is paid the floating rate by AAA, its net interest is $0.6\%$. Since BBB also pays AAA $4.35\%$, this means that it pays $4.35\%+0.6\%=4.95\%$ in total fixed rate, which is 25bp less than the market fixed rate.
>
>Suppose the banker instead envisions this arrangement:
>$$\xleftarrow{4\%}\boxed{\text{AAA}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}^{\xleftarrow{4.33\%}}\boxed{\text{Financial Inst.}}^{\xleftarrow{4.37\%}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}\boxed{BBB}\xrightarrow{\text{Floating + 0.6\%}}$$
>
>**C)** What is the new net effect of the cash flows for AAACorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>AAA's  outflow is $\text{Floating}+4\%$, whereas its inflow is $4.33\%$. This equates to a net outflow of
>>$$\text{Floating}+4\%-4.33\%=\text{Floating}-0.33\%,$$
>>which is $23$bp better than their market floating rate.
>
>**D)** What is the new net effect of the cash flows for BBBCorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- D) Solution.
>>BBB's outflow under this scheme is $\text{Floating}+4.97\%$, whereas its inflow is the floating rate. Therefore, its net outflow is $4.97\%$, which is $5.20\%-4.97\%=0.23\%$ (or 23bp) better than their fixed market rate.
>
>**E)** What is the annual fee (in dollars) effectively earned by the banker under this arrangement?
>>[!example]- E) Solution
>>The banker's outflow is $\text{Floating}+4.33\%$, and their inflow is $\text{Floating}+4.37\%$, which means that their net inflow is $(\text{Floating}+4.37\%)-(\text{Floating}+4.33\%)=0.04\%$ or 4bp.
>>
>>Since the loans are both for $\$100\text{M}$, this means that the banker earns $\$40,000$ per year for 5 years with this scheme.

492.title: 2.2a Forward Contracts
492.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.2 Derivatives/2.2a Forward Contracts.md
492.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2a Forward Contracts]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/07 21:38:02","modified":"2025/05/14 17:49:10"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Forward Contract
>A forward contract is a derivative contract between two parties to buy or sell an asset for another asset or currency at a specified **forward price** on a future **maturity date**. By **Covered Interest Parity,** the per-unit forward price of an asset that prevents arbitrage $F_{T}$, given a time to maturity $T$ (in years), can be expressed as
>$$F_{0}=S_{0}e^{(r_{f}-\rho_{f})T},$$
>where $S_{0}$ is the **spot rate** (price) of the underlying asset, $r_{f}$ is the risk-free rate over period $T$, and $\rho_{f}$ is the **carry rate** (e.g. a dividend yield on a stock, or the foreign interest rate in a currency forward). Note that both are continuously compounded.
>
>Then, the value of a forward contract at time $T$ can be expressed as
>$$\text{PV}=\begin{cases}
(F_{0}-S_{T})e^{-r_{f}T} & \text{long position}, \\
(S_{T}-F_{0})e^{-r_{f}T} & \text{short position},
\end{cases}$$
>where $S_{T}$ is the spot rate at time $T$. More particularly, if $F_{0} > S_{T}$, a long forward contract is **in-the-money**. The contract can also be **at-the-money** or **out-of-the-money**.
>
>Forward contracts trade exclusively on OTC markets via major banks, and assets only change hands at the maturity date. At maturity, assets can be paid out in two ways:
>1. **Physical delivery** requires that all of the asset is shipped/wired on the maturity date.
>2. **Cash-settlement** requires that the difference between the spot price and forward price is paid to the "winning" party on the maturity date.

# Example
>[!example] I. Hedging with Forward Contracts
>Andrew has a side business importing handcrafted furniture from Japan. He just collected payment in dollars from your US-based client for a custom table that will be shipped to the US in 90 days, at which point he will owe his Japanese business partner 12M JPY.
>
>Andrew is concerned about the volatility of the JPY-USD exchange rate and would like to lock in his gross profit by hedging with a forward contract.
>
>A bank offers him a rate of 145 JPY/USD for 12M JPY to be delivered in 90 days, and he accepts.
>
>**A)** How much must you Andrew the bank right now?
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Since assets in forward contracts only change hands at the maturity date, Andrew is not obligated to pay anything before the maturity date.
>
>Thirty days go by, and the 60-day forward rate is 140 JPY/USD. A 60-day T-bill on this day yields 4.0%.
>
>**B)** How much is the forward contract now worth from Andrew's point of view?
>>[!example]- B) Solution
>>Since the Yen gained value (i.e., $F_{0}=12\text{M} / 140 > 12\text{M} / 145$), and so the forward contract is in-the-money, and therefore positive for Andrew. Given the 60-day forward rate, $r_{f}=0.04$, and therefore after 60 days Andrew saves
>>$$12\text{M}\left( \frac{1}{140}-\frac{1}{145} \right)e^{-0.04 \cdot 60/365 }=\$2,936.29.$$
>
>**C)** How much is the forward contract worth to the bank?
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>Since Andrew gained $\$2,936.29$, the forward contract is worth exactly $-\$2,936.29$ to the bank.
>
>Sixty more days go by (i.e. you have reached the 90-day maturity date) and the JPY spot rate is 150 JPY/USD.
>
>**D)** How much must Andrew pay the bank now?
>>[!example]- D) Solution.
>>Andrew must pay the bank the value in USD agreed by the forward rate of $F_{0}=1/145$. As such, Andrew pays
>>$$12\text{M} / 145 = 82,758.62.$$
>
>**E)** How much money did Andrew make (or lose) by entering into the forward contract?
>>[!example]- E) Solution.
>>Since the forward contract is out-of-the-money (i.e., $F_{0}=1/150 < 1/145 = S_{0}$), Andrew's net gain is precisely
>>$$12\text{M}(1 / 150 - 1 / 145) = -\$2,758.62.$$
>
>**F)** Did Andrew do the right thing by hedging?
>>[!example]- F) Solution.
>>Andrew did the right thing by hedging, since JPY-USD is a volatile rate, and hedging is about eliminating risk rather than making profit. Not hedging could have done him worse.

>[!example] II. Covered Interest Parity & Arbitrage
>You are an arbitrageur looking for opportunities, and believe that there may be some misalignment in the fixed income and foreign exchange markets in New Zealand relative to the US. Let $r_{f}=0.045$ be the one-year USD risk-free rate, and let $\rho_{f}=0.035$ be the one-year NZD risk-free rate. The USD/NZD spot is currently $S_{0}=0.6$, and the USD/NZD one-year forward rate is $\hat{F}_{0}=0.601$.
>
>**A)** Is there an arbitrage opportunity? 
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>By CIP, 
>>$$F_{0}=S_{0}e^{T(r_{f}-\rho_{f})}=0.6e^{0.01} \approx 0.606>0.601=\hat{F}_{0},$$
>>and therefore there is an arbitrage opportunity. More particularly, the one-year forward for NZD is **overvalued**, since the theoretical (by CIP) is larger than the quoted rate. Therefore,
>>1. Borrow NZD and sell at $S_{0}=0.6$ USD/NZD.
>>2. Invest the US at $0.6e^{-0.045}=$
>>3. Buy NZD at the one-year forward rate $\hat{F}_{0}=0.601$ USD/NZD.
>>4. A year from now, you obtain $(0.606-0.601)e^{-0.035}=0.0048$ USD/NZD of profit.
>
>>**B)** Suppose you have the financial resources to implement your trade in part **A)** at the 1M USD  level (1M USD “notional”). How much profit would you make?
>>As calculated previously, I will make a profit of $\$57,000$.

493.title: 2.2d.1 Options
493.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.2 Derivatives/2.2d Options/2.2d.1 Options.md
493.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2d.1 Options]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/07 22:38:54","modified":"2025/05/13 21:20:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Options
>An **option** is a financial instrument (traded both OTC and on exchanges) that gives the holder **the right, but not the obligation**, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed predetermined price called the **strike price** (or **exercise price**) on or before a future maturity date, after which the option is invalidated:
>- A **call option** gives the holder the right to buy the underlier, whereas a **put option** gives the holder the right to sell the underlier.
>- **American options** can be executed before or on the maturity date, whereas **European options** (common form for non-US options) can only be executed on the maturity date.
>
>
>The price (or premium) of an option at time $t \geq 0$ can be decomposed into two components–its **intrinsic value** (payoff), and its **time value**–such that
>$$P_{t} = \text{IV}_{t} + \text{TV}_{t}.$$
>Here the intrinsic value (payoff) is the value the option would have if the TTM was zero:
>$$\text{IV}_{t}=\begin{cases}
\max(S_{t}-F_{0}, 0) & \text{call option}, \\
\max(F_{0}-S_{t}, 0) & \text{put option},
\end{cases}$$
>where $S_{t}$ is the spot at time $t$, and $F_{0}$ is the strike.
>
>Thus, if $P_{t} > \text{IV}_{t}$ (or equivalently, $\text{TV}_{t}>0$), then one should either sell the option or hold it rather than exercise it. Note that as the option approaches maturity (i.e., $t \to T$), $\text{TV}_{t} \to 0$ and $\text{IV}_{t} \to P_{t}$.
>
>The more volatile that the underlying asset is, the higher the probability that it will be in-the-money at expiration. Given the uncertainty of options pricing, complex methods can be utilized to estimate the price of an option at a given time–one of which is the [[2.2d.2i Black-Scholes Options Pricing|Black-Scholes equation]].

495.title: 2.2b Futures
495.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b Futures]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/07 22:38:38","modified":"2025/05/13 15:17:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Futures
>**Futures** are standardized [[2.2a Forward Contracts|forward contracts]] that are traded on public exchanges (e.g. CME, CBOT, ICE) rather that OTC. Standardization requirements of futures include:
>- Specifying the **notional value** per individual contract (e.g. 5,000 bushels of corn, or $100,000 face amount of 30-year treasury bonds).
>- A cash collateral, known as **margin**, adjusted daily to account for changes in futures prices, known as **marking to market**. It is done to 
>- Delivery month and location(s).
>- Quality requirements for commodities.
>
>Since futures prices converge in maturity towards the spot price of the underlier per **Covered Interest Parity**, the difference between the spot price and the futures price is known as the **futures basis**. Investors may bet on the convergence or divergence of the futures and spot prices in a **basis trade**.
>
>If an investor does not require the actual commodities associated with a future contract, they may close it out with an offsetting trade. However, there are tales of investors forgetting to close out contracts and being forced to take/receive cattle and corn.

496.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1b.1 Stocks]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/18 02:19:00","modified":"2025/03/18 02:25:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stocks
>**Stocks** represent shares of ownership in a corporation. They are traded on exchanges or over-the-counter markets, and their prices fluctuate based on supply and demand, company performance, and broader economic conditions. There exist two types of stocks:
>- **Common stock** gives shareholders voting rights and the potential for capital gains (by earning variable dividends), but they are last in line during liquidation.
>- **Preferred stock** generally provides fixed (or no) dividends and priority in dividend payments and liquidation, yet typically does not offer voting rights.
>
>Companies issue stock to raise capital for expansion, funding operations, or debt repayment, and private firms may do so through multiple rounds (e.g., Seed, Series A, B, C) before going public. After an **initial public offering (IPO)** in the primary market—where newly issued shares are sold directly to investors—public companies can also raise more capital with a f**ollow-on public offering (FPO)**, and their shares then trade on secondary markets like the NYSE or Nasdaq.
>
>>[!warning] Privately Held Stocks
>>Privately held stocks are shares of companies that are **not listed on public exchanges**, so they are typically owned by a small group of individuals, founders, or private investors. Because they are not publicly traded, these shares are often **less liquid and more difficult to value** than publicly traded stocks.

499.title: 2.1a.3 Price Sensitivity
499.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.1 Securities/2.1a Fixed-Income Securities/2.1a.3 Price Sensitivity.md
499.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.3 Price Sensitivity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/28 20:51:13","modified":"2025/03/29 14:21:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Duration & Convexity
>The **duration** of a [[2.1a.1 Bonds|bond]] measures the sensitivity of its price to changes in yield (interest). There are two types of duration:
>- **Macaulay duration** is the weighted average time until all cashflows are received, where the weights are the present values of each period's cashflow. This is formally defined as
>$$D = \frac{1}{nP}\left[\sum^{nT}_{t=1}\frac{C_{t}}{(1+y/n)^t}t+\frac{F}{(1+y/n)^{nT}}nT\right].$$
>- **Modified duration** adjusts Macaulay duration to approximate the percentage change in the price of a bond for a 1% change in yield, such that
>$$D^* = -\frac{1}{P} \cdot \frac{dP}{dy} = \frac{D}{1+y/n},$$
>where the negative sign arises from the inverse relationship between bond price and yield.
>
>Generally, price-yield curves are *convex*. Higher price-yield convexity implies a higher price regardless of which way prices or directions move: 
>
>
>The convexity of a price-yield curve is represented as the second derivative of its price with respect to yield, such that
>$$\Gamma = \frac{1}{P} \cdot \frac{d^2P}{dy^2}=\frac{1}{n^2P(1+y/n)^{2}}\left[\sum^{nT}_{t=1}\frac{C_{t}}{(1+y/n)^{t}}(t^2+t)+\frac{F}{(1+y/n)^{nT}}(n^2T^2+nT)\right].$$
>
>Convexity can be used in tandem with modified duration to create a better approximation for price:
>$$\frac{dP}{P}=-D^* \cdot dR + \frac{1}{2}\Gamma \cdot dR^2.$$

500.title: 2.1a.4 Measuring Bond Risk
500.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.1 Securities/2.1a Fixed-Income Securities/2.1a.4 Measuring Bond Risk.md
500.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.4 Measuring Bond Risk]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/29 00:51:21","modified":"2025/03/29 14:41:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Measures of Bond Risk
>[[2.1a.2 Yield Curves|Credit spread]] measures the additional risk of a fixed-income security compared to a risk-free benchmark. Aside from the trivial value $x=y-y_{0}$, where $y_{0}$ is the yield of a risk-free bond, there are multiple other ways to measure spread:
>- **Static spread** is the constant premium added to the risk-free spot rate. This is the same as $x$ for stripped bonds, but varies for coupon bonds.
>- **Option-adjusted spread (OAS)** is the static spread adjusted for embedded options by removing the value of optionality, reflecting only the credit and liquidity risks (i.e., the credit spread of a callable bond adjusted for the call provision).

501.title: 2.1a.1 Bonds
501.path: Economics/1. Finance/2. Assets/2.1 Securities/2.1a Fixed-Income Securities/2.1a.1 Bonds.md
501.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Bonds]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/25 17:46:39","modified":"2025/03/29 14:22:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bonds
>**Bonds** are a type of fixed-income security that represents a loan made by a lender (generally a corporation or government) to a borrower. Bonds are used by entities to raise capital, and in return, the lender may receive regular **coupon payments** (interest). On the bond's **maturity date**, the lender also receives the bond's **face value** (principal payment), and stops earning interest. Special types of bonds include:
>- **Zero-coupon bonds**, which pay a face value with no coupons.
>- **Treasury securities**, which 
>- **Mortgage bonds**, which pay out coupon payments for a certain period without a face value.
>- **Callable bonds**, which allow the issuer to buy back the bond before maturity. This usually occurs when the interest rates drop below the coupon rate.
>
>The price of a bond is directed by the movement of the market interest rate. When a bond is issued, the yield-to-maturity and coupon rate of the bond are matched to the market rate (i.e., $y_{0}=\frac{C}{F}=r_{0}$). After issuance, market rates move all the time and coupon rates don’t change. Therefore, the only way for the bond to stay competitive is for its price to adjust, which changes the yield. The price of a bond anytime after issuance, known as the **dirty price**, is given as
>$$P=\underbrace{\frac{C}{y}\left(1-\frac{1}{\left( 1+\frac{y}{n} \right)^{nT}}\right)}_{\text{Accrued Interest}}+\underbrace{\frac{F}{\left( 1+\frac{y}{n} \right)^{nT}}}_{\text{PV of Face Value}},$$
>for some face value $F$ and coupon rate $C$ paid $n$ times per year over $T$ years. 
>
>If a bond is bought some time after issuance, the **clean price** is used as a measure of determining the present value of all future cash flows, subtracting the interest that has already been accrued.
>
>When interest rates rise, existing bonds must lower their prices to boost their yields and stay competitive, ensuring that the opportunity cost of holding the bond aligns with current market returns. This means that:
>- If $P=F \iff y = \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at **par**.
>- If $P < F \iff y > \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at a **discount**.
>- If $P > F \iff y < \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at a **premium**.
>
>>[!warning] YTM Assumes Reinvestment
>>Inverting $P$ for the yield-to-maturity of a coupon bond $y$ assumes that all coupons are reinvested, and, of course, that the bond is held to maturity.
# Measurements of Yield

#### (*Current Yield*) $Y_{C}=\dfrac{C}{P}$.
#### (*Nominal Yield/Spot Rate*) $Y_{N}=\dfrac{C}{F}$.
#### (*Yield-to-Maturity/Yield*) $y=n\left[\left(\dfrac{F}{P}\right)^{1/nT}-1\right]$.
#### (Yield-to-Call) 
Measured as the bond's return on investment if called at the earliest opportunity.

#### (*Holding Period Return*) $R = n\left[\left( \frac{P_{T}+C_{T}}{P} \right)^{1/nT}-1 \right]$

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 23:35:05","modified":"2025/05/14 11:30:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Perpetuity
>A **perpetuity** is a financial instrument or stream of cash flows that pays a fixed amount of money indefinitely. The payments are typically made at a regular interval of $n$ times per year, and the amount of each payment $C$ remains constant over time. Formally, the [[1.2c Present Value|present value]] of a perpetuity, given an annual percentage rate $r$, is expressed as
>$$\text{PV}=\frac{nC}{r}.$$
>
>Additionally, a **growth perpetuity** is a perpetuity that grows at a constant annual rate of $g$ given a principal $C$:
>$$\text{PV}=\frac{nC}{r-g}.$$
>
>>[!warning] No Initial Payment
>>The standard perpetuity formula assumes that there is no payment at $t_{0}$. The formula for a ***perpetuity-due*** is given as 
>>$$\text{PV}=\frac{C(n+r-g)}{r-g}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1 Fisher's Equation]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 23:13:58","modified":"2025/05/14 12:50:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Fisher's Equation
>**Fisher’s equation** is an economic identity that shows that the nominal interest rate $i$ reflects both the real return on an investment $r$ and the loss of purchasing power due to inflation, $\pi$. Formally, it is expressed as
>$$i = (1 + \pi)(1 + r) - 1 \approx \pi + r.$$

505.title: 1.4 Annuities
505.path: Economics/1. Finance/1. Time Value of Money/1.4 Annuities.md
505.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.4 Annuities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 23:37:56","modified":"2025/02/24 17:00:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Annuity
>An **annuity** is a financial instrument or series of cash flows that pays a fixed amount of money at $n$ intervals per year for $t$ years, with each payment $C$ remaining constant over the term. The payments can be made at the end of each period (ordinary annuity) or at the beginning (annuity due). Formally, the present value of an ordinary annuity, given an annual percentage rate $r$, is expressed as:
>$$PV=C \times \left[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r(1+r)^{nt}}\right].$$
>
>Additionally, a **growth perpetuity** is a perpetuity that grows at a constant rate of $g$ per year given a principal $C$:
>$$PV=C \times \frac{1}{r-g} \left[1-\left(\frac{1+g}{1+r}\right)^{nt}\right].$$
>>[!warning] No Initial Payment
>>Just like with perpetuities, standard annuities do not offer payment at $t_{0}$. The formula for an **annuity-due** is given as:

506.title: 1.2c Present Value
506.path: Economics/1. Finance/1. Time Value of Money/1.2 Compounding/1.2c Present Value.md
506.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2c Present Value]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 22:58:37","modified":"2025/03/18 13:14:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Present Value
>The present value is the current worth of a [[1.2a Compounding|compounded]] sum of money or stream of cash flows, given a specific rate of return $r$, and a time period of $t$ years over $n$ periods. It is calculated by discounting the future amount(s) back to the present using the formula
>$$\text{PV} = \frac{\text{FV}}{(1+\frac{r}{n})^{nt}}.$$
>
>Given multiple cashflows $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{N}$, the **net future value** of the cashflows is calculated by compounding each cashflow to a common future date using the appropriate interest rate, and then summing these compounded amounts. Mathematically,
>$$\text{NPV} = \sum^{nt}_{i=0}\frac{C_{i}}{\left( 1+\frac{r}{n} \right)^{i}}.$$

507.title: 1.2b Future Value
507.path: Economics/1. Finance/1. Time Value of Money/1.2 Compounding/1.2b Future Value.md
507.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b Future Value]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 22:58:32","modified":"2025/02/25 21:29:09"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Future Value
>The **future value** of an investment is the amount of money it is expected to [[1.2a Compounding|compound]] over $t$ years, $n$ times per year, at a given APR $r$. Formally,
>$$\text{FV} = \left( 1+\frac{r}{n} \right)^{nt} \cdot \text{PV}.$$
>
>Given multiple cashflows $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{N}$, the **net future value** of the cashflows is calculated by compounding each cash flow to a common future date using the appropriate interest rate, and then summing these compounded amounts. Mathematically,
>$$\text{NFV} = \sum^{nt}_{i=1}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt-i} C_{i}.$$

508.title: 1.2a Compounding
508.path: Economics/1. Finance/1. Time Value of Money/1.2 Compounding/1.2a Compounding.md
508.content:
NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Compounding]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 14:07:18","modified":"2025/02/24 20:25:48"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compounding
>**Compounding** is the process by which [[1.1 Fisher's Equation|interest]] earned (or charged) on a principal $P$ also begins to earn additional interest in subsequent periods. 
>
>Cash flows can be compounded using the nominal interest rate over one compounding period per year, also known as the **Annual Percentage Rate (APR)**, or using its geometric average, the **Effective Annual Rate (EAR)**, over $n$ compounding periods per year, such that:
>$$\operatorname{EAR} = \left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^n-1.$$
>
>Letting $n \to \infty$ gives continuous compounding:
>$$\lim_{ n \to \infty }\left[\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^n-1\right] = e^r-1,$$
>for which $\ln(1 + \text{EAR})=r$.
