NOTE TITLE: [[1. Shannon Entropy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/27 17:56:22","modified":"2025/06/06 15:56:31"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Entropy
>**Entropy** quantifies the [[2.5a Expectation|average number]] of bits (uncertainty) required to convey the information in a random variable. For a discrete random variable $X$, its entropy $H(X)$ is defined as
>$$H(X)=\mathbb{E}\left[ \log_{2} \frac{1}{p_{X}(X)} \right],$$
>where $f(x)=\log_{2}\frac{1}{p_{X}(x)} \geq 0$ is a *concave* function, serving as a quantifier of the uncertainty associated with observing each $x$.

# Intuition
Given $f(x)=\log_{2}\frac{1}{p_{X}(x)}$, we can quickly see that $\lim_{ p_{X}(x) \to 1 }f(x)=0$. This implies that the larger the probability of some $x$ is, the smaller the uncertainty associated with it. The addition of the base 2 logarithm to the function captures the exact amount of bits of information yielded by the value $x$. While any base could be used, base 2 is preferred due to the binary nature of modern computers.

Now, take $X$ and find $f(x)$ for all values. multiplied by the probability of each of those values occurring. You get entropy.

# Properties
#### (*Concavity*) 

#### (*Joint Entropy*) $H(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}\left[ \dfrac{1}{p_{X,Y}(x,y)} \right]$.
#### (*Cond. Entropy*) $H(X \mid Y) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \dfrac{1}{p_{X \mid Y}(X \mid Y)} \right] = \large\sum_\limits{x}p_{X}(x)H(Y \mid X=x)$.
#### (*Chain Rule*) $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y \mid X)$.
By definition, we know that $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y \mid x)$. As such,
$$\begin{align*} 
    H(X, Y) &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x,y)\log_2p(x,y) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x,y)\log_2p(x)p(y \mid x) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x, y)(\log_2p(x) +\log_2p(y \mid x)) \\
    &= -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p(x)\log_2p(x)-\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x)p(y \mid x)\log_2p(y \mid x) \\ 
    &= H(X) + H(Y \mid X),
\end{align*}$$
where marginal probability dictates that $-\sum\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\sum\limits_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(x, y) = -\sum\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p(x)$. Essentially, the chain rule states that the joint entropy of $X,Y$ is equivalent to the information that $X$ provides on its own, as well as the extra information provided by $Y$ given $X$.
#### (*Independence*) If $X, Y$ are independent, $H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y)$, and $H(X \mid Y) = H(X)$.
#### (Entropy Bounds) $H(X \mid Y) \leq H(X)$ and $H(X,Y) \leq H(X) + X(Y)$.
#### (*Uniform Dist.*) $H(X) \leq \log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|$. where $H(X)=\log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|$ if $X \sim U(a,b)$.


# Examples

>[!example] Text Compression
>Suppose you want to transmit a message with the letters Y and N, where Y appears 95% of the time. With naive encoding, each symbol takes 1 bit on average. However, entropy tells us that the theoretical limit for compression is
>$$H(X) = 0.95 \log_{2}\frac{1}{0.95} + 0.05 \log_{2}\frac{1}{0.05} \approx 0.286 \text{ bits per symbol.}$$

>[!example] Compression of a Markov Chain
>Consider an irreducible Markov chain $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as shown below:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usetikzlibrary{automata, positioning}
>
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[->, semithick, node distance=3cm]
>    \tikzstyle{every state}=[thick, minimum size=35pt]
>
>    \node[state] (A) {0};
>    \node[state] (B) [right of=A] {1};
>
>    % Loops
>    \path (A) edge [loop left] node {\(1 - p\)} (A);
>    \path (B) edge [loop right] node {\(1 - p\)} (B);
>
>    % Arrows between states
>    \path (A) edge [bend left] node[above] {\(p\)} (B);
>    \path (B) edge [bend left] node[below] {\(p\)} (A);
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Suppose $X_{0} \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)$ and $p \neq 1/2$. Propose a scheme to represent $(X_0,\ldots,X_{n})$ in at most $n$ bits in expectation as $n \to \infty$, and state how many bits that would take.
>
>**SOLUTION:**
>We quickly find that the stationary distribution is $\pi^*=\begin{bmatrix}1/2 & 1/2\end{bmatrix}$, given the transition matrix $P$. We also find that $H(X_{0})=1$ as $X_{0} \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)$. Assuming that the chain has ran for a long time given the stationary distribution above, we find that 
>$$\begin{align} H(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})&=\sum_{x_{n} \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X_{n}}(x_{n})\sum_{x_{n+1} \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}}(x_{n+1} \mid x_{n})\log_{2}\left( \frac{1}{p_{X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}}(x_{n+1} \mid x_{n})} \right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}\right] + \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}\right] \\ &= (1-p)\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-p}+p\log_{2}\frac{1}{p}.\end{align}$$
>
>This is a crucial result. Since $H(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n}) \leq 1$ (where the result equals $1$ if $p=1/2$), this means that if we know $X_{0}$, we will need $nH(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})$ bits of information to determine the rest of the sequence. Recall that $H(X_{0})=1$. Putting this together, we find that we can recover, on average, the Markov Chain with $H(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})=nH(X_{n+1} \mid X_{n})+1 < n+1$ bits of information (strict inequality since $p \neq 1/2$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1. Standard Form Optimization]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/10 15:25:10","modified":"2025/03/10 16:58:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Standard Form 
>A standard  optimization problem is typically stated as follows:
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & f_{0}(x) \\ \text{subject to:} \quad & f_{i}(x) \leq 0, \quad i=1,\ldots,m, \end{aligned}$$
>where $p^*$ is the **optimal value**, $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the **decision variable**, $f_{0}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is the **objective function** (or cost), and $f_{i}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \space i = 1,\ldots,k$ are the $k$ optimization **constraints**.
>
>Other than inequality constraints, an optimization problem may have equality constraints $h_{i} = 0$ (equivalently represented via a pair of inequalities $h_{i} \geq 0$ and $h_{i} \le 0$), and set constraints $x \in \mathcal{X}$.
>
>Furthermore, maximization problems can be readily recast as minimization problems, such that
>$$p^* = \max\limits_{x}f_{0}(x) = -\min\limits_{x}-f_{0}(x).$$
>>[!warning] "Subject To" Notation
>>In the above, the term “$\text{subject to:}$” is sometimes replaced with the shorthand “$\text{s.t.:}$,” or simply by colon notation “$\text{:}$”.

# Properties
#### (*Feasible Set*) $\mathcal{X} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : f_{i}(x) \leq 0 \enspace \forall i = 1,\ldots,k \}$.
The feasible set is the set of points that satisfy the constraints of an optimization problem. If $\mathcal{X} = \emptyset$, the problem is said to be **infeasible**, such that $p^* = \begin{dcases}+\infty & \text{if }p^*=\min\limits_{x}f_{0}(x), \\ -\infty & \text{if }p^*=\max\limits_{x}f_{0}(x).\end{dcases}$
#### (*Optimal Set*) $\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=\{ x \in \mathcal{X} :  f_{0}(x)=p^*\}=\arg\min\limits_{x \in \mathcal{X}}f_{0}(x)$.
If $\mathcal{X}=\emptyset$, then, naturally $\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=\emptyset$. However, the converse isn't true. There may be feasible solutions to an optimization problem, but the optimal set is empty because:
1. The optimal solution is at a limit (i.e., $f_{0}$ diverges at $x^*$).
2. The constraints of the optimization problem are not satisfied.
#### (*Sub-optimality*) If $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $p^* < f_{0}(x) \le p^* + \epsilon$, then $x$ is $\epsilon$-suboptimal.

>**Fisher’s equation** is an economic identity that shows that the nominal interest rate $i$ reflects both the real return on an investment $r$ and the loss of purchasing power due to inflation, $\pi$. Formally, it is expressed as
>$$i = (1 + \pi)(1 + r) - 1 \approx \pi + r.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1 Probability Space]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/25 23:43:11","modified":"2025/06/05 17:01:55"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Probability Space
>A **probability space** is a triple $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ used to model random experiments and the associated outcomes. It consists of
>1. A **sample space** $\Upomega$, which represents the set of all possible single outcomes (**sample points**) $\omega \in \Omega$ of a random experiment. An **event** $A \subseteq \Omega$ is a subset of the sample space, and consists of one or more mutually exclusive sample points.
>2. A 
>3. A **probability measure** $\mathbb{P}: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ for each sample point (outcome) $\upomega \in \Upomega$, which follows the following axioms:
>	- (***Non-Negativity***) $0 \leq \mathbb{P}[\upomega] \leq 1$ for all $\upomega \in \Upomega$.
>	- (***Sum to One***) $\sum^{}_{\upomega \in \Upomega}\mathbb{P}[\upomega]=1$. 
>
>>[!warning] Completeness (Sum to One)
>The sum to one condition also means that a probability space must be collectively exhaustive so that no matter the outcome $\omega$ of the experiment, it will always be an element of the sample space. In other words, $P[\Omega] = 1$.

# Properties
#### (*Subsets*) If $A \subset B$, then $\mathbb{P}[A] < \mathbb{P}[B]$.

# Examples
>[!example] Birthday Paradox
>We want to calculate the probability of at least two people sharing the same birthday in a group of n people. We start by saying that $S=\set{1,...,365}$ since there are $365$ days to sample $n$ from. Then, $|\Upomega|=365^n$ (combinatorial sequence), since for each additional sample point, there are 365 available choices.
>
>We let A be the event that at least two people share the same birthday. Then we need to calculate $\mathbb{P}[A]$. However, it is easier to do so using the complement of A, $\mathbb{P}[\bar{A}]$, since it only takes into account instances where everyone has a different birthday. Since this is the case, $|\bar{A}|=\frac{365!}{(365-n)!}$ (FRC w/o replacement) since each person in the group has to have a different birthday. Therefore,
>$$\mathbb{P}[A]=1-\mathbb{P}[\bar{A}]=1-\frac{|\bar{A}|}{|\Upomega|}=1-\frac{365!}{(365-n)! \times 365^n}$$
>This means that in a group of 60 people, there is a 99% chance of two or more people sharing the same birthday.

>[!note] Decimal System
>The decimal system is a base-10 numbering system that uses digits from 0 to 9. 
>
>To convert a number $x_{10}$ from decimal to another number system base-$n$:
>1. Find $x_{10} \pmod{n}$ and write it down at the rightmost digit.
>2. Floor divide $x_{10}$ by n such that $\lfloor \frac{x}{n} \rfloor$ and repeat.
>
>Then, to reverse the conversion, 
>$$x_{10} = \sum^{k-1}_{i=0}b_i \cdot n^i,$$
>where $k$ is the length of the string in base-$n$, and $b_i$ is its $i$-th digit.
>

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1a Speed and Velocity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/29 14:29:26","modified":"2025/07/29 16:48:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Speed and Velocity
>To describe motion, we track how an object’s position changes over time using quantities like displacement, velocity, speed.
>
>The change in position of an object over a time interval is called **displacement**, defined as the difference between the final and initial position vectors, such that
>$$\Delta x = x - x_{0},$$
>where $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the initial $n$-dimensional position of the object at time $t_0$, and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is its final position at another point in time $t$.
>
>Then, **average velocity** can be defined as the overall rate of change of position,
>$$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t},$$
>whereas **instantaneous velocity** captures the object's average velocity over an infinitesimal time interval:
>$$v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta r}{\Delta t}=\frac{d x}{dt}.$$
>
>**Speed** is the scalar magnitude of instantaneous velocity, such that $s = \|v\|_{2}$. However, **average speed** is defined as the scalar that measures how much ground was covered regardless of direction, expressed as
>$$s_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{\Delta t},$$
>where $d$ is the total distance that the object traveled.

>[!note] Singly Linked List
>We can initiate a singly linked list (SLList) as:
```python
class Node:  
    def __init__(self, val, next):  # Initiates Node.  
        self.val = val  
        self.next = next  
  
  
class SLList:  
    def __init__(self, val):  # Initiates SLList.  
        self.head = Node(val, None)  
        self.size = 1  
  
    def __str__(self):  
        a = self  
        out = []
        while a.head:  
            out.append(a.head.val)  
            a.head = a.head.next  
        return str(out)  
  
    def size(self):  
        return self.size  
  
    def insert(self, val, pos=None):  
        if pos is None:  # Auto sets insert position to last position.  
            pos = self.size  
  
        if pos > self.size:  
            print("Index too large!")  
            return  
  
        a = self.head  # Removing abstraction barrier.  
        while pos - 1 > 0:  
            a = a.next  
            pos -= 1  
  
        a.next = Node(val, a.next)  
        self.size += 1
```

>Suppose a ball is dropped from the top of a building from rest. In the last $\tau$ seconds before the ball hits the ground, the ball covers the last $1/3$ of the building’s height.
>>[!example]- How much time does it take the ball to hit the ground?
>>Let $t_{f}$ be the total time the ball takes to hit the ground, and let $h$ be the height of the building. Since the ball is dropped from rest, the total height is $h = \dfrac{1}{2} g t_f^2$.
>>
>>Consider the origin to be the final destination of the ball. Then, the ball is $\frac{1}{3}h$ away from the origin in the positive direction after $t_{f}-\tau$ seconds. As such, the distance covered in the last $\tau$ seconds is $\dfrac{1}{3}h = h-\dfrac{1}{2}g(t_{f}-\tau)^2$.
>>

>>
>>Plugging into the first equation, $\dfrac{3}{4}g(t_{f}^2-2t_{f}\tau+\tau^2)-\dfrac{1}{2}gt_{f}^2=0$.
>>
>>This equation yields a solution $t_{f}=\tau(3 \pm \sqrt{ 6 })$. The only solution here is $t_{f}=\tau(3+\sqrt{ 6 })$, since $3-\sqrt{ 6 }<1$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1b Acceleration]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/29 14:29:38","modified":"2025/07/30 20:49:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Acceleration
>**Average acceleration** is the rate at which an object’s [[1.1a Speed and Velocity|velocity]] changes over a time interval. It is a vector that points in the direction of the velocity change, defined as
>$$\vec{a}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\vec{v} - \vec{v_{0}}}{t - t_{0}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t},$$
>where $\vec{v}_0$ is the initial velocity and $\vec{v}$ is the final velocity at time $t$.
>
>On the other hand, **instantaneous acceleration** is the object’s acceleration at a specific moment in time. It is defined as the derivative of velocity with respect to time, such that
>$$\vec{a} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}.$$
>
>If acceleration stays **constant** during a time interval, we can use the following equations to describe motion:
>$$
>\begin{align}
>v &= v_0 + at && \enspace \text{(Velocity)} \\
>x &= x_0+v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2 && \enspace \text{(Displacement)} \\
>v^2 &= v_0^2+2a(x-x_0) && \enspace \text{(Velocity-Displacement)}
>\end{align}
>$$

# Derivation
Let's derive the equations for motion at constant acceleration:
1. Per the definition of instantaneous acceleration, $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$.  By integrating, we get $v=\large\int adt=at+C$. The constant $C=v_{0}$ only works if $a$ is constant and can be pulled out of the integral.
2. We start with $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v_{0}+at$ and integrate to obtain $x = \large\int (v_{0}+at) dt=v_{0}t+\frac{1}{2}at^2+C$.
3. This equation combines the above and eliminates time.

# Examples
>[!example] Colliding Balls
>Thelma stands on top of a building whose height is $H$ and throws a ball upward. The speed of the ball when it leaves her hand is $v_{T}$ . Bob is standing at the bottom of the building and at the same instant throws another ball upwards with speed $v_{B}$. 
>>[!example]- What is the slowest that $v_{B}$ can be if Bob’s ball hits Thelma’s ball when still on the way up?
>>Since Bob and Thelma are trying to collide the two balls that are strictly moving in the $y$ direction, then there must be a point where $x_{B}(t)=x_{T}(t)$, such that $v_{T}-gt > 0$. 
>>
>>We solve the equality:
>>$$H+v_{T}t-\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2=v_{B}t-\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \iff t=\dfrac{H}{v_{B}-v_{T}}.$$
>>
>>Then, we satisfy the constraint, such that $v_{T}-g\dfrac{H}{v_{B}-v_{T}}>0 \iff v_{B} > \dfrac{gH+v_{T}^2}{v_{T}}.$
>>
>>So Bob's ball needs to have a starting speed of at least $\dfrac{gH+v_{T}^2}{v_{T}}$.

>[!example] Sliding Balls
>An object $A$ slides down from a frictionless ramp of angle $\theta$ and height $h$ from rest, while another object $B$ is launched from the bottom of the ramp with some initial speed and slides up along the ramp. The two objects collide at the middle point of the ramp.

>>[!example]- Find the initial speed of the object $B$.
>>Since object $B$ is moving up the ramp, it has an acceleration in its $x$-direction of $g\sin\theta$ (and therefore an acceleration in its $y$-direction of $g\cos\theta$, however we only need the $x$-direction here). Draw a plot with $g$, $x$ and $y$ to convince yourself
>>
>>Object $A$ has the exact same acceleration, and starts from rest. In order for them to meet in the middle, we deduce that the time of the collision is $v_{B_{0}}-(g\sin\theta)t=0 \iff t=\dfrac{v_{B_{0}}}{g\sin\theta}$. 
>>
>>Then, we equate the two positions, such that
>>$$x_{A_{0}}-\left(\frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\right)t^2=v_{B_{0}}t-\left(\frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\right)t^2 \iff x_{A_{0}}=v_{B_{0}}t.$$
>>
>>Notice that we can express the starting displacement of $A$ as $x_{A_{0}}=\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$ if we assume that $B$ starts at the origin. Plugging the values for $t$ and $x_{A_{0}}$ into our equation, we obtain $v_{B}=\sqrt{ gh }$.
>
>>[!example]- What are the speeds of $A$ and $B$ when they meet?
>>Given that $A$ and $B$ meet in the center of the hypotenuse with length $\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$, their ending position will be $x=\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$.
>>
>>As such, the final speed of object $A$ right before the collision is 
>>$$\begin{align}v_{A}&=\sqrt{ 0-2g\sin\theta\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta} \right) }\\&=\sqrt{gh}.\end{align}$$
>>
>>Meanwhile, object $B$ will have a speed of 
>>$$\begin{align}v_{B}&=\sqrt{ gh - 2g\sin\theta \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta} } \\ &= \sqrt{ gh - gh } \\ &= 0.\end{align}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1b Binary System]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/27 16:16:42","modified":"2024/07/07 03:17:51"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Binary System
>A binary number is a number expressed in the base-2 numeral system, which uses only two symbols: 0 and 1. Each digit in a binary number is called a **bit**. $N$ bits can represent exactly $2^N$ numbers. Binary numbers are often prefixed with **0b** to distinguish them from numbers in other bases.
>
>To convert a number $x_2$ to base-$2^k$:
>1. Group the bits into clusters of $k$ bits.
>2. Convert each bit to [[1.1a Decimal System|base-10]], and then to base $2^k$.
>
>To reverse the conversion:
>1. Convert each digit of the base-$2^k$ number to decimal.
>2. Convert to binary and cluster each digit into bit clusters of size $k$.
>
>To convert a number from and to base-$n$:
>1. Convert the number to base-10 and follow the steps for conversion.

(cont'd) >[!example] (Hard) Colliding Baseballs
>At time $t = 0$, a baseball is thrown from with an initial speed $v_{1}$ and an angle $\theta = 60\degree$ with respect to the horizontal. At a distance $L$ away a second baseball thrown straight up at initial speed $v_2$ tries to intercept the first baseball while it's still ascending.
>>[!example]- At what time $t_0$ should the second baseball be launched?
>>Let $t_1, t_2$ denote the relative times since launch at which the two balls collide. Then, $t_{1}=t_{2}+t_{0}$. Ball $1$ meets ball $2$ when they are at the same position, so $$L=v_{1}\cos\theta t_{1}=v_{1}\cos\theta(t_{2}+t_{0}) \iff t_{2}=\dfrac{L}{v_{1}\cos \theta}-t_{0}.$$
>>

>>$$v_{1}\sin \theta t_{1}-\frac{1}{2}gt_{1}^2=v_{2}t_{2}-\frac{1}{2}gt_{2}^2.$$

>>$$t_0 =\frac{L}{v_1\cos\theta} -\frac{v_2}{g} +\frac{1}{g}\,\sqrt{\,v_2^2 \;-\;2\,g\Bigl(L\tan\theta-\frac{gL^2}{2v_1^2\cos^2\theta}\Bigr)\!}\,.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1k.1 Uniform Circular Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/28 20:11:07","modified":"2024/09/28 23:53:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Uniform Circular Motion
>An object that moves in a circle at constant speed $\vec{v}$ is said to experience **uniform circular motion**. The *magnitude* of the velocity remains constant in this case, but the *direction* of the velocity continuously changes as the object moves around the circle. Thus, an object revolving in a circle is continuously accelerating, even when the speed remains constant: 
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=3, rotate=60]
>
>    % Draw the circle (part of it)
>    \draw[thick] (1.5,1.25) arc (42:-3:2cm);
>
>    % Points A and B on the circle
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above right:{B}] at (2,0) {};
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above:{A}] at ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) {};
>
>    % Center of the circle C
>    \node[fill=black,circle,inner sep=1.5pt,label=below:C] at (0,0) {};
>
>    % Draw radii
>    \draw[thick] (0,0) -- (2,0) node[midway,right] {$r$}; % Radius to A
>    \draw[thick] (0,0) -- ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) node[midway, left] {$r$}; % Radius to B
>
>    % Arc and angle
>    \draw[->] (1,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=30,radius=1] node[midway, below]{$\Delta \theta$};
>
>    % Tangential displacement arc (delta l)
>    \draw[dashed,thick] (2,0) -- ({2*cos(30)},{2*sin(30)}) node[pos=0.25, below] {$\Delta \ell$};
>
>    % Velocity vectors
>    \draw[->,thick,green] (1.55,1.25) -- +(0.35,-0.5) node[right] {$\vec{v}_1$}; % Velocity at A
>    \draw[->,thick,green] (2.025, 0.25) -- +(0.025, -0.65) node[right] {$\vec{v}_2$}; % Velocity at B
>
>	% Downward acceleration
>	\draw[->,thick,orange] (1.925,0.5) -- +(-0.45,-0.125) node[below] {$\vec{a} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Mathematically, the acceleration of an object in uniform circular motion is expressed as
>$$a_R = \frac{v^2}{r},$$
>where $r$ is the radius of curvature of the curve.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>1. In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant, but the acceleration is not zero.
>>2. Since $a_R$ is directed towards the center of the circle at all times, its **centripetal force** $\sum F_R = ma_R$ must also be directed towards the center of the circle.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1k.2 Nonuniform Circular Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/28 23:49:53","modified":"2024/09/30 12:57:07"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nonuniform Circular Motion
>Nonuniform circular motion occurs when an object moves along a circular path with a changing speed. Unlike [[1.1k.1 Uniform Circular Motion|uniform circular motion]], where the speed remains constant, nonuniform circular motion involves variations in the magnitude of the velocity, though the direction of motion is still continuously changing as the object follows the circular path:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{amsmath}
>
>\begin{document}
>
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>    % First graph: Forces (left side)
>    \begin{scope}[shift={(-2.5,0)}, rotate=90]
>        % Circle & Radius
>        \draw[dashed,thick] (0,0) circle (2);
>        
>        % Force vectors
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(0,-1) node[right] {$\vec{F}_{\text{tan}}$}; % Tangential force
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(-0.925,-0.925) node[below] {$\vec{F}$}; % Radial force
>        \draw[->, thick, magenta] (2,0) -- +(-1,0) node[below right] {$\vec{F}_R$}; % Total force
>        
>        % Labels
>        \node at (2,0) [circle,fill,inner sep=1.5pt] {}; % point on the circle
>    \end{scope}
>    
>    % Second graph: Accelerations (right side)
>    \begin{scope}[shift={(2.5,0)}, rotate=90]
>        % Circle
>        \draw[dashed,thick] (0,0) circle (2);
>        
>        % Acceleration vectors
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(0,-1) node[right] {$\vec{a}_{\text{tan}}$}; % Tangential acceleration
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(-0.925,-0.925) node[below] {$\vec{a}$}; % Total acceleration
>        \draw[->, thick, orange] (2,0) -- +(-1,0) node[below right] {$\vec{a}_R$}; % Radial acceleration
>        
>        % Labels
>        \node at (2,0) [circle,fill,inner sep=1.5pt] {}; % point on the circle
>    \end{scope}
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>Since acceleration has more than one direction, so does force. Therefore,
>$$\vec{a} = \vec{a}_R + \vec{a}_{\tan} \implies |\vec{a}| = \sqrt{|\vec{a}_R|^2 + |\vec{a}_{\tan}|^2}$$
>where $a_R = \frac{|\vec{v}^2|}{r}$ and $a_{\tan} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1p.1 Linear Momentum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/25 15:52:31","modified":"2025/08/04 13:29:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Momentum
>**Linear momentum** ($\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}$) is a measure of an object’s tendency to stay in motion and is conserved in isolated systems. Mathematically, the momentum of an object is defined as the product of its mass and its velocity, such that
>$$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}.$$
>Alternatively, since a force is required to change the momentum of an object, [[1.2a Newton's Laws|net force]] can be defined as the derivative of momentum with respect to time, such that
>$$\sum\vec{F} = \frac{d}{dt}\vec{p} = \frac{d}{dt}(m\vec{v})=m\vec{a}.$$
>The equation above implies that if no external forces act on an object, then the total momentum of that object is said to be conserved. 
>
>More generally, the sum of the momenta of $n$ colliding objects is conserved when
>$$\underbrace{m_A\vec{v}_A + m_B\vec{v}_B}_\text{momentum before collision} = \underbrace{m_A\vec{v}'_A + m_B\vec{v}'_B}_\text{momentum after collision}.$$

# Intuition
Although the law of conservation of linear momentum was discovered experimentally, we can prove it using Newton's laws of motion. Consider a large number of objects colliding, such that their linear momentum is equal to $\vec{P}=\vec{p}_1+\vec{p}_2+\ldots=\sum\vec{p}_i$. Consider also that there are external forces acting on the objects, such as friction, drag, gravity, etc. Momentum is conserved if we measure it immediately before the collision, and immediately after.

Differentiating $\vec{P}$, we find that
$$\frac{d}{dt}\vec{P}=\sum\frac{d}{dt}\vec{p}_i=\sum\vec{F}_i.$$

For any object $i$, $\vec{F}_i$ represents its net force. The forces are either external (exerted by objects outside of the system) or internal (exerted by objects inside the system). Since by Newton's third law internal forces occur in pairs, they cancel each other out. Therefore, $\vec{F}_i$ consists only of external forces. If $\vec{F}_i=0$, then the linear momentum of object $i$ is conserved.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1p.2 Elastic Collisions]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/25 17:07:35","modified":"2024/12/19 01:21:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Elastic Collision
>An **elastic collision** is a type of collision in which the total **kinetic energy** and the total **momentum** of the system are conserved. In an elastic collision, ***no energy is lost*** to heat, sound, or deformation; instead, the ***kinetic energy is fully retained*** in the system, such that
>$$\begin{alignat}{0}
>\underbrace{m_A\vec{v}_A + m_B\vec{v}_B}_\text{Momentum before collision} = \underbrace{m_A\vec{v}'_A + m_B\vec{v}'_B}_\text{Momentum after collision} \\
>\text{and} \\
>\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}m_A\vec{v}_A^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_B\vec{v}_B^2}_\text{KE before collision} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}m_A\vec{v}'^2_A + 
>\frac{1}{2} m_B\vec{v}'^2_B}_\text{KE after collision}
\end{alignat}.$$
> This implies that in $1$-dimensional calculations, the relative speed of the two objects before the collision equals their speed of separation after the collision, such that
> $$v_{A}+v_{A}'=V_{B}+V_{B}'.$$
> A consequence of this means that in an elastic collision, the colliding objects ***change their direction after the collision***.

# Examples
>[!example] Two Blocks, One Spring
>A 3.0-kg block slides along a frictionless tabletop at 8.0 m/s toward a second block (at rest) of mass 4.5 kg. A coil spring, which obeys Hooke's law and has spring constant $k = 760 \text{ N/m}$, is attached to the second block in such a way that it will be compressed when struck by the moving block. 
>
>A collision involving a spring will lead to the blocks sticking together first. Therefore, we can say that
>$$m_{A}v_{A}+m_{B}v_{B}=(m_{A}+m_{B})v_{f} \iff v_{f}=\frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}}v_{A}$$
>Since block $B$ is at rest, $m_{B}v_{B}=0$. Since the system is elastic, $v_{f}=v_{A}$, as all energy is conserved. We can then apply the law of conservation of energy in the same way, such that
>$$\frac{1}{2}m_{A}v_{A}^2=\frac{1}{2}(m_{A}+m_{B})v_{f}^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \iff kx^2 = m_{A}v_{A}^2-(m_{A}+m_{B})\left(\frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}} \right)^2v_{A}^2$$
>This yields $x \approx 0.39$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/21 01:09:59","modified":"2024/12/18 18:56:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
>Any oscillating system for which the net restoring force is directly proportional to the negative of the displacement is said to exhibit **simple harmonic motion (SHM)**, as it is sinusoidal with a single frequency. Such a system is often called a **simple harmonic oscillator (SHO)**. Due to its sinusoidal nature, the displacement of any system in simple harmonic motion can be modeled as
>$$x = x_{0}\cos(\omega t + \phi),$$
>where $x_{0}$ is the waveform's amplitude, representing the initial displacement of the oscillator from its equilibrium position), $\omega = 2\pi f = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ is its natural frequency, and $\phi$ is its phase.
>
>The total energy of the simple harmonic oscillator is then given by
>$$E=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_{0}^2\sin^2(\omega t+\phi)+\frac{1}{2}kx_{0}^2\cos^2(\omega t + \phi).$$

# Intuition
We start with Newton's second law: $\sum F=ma$. Since $a=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, and the total force exerted by a spring is given as $\sum  F =-kx$. Therefore,
$$m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-kx \iff \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+\frac{k}{m}x=0.$$
This is an un(der)damped ($\zeta = \frac{\alpha}{\omega_{0}}=0$) second order differential equation with natural frequency $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{k}{m} }.$ Solving for it by definition, we get
$$\begin{align}
x(t)&=K_{1}\cos(\omega_{n}t)+K_{2}\sin(\omega_{n}t).
\end{align}$$
At $t=0$, $x(0)=K_{1}\cos(\omega_{n}0)=K_{1}=x_{0}$. Therefore, $K_{1}=x_{0}$.

If we take the derivative of $x(t)$, we get:
$$\dot{x}(t)=-\omega_{n}x_{0}\sin(\omega_{n}t)+\omega_{n}K_{2}\cos(\omega_{n}t).$$
Setting $t=0$, we get 
$\dot{x}(0)=\omega_{n}K_{2}=\dot{x_{0}}=v_{0}$. Therefore, $K_{2}=\frac{v_{0}}{\omega_{n}}$. We find that the general solution to the simple harmonic model is
$$x(t)=x_{0}\cos(\omega_{n} t)+\frac{v_{0}}{\omega_{n}}\sin(\omega_{n} t),$$
where $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$. If we assume that $v_{0}=0$ (i.e. the SHO starts motion after $t=0$), we get the final form,
$$x(t)=x_{0}\cos(\sqrt{ \frac{k}{m} }t).$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1u.2 Simple Pendulum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/18 18:40:42","modified":"2024/12/18 19:22:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Simple Pendulum
>A simple pendulum is a [[1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion|simple harmonic oscillator]] consisting of a small, massive objet (called the **bob**) suspended from the end of a lightweight cord, which swings back and forth under the influence of gravity. Its angular displacement follows the formula,
>$$\theta(t)=\theta_{\text{max}}\cos(\omega_{n}t+\phi),$$
>where $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{g}{\ell } }$ is the natural frequency of the pendulum with $\ell$ being the length of the string, and $\theta_{\text{max}}$ is its peak angle of displacement.

# Intuition
The restoring force exerted on a pendulum when it is displaced from its equilibrium (resting) position can be modeled as
$$F=-mg\sin\theta,$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between the pendulum's equilibrium position and current position. For small angles, the following holds:
$$\sin \theta \approx \theta \enspace \text{ (for } \theta < 15\degree\text{)}.$$
Therefore, 
$$F=-mg\theta \enspace \text{ (for } \theta < 15\degree\text{)}.$$
A swinging pendulum always makes an arc with its equilibrium position. Therefore, $s=\theta \ell,$ where $\ell$ is the length of the pendulum's string (and the radius if hypothetically the pendulum makes a circle). We get:
$$F=-\frac{mg}{\ell}s.$$
This formula roughly resembles $-kx$. Therefore, we can approximate $k=\frac{mg}{\ell}$. Since a simple pendulum follows SHM, we get $\omega_{n}=\sqrt{ \frac{mg}{\ell m} }=\sqrt{ \frac{g}{\ell} }$. This means that the equation for angular displacement becomes
$$\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}+\frac{g}{\ell}\theta=0 \iff \theta(t)=\theta_{\text{max}}\cos(\omega_{n}t+\phi).$$
The amplitude equals $\theta_{\text{max}}$ since it is assumed that SHM starts when the pendulum is at $\theta_{\text{max}}$ before being released for the first time.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1u.3 Physical Pendulum]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/18 19:06:32","modified":"2024/12/18 19:24:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Physical Pendulum
> A **physical pendulum** is a [[1.1u.1 Simple Harmonic Motion|simple harmonic oscillator]] that is free to oscillate about a fixed horizontal axis that does not pass through its center of mass. Unlike a simple pendulum, which assumes all mass is concentrated at a single point, a physical pendulum **takes into account the distribution of mass throughout the body.**

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1v.1 Transverse Waves]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/02 17:12:08","modified":"2024/12/18 21:07:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Transverse Wave
>A **transverse wave** is a wave in which particles of the medium move perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation (e.g. light waves, water waves). A series of crests and troughs travel along a transverse wave:
>1. The **crests** of a transverse wave represent the ***positive*** peaks of its oscillation.
>2. The **troughs** of a transverse wave represent the ***negative*** peaks of its oscillation.
>
>A transverse wave's vertical displacement at distance $x$ and time $t$ can be modeled as a function, 
>$$D(x, t)=A\sin(kx \pm  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$$
>where $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ is the wave's wavenumber ($\lambda$ is the wave's wavelength), $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ is the wave's natural frequency ($T$ is its period), and $A$ is its peak $y$-axis displacement (amplitude). The $\pm$ sign is negative as the wave is moving towards the ***right*** of the x-axis.
>
>Furthermore, the speed of a transverse wave is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{F_{T}}{\mu}} = \lambda f,$$
>where $F_{T}$ is the tension on the cord, and $\mu = \frac{m}{\ell}$ is the mass per unit length of the cord, whereas $\lambda$ and $f$ are the sinusoidal wavelength and frequency respectively.


# Intuition

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1v.2 Longitudinal Waves]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/02 17:12:15","modified":"2024/12/05 11:47:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Longitudinal Wave
>A **longitudinal wave** is a wave in which particles of the medium move parallel to the direction of wave propagation (e.g., sound waves, movement of a slinky). A series of compressions and expansions travel along a longitudinal wave. 
>1. **Compressions** are those areas where the coils are momentarily close together. 
>2. **Expansions** (sometimes called rarefactions) are regions where the coils are momentarily far apart. 
>
>Compressions and expansions correspond to the crests and troughs of a transverse wave. As such, a longitudinal wave can be graphically represented by plotting density versus position, resembling a transverse wave and visually clarifying the wave’s behavior.
>
>Moreover, the speed of a longitudinal wave over a solid is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}},$$
>whereas its speed over a fluid is given as
>$$v = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}},$$
>where $E$ is the elastic modulus of the material, $B$ is the bulk modulus of the liquid, and $\rho$ is the material's density.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>Since longitudinal waves can be represented as transverse, we can use the equation $v=\lambda f$ to find the wave's wavelength, frequency and period.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.1v.3 Standing Waves]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/18 20:00:57","modified":"2024/12/18 22:08:57"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Standing Wave
>A standing wave is a wave pattern that results from the constructive interference (superposition) of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude traveling in opposite directions. Unlike traveling waves, standing waves appear stationary, with certain points (called nodes) remaining at rest, while other points (called antinodes) oscillate with maximum amplitude. The vertical displacement of a standing wave at distance $x$ and time $t$ is represented by the function
>$$D(x, t) = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega_{n}t),$$
>where $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ is the wave's wavenumber ($\lambda$ is the wave's wavelength), $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ is the wave's natural frequency ($T$ is its period), and $A$ is its peak $y$-axis displacement (amplitude).
>
>A standing wave contains two types of points:
>1. **Nodes**, where the wave displacement is always $0$ due to destructive interference.
>2. Antinodes, where the wave displacement is always $D$ due to constructive interference.
>
>Furthermore, a standing wave can occur at multiple frequencies $f_{n}$, known as **resonant frequences**. More specifically,
>$$f_{n} = \frac{v}{2\ell}n = nf_{1}$$
>where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, guides the frequencies at which a standing wave occurs. Here, $f_{1}=\frac{v}{2\ell}$ represents the **first harmonic** of the wave, whereas frequencies of $n>1$ are known as $n$-th **harmonics**, or $(n-1)$-th **overtones**.
# Intuition
Since the only thing that distinguishes the two waves from one another is their direction, and we have
$$D(x, t)=A\sin(kx \pm  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$$
by the definition of the transverse wave, we have the superimposed wave
$$D_{3}(x, t)=D_{1}(x, t)+D_{2}(x,t),$$
where $D_{1}(x,t)=A\sin(kx -  \omega_{n} t + \phi),$ is the wave traveling to the right of the $x$-axis, and $D_{2}(x,t)=A\sin(kx +  \omega_{n} t + \phi)$ is the wave traveling to the left. Then,
$$\begin{align}
D_{3}(x, t) &= A\sin(kx -  \omega_{n} t + \phi) + A\sin(kx + \omega_{n} t + \phi) \\
&= 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega_{n}t).
\end{align}$$

>[!note] Scattering
>**Scattering** refers to the interaction of waves with a boundary or medium, resulting in portions of the wave being reflected, transmitted, or absorbed. There are two types of general scattering:
>1. **Reflection** occurs when a wave hits a new medium (such as a fixed support), and by Newton's third law, the support invokes an equal and opposite in magnitude reaction, thereby causing the wave to invert and proceed to travel in the opposite direction.
>2. Transmission occurs when a wave passes through a medium or boundary and continues to propagate in the new medium.

>[!note] Doppler Effect
>The **Doppler Effect** is the apparent change in the frequency (or wavelength) of a wave as observed by an observer moving relative to the source of the wave. NOTE TITLE: [[1.2 Mutually Exclusive Events]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/02 22:27:52","modified":"2025/06/11 00:07:58"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Mutually Exclusive Events
>If events $A_1,...,A_N \subseteq \Omega$ in the same [[1.1 Probability Space|probability space]] are disjoint, such that $A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset$ for all $i \neq j$ (i.e. the events do not share common sample points), then by the **Law of Finite Additivity**, the probability that one of the events occurs is equal to the sum of their probabilities,
>$$\mathbb{P}[A_{1} \cup \ldots \cup A_{N}]=P[A_{1}] + \ldots + P[A_{N}].$$
>Such events are called **mutually exclusive**, and cannot occur simultaneously.
# Examples
>[!example] Dice Roll
>A 6-sided dice may have many events. Two of these events are $A = \{ 2, 4, 6 \}$ (i.e. rolling even), and $B = \{ 1, 3, 5 \}$ (i.e. rolling odd). Their intersection is $A \cap B = \emptyset$. Therefore, these events are mutually exclusive; you cannot roll odd and even at the same time.
>
>However, consider the event $C = \{ 3, 6 \}$ (rolling a multiple of 3). Then, $A \cap C = \{ 6 \}$, and $B \cap C = \{ 3 \}$. Therefore, neither $A$ nor $B$ are mutually exclusive to $C$, since you can both roll a multiple of 3 and an even number, or roll a multiple of 3 and an odd number.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2 Quantifiers]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 09:40:05","modified":"2025/07/12 15:41:38"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Quantifier
>A quantifier of a [[1.1 Propositional Logic|proposition]] is a logical operator that specifies how many elements in a domain satisfy a statement which refers to a variable, known as a *propositional formula*. For the *propositional formula* $P(x)$, we can define the *duals*:
>1. ***Universal Quantifier:*** $\forall x P(x) \iff P(x)\text{ is true for all x.}$
>2. ***Existential Quantifier:*** $\exists x P(x) \iff \text{There exists at least one }x\text{ for which } P(x) \text{is true.}$

# Understanding
We can translate any propositional formula from the duals back to propositional forms. For example, take a variable $x$ such that $x \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. Then,
1. $\forall x P(x) \iff P(1) \land P(2) \land P(3)$.
2. $\exists x P(x) \iff P(1) \lor P(2) \lor P(3)$.

# Properties
##### *(DeMorgan's Laws)* $\neg[\forall x P(x)] \equiv \exists x \neg P(x)$, and $\neg [\exists x P(x)] \equiv \forall x \neg P(x)$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Compounding]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 14:07:18","modified":"2025/02/24 20:25:48"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compounding
>**Compounding** is the process by which [[1.1 Fisher's Equation|interest]] earned (or charged) on a principal $P$ also begins to earn additional interest in subsequent periods. 
>
>Cash flows can be compounded using the nominal interest rate over one compounding period per year, also known as the **Annual Percentage Rate (APR)**, or using its geometric average, the **Effective Annual Rate (EAR)**, over $n$ compounding periods per year, such that:
>$$\operatorname{EAR} = \left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^n-1.$$
>
>Letting $n \to \infty$ gives continuous compounding:
>$$\lim_{ n \to \infty }\left[\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^n-1\right] = e^r-1,$$
>for which $\ln(1 + \text{EAR})=r$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Least Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/10 00:16:22","modified":"2025/03/10 20:28:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Optimization
>**Least squares** optimization is a method for finding an approximate solution to a system of equations $A\vec{x}=\vec{y}$ for which $\nexists\vec{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$. Formally, given a real matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and a vector $\vec{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the least squares problem finds (at least one) vector $\vec{x}^* \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $A\vec{x}^*$ is the [[10. Projection Theorem|orthogonal projection]] of $\vec{y}$ onto $\mathcal{R}(A)$,
>$$\vec{x}^* \in \arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|A\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|_{2}^2,$$
>where $\vec{x}^*$ is always an optimal solution to the system of normal equations $A^TA\vec{x}=A^T\vec{y}$.
>
>Particularly, if $A$ is in full column rank (i.e., $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n$), and therefore $Ax=y$ is *overdetermined*, then the least squares solution is given as
>$$\vec{x}^* = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T\vec{y}.$$
>
>Moreover, if $A$ is in full row rank (i.e., $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$), and therefore $A\vec{x}=\vec{y}$ is *undetermined* with infinite solutions, then the least squares solution is defined as the solution of the system with the smallest Euclidean norm, such that
>$$\vec{x}^* = \arg\min\limits_{\vec{x}:A\vec{x}=\vec{y}}\|\vec{x}\|_{2} = A^T(AA^T)^{-1}\vec{y}.$$
>>[!warning] LS and the Pseudoinverse
>>Note that the set of optimal solutions to the least squares problem can be expressed as
>>$$\mathcal{X}_{\text{opt}}=A^\dagger \vec{y} + \mathcal{N}(A),$$
>>where $A^\dagger \vec{y}$ is the minimum-norm point in the optimal set. This means that if $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = \min(m, n)$ (i.e., $A$ is full rank), then the optimal solution $x^* = A^{\dagger}\vec{y}$.
# Proofs
### 1. General Solution
Per the Projection Theorem, we know that given any $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, there exists some $\bar{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$ at minimal distance from $\vec{y}$. We also know that $(y-\bar{y}) \perp \mathcal{R}(A) \equiv (y-\bar{y}) \in \mathcal{N}(A^T)$. As such, for all $y$,
$$A^T(y-\bar{y}) = 0.$$
Furthermore, since $\bar{y} \in \mathcal{R}(A)$, there certainly exists some $x$, such that $Ax = \bar{y}$. Combining the two equations,
$$A^Ty-A^TAx=0 \iff A^TAx=A^Ty.$$
### 2. Full Col. Rank Solution
Since $A^TA$ is invertible for wide matrices of full column rank, we have $x^*=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Ty$.
### 3. Full Row Rank Solution
When a tall matrix $A$ has full row rank $m \leq n$, the rank-nullity theorem implies that the nullspace of $A$ is nontrivial, such that $\text{Nullity}(A) = n-m \geq 1$. 

### 4. Pseudoinverse Solution


# Variants
#### (*Weighted LS*) For $W = \operatorname{diag}(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{m})$, $\exists\vec{x}^*_{w}=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|W(A\vec{x}-\vec{y})\|_{2}^2$, such that $A^TW^TWA\vec{x}_{w}^* = A^TW^TW\vec{y}$.
The proof is simple. We know from the proof of general LS that $x^*$ is the optimal solution to $A^TAx=A^Ty$. We then take $A_{w}=WA$, $y_{w} = Wy$, and substitute for the solution, such that
$$A_{w}^TA_{w}\vec{x}=A_{w}^Ty_{w} \iff A^TW^TWAx=A^TW^TWy.$$
#### (*Linearly Constrained LS*) For $\begin{aligned} \min_\limits{x} \quad & c^T x \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b\end{aligned}$

#### (*$\ell^2$-Regularized LS*) For $\lambda > 0$, $x^*=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n}\|A\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|_{2}^2+\lambda\|\vec{x}\|_{2}^2$ is the optimal solution to $(A^T A + \lambda L^T L)\vec{x} = A^T \vec{y}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2a Newton's Laws]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:14:49","modified":"2025/08/11 20:01:30"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Newton's Laws
>**Newton’s Laws** describe the relationship between force, motion, and interaction: how objects behave when forces act on them or when they interact with other objects:
>1. **Newton’s First Law** states that ***an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force***. This only holds in inertial reference frames, where motion is not observed to spontaneously accelerate or decelerate.
>‎ 
>2. **Newton’s Second Law** defines the precise relationship between force and motion: the net force **exerted** on an object is equal to the product of its mass and [[1.1b Acceleration|acceleration]], such that
>$$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}.$$
>The First Law is a special case of the Second Law, where $\sum \vec{F} = 0$.
>‎ 
>3. **Newton’s Third Law** states that if object $A$ exerts a force on object $B$, then $B$ simultaneously exerts a force of ***equal magnitude*** and ***opposite direction*** on $A$. These action–reaction pairs act on different objects and therefore do not cancel.
>
>>[!warning] Fictitious Forces

>>$$M_{1} < M_{2} < M_{3}.$$


>[!example] Two Masses
>Consider two objects $A$ and $B$. When we apply a force $F$ on object $A$, it obtains an acceleration of $3 m/s^2$. The ratio of the two objects’ masses is $m_{A}$ : $m_{B} = 3 : 2$. The two objects are placed together, and $F$ is applied to them such that the two move together.
>>[!example]- What is the acceleration of the combined system?

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b Future Value]]

>[!note] Future Value
>The **future value** of an investment is the amount of money it is expected to [[1.2a Compounding|compound]] over $t$ years, $n$ times per year, at a given APR $r$. Formally,
>$$\text{FV} = \left( 1+\frac{r}{n} \right)^{nt} \cdot \text{PV}.$$
>
>Given multiple cashflows $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{N}$, the **net future value** of the cashflows is calculated by compounding each cash flow to a common future date using the appropriate interest rate, and then summing these compounded amounts. Mathematically,
>$$\text{NFV} = \sum^{nt}_{i=1}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt-i} C_{i}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b Signed Integers]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/07 03:35:16","modified":"2024/07/07 03:50:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Signed Integer
>A signed integer is a data type in computer science and mathematics that can represent both positive and negative whole numbers by assigning $1$ or $0$ to the leftmost bit to indicate the sign of the integer. Signed integers can therefore represent numbers between $-2^{N-1}-1$ and $2^{N-1}-1$ inclusive, where $N$ represents the number of bits representing the integer.

# Intuition
Let's start with formulating the range of signed integers. We previously said that [[1.2a Unsigned Integers|unsigned integers]] can represent numbers in the range $[0,2^N-1]$. However, when using signed integers, two issues arise: 
1. There is a -0 and +0! We can see this with a quick example: as the leftmost bit is allocated to the number sign, 0b1000 and 0b0000 are the same number! 
2. Similarly, because the leftmost bit takes up space, we can only utilize $N-1$ bits for our signed integer.
Combining the two facts, we get our desired range: $[-2^{N-1}-1, 2^{N-1}-1]$.

We also arise into something else here: adding a positive and a negative number always leads to a negative number!

>**Gravity** is the **attractive force** exerted by a massive body on another object with mass. Near Earth’s surface, this force causes all objects to accelerate downward at approximately $9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2$, regardless of their mass.
>
>The gravitational force on an object is given by the equation
>$$\vec{F}_G = m \vec{g},$$
>where $m$ is the object’s **mass**, $\vec{g}$ is the **acceleration due to gravity** (typically $\vec{g} = -9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2$), and $\vec{F}_G$ is the **weight** of the object, directed downward toward the center of the Earth.
>
>When an object is in contact with a surface, the surface resists compression by exerting a **normal force**, per [[1.2a Newton's Laws|Newton's Third Law]]. Normal Force is denoted as $\vec{F}_N=-\vec{F}_G$, and **always acts perpendicular** to the surface, even on slopes:
>```tikz

>
>\begin{tikzpicture}
>
>    % Draw the table
>    \draw[thick] (-2,0) -- (2,0); % table surface
>
>    % Draw the box
>    \draw[thick, fill=black, fill opacity=0.1] (-0.5,0) rectangle (0.5,1);
>
>    % Label the box
>    \node at (0, 0.5) {m};
>
>    % Draw the force of gravity (downward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,0) -- (0,-1) node[below] {$\vec{F}_G$};
>
>    % Draw the normal force (upward)
>    \draw[->, thick] (0,1) -- (0,2) node[above] {$\vec{F}_N$};
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>
>\end{document}
>```
>>[!warning] Mass vs. Weight
>>Note that mass is a scalar and does not change with location. Weight is a **force** and depends on the gravitational field strength at a given place.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Stuck Ball
>A sphere of mass M is placed between two perpendicular inclined planes. The two planes form angles of $\theta_{1}=60\degree$ and $\theta_{2}=60\degree$ with respect to the horizontal. We assume the contact between the planes and the sphere is frictionless. 
>>[!example]- Find the normal forces between the ramps and the sphere.
>>Since the normal force is in the opposite direction of the perpendicular to the incline component  of gravity, we have that $-N_{1}\cos\theta_{1}+N_{2}\cos\theta_{2}$


>[!example] (Easy) Sliding Blocks
>Two blocks of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are placed on a frictionless ramp with an inclination angle $\theta$. The two blocks are then released and slide down.
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of block $m_{2}$.
>>To proceed, observe $m_{1}$ and $m_2$ as one system. Since $m_{1}>m_{2}$, then both blocks will move together, such that $(m_{1}+m_{2})a=(m_{1}+m_{2})g\sin\theta$. Therefore, $a=g\sin\theta$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force between the two blocks.
>>Now observe only block 1. Per Newton's Second Law, $m_{1}a=m_{1}g\sin\theta-N_{21}$. Substitute for $a$ and obtain
>>$$m_{1}g\sin\theta=m_{1}g\sin\theta-N_{21} \iff N=0.$$

>[!note] The Normal Force
>**Normal force** is the contact force that acts **perpendicular** to the surface between two objects. It arises when two surfaces are pressed together and prevents them from passing through each other.
>
>When an object rests on a surface, the normal force balances the component of the object’s weight perpendicular to that surface. For an object of mass m resting on a horizontal surface:

>as shown in the following figure:

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 20:55:57","modified":"2025/08/01 13:50:40"}

>[!note] Friction
>**Friction** is a resistive force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact, and it always **acts parallel to the contact surface**:
>1. **Static friction** acts when two surfaces are in contact but not moving relative to each other. It prevents motion from starting and adjusts its magnitude up to a maximum limit, such that
>$$|\vec{F}_{\text{fr}}| \leq \mu_s |\vec{F}_N|,$$
>where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction, and $\vec{F}_N$ is the normal force.
>‎ 
>2. **Kinetic friction** (or sliding friction) acts when two surfaces slide against each other. It has a constant magnitude given by
>$$|\vec{F}_{\text{fr}}| = \mu_k |\vec{F}_N|,$$
>where $\mu_k$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction. Kinetic friction is typically smaller than the maximum static friction.

>[!note] Spring Force
>**Spring force** is the restoring force exerted by a spring when it is compressed or stretched from its equilibrium position. It acts in the direction opposite to the displacement and is given by **Hooke’s Law**, such that
>$$\vec{F}_s = -k\vec{x},$$
>where $\vec{F}_s$ is the spring force, $\vec{x}$ is the displacement from equilibrium, and $k$ is the spring constant (in N/m), which quantifies the stiffness of the spring. The negative sign indicates that the force always acts to restore the spring to equilibrium.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2b.5 Drag Force]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/30 21:12:22","modified":"2025/08/01 14:00:48"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Drag Force
>**Drag force** is the resistive force experienced by an object moving through a fluid (such as air or water). It always acts in the direction **opposite** to the object’s velocity relative to the fluid and depends on the **speed**, **shape**, and **surface properties** of the object, as well as the **viscosity** of the fluid.
>
>When the relative speed is small and the fluid flow is smooth (laminar), the drag force is approximately **proportional** to the object’s speed, such that
>$$\vec{F}_{\text{drag}} = -b \vec{v},$$
>where $b$ is a positive constant depending on the fluid’s viscosity and the object’s geometry. The negative sign indicates that drag opposes motion.
>
>When the object moves faster and the flow becomes more **turbulent**, the drag force becomes roughly **proportional to the square of the speed**, such that $\vec{F}_{\text{drag}} \propto -v^2$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.2c Present Value]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 22:58:37","modified":"2025/03/18 13:14:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Present Value
>The present value is the current worth of a [[1.2a Compounding|compounded]] sum of money or stream of cash flows, given a specific rate of return $r$, and a time period of $t$ years over $n$ periods. It is calculated by discounting the future amount(s) back to the present using the formula
>$$\text{PV} = \frac{\text{FV}}{(1+\frac{r}{n})^{nt}}.$$
>
>Given multiple cashflows $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{N}$, the **net future value** of the cashflows is calculated by compounding each cashflow to a common future date using the appropriate interest rate, and then summing these compounded amounts. Mathematically,
>$$\text{NPV} = \sum^{nt}_{i=0}\frac{C_{i}}{\left( 1+\frac{r}{n} \right)^{i}}.$$

(cont'd) >[!example] Monty Hall Problem
>You are a contestant on a game show and can choose to open one of 3 doors, two of them containing a goat, and one of them containing a brand new car. You choose one of the doors, and Monty Hall opens another one, knowing that he's opening a door with a goat behind it. 
>
>>[!example]- Should you switch, or should you keep your original choice?
>>Let $A, B, C$ be the events that the car is behind door A, B, or C. Then $\mathbb{P}[A]=\mathbb{P}[B]=\mathbb{P}[C]=\frac{1}{3}$. Let's say you pick door A. This means that $\mathbb{P}[B \cup C]=\frac{2}{3}$. If Monty opens door C, then $\mathbb{P}[C]=0$, and so $\mathbb{P}[B]=\frac{2}{3}$. In most cases, it is therefore better to switch.
>
>>What is the sample space here? Consider a triple $(A, B, C)$, which represents:
>>1. A: The location of the prize.
>>2. B: The initial door opened by the contestant.
>>3. C: The door opened by Monty.
>>
>Note that some triples are not possible, e.g. $(A, B, A)$, since Monty cannot open the door that contains the car or the door that the contestant has picked. It turns out that there are 12 different permutations of triples that can be made. These include:
>$$
>\begin{align}
>(A, B, C) \\
>(A, C, B) \\
>(B, C, A) \\
>(B, A, C) \\
>(C, B, A) \\
>(C, A, B) \\
>(A, A, B) \\
>(A, A, C) \\
>(B, B, A) \\
>(B, B, C) \\
>(C, C, A) \\
>(C, C, B)
>\end{align}
>$$
>We note that there are only two events that could happen: $E_1=$ Monty has one door to pick (as in the first 6 triples), and $E_2=$ Monty has two doors to pick (as in the last 6 triples). Then:
>$$
>\begin{alignat}{0}
>\mathbb{P}[E_1]=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times 1 = \frac{1}{9}
>\\
>\mathbb{P}[E_2]=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{18}
>\end{alignat}
>$$
>Note that in the first equation we multiply by 1 because Monty has 1 door to choose, and in the second equation we multiply by $\frac{1}{2}$ because he can choose between 2 doors.
>
>Let's suppose the contestant wants to switch doors. Now, let $W$ be the event that the contestant wins. Which sample points $(A, B, C)$ are in W? Since we are interested in the event that the contestant **has to win**, the only way this could happen is if they didn't initially pick the prize door (that is, the first 6 triples). Therefore, the contestant has a $\mathbb{P}[W]=6 \times \frac{1}{9} = \frac{2}{3}$ chance of winning.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3 Conditional Probability]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/28 18:11:42","modified":"2025/06/11 02:15:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Conditional Probability
>For two events $A, B \subseteq \Omega$ in the same [[1.1 Probability Space|probability space]], the law of conditional probability states that the probability of $B$ given that $A$ has happened is
>$$\mathbb{P}[B \mid A]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[A]}.$$
>This implies that the probability of $A$ is nonzero ($\mathbb{P}[A]>0$).
>
>>[!warning] Non-Associativity
>>Conditional probabilities are non-associative. This means that generally, $\mathbb{P}[B \mid A] \neq \mathbb{P}[A \mid B]$, unless $\mathbb{P}[A]=\mathbb{P}[B]$.
# Intuition
The joint probability $\mathbb{P}(A \cap B)=\mathbb{P}(B \cap A)$ is the probability that both $A$ and $B$ happen. It is restricted to the sample points that occur in both events. In a Venn diagram, it can be represented as the overlap between two circles, $A$ and $B$:
```tikz
\begin{document}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  % Define circles for A and B
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (2cm) node[left] {\(A\)};
  \draw[thick] (2.5,0) circle (2cm) node[right] {\(B\)};

  % Label A ∩ B
  \begin{scope}
    \clip (0,0) circle (2cm);
    \fill[gray, opacity=0.15] (2.5,0) circle (2cm);
  \end{scope}
  \node at (1.25,0) {\(A \cap B\)};

  % Label sample space
  \draw[thick] (-3,-2.5) rectangle (6,2.5) node[below left] {\(\Omega\)};
\end{tikzpicture}

\end{document}
```
By dividing the joint probability by the probability of the event that has already happened we are “zooming in” on the world where $A$ happened and renormalizing so that those remaining outcomes sum to 1.  In effect, we:
1. Throw out all outcomes where A didn’t occur.
2. Rescale the probabilities of the leftover outcomes (i.e., $A \cap B$, $A \cap \bar{B}$) by $1/\mathbb{P}(A)$ so they total 1.
Essentially, $A$ becomes our new sample space.

# Examples
>[!example] Boys and Girls
>A company is holding a dinner for working mothers with at least one son.
>>[!example]- Jackson, a mother with two children, is invited. What is the probability that both her children are boys?
>>We have the following sample space: $\Omega = \{ (b, b), (b, g), (g, b), (g, g) \}$. Let $B_{i}$ be the probability that her $i$-th child is a boy. We need to find $\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cap B_{2} \mid B_{1} \cup B_{2})$. We have:
>>$$\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cap B_{2} \mid B_{1} \cup B_{2}) = \frac{\mathbb{P}([B_{1} \cap B_{2}] \cap [B_{1} \cup B_{2}])}{\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cup B_{2})}=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cap B_{2})}{\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cup B_{2})}=\frac{1/4}{1/3}=\frac{1}{3},$$
>>since $B_{1} \cap B_{2} = \{ (b,b) \}$ and $B_{1} \cup B_{2}=\{  (b, b), (b, g), (g,b) \}$.
>
>A few days before the party, you are taking a walk and see your new colleague, Ms. Parker, who is known to have two children.
>>[!example]- If you see her walking with one of her children, and that child is a boy, what is the probability that both children are boys?
>>Note the slight distinction in the two questions. Here, we know that one of her children is a boy. Label the observed child as $B_{1}$. Then, we are solving for
>>$$\mathbb{P}(B_{1} \cap B_{2} \mid B_{1})=\mathbb{P}(B_{2} \mid B_{1})=\mathbb{P}(B_{2})=\frac{1}{2},$$
>>since whether the observed child is a boy is independent of her other child being a boy.

>[!example] Scratched CDs
>You just bought 3 used movie CDs from Blockbuster! Unfortunately for you, one of the CDs is scratched on one side, while a second one is scratched on both sides. In a fit of rage, you shove the CDs back in the bag and shuffle it.
>>[!example]- Later in the day, you take out one of the CDs, and observe that it has a scratched side. What is the probability that the other side of the CD will be scratched too?
>>Here, it is easy to make a mistake here and say that the sample space is $\Omega = \{ (S, S), (S, C) \}$, and therefore the probability is $3/6=1/2$, since there are 3 clean sides and 3 scratched sides. 
>>
>>However, we are recording each of the 6 sides here, rather than recording each CD. Therefore, the conditional sample space is $\Omega = \{ SS_{1}, SS_{2}, SC_{S}\}$, (i.e., the two sides of the double-scratched CD and the scratched side of the CD with a single scratched side). In $2/3$ of cases, the CD with both sides scratched is selected. 
>>
>>As a sanity check, consider $S_{i}$ being an indicator of whether the $i$-th side is scratched. Then,
>>$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}(S_{2} = 1 \mid S_{1} = 1) &= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{1} = 1 \cap S_{2} = 1)}{\mathbb{P}(S_{1}=1)} \\
&= \frac{1/3}{1/2} \\
&= 2/3.
\end{align}$$

>[!note] Perpetuity
>A **perpetuity** is a financial instrument or stream of cash flows that pays a fixed amount of money indefinitely. The payments are typically made at a regular interval of $n$ times per year, and the amount of each payment $C$ remains constant over time. Formally, the [[1.2c Present Value|present value]] of a perpetuity, given an annual percentage rate $r$, is expressed as
>$$\text{PV}=\frac{nC}{r}.$$
>
>Additionally, a **growth perpetuity** is a perpetuity that grows at a constant annual rate of $g$ given a principal $C$:
>$$\text{PV}=\frac{nC}{r-g}.$$
>
>>[!warning] No Initial Payment
>>The standard perpetuity formula assumes that there is no payment at $t_{0}$. The formula for a ***perpetuity-due*** is given as 
>>$$\text{PV}=\frac{C(n+r-g)}{r-g}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3b Kinetic Energy]]

>[!note] Kinetic Energy
>**Kinetic energy** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) quantifies the motion of an object in terms of how difficult it would be to stop it. The faster and more massive an object, the harder it is to stop, and the more kinetic energy it has.
>
>Mathematically, the kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving with speed v is given by the equation
>$$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3c Work-Energy Principle]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/01 16:10:12","modified":"2025/08/02 15:33:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Work-Energy Principle
>The **Work–Energy Principle** states that when a net force acts on an object and changes its speed, the total work done by the force equals the change in the object’s kinetic energy.
>
>If an object of mass $m$ is subject to a net force that causes it to speed up or slow down from an initial speed $v_i$ to a final speed $v_f$, then the net work $W$ done on the object is
>$$\sum W = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2.$$

# Proof
Proceed using Newton's Second Law, such that $F_{\text{net}}=m\vec{a}=m\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$. Work is then defined as
$$\begin{align}
W&=\int_{\mathcal{P}} F_{\text{net}} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&=m\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&=m \int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \vec{v} \cdot d\vec{v} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}^2\Big|_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}_{f}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}m\vec{v}_{i}^{2} \\
&= \Delta K.
\end{align}$$
# Examples

>[!example] Hemisphere Pulling Problem
>A small sphere of mass $m$ is attached to a string being pulled from the bottom of a hemisphere $\theta=0$ to the top $\theta = \pi / 2$. It is pulled slowly, such that at every moment the sphere is nearly in equilibrium. Throughout the entire process, the string is tangent to the hemisphere.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-01 at 21.19.51.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- When the sphere is at an angle $\theta$, what is magnitude of the string’s tension?
>>In the $x$ direction of the tangent, there is tension $T$, which is opposed by gravity with an $x$ component of $mg\cos\theta$. Given that the sphere is "nearly" at equilibrium, $a=0$, then $T-mg\cos\theta=0 \iff T=mg\cos \theta$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by the string on the sphere throughout the process?
>>It holds that $W = \int |\vec{F}| \cdot |d\vec{r}|$. From the previous part, $|\vec{F}|=T=mg\cos\theta$. Here, $|d\vec{r}|=Rd\theta$ since $|\vec{r}|=R\theta$, which is the arc length. Since both $T$ and $d\vec{r}$ are in the same direction, the angle between them is $0$, and therefore $\cos0 = 1$:
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{T} &=\int T \cdot dr \cdot \cos0 \\
>>&= \int mg \cos\theta \cdot R \cdot d\theta \\
>>&= mgR \sin\theta \Big |^{\pi / 2}_{0} \\
>>&= mgR.
>>\end{align}$$
>> A quicker way to derive this would be to label the positive axis as the axis of direction, As such, $W_{T}=$
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by the normal force throughout the process?
>>The normal force exerted on the ball by the hemisphere is upward, whereas the vertical component of gravity in terms of the ball's reference frame is $mg \sin\theta$. Once again, because the sphere is in quasi-equilibrium, then $N-mg\sin\theta=0 \iff N=mg\sin\theta$. However, because the angle between $N$ and $dr$ is $90 \degree$, it turns out that
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{N} &=\int N \cdot dr \cdot \cos \pi / 2 \\
>>&= \int mg \sin\theta \cdot R \cdot d\theta \cdot 0 \\
>>&= 0
>>\end{align}$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the work done by gravity throughout the process?
>>Opposite to the direction of displacement, the horizontal component relative to the ball's reference frame is $F_{G}=mg\cos\theta$. Then, 
>>$$\begin{align}
>>W_{G} &=\int F_{G} \cdot dr \cdot \cos \pi \\
>>&= -mgR\int \cos\theta \; d\theta \\
>>&= -mgR \sin\theta \Big|^{\pi / 2}_{0} \\
>>&= -mgR.
>>\end{align}$$
>
>>[!example]- Is there a relationship between parts 2 and 4?
>>Since the sphere moves slowly and remains in quasi-equilibrium, its speed does not change, so $\Delta K = 0$. By the work–energy principle:
>>$W_{\text{net}} = W_T + W_G = \Delta K = 0$
>>
>>As such, the work done by tension exactly cancels the work done by gravity ($W_T = -W_G$).
>>

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.1 Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/02 16:21:42","modified":"2025/08/04 11:53:09"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Potential Energy
>**Potential energy** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) is a scalar quantity that denotes how much work a system can release or absorb due to the relative positions of its parts. 
>
>It is defined for systems where internal forces do work that depends only on the initial and final positions–and not on the path taken–called **conservative forces**, for which it holds that
>$$\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0.$$
>
>Mathematically, the change in potential energy is defined as the negative of the work done by conservative forces, where
>$$\Delta U = -W_{\text{ext}}.$$
# Intuition
Potential energy is introduced a configuration-based quantity that depends on the relative position of interacting objects. Consider the gravitational interaction between two objects, say Earth and an apple. There are **two perspectives**:
1. **External Force View (apple only)**
	- Gravity is an external force.
    - The work done by gravity leads to a change in kinetic energy, such that $\Delta K = W_{\text{ext}}$.
2. **System View (apple + Earth)**
    - Gravity is internal to the system.
    - No external work is done, so the total mechanical energy stays constant, such that $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0 \implies \Delta K = -\Delta U$.

From both, we conclude that $\Delta U = -W_{\text{ext}}$.

# Examples

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.2 Gravitational Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 15:44:29","modified":"2025/08/03 20:29:11"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Gravitational Potential Energy
>**Gravitational [[1.3d.1 Potential Energy|potential energy]]** (SI: Joule / $\text{J} \equiv \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}$) describes the interaction between two objects with mass based on how far apart they are. It is defined for systems where gravity is the internal conservative force.
>
>If two spherical objects of mass $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are separated by a center-to-center distance $r$, the gravitational potential energy of the system is given by
>$$U(r) = -G\frac{ m_{1} m_{2}}{r},$$
>where $G$ is the [[1.2b.6 Law of Universal Gravitation|gravitational constant]].
>
>For **objects near Earth's surface**, it holds that for $r=R+h$ such that $R$ is Earth's radius and $h$ is the height of the object between sea level and the Kármán line (i.e., $h_{max} \approx 100 \; \text{km}$),
>$$U(r) \approx U(R)+mgh = mgh,$$
>where $m$ is the object's mass, $g=G \dfrac{M}{R^2}$ is the gravitational field strength near Earth's surface, and $h$ is the height of the object from Earth's surface. Note that $U(R) = 0$ since the baseline is defined as Earth's surface.
>
>>[!warning] Infinity as the Potential Energy Baseline
>The general formula assumes that $U(\infty) \equiv 0$, meaning the potential energy is zero when the two objects are infinitely far apart and $U(0) \equiv -\infty$ if they are at a singularity. The negative sign indicates that energy must be added to the system (i.e., work must be done) to separate the objects and overcome gravity.
# Intuition
Observe the gravitational force on $m_{2}$ an external force. Define $\hat{r}$ as the positive unit vector, and $\vec{r}$ as the displacement vector from $m_{1}$ to $m_2$. Then, the work done by the gravity of the left object with mass $m_1$ on the right object with mass $m_{2}$ between center-to-center distances $r_{i}$ and $r_{f}$ can be defined as
$$\begin{align}
W_{G} &= \int^{\vec{r}_{f}}_{\vec{r}_{i}} F_{G} \cdot d\vec{r}  \\
&= \int^{\vec{r}_{f}}_{\vec{r}_{i}} -G \frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^2}\hat{r} \cdot d\vec{r} \\
&= -Gm_{1}m_{2} \int^{r_{f}}_{r_{i}} \frac{1}{r^2}dr \\
&= G \frac{Mm}{r_{f}} - G \frac{Mm}{r_{i}}.
\end{align}$$
Because $W_G$ has been regarded as an external force, it follows that the change in potential energy between $r_{i}$ and $r_{f}$ is equal to $\Delta U = -W_{G}=G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{i}} - G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{f}}$.

Here is where the reference point of $U(\infty) \equiv 0$ comes in. Given this reference point, it follows that the potential energy at a center-to-center distance of $r$ is equal to the potential energy at an infinite distance away, plus the change from infinity to $r$, such that
$$\begin{align}
U(r) &= U(\infty) + \Delta_{\infty \to r}U \\
&=0+G \dfrac{Mm}{\infty} - G \dfrac{Mm}{r} \\
&= -G \frac{Mm}{r}.
\end{align}$$

### GPE at Earth's Surface
Now we proceed to our definition for potential energy near Earth's surface. here, the reference point is sea level, such that $U(R) = 0$. Let an object be $h$ meters above sea level (or more generally, Earth's surface). Then,
$$\begin{align}
U(R+h) &= -G \frac{Mm}{R+h} \\
&= -G \frac{Mm}{R} + G \frac{Mm}{R^2}h+\ldots \\
&\approx -G \frac{Mm}{R}+m \frac{GM}{R^2}h \\
&= U(R)+mgh \\
&= mgh
\end{align}$$
using Taylor Series decomposition with the fact that $h \ll R$ near Earth's surface, thereby making all but the first two components irrelevant.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Diverting an Asteroid
>An asteroid of mass $m$ is flying toward Earth. When it is a distance $r_{0}$ away from Earth’s center, it has a speed $v_{0}$. Superman tries to intercept the asteroid and push it away, so that it will not be attracted by earth again.
>
>>[!example]- What is the minimal work Superman needs to apply on the asteroid?
>>The total mechanical energy of the asteroid is $E_{i}=K+U=\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^2-G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{0}}$. Since Superman must oppose that energy, $E_{f}=0$. As such, the work that Superman must exert on the asteroid to divert its course is 
>>$$W_{S}=E_{f}-E_{i}=0+G \dfrac{Mm}{r_{0}}-\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^2.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3d.3 Elastic Potential Energy]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/03 18:29:27","modified":"2025/08/03 23:50:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Elastic Potential Energy
>**Elastic potential energy** $U_s$ is the scalar quantity stored in a system when it is deformed from its equilibrium configuration by an internal restoring force, assuming it obeys [[1.2b.4 Spring Force|Hooke's Law]].
>
>Mathematically, the elastic potential energy given a displacement $x$ from equilibrium is
>$$U(x) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2,$$
>where $k$ is the spring constant (a measure of stiffness), and $x$ is the displacement from the system’s equilibrium length. 
>
>This energy is always non-negative and reaches zero when the system is at rest in its natural, undeformed configuration.

# Examples
>[!example] (Easy) Spring-Loop Track Energy Transfer
>A block of mass $m$ is first pushed against a spring of force constant $k$ by a length $R$ and released from rest. After the release it moves toward a vertical circular track of radius $R$, as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-03 at 20.35.22.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Assuming the block gains enough speed to reach to the top of the vertical track, what is the kinetic energy of the block when it reaches the top?
>>The elastic potential energy before release is $U=\dfrac{1}{2}kR^2$. The potential energy is transformed to kinetic energy and as such, the total energy before the loop is $E_i=\dfrac{1}{2}kR^2+0$. After the loop, the box is displaced by $2R$ in the $y$ direction. This means that the total energy $E_{f}=K_{f}+U_{f}$, where $U_{f}=2mgR$ is the gravitational potential energy, as it is conservative, and therefore relies only on the initial and final displacement of $0$ and $2R$ respectively. Since the system is conserved (i.e., there are no other outside forces to consider since we assume the surface is frictionless and there is no drag), $E_{f}-E_{i}=0$. Therefore, 
>>$$K_{f}+2mgR-\frac{1}{2}kR^2=0 \iff K_{f}=\frac{1}{2}kR^2-2mgR.$$
>
>>[!example]- Find the normal force between the track and the block when the block reaches the top of the track.
>>The block pushes on the loop, and therefore the loop pushes black at the block. Since the two vertical forces in play here are the normal force and the force of gravity $mg$, and both are downward, then $\dfrac{mv^2}{R}=N+mg$ per circular motion. Given the answer for $K_{f}$ in the previous step,
>>$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{1}{2}kR^2-2mgR = \frac{1}{2}(RN+mgR),$$
>>
>>which when solved yields $N=kR-5mg$.

>[!example] (Medium) Critical Friction in a Coupled Spring-Pulley System
>A block of mass $m_2$ is placed on a frictionless table with another block $m_3$ placed on top of it. The surface between $m_2$ and $m_3$ has a coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$. 
>
>The block $m_2$ is connected with another block $m_1$ by a massless rope which wraps around a massless pulley as shown in the figure. The rope does NOT slip over the pulley when moving. 
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-03 at 21.18.12.png|300]]
>
>The block $m_1$ is connected with a spring of force constant $k$ whose other end is fixed to the ground. The spring is stretched with an amount $h$ away from its equilibrium point and the whole system is released from rest.
>
>
>>[!example]- Find the minimum value of $\mu_{s}$ such that the block $m_{3}$ can remain on block $m_{2}$ without falling off.
>>For block $m_{3}$, static friction is what accelerates the block rightward. Therefore, $f_{s}=m_{3}a$. 
>>
>>For block $m_{2}$, tension opposes static friction, such that $T-f_{s}=m_{2}a \iff T=(m_{2}+m_{3})a$. 
>>
>>For block $m_{1}$, tension opposes gravity and the spring force, such that $T-F_{s}-m_{1}g=-m_{1}a$, as block $m_{1}$ accelerates downward, in the negative direction. Additionally, since the displacement of the spring force from equilibrium is in the positive direction, $F_{s}=-kh$. Solving for tension, one obtains
>>$$(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})a=m_{1}g-kh \iff a=\frac{m_{1}g-kh}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}.$$
>>
>>From the definition of static friction force, it is known that $F_{\text{s}} \leq\mu_{s}N$, where $N-m_{3}g=0$. As such,
>>$$m_{3}\frac{m_{1}g-kh}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}} \leq \mu_{s} m_{3}g,$$
>>and therefore $\mu_{s} \geq \dfrac{m_{1}g-kh}{g(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})}$.
>
>>[!example]- After we release the system, what is the speed of $m_{1}$ when the spring returns to its equilibrium position?
>>Before release, $E_{i}=0+\dfrac{1}{2}kh^2+m_{1}gh$. However, because the whole system moves, $E_{f}=\dfrac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3})v^2$. Per conservation of energy, $E_{i}=E_{f}$, and therefore,
>>$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2m_{1}gh+kh^2}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.3e Power]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/02 15:37:42","modified":"2025/08/02 15:50:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Power
>Power (SI: Watt / $\text{W} \equiv \text{J} / \text{s}$) quantifies how rapidly energy is transferred or transformed. It measures the rate at which a system does work or converts energy, providing insight into how fast a physical process occurs.
>
>More particularly, **average power** denotes the total amount of energy transferred, divided by the total time it takes, such that
>$$\bar{P} = \frac{E}{\Delta t} = \frac{W}{\Delta t},$$
>where $W$ is the net work done and $E$ is the energy transferred over some time frame $\Delta t = t_{f}-t_{i}$.
>
>Similarly, **instantaneous power** describes the rate of energy transfer at a specific infinitesimal point in time, such that
>$$P = \frac{dE}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}.$$
