>[!note] Annuity
>An **annuity** is a financial instrument or series of cash flows that pays a fixed amount of money at $n$ intervals per year for $t$ years, with each payment $C$ remaining constant over the term. The payments can be made at the end of each period (ordinary annuity) or at the beginning (annuity due). Formally, the present value of an ordinary annuity, given an annual percentage rate $r$, is expressed as:
>$$PV=C \times \left[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r(1+r)^{nt}}\right].$$
>
>Additionally, a **growth perpetuity** is a perpetuity that grows at a constant rate of $g$ per year given a principal $C$:
>$$PV=C \times \frac{1}{r-g} \left[1-\left(\frac{1+g}{1+r}\right)^{nt}\right].$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.4 Bank runs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/29 14:47:08","modified":"2025/03/29 14:47:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bank Run
>A bank run occurs when a large portion of a bank's customers withdraws money in a short period of time driven by fears of bank failure. As bank runs progress, they may become **self-fulfilling prophecies**, as the chance of sudden bankruptcy increases. In case a bank lacks liquidity, it may use lenders of last resort such as the [[6.3b Discount Window|discount window]] to prevent bankruptcy.

# Intuition
In fractional-reserve banking systems, banks only keep part of the money that its customers deposit, and loan out the rest of the money. As such, if enough customers withdraw over a short period of time, the bank may not have enough liquidity to satisfy all of the withdrawals. This could be prevented by suspension of payments, which albeit generally a temporary measure while banks sell loans, may be a potential situation for bankruptcy.

Bank runs may also happen as a result of self-fulfilling prophecies. Customers may believe that the bank is inept in some way and may withdraw their money. Since the bank cannot react on time, a bank run occurs.

We can formulate bank run problems based on the [[Prisoner's Dilemma]]: suppose that two investors deposit a $D$ dollars in a bank. The bank has invested $2D$ into a long-term project, yielding $2R$ upon maturity ($R > D$). If the bank is forced to liquidate the project before completion, it will recover $2r$, where $D > r > \frac{D}{2}$. We can create a table to help us with the cases of this problem:
- Before maturity:
	- One of the investors withdraws: the one that withdraws gets $D$, whereas the other gets $2r - D$.
	- Both investors withdraw: each investor receives $r$.
- After maturity:
	- One of the investors withdraws: the one that withdraws gets $D$, whereas the other gets $2R-D$.
	- Both investors withdraw: each investors receives $D$ and the bank profits $2R-2D$.
	- None of the investors withdraws: both investors get $R$.

Here, there are two Nash equilibria:
1. Both investors withdraw and get $r$ each. 
2. Both investors keep their money in the bank and get $R$ each.

Option 1 leads to a bank run, since the investors did not get the full quantity of their money $D$ back. However, the FDIC insures deposits up to some limit such that the minimum amount of money an investor gets is always $D$. Also, if the bank has some backup money, it may also be able to pay off the original investment.

The FDIC's establishment, although beneficial, greatly downplays the credibility of banks, as depositors have weaker incentives to monitor the quality of banks.

# Example
>[!example] Bank Runs During the Great Depression
>During the Great Depression, different federal banks in Mississippi had different approaches to banking panics:
>- Federal Bank of Atlanta (in the south of MS) believed the FED should serve as a lender of last resort, responding to the panics with large infusions of cash.
>- Federal Bank of St. Louis (in the north of MS) believed in the real bills doctrine, only lending backed money and therefore being tougher on discount.
>
>However, at the end, economic characteristics were similar in both parts of Mississippi, and although quality of bank assets was higher in banks governed by the St. Louis fed, more banks were suspended, and lending and trade declined more.
>
>Since the panic was due to illiquidity, FED's action should've been aggressive on a national scale.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.4 Chain Rule]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/28 18:33:45","modified":"2025/02/26 13:12:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

> [!note] Chain Rule
> For a finite number of events $A_1, ..., A_N \subseteq \Omega$ in the same probability space, the chain rule states that the probability of all $N$ events occurring is equal to the product of the [[1.3 Conditional Probability|conditional probabilities]] of each event given the events that came before it, such that
> $$\mathbb{P}[\cap_{i = 1}^N A_i]=\mathbb{P}[A_1] \times \mathbb{P}[A_2 \mid A_1] \times \mathbb{P}[A_3 \mid A_1 \cap A_2] \times ... \times \mathbb{P}[A_N \mid \cap_{i = 1}^{N-1}A_i].$$
# Intuition. 
For two events, the chain rule is simply
$$\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[A] \times \mathbb{P}[B \mid A] = \mathbb{P}[B] \times \mathbb{P}[A \mid B],$$
which looks very similar to a reordering of the conditional probability theorem. We can say that the probability of both $A$ and $B$ happening is equal to the scaled probability of $B$ happening given that $A$ has already happened.  Let's expand our use case for 3 events using :
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[A \cap B \cap C] &= \mathbb{P}[(A \cap B) \cap C]  \\
&= \mathbb{P}[A \cap B] \times \mathbb{P}[C \mid A \cap B] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[A] \times \mathbb{P}[B \mid A] \times \mathbb{P}[C \mid A \cap B].
\end{align}$$
This comes from the fact that sets are associative (as seen in the first line of the equation). Therefore, we can implicitly substitute $D = A \cap B$, and first solve for the two-event scenario.

# Examples
>[!example] Monty Hall Revisited
>Let's figure out the Monty Hall problem using another set of events. For $i \in \{ 1, 2, 3 \}$:
>- $C_i$ is the event that the contestant chooses door $i$.
>- $P_i$ is the event that the prize is behind door $i$.
>- $H_i$ is the event that the host opens door $i$.
>
>Considering the rules from the previous instance, what is the probability of the contestant choosing door 1, the prize is behind door 2, and the host opens door 3 ($C_1 \cap P_{2} \cap H_3$)? We have:
>$$\mathbb{P}[C_1 \cap P_2 \cap H_3]=\mathbb{P}[C_1] \times \mathbb{P}[P_2 | C_1] \times \mathbb{P}[H_3 | C_1 \cap P_2]$$
>Which is equal to $\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times 1 = \frac{1}{9}$.
>Note that if the contestant chooses the same door that the prize is behind, then $\mathbb{P}[C_1 \cap P_2 \cap H_3]=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{18}$ Since the host has two doors with goats to pick from.
>
>Going back to the original question, noting that $\mathbb{P}[C_1 \cap H_3]=\mathbb{P}[C_1] \times \mathbb{P}[H_3 | C_1]=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{6}$,
>$$\mathbb{P}[P_2 | C_1 \cap H_3] = \frac{\mathbb{P}[C_1 \cap P_2 \cap H_3]}{\mathbb{P}[C_1 \cap H_3]}=\frac{\frac{1}{9}}{\frac{1}{6}}=\frac{2}{3}.$$
>If instead the contestant chooses door 2, and the prize is behind door 2, then

>[!note] Direct Proof
>A direct proof is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given [[1.2 Implication|hypothesis]] $P$ by assuming its truth and demonstrating that the [[1.2 Implication|conclusion]] $Q$ necessarily follows, such that
>$$P \implies Q.$$

# Examples
>[!example] Prove that for any $a,b,c \in Z$, if $a \mid b$ and $a\mid c$, then $a \mid (b + c)$.
>We can express the n[](1.3%20Implication.md)c=q_2a$ for some quotients $q_1,q_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then, $b+c=a(q_1 + q_2)$, which has a factor of $a$ and therefore can be divided by $a$.
>
>Alternatively, this theorem can be expressed in quantifier form as $(\forall a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z})(P(a,b) \land P(a,c)) \implies P(a, b+c)$.

>[!example] Prove that an integer $0 < n < 1000$ is divisible by 9 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
>We can express $n$ as a number $abc$ such that $n=100a+10b+c$. Then, we can express the sum of its digits as a multiple of 9 as $a+b+c=9q$ for some quotient $q \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting for $c=9q-a-b$, it follows that $n=99a+9b+9q=9(11a+b+q)$. Since $9$ factors out, $n$ is divisible by $9$.
>
>Since we are solving for $P \iff Q$, we must also prove for the converse, $Q \implies P$. Suppose that $n=9q$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ is (clearly) divisible by $9$. Then, it follows that $100a+10b+c=9q$ is also divisible by $9$. We can massage the equation such that $99a+9b+(a+b+c)=9q$. This leads to
>$$a+b+c=9(q-11a-b),$$
>which is clearly divisible by $9$.

>[!note] Linear Momentum
>**Linear momentum** (SI: $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}$) is a vector quantity that measures how difficult it is to stop an object in motion. For a particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$, its momentum is defined as
>$$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}.$$
>Linear momentum is also the integral of [[1.2a Newton's Laws|net force]] with respect to time, such that $\frac{d}{dt}\vec{p}=m\vec{a}$. This implies that **if no external force** acts on objects in a system, then the total momentum of said objects is **conserved**, such that $\vec{P}_{i}=\vec{P}_{f}$, where $\vec{P}$ represents the total momentum of the system.
>
>This conservation law is especially useful when analyzing **collisions**, where two or more objects transfer momentum over short timescales:
>- In an **elastic collision**, both **momentum and mechanical energy** are conserved.
>
>- In an **inelastic collision**, **momentum is conserved**, but **mechanical energy is not**. Some of the energy is converted to other forms (e.g., thermal energy or sound).
>	- Furthermore, a **perfectly inelastic collision** is one where the objects stick together after impact, maximizing energy loss from the system’s mechanical energy..


# Examples

>
>>[!example]- If the system includes the bead, Earth, and the gravitational interaction between them, is the momentum of this system conserved?
>>The momentum is not conserved, as some of the speed of the ball converts to gravitational potential energy.

>>Maximum compression occurs when both objects have the same instantaneous speed. Since the collision contains an elastic spring, both momentum and kinetic energy are preserved: 
>>- For energy, $E_{i}=\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v_{0}^2$ is purely kinetic energy, whereas $E_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{1}+\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ is both elastic potential and the kinetic energy of both objects moving together at the same speed $v_{1}$.

>[!note] Center of Mass
>The **center of mass** (CoM) is the average position of mass in a system, weighted by how much mass is at each point. It denotes where the “balance point” of the system is. For a system of particles with masses $m_i$ at positions $\vec{r}_i$, the center of mass is defined as
>$$\vec{r}_{\text{C.M.}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i \vec{r}_i,$$
>where $M = \sum_i m_i$ is the total mass of the system.
>
>For continuous systems, the center of mass is defined as
>
>The center of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated at that point and all external forces were applied there. If **no external force** acts on a system, then the **center of mass moves at constant velocity**, regardless of internal motion or deformation.
>
>As such, the **momentum of the center of mass** equals the **total momentum** of the system, where
>$$\vec{P} = M \vec{v}_{\text{C.M.}}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.4b Proof by Contraposition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 05:12:18","modified":"2025/07/12 17:45:02"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Proof by Contraposition
>A proof by contraposition is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given [[1.2 Implication|implication]] $P \implies Q$ by assuming the truth of the negation of the conclusion $\neg Q$, and demonstrating that the negation of the hypothesis $\neg P$ necessarily follows, such that
>$$\neg Q \implies \neg P.$$

# Examples
>[!example] Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $d$ divide $n$. If $n$ is odd, then $d$ is odd.
>We proceed by contraposition; it is easier to prove that if $d$ is even, then $n$ is even, since any even number is a multiple of $2$. We proceed by expressing $d$ as $d=2k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Because $d \mid n$, then $n=qd$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$. When we substitute for $d$, $n=2(qk)$, which is definitely even since it is divisible by $2$. Since the contraposition holds, so does the original statement.

>[!example] If $a^2$ is even, then $a$ is even.
>We proceed by contraposition. Since $a$ is odd, it can be expressed as $2q+1$ for some quotient $q$. Then, $a^2$ can be expressed as $a^2=4q^2+4q+1=2(2q^2+2q)+1$. Since $2(2q^2+2q)$ is a multiple of $2$, it is clearly even. However, when we add $1$ to it it clearly becomes odd. Therefore, $a^2$ is also odd.

>[!example] *(Pigeonhole Principle)* Let $n,k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. Place $n$ objects into $k$ boxes. If $n > k$, then at least one box must contain multiple objects.
>We proceed by contraposition. If all boxes contain exactly one object, then the number of objects is at most equal to the number of boxes, such that $n \leq k$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.4c Proof by Contradiction]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/14 05:12:51","modified":"2025/06/02 18:07:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Proof by Contradiction
>A proof by contradiction is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a given proposition $P$ by assuming the negation $\neg P$ and demonstrating that this assumption leads to a contradiction of two conclusions, $R$, thereby [[1.3 Implication|implying]] that $P$ must be true, such that
>$$\neg P \implies \neg R \land R.$$

# Examples
>[!example] There are infinitely many prime numbers.
>We proceed by contradiction. Assume there is a finite number of $k$ prime numbers, $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$. Then, there is a numbe[](1.3%20Implication.md)ot be prime since it is larger than any prime number. Since every natural number greater than $1$ is either prime or has a prime divisor (proven in 2.5a), then there is a prime number $p \in \{p_1, \ldots, p_k\}$ such that $p \mid n$, which is our statement $R$.
>
>However, by the same logic $p$ must also divide $r = p_1p_2p_3\ldots p_n$. Then, as proven in 2.1, $p \mid n-r$. But $n-r=1$! Since the only positive number that divides $1$ is $1$, $p=1$ is not prime. This is our statement $\neg R$.
>
>Since we have proven $R \land \neg R$, we have a contradiction!

>[!example] $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
>We proceed by contradiction. Assume that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational. By the definition of rational numbers, there exist some $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with no common factors other than $1$ for which $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$ (this is our $R$). 
>
>It follows that $2 = \frac{a^2}{b^2} \iff a^2 = 2b^2$. Since $2b^2$ is a multiple of $2$, it is even, and so is $a^2$. This means that $a$, too, is even (proven in 2.2). Hence, there is some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ for which $a=2q$. We have that $b^2=2q^2$. Since $q$ is an integer, so is $q^2$, and since $b^2$ is even, so is $b$. As such, both $a$ and $b$ are even. 
>
>However, if $a$ and $b$ are even, then they share a common factor of $2>1$. This is our statement $\neg R$, and we have a contradiction since $\neg R \land R$ holds.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.5a Rotational Kinematics]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/04 11:43:15","modified":"2025/08/11 20:45:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rotational Motion
>To describe an object's rotational motion, we track its angular displacement $\Delta\theta$, where
>$$\Delta \theta = \theta - \theta_{0},$$
>such that if $\Delta \theta > 0$, the rotation is counter-clockwise, and vice-versa.
>
>Then, **angular velocity** can be defined as the overall rate of change of the object's rotation, where
>$$\omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}, \enspace \text{and} \enspace \omega = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}=\frac{d \theta}{dt}.$$
>
>Just like in translational kinematics, **angular acceleration** denotes the rate of change in angular velocity over time, such that 
>$$\alpha_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\omega - \omega_{0}}{t - t_{0}} = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t}, \enspace \text{and} \enspace \alpha = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\omega}{dt}.$$
>
>Similarly, the equations for motion at constant acceleration still hold, such that
>$$
>\begin{align}
>\omega &= \omega_0 + \alpha t && \enspace \text{(Angular Velocity)}, \\
>\theta &= \theta_0+\omega_0t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 && \enspace \text{(Angular Displacement)}, \\
\omega^2 &= \omega_0^2+2\alpha(\theta-\theta_0) && \enspace \text{(Angular Velocity-Displacement)}.
>\end{align}
>$$
>
>In addition, angular motion can be used to describe an object's translational motion. Let $r$ be the distance of a point from the rotational axis. Then, one can express the distance traveled as $d=r\Delta \theta$. As such, $v=rd\theta=\omega r$, and $a=\alpha r$.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.5b Rotational Inertia]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/11 19:28:33","modified":"2025/08/13 03:17:42"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Rotational Inertia
>**Rotational inertia** (also called the **moment of inertia**) is the rotational analogue of mass. While mass $m$ in translational motion measures resistance to changes in linear velocity, rotational inertia measures a rigid body’s resistance to changes in angular velocity. It depends on both the distribution of mass and the distance of each mass element from the axis of rotation, such that
>$$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2,$$
>where $m_{i}$ is the mass of each object in the system, and $r_{i}$ is its distance from the axis of rotation.

# Derivation
Given the definition of rotational inertia, we can redefine kinetic energy $K=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ as rotational kinetic energy $K_{\text{rot}}=\dfrac{1}{2}I \omega^2$. Now imagine a circle, and draw its radius as a line. Given two points on the same line, one will have traveled more distance than the other. As such, we can say that **the rotational kinetic energy of a rotating object is the sum of translational kinetic energy of the points that make up the object**, such that
$$K=\sum_{i} \frac{1}{2}m_{i}v_{i}^2.$$
This is shown in the following graph, given a 2D disk:

```tikz
\begin{document}
\begin{tikzpicture}[line width=0.8pt, scale=0.95, rotate=60]
  % Disk outline (no fill)
  \draw (0,0) circle [radius=3cm];

  % Axis (pivot)
  \fill (0,0) circle (2pt);
  \node[below left] at (0,0) {axis};

  % Dotted radius (instead of the red rod)
  \draw[dotted] (0,0) -- (3,0);

  % Rotation arrow and label
  \draw[->] (1.1,0.7) arc[start angle=35, end angle=155, radius=1.2cm];
  \node at (0,1.5) {$\omega$};

  % Mass points along the radius
  \def\rone{2.7}  % r1
  \def\rtwo{1.7}  % r2
  \fill (\rone,0) circle (2pt);
  \fill (\rtwo,0) circle (2pt);

  % Velocity vectors (perpendicular to radius)
  \draw[->] (\rone,0) -- ++(0,0.9);
  \draw[->] (\rtwo,0) -- ++(0,0.6);

  % Labels
  \node[below] at (\rone,-0.15) {$m_1$};
  \node[below] at (\rtwo,-0.15) {$m_2$};
  \node[right] at (\rone,0.85) {$v_1$};
  \node[right] at (\rtwo,0.55) {$v_2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{document}
```

As such, given $v_{i}=\omega r_{i}$, this becomes
$$K=\sum_{i} \frac{1}{2}m_{i}r_{i}^2\omega^2,$$
which leads us to the definition of the moment of inertia, $I=\sum_{i}m_{i}r_{i}^2$.

>[!note] Angular Momentum
>In rotational motion, the angular equivalent of linear momentum is called **angular momentum**, and measures the quantity of rotation a rigid body has about a given axis. It is defined as
>$$L = I\omega,$$
>where I is the rotational inertia of the body about the axis of rotation, and $\omega$ is the [[1.5a Rotational Kinematics|angular velocity]]. Angular momentum is a vector quantity, with a direction given by the right-hand rule, and can be positive or negative depending on the sense of rotation.
>
>Just as linear momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$ is conserved in the absence of net external forces, angular momentum is conserved in the absence of net external torques.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.5e Rolling Motion]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/11 20:42:42","modified":"2025/08/13 05:39:30"}

>[!note] Rolling Motion
>**Rolling motion** is the combination of translational motion of a rigid body’s center of mass and rotational motion about its center of mass. 
>
>A common example is a wheel rolling on a surface. In this motion, the center of mass translates with velocity $v_{\text{C.M.}}$ while every point on the body also rotates with angular velocity $\omega$:
>
>
>If the wheel **rolls without slipping**, experiencing static friction, then the translational and rotational speeds are related by
>$$v_{\text{C.M.}} = R\omega \iff a_{\text{C.M.}}=R\alpha,$$
>where $R$ is the radius of the wheel. The point of contact with the ground has zero instantaneous velocity relative to the surface.
>
>If **slipping occurs**, $v_{\text{C.M.}} \neq R\omega$, and the point of contact moves relative to the ground. Rolling without slipping is a key condition in problems involving rotational dynamics, energy conservation, and torque analysis.

# Derivation
# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Rolling Cylinder I
>A cylinder of uniform mass $M$ and radius $R$ is placed on a frictional surface. The rotational inertia of the cylinder with respect to its central axis is $I$. A constant force of magnitude $F$ is applied to the top of the cylinder in the horizontal direction as shown in the figure.
>
>![[Screenshot 2025-08-13 at 0.32.16.png|300]]
>
>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the cylinder, assuming that it does not skid or slide on the surface.
>>Since we have static friction in the backward direction, it holds that $F-f_{s}=Ma$ in the horizontal. We also calculate torque as $I \alpha = R(F + f_{s})=R(2F-Ma)$. Since $a = R\alpha$, then
>>$$\frac{Ia}{R}=R(2F-Ma) \iff a=\frac{2FR^2}{I+R^2M}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the minimal value of the coefficient of static friction $\mu_{s,\min}$ needed in order for the perfect rolling condition (no skidding, no sliding) to hold?
>>Since $f_{s}=F - Ma$ as found before, we substitute for $a$ and solve:
>>$$f_{s}=\frac{I-R^2M}{I+R^2M}F \le \mu_{s, \min}Mg \iff \mu_{s} \geq \frac{I-R^2M}{I+R^2M} \frac{F}{Mg},$$
>>where the equality is the value of $\mu_{s, \min}$.

A constant force of magnitude $F$ is applied to the bottom right of the cylinder, at a point that is $45\degree$ to the vertical line, and with a direction that is $45\degree$ above the horizontal, as shown in the figure.

>>[!example]- Find the acceleration of the cylinder, including the magnitude and direction.
>>We have that $I\alpha=R(F-f_{s})$ This is because the movement is to the left, but the force of friction that assists the rolling motion is clockwise as opposed to the force. Then, we also have $-Ma=F\cos 45\degree$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.6 Bayes' Rule]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/24 16:50:57","modified":"2025/08/07 18:23:15"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bayes' Rule
>For a finite set of [[1.2 Mutually Exclusive Events|mutually exclusive events]] $A_1, \ldots, A_{N} \subseteq \Omega$ ($A_{i} \cap A_{j} = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$) with nonzero probabilities ($\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]>0$ for all $i$) that form a partition of the sample space, **Bayes' rule** states that for any event $B \subseteq \Omega$ with nonzero probability ($\mathbb{P}[B]>0$),
>$$\mathbb{P}[A_i \mid B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\sum^{N}_{j=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_j]\mathbb{P}[A_j]}.$$
# Intuition
In its essence, Bayes' rule is just a substitution. To see why, let's start from the basics. By the [[1.3 Conditional Probability|law of conditional probability]], we have:
$$\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] = \frac{\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}.$$
Then:
1. Again by conditional probability, we have $\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] \mathbb{P}[B] = \mathbb{P}[B \mid A_{i}]\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]$. 
2. By [[1.5 Total Probability Theorem|total probability]], we have $\mathbb{P}[B]=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_{i}]\mathbb{P}[A_{i}]$.

Therefore,
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B] &= \frac{\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\mathbb{P}[B]} \\
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_i]\mathbb{P}[A_i]}{\sum^{N}_{j=1}\mathbb{P}[B \mid A_j]\mathbb{P}[A_j]}.
\end{align}$$

However, Bayes' theorem is **crucial for Bayesian inference**; a method of statistical inference with the goal of **belief updating**, or updating the probability of a hypothesis as more information is taken into account. For example, we may estimate the **prior probability** $\mathbb{P}[A]$ of an event $A$, and then update the probability to $\mathbb{P}[A \mid B]$, known as the **posterior probability**, once we know that event $B$ has occurred. Real-world data is often conditional rather than joint or marginal, and Bayes' rule helps bridge the gap between posterior and prior beliefs.
# Examples
>[!example] Pharmaceutical Company
>A pharmaceutical company is marketing a new test for a medical disorder. It has the following probabilities:
>1. When applied to an affected person, the test is positive in 90% of the cases and negative in 10% (**false negatives**).
>2. When applied to a healthy person, the test is negative 80% of the time and positive 20% of the time (**false positive**).
>
>Suppose that the incidence of the disease in the U.S. is 5%; this is our prior knowledge. When a person tests positive, what is the updated probability that they have the disease?
>
>Let A be the event that the person is affected, and let B be the event that the person tests positive. Then,
>$$
>\begin{alignat}{0}
>\mathbb{P}[A]=0.05 \\
>\mathbb{P}[B|A]=0.90 \\
>\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}]=0.20
\end{alignat}
>$$
>Since 90% of affected people test positive, and so do 20% of healthy people ($B|\bar{A}$).
>
>We want to calculate $\mathbb{P}[A|B]$. We proceed as follows:
>$$\mathbb{P}[A|B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]}{\mathbb{P}[B]}$$
>We only need to find $\mathbb{P}[B]$. How? Well, we can picture $\mathbb{P}[A|B]$ in the following graph of $\Upomega$:
>```tikz
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[domain=0:4]
>\draw[] (0, 0) ellipse (4 and 2) node[left]{};
>\draw[] (-1, 0) ellipse (2 and 1) node[below]{$A$};
>\draw[] (1.25, 0) circle (1) node[below]{$B$};
>\draw[->] (0.6,0) -- (0.4,-1.25) node[below]{$A \cap B$};
>\draw[->] (1.25,0) -- (2,-1) node[below]{$\bar{A} \cap B$};
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>This means that $\mathbb{P}[B]=\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]+\mathbb{P}[\bar{A} \cap B]$. Applying the rules of conditional probability, we have:
>$$
>\begin{equation}{}
>\begin{aligned}
>\mathbb{P}[B] &= \mathbb{P}[A \cap B]+\mathbb{P}[\bar{A} \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}]\mathbb{P}[\bar{A}]= \\ &= \mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}](1-\mathbb{P}[A])
>\end{aligned}
>\end{equation}
>$$
>Finally, combining the two equations, we have:
>$$\mathbb{P}[A|B]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]}{\mathbb{P}[B|A]\mathbb{P}[A]+\mathbb{P}[B|\bar{A}](1-\mathbb{P}[A])}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.6a Independence of Two Events]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/01/12 13:51:49","modified":"2025/01/12 17:57:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Pairwise Independence
>Two events $A, B \subseteq \Omega$ in the same [[1.1 Probability Space|probability space]] are said to be **pairwise independent**, if their joint probability is equal to the product of their marginal probabilities, such that
>$$\mathbb{P}[A \cap B] = \mathbb{P}[A] \times \mathbb{P}[B].$$
>Moreover, if $\mathbb{P}[A] > 0$, independence is equivalent to the condition,
>$$\mathbb{P}[B \mid A] = \mathbb{P}[B],$$
>and vice-versa.

# Intuition
Consider the law of conditional probability, which states that, given events $A,B \in \Omega$, the probability of $B$ given $A$ is $\mathbb{P}[B \mid A] = \frac{\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]}{\mathbb{P}[A]}$. However, if $B$ is not updated given the information that $A$ has occurred, then equivalently, $\mathbb{P}[B \mid A] = \mathbb{P}[B]$. Then, $A$ and $B$ are **independent**, and in order for the equivalence to hold, $\mathbb{P}[A \cap B]=\mathbb{P}[A] \times \mathbb{P}[B]$.

We adopt the latter definition of independence, since it can be used even when $\mathbb{P}[A]=0$, where $\mathbb{P}[B \mid A]$ is undefined.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.6b Independence of Several Events]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/01/12 13:52:00","modified":"2025/01/13 06:43:18"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Mutual Independence
>Events $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{N} \subseteq \Omega$ are said to be **mutually independent** if, for every single combination $S$ of the interval $[1, N]$, such that  $S \subseteq \{ 1, 2, \ldots, N \}$ and $|S| \geq 2$, the joint probability of all events $A_{i}$ for $i \in S$ is equal to the product of their marginal probabilities. Mathematically,
>$$\mathbb{P}\Big[\bigcap_{i \in S}A_i\Big]=\prod^{}_{i \in S}\mathbb{P}[A_i].$$

# Intuition
Mutual Independence is simply an extension of the [[1.6a Independence of Two Events|pairwise independence principle]]. Consider for simplification the events $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$. 

# Examples
>[!example] Pairwise Independent but Not Mutually Independent
>Suppose you flip a fair coin twice. Let three events be:
>- A: The first flip is heads.
>- B: The second flip is heads.
>- C: Both flips are the same (HH or TT).
>
>The first and the second events are independent. So are the first and the third, since $\mathbb{P}[A \cap C]=\mathbb{P}[A]\mathbb{P}[C]=\frac{1}{4}$.
>
>However, these events are not mutually independent: if we are given that A and B occurred, the probability of C occurring is 1. These events are independent by pairs, but not mutually.

NOTE TITLE: [[1.6c~ Conditional Independence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/01/12 13:52:12","modified":"2025/01/12 17:34:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Conditional Independence (IN PROGRESS)
>Events $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{N} \in \mathbb{\Omega}$ in the same probability space are **conditionally independent** given any event $B$ with $\mathbb{P}[B]>0$ if, for every subset $S \subseteq \{ 1, 2, \ldots, N \}$ where $|S| \geq 2$, the joint probability of the events $A_{i}$ for all $i \in S$ , given $B$, equals the product of their individual conditional probabilities given $B$. Formally, this means:
>$$\mathbb{P}\Big[\bigcap_{i \in S} A_{i} \mid B] = \prod_{i \in S}\mathbb{P}[A_{i} \mid B].$$
>If in addition, for any specific event $A_{k}$ with $k \in S$, if $\mathbb{P}[\cap_{S \backslash k} A_{i} \cap B] >0$, then $A_{k}$ is conditionally independent of the other events given $B$, such that
>$$\mathbb{P}[A_{k} \mid \cap_{i \in S \setminus k} A_{i} \cap B] = \mathbb{P}[A_{k} \mid B].$$

# Intuition
Consider events $A$, $B$ and $C$ in the same sample space. Then, $A$ and $B$ are considered conditionally independent if, for any $C$,
$$\mathbb{P}[A \cap B \mid C] = \mathbb{P}[A \mid C] \times \mathbb{P}[B \mid C].$$
Let's see why this is the case: with a quick proof:
$$\mathbb{P}[A \cap B \mid C] = \frac{\mathbb{P}[A \cap B \cap C]}{\mathbb{P}[C]}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.7 Independence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/06/06 16:01:25","modified":"2025/08/07 12:48:00"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Independence
>Events $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$ in the same [[1.1 Probability Space|probability space]] are said to be **pairwise independent** if for all $i \neq j$ ,
>$$\mathbb{P}[X_{i} \cap X_{j}] = \mathbb{P}(X_{i}) \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_{j}).$$
>
>Furthermore, the events are **mutually independent** if
>$$\mathbb{P}\left( \bigcap\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} \right) = \prod^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}(X_{i}).$$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.8 Inclusion-Exclusion Principle]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/28 18:33:13","modified":"2025/02/17 05:10:13"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) >[!example] Joint Occurrence
>You know that at least one of the events $A_{i}, \space i = 1,\ldots,N$, is certain to occur, but certainly no more than two occur. $N$ is an integer $\geq 2$. Show that if the probability of occurrence of any single event is $p$, and the probability of joint occurrence of any two distinct events is $q$, we have $p \geq \frac{1}{N}$, and $q \leq \frac{2}{N(N-1)}$.
>
>>[!example] Solution
>>We know that:
>>1. One of the events $A_{i}$ is certain to occur with $\mathbb{P}(A_{i})=p$.
>>2. No more than two events $A_{i} \cap A_{j}$ can occur, and $\mathbb{P}(A_{i} \cap A_{j})=q$.
>>3. Since at least one event is certain to occur, $\mathbb{P}\Big[\bigcup^{N}_{i=1} A_i\Big]=1$
>>
>>We proceed using the inclusion-exclusion principle. We know that:
>>$$1=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}(A_{i})-\sum^{}_{i < j}\mathbb{P}(A_{i} \cup A_{j}).$$
>>There are exactly $\binom{N}{2}$ ($N$ choose two) pairs of distinct events $A_{i} \cap A_{j}$. Therefore,
>>$$Np - \frac{N!}{2(N-2)!}=Np - \frac{N(N-1)}{2}q=1.$$
>>Since the difference equation results in a positive sum, $Np \geq 1 \iff p \geq \frac{1}{N}$. Additionally, $q=\frac{2(Np-1)}{N(N-1)}$. For the minimum value of $p \geq \frac{1}{N}$, this equates to $q=\frac{2(0)}{N(N-1)}$

NOTE TITLE: [[1.9 Union Bound]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/02 23:06:24","modified":"2025/08/07 19:09:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Union Bound
>For any events $A_1,\ldots,A_N \subseteq \Omega$ in the same probability space, the **union bound** states that the probability of the union of the events is at most the sum of their individual probabilities. Formally,
>$$\mathbb{P}\Big[\bigcup^{N}_{i=1}A_i\Big] \leq \sum^{N}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[A_i].$$
# Intuition
Let's consider why the union bound is true:
1. In the case of [[1.2 Mutually Exclusive Events|mutually exclusive events]], their union is exactly equal to the sum of their marginal probabilities.
2. In the case of all other events, per the [[1.8 Inclusion-Exclusion Principle|inclusion-exclusion principle]], their union is less than their marginal probabilities.

There are no scenarios where the probability of the union exceeds the sum of the individual probabilities. This would imply the inclusion of probability mass outside the defined events, which violates the basic principles of both the union operation and probability as a whole. If you are still unsure, draw a Venn diagram and think about it!


# Examples
>[!example] Matching Beads
>Sinho has a set of 2n beads (n ≥2) of n different colors, such that there are two beads of each color.

NOTE TITLE: [[10. Projection Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/07 16:55:35","modified":"2025/05/14 03:30:20"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Projection Theorem
>For any vector $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a subspace $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the projection of $\vec{x}$ onto $\mathcal{S}$ is the unique linear operator in $\mathcal{S}$ that minimizes the distance between $\vec{x}$ and $\mathcal{S}$, defined as
>$$\Pi_\mathcal{S}(\vec{x})=\arg\min\limits_{\vec{y} \in \mathcal{S}} ||\vec{x}-\vec{y}||,$$
>such that $\Pi_\mathcal{S}(\vec{x}) \in \mathcal{S}$ and the residual vector $\vec{x}-\Pi_S(\vec{x}) \perp \mathcal{S}$.
>
>Then, the general solution of $\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x})$, given a matrix $S \in \mathcal{S}^n$, such that $\operatorname{rank}(S)=n$ (i.e., $S$ is full-rank),
>$$\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = S(S^TS)^{-1}S^T\vec{x},$$
>where $P = S(S^TS)^{-1}S^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is called the **projection matrix**.
>
>If $S$ is not full rank (i.e., $\operatorname{rank}(S)<n$), given an orthonormal basis matrix $B_{S}$ of $\mathcal{S}$, the orthonormal projection of $\vec{x}$ onto $\mathcal{S}$ can be expressed as
>$$\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = B_{S}^TB_{S}\vec{x} = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\langle \vec{(B_{S})}_{i}, \vec{x} \rangle \vec{(B_{S})}_{i},$$
>which can be equivalently written as $\Pi_{\mathcal{S}}(\vec{x}) = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\langle \vec{s}_{i}, \vec{x} \rangle}{\|\vec{s}_{i}\|^2} \vec{s}_{i}$ if the basis vectors $s_{i}$ are orthogonal rather than orthonormal.
# Proof
# Properties
#### (*Linearity*) 

#### (*Orthogonal Decomp.*) If $S^\perp=\{ x \in \mathcal{X} : \langle x, s \rangle=0 \enspace \forall s \in S \}$, then $\mathcal{X}=S \oplus S^\perp$.

# Examples
>[!example] Projection Onto a Hyperplane
>**Conditions:** Let $y = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$, and let $\mathcal{H} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : c^Tx = 0 \}$ be a hyperplane<sup>[[3.4f Hyperplanes|3.4c]]</sup> in $\mathbb{R^2}$, such that $c=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$. 
>
>**Task:** Compute the minimum distance from $y$ to $\mathcal{H}$.
>
>**Solution:** Since $c$ is the normal direction of the hyperplane, it follows that $y - p^* \parallel c$ (since the error term of a projection is always perpendicular to the space of the projection). This, in turn, implies that the error term is some scaling of $c$, such that 
>$$y-p^* = \alpha c.$$
>
>Since $p^* \in \mathcal{H} \perp c$, it also follows that $c^Tp^*=0$.  As such, 
>$$c^T(y-p^*) = \langle c, y \rangle - 0 = \alpha \|c\|^2_{2} \iff \alpha = \frac{\langle c, y \rangle}{\|c\|^2_{2}}.$$
>
>Therefore, $\alpha = \frac{2}{2} = 1$, meaning that the distance $\|y-p^*\|_{2}=\|c\|_{2}=\sqrt{ 2 }$.

NOTE TITLE: [[12.2 Eigendecomposition]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 16:23:15","modified":"2025/05/14 22:42:13"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Eigendecomposition
>A [[4.2c Square Matrix|square matrix]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is diagonalizable if it admits $n$ linearly independent [[5.1 Eigenvectors|eigenvectors]], allowing it to be decomposed as
>$$A = V \Uplambda V^{-1},$$
>where $V = \begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \vec{v}_2 & \dots & \vec{v}_n\end{bmatrix}$ forms the eigenbasis of $A$, and $\Uplambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n})$ is a diagonal square matrix that holds the *strictly real* eigenvalues of $A$. 
>
>The **Spectral Theorem** extends this result to symmetric matrices ($A = A^T$), ensuring that they can be diagonalized as 
>$$A= \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}q_{i}q_{i}^T = \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}\Pi_{\operatorname{span}(u_{i})} = Q\Lambda Q^T,$$ where $Q$'s columns form an *orthonormal* eigenbasis of $A$, and  $\Uplambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n})$.

# Intuition
We use diagonalization to make linear transformations between matrices easier. We do so by changing the basis of a matrix $A$ so that it is strictly diagonal. We then perform our necessary calculations and change it back to our initial basis.
### Why eigenvectors and eigenvalues?
Essentially, 

# Properties
#### $A^n=V \Uplambda^n V^{-1}$
$$
\begin{align}
A^n &= (V\Uplambda V^{-1})(V\Uplambda V^{-1})...(V\Uplambda V^{-1}) \\ 
&=
V\Uplambda (V^{-1}V)\Uplambda(V^{-1}V)...\Uplambda V^{-1}\\
&=
V\Uplambda^nV^{-1}
\end{align}
$$
# Example
>[!example] Computing Powers of Matrices
>We want to compute the 5th power of $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}$. This is hard, since we will have to perform matrix-matrix multiplication 4 times. Instead, we will find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$, change its basis, perform the calculation and change it back into standard basis. Using simple calculation we find the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2}=5,4$. The corresponding eigenvectors are therefore $\vec{x}_{\lambda_1}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\vec{x}_{\lambda_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$. As such, the eigenbasis of $A$ is $V=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Its inverse is $V^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and the diagonal matrix of eigenvectors is $\Uplambda=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$. We can then perform the computation extremely easily:
>$$\Uplambda^{5}=\begin{bmatrix}5^5 & 0 \\ 0 & 4^5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 3125\end{bmatrix}.$$
>A quick change of basis to reverse the diagonalization will yield:
>$$V \Uplambda^5 V^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}3125 & 6303 \\ 0 & 1024\end{bmatrix}=A^5.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[13.2 Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/25 15:58:44","modified":"2025/03/09 23:42:38"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
>Any matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \mathrm{min}(m, n)$ and [[13. Singular-Value Decomposition|SVD]] $A=U\Sigma V^T$ has a **Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse**, defined as 
>$$
>A^\dagger = V\Sigma^\dagger U^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m},
>$$
>where $\Sigma^\dagger = \begin{bmatrix}\Upsigma_r^{-1} & 0_{r \times (m-r)} \\ 0_{(n-r) \times r} & 0_{(n-r) \times (m-r)}\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$, with $\Upsigma^{-1}_{r} = \operatorname{diag}(\dfrac{1}{\sigma_{1},}, \ldots, \dfrac{1}{\sigma_{r}}) \in \mathbb{S}^r_{++}$.

# Properties
#### (*Left Inverse*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n \leq m$ (full col. rank), $A^{\dagger}A = V_{r}V_{r}^T=VV^T=I_{n}$.

#### (*Right Inverse*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$ (full row rank), $AA^{\dagger} = U_{r}U_{r}^T = UU^T=I_{m}$.

#### (*Left Decomposition*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = n \leq m$, then $A^{\dagger} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T$.
#### (*Right Decomposition*) If $\operatorname{Rank}(A) = m \leq n$, then $A^{\dagger} = A^T(AA^T)^{-1}$.
#### (*Reflexivity*) $AA^{\dagger}A = A$ and $A^{\dagger}AA^{\dagger} = A^{\dagger}$.
#### (Invertibility Equality) If $A$ is invertible, $A^{\dagger} = A^{-1}$.
#### (*Orthogonal Projectors*) $P_{\mathcal{R}(A)}=AA^{\dagger} = U_{r}U_{r}^T$ and $P_{}A^{\dagger}A = V_{r}V_{r}^T$.

NOTE TITLE: [[13.3 Low-Rank Approximation]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/26 18:45:48","modified":"2025/03/09 23:54:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Eckart-Young-Minsky Theorem
>A general matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \mathrm{min}\{m, n\}$ can be approximated by a lower-rank matrix $A_k$ with rank $1 \leq k \leq r$, such that $A_k$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation to $A$,
>$$A_k = \arg\min\limits_{A_{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}} \|A-A_{k}\|_F^2.$$
>We may then approximate our matrix $A$ using [[13. Singular-Value Decomposition|singular value decomposition]] as
>$$A_{k}=\sum^{k}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=U_{k}\Sigma_{k}V_{k}^{T}.$$
# Intuition
Essentially, the above definition states that $A_\mathscr{l}$ is found inside the set of matrices $B$ that minimize the square of the [[4.9a Frobenius Norm|Frobenius norm]] of $A-B$ (in other words $A \approx B$). This holds mostly if the data is real, and therefore has some linear, low-rank structure with some singular values being large, and some very small. Then, we can equivalently say that the first $\mathscr{l}$ ordered singular values are large, and the remaining $r-\mathscr{l}$ are small:
$$\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=\sum^{\mathscr{l}}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T+\sum^{r}_{i=\mathscr{l}+1}\underbrace{\sigma_i}_{\approx 0}\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T=\sum^{\mathscr{l}}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2. Mutual Information]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/07 14:50:45","modified":"2025/06/06 15:56:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Mutual Information
>The **mutual information** between two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is a non-negative measure of the reduction in [[1. Shannon Entropy|entropy]] of one variable given knowledge of the other. For discrete variables, it is defined as
>$$\begin{align}
I(X;Y)&=\mathbb{E}\left( \log_{2}\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)} \right) \\
&= \sum_{x,y \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log_{2}\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)} \\
&=H(X)-H(X \mid Y) \\
&= H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y) 
\end{align}$$
>>[!warning] Independence
>>Note that for independent variables, $I(X;Y)=0$.


# Rationale
We begin by rationalizing about the definition of mutual information. Per the definition, mutual information quantifies the reduction in entropy given two variables $X$ and $Y$, compared to just $X$ or $Y$. It is only logical that $I(X;Y)=0$ if $X$ and $Y$ are independent; one will gain no information by observing $X$ (resp. $Y$) given $Y$ (resp. $X$). However, we must reason about the key equation here: $$p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2. Stable Matching]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/10 12:35:55","modified":"2025/08/11 15:07:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stable Matching
>Consider the problem of pairing $n$ jobs and $n$ candidates, each with a complete preference list, so that no pair (candidate, job) would prefer each other over their current partners. Such a pairing is called a **stable matching**, and requires that **no rogue couples** (i.e., job-candidate pairs where both parties prefer other agents).
>
>The process of finding it is often done using the **Gale–Shapley Propose-and-Reject algorithm**, where in each iteration:
>1. Each job proposes to the most preferred candidate who hasn’t rejected it yet.
>2. Each candidate keeps the best offer so far (_on a string_) and rejects all others.
>3. Rejected jobs cross off those candidates and prepare to propose to the next in line.
>
>The propose-and-reject algorithm **always halts** once no rejections occur in an iteration.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1 Linear Programing]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/05 02:54:56","modified":"2025/03/11 04:21:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Linear Program
>A **Linear Program (LP)** is an [[1. Standard Form Optimization|optimization problem]] where the objective function and constraints are all affine. Its **standard form** is given as
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & c^T x \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b, \\ & x \geq 0\end{aligned}$$
>where $f_{0}(x)=\langle c, x \rangle$ for some decision variable $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constants $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $d \in \mathbb{R}$.
>
>The feasible set of an LP is a *polyhedron* (or a *polytope* if fully bounded). 
# Intuition
Intuitively, in linear programming:
- You have a collection of variables $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.
- You form a linear expression $c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 + \dots + c_n x_n$ (the “objective”) that you want to make as large (maximize) or as small (minimize) as possible.

At the same time, each variable combination must satisfy a series of linear constraints, such as:
- $a_{1,1} x_1 + a_{1,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{1,n} x_n \;\le\; b_1,$
- $a_{2,1} x_1 + a_{2,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{2,n} x_n \;\le\; b_2,$
and possibly some equalities, like
- $a_{3,1} x_1 + a_{3,2} x_2 + \dots + a_{3,n} x_n \;=\; b_3.$

Each constraint chops off a portion of the space of all possible $x$. Because the constraints are linear, the feasible region (the set of all allowable solutions) is a **convex polytope** (think of a polygon in 2D, a polyhedron in 3D, etc.).
# Properties

# Examples
>[!example] Revenue Maximization

>[!example] Slack Variables
>Express the following problems as LPs:
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \left[\max\limits_{i=1,\ldots,n} x_{i} - \min\limits_{j=1,\ldots,n}x_{j} \right] \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b\end{aligned}$$
>>[!example]- Solution
>>**Solution:** We can introduce *slack variables* that form a high and low bound on the elements of $x$, such that
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x, u, t} \quad & u-t \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b, \\ & u \geq x_{i}, \space i=1,\ldots,n, \\ & t \leq x_{i}, \space i=1,\ldots,n. \end{aligned}$$
>
>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \sum^{n}_{i=1}|x_{i}| \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b\end{aligned}$$
>>[!example]- Solution
>>We introduce a single bounded slack variable $t$, such that
>>$$\begin{aligned}\min_\limits{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \sum^{n}_{i=1}t \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax = b, \\ \quad & t \geq x_{i}, \space i = 1,\ldots,n \\ \quad & t \geq -x_{i}, \space i = 1, \ldots, n, \end{aligned}$$
>>to cover both positive and negative elements of $x$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1 Loop-Invariant Proofs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/01/17 18:42:01","modified":"2025/01/17 19:02:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Loop Invariant
>A **loop-invariant proof** is a proof based on the principles of [[2.5a Simple Induction|mathematical induction]] that proves the correctness of an algorithm using a property or condition that holds true before and after each iteration of a loop throughout its execution, called a **loop invariant**. A loop-invariant proof consists of the following steps:
>1. **Initialization**: Proving that the loop invariant is true before the execution of the loop *(Base Case)*.
>2. **Maintenance**: Assuming that the loop invariant is true before an iteration of the loop (*Inductive Hypothesis*), and proving that it remains true after the iteration (*Inductive Step*).
>3. **Termination**: Proving that when the loop terminates, the invariant, combined with the termination condition, implies the correctness of the algorithm.
>
>>[!warning] Finiteness
>>Since all loops are finite, we must make a distinction between induction and loop-invariant proofs. This also suggests that although step two shows that the loop invariant must hold true after the iteration, it does not necessarily need to

>[!note] Random Variable
>A **random variable** is a real-valued function $X$: $\Upomega \to \mathbb{R}$ that assigns to each [[1.1 Probability Space|sample point]] (outcome) $\upomega \in \Upomega$ a real number, $X(\upomega) \in \mathbb{R}$. 
>
>- **Discrete random variables** feature a *countable* range $\mathcal{X} = \set{X(\upomega): \upomega \in \Upomega}$, such that for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$, the set
>$$\set{\upomega \in \Upomega: X(\upomega) = x} \in \mathcal{F}$$
>is an **event** in the sample space containing all the outcomes where the random variable $X$ equals the specific value $x \in \mathcal{X}$.
>‎ 
>- **Continuous random variables** can take on any value within a given interval of the [[1.1 Probability Space|continuous sample space]], such that they feature an *uncountable* range $\mathcal{X}=[a, b]$ for some bounds $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.10a Sampling]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/17 04:34:08","modified":"2024/12/17 15:30:36"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
>**Sampling** is the process of converting a **continuous-time signal** into a **discrete-time signal** by taking measurements (samples) of a continuous-time signal $x_{C}(t)$ at a regular sampling period of $T_{s}$ to create a discrete-time signal $x_{D}[n]$ , such that
>$$x_{D}[n]=\left.x_{C}(t) \right\vert_{t=kT_{S}} \text{ for } k \in \mathbb{N}.$$
>This process is also outlined in the block diagram below, where a spike train $z(t)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(t-kT_{S})$ is multiplied with the input to produce the sampled signal $x_{Z}(t)= x_{C}(t) \times z(t)$, which is then converted to a discrete-time signal, $x_{D}[n]$:
>```tikz
>\usepackage{tikz}
>\usetikzlibrary{arrows.meta, positioning}
>
>\begin{document}
>\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2cm, >=Stealth, thick]
>
>% Nodes
>\node (input1) at (0,0) {};
>\node[draw, circle, minimum size=0.5cm, right=of input1] (adder) {$\times$};
>\node[below=1.5cm of adder] (input2) {};
>\node[draw, rectangle, minimum height=1.2cm, minimum width=1.8cm, right=of adder] (box) {Dirac-to\newline-Kronecker};
>\node[right=of box] (output) {};
>
>% Arrows
>\draw[->] (input1.east) -- (adder.west) node[at start, left] {$x_{C}(t)$};    % Input from the left to adder
>\draw[->] (input2.north) -- (adder.south) node[at start, below] {$z(t)$};  % Input from below to adder
>\draw[->] (adder.east) -- (box.west) node[midway, above]{$x_{Z}(t)$};       % Adder output to box
>\draw[->] (box.east) -- (output.west) node[right] {$x_{D}[n]$};      % Box output to the right
>
>\end{tikzpicture}
>\end{document}
>```
>
>Sampling theory is primarily governed by the **Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem**, which states that a signal $x_{C}(t)$ that is band-limited (i.e. bounded) to a frequency $B$, such that $X(\omega) = 0 \text{ for all }|\omega| \geq B$, can be fully recovered from its sample $x_{D}[n]$ if
>$$\omega_{S} \geq 2B,$$
>where $\omega_{S}=\frac{2\pi}{T_{S}}$ is the sampling frequency, and $B$ is called the **Nyquist rate**.
>
>>[!warning] Note (Aliasing)
>>If the condition is not met ($\omega_{s} < 2B$), frequency components overlap with one another and cause distortion known as **aliasing**. Aliasing makes it impossible to distinguish higher frequencies from lower ones, leading to an inaccurate representation of the original signal. The effects of aliasing can be mitigated by pre-processing the $x_{D}[n]$ with a low pass (anti-aliasing) filter, as explained below.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.12d.1 Outer Product SVD]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/15 15:55:51","modified":"2025/03/09 23:57:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Outer Product Form of the SVD
>A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \min\{m,n\}$ can be decomposed using the outer product form of the SVD as
>$$A = \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T$$
>where $\{\vec{u}_1, \vec{u}_2, \dots, \vec{u}_r\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, \dots, \vec{v}_r\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ are sets of orthonormal vectors known respectively as the ***left singular vectors*** and ***right singular vectors*** of $A$, whereas $\sigma_1 > \dots > \sigma_r > 0$ are positive ordered scalars known as the ***singular values*** of $A$.

# Intuition
Essentially, we can algorithmically compute the SVD as follows:
1. Find and sort $(\lambda_1, \vec{v}_1),...,(\lambda_r, \vec{v}_r)$, the orthogonal eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs of $A^TA$.
2. For each pair, find:
	1. $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$
	2. $\vec{u}_i=\frac{1}{\sigma_i}A\vec{v}_i$
We can prove the second step using $\frac{1}{\sigma_k}A\vec{v}_k=\frac{1}{\sigma_k}\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k$. Then $\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k=\left<\vec{v}_k, \vec{v}_i\right>$ will be 0 for $i \neq k$ and 1 for $i = k$ since the right singular vectors are orthonormal. As such, $\frac{1}{\sigma_k}\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k=\vec{u}_k$.

Alternatively, we can find and sort $(\lambda_1, \vec{u}_1),...,(\lambda_r, \vec{u}_r)$, which are the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs of $AA^T$. Then, $\vec{v}_i=\frac{1}{\sigma_i}A^T\vec{u}_i$ or $\vec{v}_i^T=\frac{1}{\upsigma_i}A\vec{u}_i^T$.

This SVD form is messy, albeit the most efficient to compute since it decomposes $A$ into $r$ rank-1 matrices.

# Properties
##### $\{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{Col}(A)$
Since $\{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$, we only need to prove that it spans $\mathrm{Col}(A)$:
$$
\begin{align}
A\vec{x} &= \left(\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\right)\vec{x} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\left(\vec{v}_i^T\vec{x}\right) \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\left<\vec{x},\vec{v}_i\right>\vec{u}_i.
\end{align}
$$
The result is a linear combination of $\vec{u}_i$. Therefore, $\mathrm{Col}(A) \subseteq \mathrm{Span}(\vec{u}_1,\dots,\vec{u}_r)$. Since both $\mathrm{Col}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Span}(\vec{u}_1,\dots,\vec{u}_r)$ have the same dimension $r$, they are equal.

#### $\{\vec{v}_1, \dots, \vec{v}_r\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{Row}(A)=\mathrm{Col}(A^T)$
Since $A^T=\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{v}_i\vec{u}_i^T$, we can proceed using the same reasoning as above.



#### $(\sigma_i^2,\vec{u}_i)$ is an eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of $AA^T$
For any $\vec{u}_k \in \{\vec{u}_1, \dots, \vec{u}_r\}$:
$$
\begin{align}
AA^T\vec{u}_k
&=
\left(\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\right)\left(\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_j\vec{v}_j\vec{u}_j^T\right)\vec{u}_k \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_i\sigma_j\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_j\vec{u}_j^T\vec{u}_k \\
&=
 \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sum^{r}_{j=1}\sigma_i\sigma_j\vec{u}_i\left<\vec{v}_j,\vec{v}_i\right>\left<\vec{u}_k,\vec{u}_j\right> \\
&=
\sigma^2_k\vec{u}_k.
\end{align}
$$
We obtain this from the fact that $\left<\vec{v}_j,\vec{v}_i\right>=\begin{cases}0 & \text{ } i \neq j \\ 1 & \text{   } i = j\end{cases}$  and $\left<\vec{u}_k,\vec{u}_j\right>=\begin{cases}0 & \text{ } k \neq j \\ 1 & \text{   } k = j\end{cases}$ since all elements of both sets are orthonormal to each other by set orthonormality. Therefore the equation is non-zero if and only if $k=i=j$.
#### $(\sigma_i^2,\vec{v}_i)$ is an eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of $A^TA$
Proceed by same reasoning as above.
#### $A\vec{v}_i=\sigma_i\vec{u}_i \iff A^T\vec{u}_i=\sigma_i\vec{v}_i$
$$
\begin{align}
A\vec{v}_k&=\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T\vec{v}_k \\
&= \sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\left<\vec{v}_k,\vec{v}_i\right>\vec{u}_i \\
&=\sigma_i\vec{u}
_i\end{align}
$$
Since due to orthonormality the equation is non-zero only when $k=i$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.12d.2 Compact SVD]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/15 18:10:01","modified":"2025/03/09 23:57:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compact SVD
>A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r \leq \min\{m,n\}$ can be decomposed using the compact form of the SVD as
>$$A = U_r\Upsigma_rV_r^T$$
>where $U_r \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $V_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$ are matrices with orthogonal columns known respectively as the ***left singular vectors*** and ***right singular vectors*** of $A$, whereas $\Upsigma_r \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$ is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries  are positive ordered scalars known as the ***singular values*** of $A$.

# Intuition
The compact SVD is connected to the outer product SVD as follows:
$$
\begin{align}
\begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & \sigma_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1 & \dots & \vec{v}_r\end{bmatrix}^T &= \begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & \sigma_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vec{v}_1^T \\ \vdots \\ \vec{v}_r^T\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}\vec{u}_1 & \dots & \vec{u}_r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1\vec{v}_1^T \\ \vdots \\ \sigma_r\vec{v}_r^T\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\sum^{r}_{i=1}\sigma_i\vec{u}_i\vec{v}_i^T
\end{align}
$$
Additionally, the compact SVD has a square and invertible $\Upsigma_r$ and is easier than the full SVD to construct by hand, but $U_r$ and $V_r$ aren't square and do not have an inverse, and there is no characterization of null spaces like in the full SVD.
# Properties
We can see that our properties are simply the properties of the outer product SVD in matrix form.
##### $\mathrm{Col}(U_r)=\mathrm{Col}(A).$
Same as outer product SVD.
##### $\mathrm{Col}(V_r)=\mathrm{Row}(A)=\mathrm{Col}(A^T).$
Same as outer product SVD.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Bonds]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/25 17:46:39","modified":"2025/03/29 14:22:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bonds
>**Bonds** are a type of fixed-income security that represents a loan made by a lender (generally a corporation or government) to a borrower. Bonds are used by entities to raise capital, and in return, the lender may receive regular **coupon payments** (interest). On the bond's **maturity date**, the lender also receives the bond's **face value** (principal payment), and stops earning interest. Special types of bonds include:
>- **Zero-coupon bonds**, which pay a face value with no coupons.
>- **Treasury securities**, which 
>- **Mortgage bonds**, which pay out coupon payments for a certain period without a face value.
>- **Callable bonds**, which allow the issuer to buy back the bond before maturity. This usually occurs when the interest rates drop below the coupon rate.
>
>The price of a bond is directed by the movement of the market interest rate. When a bond is issued, the yield-to-maturity and coupon rate of the bond are matched to the market rate (i.e., $y_{0}=\frac{C}{F}=r_{0}$). After issuance, market rates move all the time and coupon rates don’t change. Therefore, the only way for the bond to stay competitive is for its price to adjust, which changes the yield. The price of a bond anytime after issuance, known as the **dirty price**, is given as
>$$P=\underbrace{\frac{C}{y}\left(1-\frac{1}{\left( 1+\frac{y}{n} \right)^{nT}}\right)}_{\text{Accrued Interest}}+\underbrace{\frac{F}{\left( 1+\frac{y}{n} \right)^{nT}}}_{\text{PV of Face Value}},$$
>for some face value $F$ and coupon rate $C$ paid $n$ times per year over $T$ years. 
>
>If a bond is bought some time after issuance, the **clean price** is used as a measure of determining the present value of all future cash flows, subtracting the interest that has already been accrued.
>
>When interest rates rise, existing bonds must lower their prices to boost their yields and stay competitive, ensuring that the opportunity cost of holding the bond aligns with current market returns. This means that:
>- If $P=F \iff y = \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at **par**.
>- If $P < F \iff y > \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at a **discount**.
>- If $P > F \iff y < \frac{C}{F}$, then the bond is offered at a **premium**.
>
>>[!warning] YTM Assumes Reinvestment
>>Inverting $P$ for the yield-to-maturity of a coupon bond $y$ assumes that all coupons are reinvested, and, of course, that the bond is held to maturity.
# Measurements of Yield

#### (*Current Yield*) $Y_{C}=\dfrac{C}{P}$.
#### (*Nominal Yield/Spot Rate*) $Y_{N}=\dfrac{C}{F}$.
#### (*Yield-to-Maturity/Yield*) $y=n\left[\left(\dfrac{F}{P}\right)^{1/nT}-1\right]$.
#### (Yield-to-Call) 
Measured as the bond's return on investment if called at the earliest opportunity.

#### (*Holding Period Return*) $R = n\left[\left( \frac{P_{T}+C_{T}}{P} \right)^{1/nT}-1 \right]$

>[!note] Dirac Delta
>The **Dirac delta function**, denoted as  $\delta(t)$, is a mathematical construct used to model an idealized point impulse. Mathematically, it is defined by the piecewise equation
>$$\delta(t) = 
>\begin{cases}
>\infty & \text{for } t = 0 \\
>0 & \text{for } t \neq 0
>\end{cases}.$$
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The Dirac delta is actually not a function. Rather it is a distribution, or a generalized function.

# Properties
#### (Sampling) $x(t)\delta(t - t_0) = x(t_0)\delta(t-t_{0})$

#### (Sifting) $\int^{B}_{A}x(t)\delta(t-t_0)dt = \begin{cases}x(t_0) & \text{if } A < t_0 < B \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$
#### (Convolution) $y(t) = \alpha\delta(t-t_0) \implies (x \textasteriskcentered y)(t) = \alpha x(t-t_0)$
We can easily prove this using the two previous properties:
$$ \begin{align}
(x \textasteriskcentered y)(t) &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)y(t-\tau)d\tau \\
&= \alpha\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau-t_0)d\tau \\
\end{align}$$
Note here that $\delta(t-\tau-t_0) \neq 0 \iff \tau = t-t_0$, so
$$\alpha\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau-t_0)d\tau = \alpha x(t-t_0).$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Discrete-Time LTI System]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/30 19:06:05","modified":"2024/12/13 02:11:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] State Trajectory In Discrete-Time LTI Model
>The solution to the discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI model]]
>$$\vec{x}[i+1]=A \vec{x}[i]+B \vec{u}[i]$$
>$$\vec{x}[0]=\vec{x}_0,$$
>for the state vector as a function of timestep $\vec{x}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the control inputs as a function of timestep $\vec{u}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and matrices $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ is
>$$\vec{x}[i]=A^i \vec{x}_0 + \sum^{i-1}_{k=0}A^{i-k-1}B \vec{u}[k].$$

# Proof
The proof to this solution is very straightforward. We will use the principle of mathematical induction to figure it out. We will start with the base case,
$$\vec{x}[0]=\vec{x}_0.$$
Knowing this, we can assume the LTI model is true for timestep $i$:
$$\vec{x}[i]=A \vec{x}[i-1]+B \vec{u}[i-1].$$
We will then prove it for $i+1$ as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
	\begin{aligned}
		\vec{x}[i+1] &= A\vec{x}[i]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= A^2\vec{x}[i-1]+AB\vec{u}[i-1]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= A^3\vec{x}[i-2]+A^2B\vec{u}[i-2]+AB\vec{u}[i-1]+B\vec{u}[i] \\
					 &= \text{...} \\
					 &= A^{i+1} \vec{x}_0+\sum^{i}_{k=0}A^{i-k}B\vec{u}[k].
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Therefore, for timestep $i$, the solution is
$$\vec{x}[i]=A^i \vec{x}_0 + \sum^{i-1}_{k=0}A^{i-k-1}B \vec{u}[k].$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 18:01:06","modified":"2024/12/13 15:19:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Kronecker Delta (Discrete-Time Unit Impulse)
>The **kronecker delta** (i.e. the discrete-time unit impulse) is defined as
>$$\delta[n]=\begin{cases}0 && \text{if } n=0 \\ 1 && \text{if } n \neq 0\end{cases}.$$
>Any arbitrary discrete-time signal $x(n)$ can be decomposed into a linear combination of discrete-time impulses (Kronecker deltas), such that
>$$x[n] = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x[k]\delta[n-k].$$

# Properties
#### (Step Representation) $\delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]$.
The RHS is $1$ only at $n=0$. Any value $n < 0$ will lead to $0-0=0$, whereas any value $n > 0$ will lead to $1-1=0$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.2 C-T Unit Step]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/13 04:48:19","modified":"2024/12/13 18:52:01"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Continuous-Time Unit Step
>The continuous-time unit step can be defined as a signal $u$, such that
>$$u(t) = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if } t < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } t \geq 0 \end{cases}.$$
>The unit step can be written as the integral of the [[2.1a.1 Dirac Delta|Dirac delta]], such that
>$$u(t) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\delta(\tau)d\tau.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.2 D-T Unit Step]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 18:01:47","modified":"2024/12/13 04:48:42"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Discrete-Time Unit Step
>The discrete-time unit step can be defined as a signal $u: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$, such that
>$$u[n] = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if } n < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } n \geq 0 \end{cases}.$$
>The unit step can be written in terms of a linear combination of shifted [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta| impulses]] as 
>$$u[n] = \sum^{}_{k=0} \delta[n-k] \iff u[n] = \sum^{n}_{l=-\infty}\delta[l] \impliedby l=n-k.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.3 Price Sensitivity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/28 20:51:13","modified":"2025/03/29 14:21:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Duration & Convexity
>The **duration** of a [[2.1a.1 Bonds|bond]] measures the sensitivity of its price to changes in yield (interest). There are two types of duration:
>- **Macaulay duration** is the weighted average time until all cashflows are received, where the weights are the present values of each period's cashflow. This is formally defined as
>$$D = \frac{1}{nP}\left[\sum^{nT}_{t=1}\frac{C_{t}}{(1+y/n)^t}t+\frac{F}{(1+y/n)^{nT}}nT\right].$$
>- **Modified duration** adjusts Macaulay duration to approximate the percentage change in the price of a bond for a 1% change in yield, such that
>$$D^* = -\frac{1}{P} \cdot \frac{dP}{dy} = \frac{D}{1+y/n},$$
>where the negative sign arises from the inverse relationship between bond price and yield.
>
>Generally, price-yield curves are *convex*. Higher price-yield convexity implies a higher price regardless of which way prices or directions move: 
>
>
>The convexity of a price-yield curve is represented as the second derivative of its price with respect to yield, such that
>$$\Gamma = \frac{1}{P} \cdot \frac{d^2P}{dy^2}=\frac{1}{n^2P(1+y/n)^{2}}\left[\sum^{nT}_{t=1}\frac{C_{t}}{(1+y/n)^{t}}(t^2+t)+\frac{F}{(1+y/n)^{nT}}(n^2T^2+nT)\right].$$
>
>Convexity can be used in tandem with modified duration to create a better approximation for price:
>$$\frac{dP}{P}=-D^* \cdot dR + \frac{1}{2}\Gamma \cdot dR^2.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1a.4 Measuring Bond Risk]]

>[!note] Measures of Bond Risk
>[[2.1a.2 Yield Curves|Credit spread]] measures the additional risk of a fixed-income security compared to a risk-free benchmark. Aside from the trivial value $x=y-y_{0}$, where $y_{0}$ is the yield of a risk-free bond, there are multiple other ways to measure spread:
>- **Static spread** is the constant premium added to the risk-free spot rate. This is the same as $x$ for stripped bonds, but varies for coupon bonds.
>- **Option-adjusted spread (OAS)** is the static spread adjusted for embedded options by removing the value of optionality, reflecting only the credit and liquidity risks (i.e., the credit spread of a callable bond adjusted for the call provision).

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1b.1 Scalar Model]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/30 20:34:56","modified":"2024/03/30 21:26:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] State Trajectory in Scalar Continuous-Time LTI Differential Equation Model
>The solution to the scalar (vector-less) continuous-time LTI model
>$$\frac{d}{dt}x(t)=ax(t)+bu(t)$$
>$$x(0)=x_0$$
>for the state scalar as a function of time $x: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}$, the control input as a function of timestep $u: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}$ and scalar coefficients $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ is
>$$x(t)=e^{at}x_0+\int^{t}_{0}e^{a(t-\tau)}bu(\tau)d \tau.$$
# Proof
Since this is a first-order differential equation, we can solve it using the solution for non-homogeneous first-order differential equations $x(t)=e^{\lambda t}x_0+\int^{t}_{0}e^{\lambda (t-\tau)}u(\tau)d\tau$ (see Note 2).

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1b.1 Stocks]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/18 02:19:00","modified":"2025/03/18 02:25:34"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stocks
>**Stocks** represent shares of ownership in a corporation. They are traded on exchanges or over-the-counter markets, and their prices fluctuate based on supply and demand, company performance, and broader economic conditions. There exist two types of stocks:
>- **Common stock** gives shareholders voting rights and the potential for capital gains (by earning variable dividends), but they are last in line during liquidation.
>- **Preferred stock** generally provides fixed (or no) dividends and priority in dividend payments and liquidation, yet typically does not offer voting rights.
>
>Companies issue stock to raise capital for expansion, funding operations, or debt repayment, and private firms may do so through multiple rounds (e.g., Seed, Series A, B, C) before going public. After an **initial public offering (IPO)** in the primary market—where newly issued shares are sold directly to investors—public companies can also raise more capital with a f**ollow-on public offering (FPO)**, and their shares then trade on secondary markets like the NYSE or Nasdaq.
>
>>[!warning] Privately Held Stocks
>>Privately held stocks are shares of companies that are **not listed on public exchanges**, so they are typically owned by a small group of individuals, founders, or private investors. Because they are not publicly traded, these shares are often **less liquid and more difficult to value** than publicly traded stocks.

>[!note] State Trajectory in Diagonal Continuous-Time LTI Differential Equation Model
>The solution to the diagonal continuous-time LTI model
>$$\frac{d}{dt}\vec{x}(t)=\Uplambda \vec{x}(t)+B \vec{u}(t)$$
>$$\vec{x}(0)=\vec{x}_0,$$

>$$\vec{x}(t)=e^{\Uplambda t}\vec{x}_0+\int^{t}_{0}e^{\Uplambda(t-\tau)}B\vec{u}(\tau)d\tau.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1c Signal Periodicity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/12/15 00:22:00","modified":"2024/12/17 04:37:15"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Periodicity of Signals
>A ***continuous-time*** signal $x$ is said to be periodic if there is a real number $p > 0$, such that
>$$x(t + p) = x(t) \enspace \text{for all } t.$$
>The smallest $p$ for which the above equation holds is called the fundamental period of $x$. The fundamental frequency of $x$ is denoted by
>$$w_{0}=\frac{2\pi}{p}.$$
>
>Additionally, all periodic ***discrete-time*** signals share a fundamental period $p=1$, as well as a fundamental frequency $\omega_{0} = 2\pi$.
>
>>[!warning] Note 1 (Constant Signals)
>>Constant signals (i.e. DC signals) have an undefined period and a fundamental frequency $\omega_{0} = 0$.
>
>>[!warning] Note 2 (Compound Signals)
>>If a signal  $x$ is formed by combining several periodic signals, its overall period is the least common multiple of their individual periods.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1c.2 Shifting Operations]] METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/05 14:11:54","modified":"2024/07/10 13:17:28"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!note] RISC-V Bitwise Shifting >The following are the RISC-V shifting operations. All operations follow the form **operand** **rd** **rs1** **rs2**. They also have immediate equivalents that follow the format **operand** **rd** **rs1** **imm**: > >| Operation | Description | | :-------: | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | sll(i) | Shifts the value of `rs1` by `rs2`/`imm` bits to the **left** and stores the result in `rd`. | | srl(i) | Shifts the value of `rs1` by `rs2`/`imm` bits to the **right** and stores the result in `rd`. | | sra(i) | Shifts the value of `rs1` by `rs2`/`imm` bits to the **right**, preserves the MSB and stores the result in `rd`. | >>[!warning] Important! >>Shifting **left** **logically** will append zeros to the beginning (least significant bit) of the binary string. Shifting **right logically** will append zeros the the end (most significant bit). Shifting **right** **arithmetically** will append ones to the end (most significant part) of a negative binary string and will append zeros to the most significant bit of a positive binary string. # Understanding What is the difference between `srl` and `sra`? - The first "logically" shifts the bits, meaning it only shifts them without further action. It is best used for division of unsigned integers. - The latter "arithmetically" shifts the bits, thus preserving the most significant bit and therefore the sign of the number. It is best used for signed bits. You can use the aforementioned operations for division of unsigned and signed integers by a power of two. As for `sll`, you can use it for multiplication by powers of two. Test it yourself!

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1d Memory Instructions]] METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/05 13:52:45","modified":"2024/07/10 14:29:15"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!note] RISC-V Memory Instructions >The following are the storing/loading instructions in 32-bit RISC-V. If the arguments of an instruction are not defined, then they are equivalent to the arguments of the first instruction with defined arguments. Instructions in italic are pseudoinstructions: > >| Operation | Description | | :-------: | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | **lw(u) ** **rd** **imm****(****rs1****)** | Loads a 4-byte "word" of memory into the destination register `rd` from address `rs1 + imm`. | | lb(u) | Loads 1 byte of memory into the destination register `rd` from address `rs1 + imm`. | | lh(u) | Loads a 2-byte "half word" of memory into the destination register `rd` from address `rs1 + imm`. | >**sw** **rs2** **imm****(****rs1****)** | Stores in `rs1 + imm` a 4-byte "word" address from `rs2`. | >| sb | Stores in `rs2` a 1-byte address starting at `rs1 + imm` in memory. | | sh | Stores in `rs2` a 2-byte "half word" address starting at `rs1 + imm` in memory. | | **lui** **rd** **imm** | Absolute addressing: loads a 20-bit "upper" immediate with the last 12 bits set to 0 (shifted left by 12 bits) into `rd` (`rd = imm << 12`). | | auipc | Relative addressing: adds a 20-bit upper immediate to the current address of the program counter and sets `rd` to the immediate relative to the program counter (`rd = (imm << 12) + PC`). | | ***li*** ***rd*** ***imm*** | Sets the register `rd` to a 32-bit immediate value. | | ***li*** ***rd*** ***label*** | Sets the register `rd` to the 32-bit address of `label`. | >>[!warning] Note! >>Your **imm** value must be equal to the amount of bytes (and not pointers/elements) you want to shift **rs1** by. # Intuition Let's talk about the elephant in the room here: `lui` and `auipc`. What the heck do these do? Well, they are in fact custom instructions simply made for the `li` and `la` pseudoinstructions. Consider the `li t0 0x12345678` pseudoinstruction, with a pretty long address. It can be written as: ``` addi t0, x0, 0x678 // t0 = 0x678 slli t0, t0, 12 // t0 = 0x678 << 12 = 0x678000 addi t0, t0, 0x345 // t0 = 0x678000 + 0x345 = 0x678345 slli t0, t0, 12 // t0 = 0x678345 << 12 = 0x678345000 addi t0, t0, 0x12 // t0 = 0x678345000 + 0x12 = 0x12345678 ``` However, that is pretty inefficient, right? Therefore we need to find a more efficient method to store big immediates. Enter `lui`. As stated above, `lui rd 0x12345` stores the most significant 20 bits into the 32-bit address of `rd`. However, `0x12345678` is a 32-bit string! Turns out that `addi rd 0x678` can simply do the rest. Then, we get `rd = 0x12345000 + 0x678`. The pseudoinstruction `la` follows a similar approach, but with `auipc` as its first instruction. Consider `la t0 label` where the address of label is `0x12345`. - The `auipc` instruction takes the current PC value, `0x1000` (for example). - It shifts the immediate `0x12345` left by 12 bits to get `0x12345000`. - It adds the current PC value `0x1000` to this shifted immediate value to get `0x12346000`. - The result `0x12346000` is stored in register `t0`.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1e.2 Unconditional Jump Operations]] METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/06 12:18:11","modified":"2024/07/07 15:20:36"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!note] RISC-V Unconditional Jump Operations >The following are the direct jump and link operations in 32-bit RISC-V: > >| Operation | Description | | :-------: | :-----------------------------------------------------------: | | **jal** **rd** **label** | Set `rd` to PC+4 (the line after the current line) and branch to `[label]`. | | **jalr** **rd** **rs1** **imm** | Set `rd` to PC+4 and jump to the line of code at `rs1 + imm`. | >>[!warning] Note! >>There are two pseudoinstructions used when we do not need to return after a call: >>- Direct jumps to label using **j** **label**, which stands for **jal** **x0** **label**. >>- Direct jumps to address using **jr** **rs1**, which stands for **jalr** **x0** **rs1** **0**. >[!example] C Loop >In C or any high-level programming language, one would write code in the following manner: >```run-c >int A[20]; >int sum = 0; >for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { > sum += A[i] >} >printf("%d\n", sum) >``` >In the RISC-V low-level language, however, such abstractions are not possible. However, we can roughly translate the C code above into RISC-V, assuming that `x8` contains the address of the int array: >``` > mv x9 x8 # x9 = &A[0] > mv x1 x0 # sum = 0 > mv x2 x0 # i = 0 > addi x3 x0 20 # x2 = length of A > >Loop: > bge x1 x2 Done # if x1 >= x2 break > lw x10 0(x9) # x10 = *(&A[i]) > add x1 x1 x10 # sum += A[i] > addi x9 x9 4 # x9 = &A[i+1] > addi x2 x2 1 # i++ > j Loop >Done
