NOTE TITLE: [[2.1f.3i Inductor Series Equivalence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/04 05:01:22","modified":"2024/02/20 16:29:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Series Equivalence
>Two [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductors]] in series are equivalent to
>```tikz
>\usepackage{circuitikz}
>\begin{document}
>\begin{circuitikz}[american]
>  \draw (3,3) to [inductor, v=$V_1(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_1$] (3,0)
>  to [inductor, v=$V_2(t)$, L=$L_2$] (3, -3)
>  to [short] (0, -3)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (0, 3)
>  to [short] (3, 3);
>  \draw [->] (4, 0)--(6, 0) node[below=5pt, xshift=-28]{$L_{eq}=L_1+L_2$};
>  \draw (10,2) to [inductor, v=$V_{eq}(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_{eq}$] (10,-2)
>  to [short] (8, -2)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (8, 2)
>  to [short] (10, 2);
\end{circuitikz}
\end{document}
>```
# Proof
Using $V_{test} = V_{eq}$ and KVL, we deduce that
$$V_{eq} = V_1 + V_2.$$
We then plug-in the equations of the inductors,
$$V_{eq}=L_1\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}+L_2\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}$$
Which leads to
$$V_{eq}=(L_1+L_2)\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1f.3ii Inductor Parallel Equivalence]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/04 05:02:06","modified":"2024/10/04 23:25:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Parallel Equivalence
>Two [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductors]] in parallel are equivalent to
>```tikz
>\usepackage{circuitikz}
>\begin{document}
>\begin{circuitikz}[american]
>\draw (-4.5, 6) to [short] (0, 6)
>to [short, i=$I_{test}(t)$] (0, 5)
>to [short] (1.5, 5)
>to [inductor, l=$L_1$, v=$V_1(t)$, i>^=$I_1(t)$] (1.5, 1)
>to [short] (0,1)
>(0, 5) to [short] (-1.5, 5)
>to [inductor, l=$L_2$, v=$V_2(t)$, i>^=$I_2(t)$] (-1.5, 1)
>to [short] (0, 1)
>to [short] (0, 0)
>to [short] (-4.5, 0)
>to [I, l=$I_{test}$, v=$V_{test}(t)$] (-4.5, 6);
>\draw [->] (3, 3)--(5, 3) node[below=5pt, xshift=-28]{$L_{eq}=\left(\frac{1}{L_1}+\frac{1}{L_2}\right)^{-1}$};
>\draw (9,6) to [inductor, v=$V_{eq}(t)$, i>^=$I_{test}(t)$, L=$L_{eq}$] (9,0)
>  to [short] (7, 0)
>  to [I, l=$I_{test}$] (7, 6)
>  to [short] (9, 6);
\end{circuitikz}
\end{document}
>```
# Intuition
Using NVA,
$$
\begin{alignat}{0}
V_{test} =V_1=V_2 \\
L_{eq}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=L_1\frac{dI_1}{dt}+L_2\frac{dI_2}{dt}
\end{alignat}
$$
Since by KCL $I_{eq}=I_1+I_2$,
$$\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=\frac{dI_1}{dt}+\frac{dI_2}{dt}.$$
From the first and second equations,
$$\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}=\frac{L_{eq}}{L_1}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}+\frac{L_{eq}}{L_2}\frac{dI_{test}}{dt}.$$
Simplifying, we get
$$L_{eq}=\left(\frac{1}{L_1}+\frac{1}{L_2}\right)^{-1}.$$

>[!note] Difference Amplifier

NOTE TITLE: [[2.1i.2 Stored Energy of Inductors]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/02/03 22:05:16","modified":"2024/02/20 16:29:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stored Energy of an Inductor
>The stored energy $E_L$ of an [[2.1i.1 Inductor|inductor]] can be written as
>$$E_L=\frac{1}{2}LI_L(t)^2.$$

# Proof
Since we already know that $P=IV$ and that power is the time-integral of energy (work), we can substitute $V_L=L \frac{dI_L(t)}{dt}$: $$P_L= LI_L(t) \frac{dI_L(t)}{dt}.$$We then manipulate and integrate:
$$\int P_Ldt= L \int I_L(t) dI_L(t).$$
Completing the integration we get:
$$E=\frac{1}{2}LI_L(t)^2.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2 Asymptotic Analysis]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/01/17 19:05:40","modified":"2025/01/26 14:26:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Asymptotic Analysis
>**Asymptotic analysis** is a mathematical approach to evaluate the performance of algorithms in terms of their resource usage (e.g. time or space) as the size of the input data ($n$) grows infinitely large. Instead of focusing on exact execution times, it provides a generalized way to express the efficiency of algorithms by describing their growth rates and behavior as input sizes increase using the following notations:
>- **$O$-notation** (big-oh notation) characterizes an *upper bound* on the asymptotic behavior of a function $f$, such that it may not run faster than a certain rate. In other words, $O$-notation is the set of all functions that run slower than (or equivalently slow to) $f$. Formally, for a given function $g$, $O$-notation states that there exist positive constants $c, n_{0} > 0$ such that
>$$O(g(n)) = \{ f(n) \space \colon \space 0 \leq f(n) \leq cg(n) \text{ for all } n \geq n_{0} \}.$$
>- **$\Omega$-notation** characterizes a *lower bound* on the asymptotic behavior of a function $f$, such that it grows at least as fast as a certain rate. In other words, $\Omega$-notation is the set of all functions that run faster than (or equivalently fast to) $f$. Formally, for a given function $g$, $\Omega$-notation states that there exist positive constants $c, n_{0} > 0$ such that
>$$\Omega(g(n)) = \{ f(n) \space \colon \space 0 \leq cg(n) \leq f(n)  \text{ for all } n \geq n_{0} \}.$$
>- **$\Theta$-notation** characterizes a *tight bound* on the asymptotic behavior of a function $f$, such that it runs precisely at a certain rate. It is the set of all functions that run *just as fast* as $f$. Formally, for a given function $g$, $\Theta$-notation states that there exist positive constants $c_{1}, c_{2}, n_{0} > 0$ such that
>$$\Theta(g(n)) = \{ f(n) \space \colon \space 0 \leq c_{1}g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_{2}g(n) \text{ for all } n \geq n_{0} \}.$$
>
>Moreover, for any two functions $f(n)$ and $g(n)$, if $f(n)=O(g(n))$ and $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$, then $f(n) = \Theta(g(n))$, meaning that $f(n)$ is tightly bound by $g(n)$ from both above and below.
>
>>[!warning] Proper Abuse
>>Although we formally define asymptotic notation in terms of sets, we use the equal sign ($=$) instead of the set membership sign ($\in$) within formulae. There are two different ways of interpreting this notation:
>>- When the asymptotic notation **stands alone** (e.g. $O(n^2)=4n^2+100n+500$), the equals sign means **set membership** ($\iff 4n^2+100n+500 \in O(n^2)$).
>>- When the asymptotic notation **appears in a formula** (e.g. $2n^2+3n+1=2n^2+\Theta(n)$), it stands for some **function that has been abstracted** ($\iff 2n^2+3n+1=2n^2+f(n)$ where $f(n) = 3n+1 \in \Theta(n)$).

>[!note] Quadratic Program
>A **Quadratic Program (QP)** is an [[1. Standard Form Optimization|optimization problem]] where the objective function is quadratic, and the constraints are affine. Its **standard form** is given as
>$$\begin{aligned} p^* = \min_\limits{x} \quad & \frac{1}{2}x^THx+c^Tx \\ \text{s.t.:} \quad & Ax \leq b, \end{aligned}$$
>where $f_{0}(x)=\langle c, x \rangle$ for some decision variable $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constants $H \in \mathbb{S}^n$ (and $H \in \mathbb{S}^n_{+}$ for the QP to be convex), $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2a Forward Contracts]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/07 21:38:02","modified":"2025/05/14 17:49:10"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Forward Contract
>A forward contract is a derivative contract between two parties to buy or sell an asset for another asset or currency at a specified **forward price** on a future **maturity date**. By **Covered Interest Parity,** the per-unit forward price of an asset that prevents arbitrage $F_{T}$, given a time to maturity $T$ (in years), can be expressed as
>$$F_{0}=S_{0}e^{(r_{f}-\rho_{f})T},$$
>where $S_{0}$ is the **spot rate** (price) of the underlying asset, $r_{f}$ is the risk-free rate over period $T$, and $\rho_{f}$ is the **carry rate** (e.g. a dividend yield on a stock, or the foreign interest rate in a currency forward). Note that both are continuously compounded.
>
>Then, the value of a forward contract at time $T$ can be expressed as
>$$\text{PV}=\begin{cases}
(F_{0}-S_{T})e^{-r_{f}T} & \text{long position}, \\
(S_{T}-F_{0})e^{-r_{f}T} & \text{short position},
\end{cases}$$
>where $S_{T}$ is the spot rate at time $T$. More particularly, if $F_{0} > S_{T}$, a long forward contract is **in-the-money**. The contract can also be **at-the-money** or **out-of-the-money**.
>
>Forward contracts trade exclusively on OTC markets via major banks, and assets only change hands at the maturity date. At maturity, assets can be paid out in two ways:
>1. **Physical delivery** requires that all of the asset is shipped/wired on the maturity date.
>2. **Cash-settlement** requires that the difference between the spot price and forward price is paid to the "winning" party on the maturity date.

# Example
>[!example] I. Hedging with Forward Contracts
>Andrew has a side business importing handcrafted furniture from Japan. He just collected payment in dollars from your US-based client for a custom table that will be shipped to the US in 90 days, at which point he will owe his Japanese business partner 12M JPY.
>
>Andrew is concerned about the volatility of the JPY-USD exchange rate and would like to lock in his gross profit by hedging with a forward contract.
>
>A bank offers him a rate of 145 JPY/USD for 12M JPY to be delivered in 90 days, and he accepts.
>
>**A)** How much must you Andrew the bank right now?
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Since assets in forward contracts only change hands at the maturity date, Andrew is not obligated to pay anything before the maturity date.
>
>Thirty days go by, and the 60-day forward rate is 140 JPY/USD. A 60-day T-bill on this day yields 4.0%.
>
>**B)** How much is the forward contract now worth from Andrew's point of view?
>>[!example]- B) Solution
>>Since the Yen gained value (i.e., $F_{0}=12\text{M} / 140 > 12\text{M} / 145$), and so the forward contract is in-the-money, and therefore positive for Andrew. Given the 60-day forward rate, $r_{f}=0.04$, and therefore after 60 days Andrew saves
>>$$12\text{M}\left( \frac{1}{140}-\frac{1}{145} \right)e^{-0.04 \cdot 60/365 }=\$2,936.29.$$
>
>**C)** How much is the forward contract worth to the bank?
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>Since Andrew gained $\$2,936.29$, the forward contract is worth exactly $-\$2,936.29$ to the bank.
>
>Sixty more days go by (i.e. you have reached the 90-day maturity date) and the JPY spot rate is 150 JPY/USD.
>
>**D)** How much must Andrew pay the bank now?
>>[!example]- D) Solution.
>>Andrew must pay the bank the value in USD agreed by the forward rate of $F_{0}=1/145$. As such, Andrew pays
>>$$12\text{M} / 145 = 82,758.62.$$
>
>**E)** How much money did Andrew make (or lose) by entering into the forward contract?
>>[!example]- E) Solution.
>>Since the forward contract is out-of-the-money (i.e., $F_{0}=1/150 < 1/145 = S_{0}$), Andrew's net gain is precisely
>>$$12\text{M}(1 / 150 - 1 / 145) = -\$2,758.62.$$
>
>**F)** Did Andrew do the right thing by hedging?
>>[!example]- F) Solution.
>>Andrew did the right thing by hedging, since JPY-USD is a volatile rate, and hedging is about eliminating risk rather than making profit. Not hedging could have done him worse.

>[!example] II. Covered Interest Parity & Arbitrage
>You are an arbitrageur looking for opportunities, and believe that there may be some misalignment in the fixed income and foreign exchange markets in New Zealand relative to the US. Let $r_{f}=0.045$ be the one-year USD risk-free rate, and let $\rho_{f}=0.035$ be the one-year NZD risk-free rate. The USD/NZD spot is currently $S_{0}=0.6$, and the USD/NZD one-year forward rate is $\hat{F}_{0}=0.601$.
>
>**A)** Is there an arbitrage opportunity? 
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>By CIP, 
>>$$F_{0}=S_{0}e^{T(r_{f}-\rho_{f})}=0.6e^{0.01} \approx 0.606>0.601=\hat{F}_{0},$$
>>and therefore there is an arbitrage opportunity. More particularly, the one-year forward for NZD is **overvalued**, since the theoretical (by CIP) is larger than the quoted rate. Therefore,
>>1. Borrow NZD and sell at $S_{0}=0.6$ USD/NZD.
>>2. Invest the US at $0.6e^{-0.045}=$
>>3. Buy NZD at the one-year forward rate $\hat{F}_{0}=0.601$ USD/NZD.
>>4. A year from now, you obtain $(0.606-0.601)e^{-0.035}=0.0048$ USD/NZD of profit.
>
>>**B)** Suppose you have the financial resources to implement your trade in part **A)** at the 1M USD  level (1M USD “notional”). How much profit would you make?
>>As calculated previously, I will make a profit of $\$57,000$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2a Kernel Density Estimate]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/07 11:25:04","modified":"2024/03/07 11:50:51"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] KDE Formula
>A kernel density estimate is a smooth, continuous function that approximates the underlying probability distribution of a dataset. Mathematically,
>$$f_a(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}K_\alpha(x, x_i),$$
>where $K_\alpha(x, x_i)$ is the kernel centered at observation $x_i$, $x$ represents a vector of all values in the dataset (or on the number line), and $\alpha$ is the bandwidth/smoothing parameter. Note that we divide the sum by $\frac{1}{n}$ to normalize the area under the curve.

# Examples
>[!example] Gaussian Kernel
> The Gaussian kernel can be expressed as
> $$K_\alpha(x, x_i)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \alpha^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-x_i)^2}{2\alpha^2}},$$
> where the bandwidth $\alpha$ acts as a standard deviation and $x_i$ acts as the mean (since the curve is centered around it).

>[!example] Boxcar Kernel
>The Boxcar kernel can be expressed as the piecewise
>$$K_\alpha(x,x_i)=
>\begin{cases}
>\frac{1}{\alpha} & \text{if } |x-x_i| \leq \frac{\alpha}{2} \\
>0 & \text{if else}
>\end{cases}.
>$$

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI System
>A linear time-invariant (LTI) system $H$ is one that is both:
>1. **Linear**, such that its system response follows the principle of superposition (composed of linearity and additivity):
>	1. Homogeneity: $y(\alpha x)$
>
>1. **Time-invariant**, such that a time shift in its input signal results in a time shift in its output signal:
>$$x(t) \to \boxed{h(n)} \to y(t) \implies x(t-t_0) \to \boxed{h(n)} \to y(t-t_0),$$
>where $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$.

>- $y(n) = 7x(n+1)$
>- $y(n) = x(n)x(n-1)$
>- $y(n) = e^{x(n)}$

>[!note] Futures
>**Futures** are standardized [[2.2a Forward Contracts|forward contracts]] that are traded on public exchanges (e.g. CME, CBOT, ICE) rather that OTC. Standardization requirements of futures include:
>- Specifying the **notional value** per individual contract (e.g. 5,000 bushels of corn, or $100,000 face amount of 30-year treasury bonds).
>- A cash collateral, known as **margin**, adjusted daily to account for changes in futures prices, known as **marking to market**. It is done to 
>- Delivery month and location(s).
>- Quality requirements for commodities.
>
>Since futures prices converge in maturity towards the spot price of the underlier per **Covered Interest Parity**, the difference between the spot price and the futures price is known as the **futures basis**. Investors may bet on the convergence or divergence of the futures and spot prices in a **basis trade**.
>
>If an investor does not require the actual commodities associated with a future contract, they may close it out with an offsetting trade. However, there are tales of investors forgetting to close out contracts and being forced to take/receive cattle and corn.

(cont'd) >[!example] Cascade
>Suppose we have two FIR filters, $a(n)$ and $b(n)$, such that their impulse response is given by
>$$\begin{align}
>a(n) &= a_0\delta(n) + a_1\delta(n-1)+ \ldots + a_N\delta(n-N) && (\text{where } N \in \mathbb{N}), \\  &\text{and} \\ b(n) &= b_0\delta(n) + b_1\delta(n-1)+ \ldots + b_M\delta(n-M) && (\text{where } M \in \mathbb{N}).
>\end{align}$$
>The two filters are placed in a cascade $C$, such that the final system is
>$$x \rightarrow \boxed{\boxed{A} \rightarrow \boxed{B}}^C \rightarrow y.$$
>We can find the cascade by setting $x(n) = \delta(n)$. Then,
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= [(x * a) * b].
>\end{align}$$
>Since the impulse response of any system is its filter, we can simplify this into
>$$\begin{align}
>c(n) &= (a * b) \\
>&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} a(k)b(n-k) \\
>\end{align}$$
>Here, we can see that $a(k)b(n-k)$ is equal to
>$$a_0b_0\delta(k)\delta(n-k) + a_0b_1\delta(k)\delta(n-k-1) + a_1b_0\delta(k-1)\delta(n-k) + a_1b_1\delta(k-1)\delta(n-k-1) + \ldots,$$
>and therefore
>$$\begin{align}
>c(n) &= a_0b_0\delta(n) + (a_0b_1 + a_1b_0)\delta(n-1) + (a_0b_2 + a_1b_1 + a_2b_0)\delta(n-2) + \ldots
>\end{align}$$
>This means that we can model any coefficient $c_n$ of the cascade ($n \leq N$) as
>$$c_n = \sum^{n}_{k=\max(0, n - M)}a_kb_{n-k},$$
>where $k=\max(0, n-M),$ as the two systems are of different sizes, and we need to account for cases where $M < N$. Finally, we can express $c$ as
>$$c(n) = c_0\delta(n) + c_1\delta(n-1) + \ldots + c_{N+M}\delta(n-N-M).$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b LTI Convolution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/10 21:55:20","modified":"2024/12/17 00:04:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Convolution Representation
>Given a discrete-time input signal $x(n)$, the output of a discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] $y(n)$ can be represented as a weighted combination of impulse responses $h[n]$, such that
>$$y(n) = x(n) * h(n) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(k)h(n-k)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(n-k)h(k).$$ 
>Similarly, given a continuous-time input signal $x(t)$, the output of a continuous-time LTI system $y(t)$ can be represented as
>$$y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}x(t - \tau)h(\tau)d\tau.$$

# Intuition

# Properties
#### (*Polynomialization*) If for the polynomials $\hat{y}(z)=\hat{x}(z)\hat{h}(z)$, then $y_k=(h * x)_k$ where $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}y_kz^k$.
We start by expanding with the fact that $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{i=-\infty}\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}(x_iz^i)(h_jz^j)$. We can perform a change of variables for $k=i+j$, such that
$$\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}x_kh_{k-i}z^k.$$
By definition, $\hat{y}(z)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}y_kz^k$, and therefore $y_k=\sum^{\infty}_{j=-\infty}y_kz^kx_kh_{k-i}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b Strategic Dominance]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/30 07:44:09","modified":"2024/06/30 07:46:58"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Strategic Dominance
>**Strategic dominance** in game theory occurs when there is a certain single strategy $s_i' \in S_i$ for a player $i \in N$ that is the [[2.2a Best Response|best response]] for any combination of other players' strategies $s_{-i}$. There are two cases in which this happens:
>- Strategy $s_i'$ **strongly dominates** all other strategies $s_i$ of player $i$ if the payoff of $s_i'$ is *strictly greater* than all of $i$'s other strategies $s_i$ for some strategies of other players $s_{-i}$, such that
>$$u_i(s_i', s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i}).$$
>- Strategy $s_i'$ **weakly dominates** another strategy $s_i^\# \in S_i$ if it does at least as well as $s_i^\#$ for all possible strategies of other players $s_{-i}$, and does better than $s_i^\#$ for certain strategies $\hat{s}_{-i}$ of the other players, such that
>$$\begin{equation}\begin{aligned}u_i(s_i', s_{-i}) &\geq u_i(s_i^\#, s_{-i}) && \text{for all $s_{-i}$}  \\ u_i(s_i', \hat{s}_{-i}) &> u_i(s_i', \hat{s}_{-i}) && \text{for some } \hat{s}_{-i}\end{aligned}\end{equation}$$
>
>A strategy profile to a game in which each player is using their dominant strategy is said to be a **dominant strategy solution**.

# Intuition
Strategic dominance follows the principle of rational choice. Obviously, considering the other players' strategies, one will choose that strategy which puts them at the best position possible. 
- Strongly dominant strategies can be interpreted as strategies that are the only rational response of a player $i$ in a game.
- Weakly dominant strategies can be interpreted as a set of rational strategies that can be used as a best response depending on the other players' strategies.
Here, it is important to note that ==not all games have dominant strategies==.

Let's now look at the solvability of dominance. pg 69-71 (Optional?)

# Examples
>[!example] EASY: Dominant Strategy in Auctions
>Suppose you want to buy a painting of Renoir. You value it at $300,000, meaning this is the true valuation that you give the painting. Then, the rules of game theory dictate that actively bidding until $300,000 and either giving up or winning the auction is the dominant strategy. Consider the other two cases:
>- Suppose you set yourself a lowball limit of $250,000. Then, bidding either continues above your true price of $300,000, or somebody wins the auction with a bid of $270,000. In that case, you're bummed, since you could've gotten a sweet painting for less than it's worth to you.
>- Suppose now you overextended yourself and decide to bid until $350,000. Then, either somebody saves you by bidding higher, or you win the auction. However, you're still bummed, since you are now stuck with a painting that you paid more for than you think is worth.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/04 01:27:20","modified":"2025/06/06 17:15:29"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Probability Mass Function (PMF)
>The probability [[2.2a Probability Distribution|distribution]] of a discrete random variable $X$ is fully described by a non-negative **probability mass function (PMF)** $p_{X}: \mathcal{X} \to [0,1]$, formally defined as
>$$p_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}[X=x],$$
>where $\set{ X=x } \in \mathcal{F}$ is the event consisting of all outcomes where the random variable $X$ equals the specific value $x \in \mathcal{X}$.
>
>The cumulative probability that $X$ takes on a value less than or equal to $x$ in the PMF is given by the monotonically non-decreasing **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** $F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$, formally defined as
>$$F_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}[X \leq x]=\sum^{}_{k \leq x}p_{X}(k),$$
>implying that the PDF is the rate of change of the CDF, $p_{X}(x)=F_{X}(x)-F_{X}(x-1)$.
>>[!warning] PMFs Sum to One
>>For a PMF to meet the sum-to-one criterion of any probability function,
>>$$\sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}p_{X}(x)=1.$$

# Properties
#### (*Joint Distribution*) $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}[X=x \space \cap \space Y=y]$.
#### (*Conditionality*) $p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\cfrac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_{Y}(y)}$.
#### (*Marginality*) $p_{X}(x)=\sum\limits_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}p_{X,Y}(x,y)$.
#### (*Independence*) If $X,Y$ are independent, then $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{X}(x) \cdot p_{Y}(y)$ and $p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=p_{X}(x)$.

> [!note] Bernoulli Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \in \{ 0, 1 \}$ follows the **Bernoulli distribution** $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$ if it represents a **single trial** with binary outcomes. Formally, the Bernoulli distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}p & \text{if } x=1, \\ 1-p & \text{if } x=0, \end{cases}$$
>where $p$ is the probability of a successful outcome.
### Explanation.
The Bernoulli [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|distribution]] is used for probabilities where the event either happens, or does not happen. Following this, the random variable can only take two values (1 or 0).

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)]=p.$
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)]=p(1-p)$.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.4 Binomial Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 16:48:10","modified":"2025/08/08 19:57:49"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Binomial Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Binomial distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ if it represents the number of **successes** in (i.e., the sum of) $n$ independent [[2.2b.3 Bernoulli Distribution|Bernoulli trials]], where each trial has a probability $p$ of success. Formally, the Binomial distribution of a random variable is given by the PMF,
>$$p_{X}(x)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x},$$
>where $\binom{n}{x}=\frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}$ is the binomial coefficient, $p^{k}$ is the probability of exactly $k$ successes, and $(1-p)^{n-x}$ is the probability of the remaining trials being failures.


# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)]=np.$
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)]=np(1-p)$.
$$\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(X) &= \mathbb{E}(X^2) - \mathbb{E}(X)^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}(I_{i}) + \sum_{i \ne j}^{n}\mathbb{E}(I_{i}I_{j}) - n^2p^2 \\
&= np + n(n-1)p^2 - n^2p^2 \\
&= np + n^2p^2-np^2-n^2p^2 \\
&= np-np^2 \\
&= np(1-p).
\end{align}$$
Since there are exactly $n(n-1)$ ordered distinct pairs of $i, j$ and $I_{i} \sim_{\text{iid}} \text{Ber}(p)$, so $\mathbb{E}(I_{i}I_{j})=\mathbb{E}(I_{i})\mathbb{E}(I_{j})$ for $i \neq j$.

#### (*MGF*) $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=(1-p+pe^t)^n$.
#### (Sum) Let $X=\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$, where $X_{i} \sim_{\text{iid}} \text{Bin}(n_{i}, p)$. Then, $X \sim \text{Bin}\left( \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}n_{i}, \; p \right)$.

# Examples
>[!example] Packet Routing
>Consider a system with $n$ inputs and $n$ outputs. At each input, a packet appears independently with probability $p$. If a packet appears, it is destined for one of the $n$ outputs uniformly randomly, independently of the other packets.
>
>
>>[!example]- Let $X$ denote the number of packets destined for the first output. What is the distribution of $X$?
>>Let $A$ be the event that the packet appears, and let $B_{i}$ be the event that the packet hits the $i$-th output. Then, $\mathbb{P}(A \cap B_{i})=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B_{i})=p\frac{1}{n}=\frac{p}{n}$ by independence. The distribution of $X$ can be modeled as $\operatorname{Bin}(n, \frac{p}{n})$. There are $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, and each trial has the same probability of success $\frac{p}{n}$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the probability of a *collision* (that is, more than one packet heading to the same output)?
>>Let $X=X_{1}+X_{2}+\ldots+X_{n}$ denote the total number of packets, where each $X_{i}$ denotes the number of packets destined for the $i$.-th output. Then, $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, p)$, since every packet is generated by one of the $n$ inputs with probability $p$ and goes to exactly one output with probability $\frac{1}{n}$, so counting the packets at each output and summing them gives the total number of packets generated. We have that:
>>$$$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:56:00","modified":"2025/08/06 13:17:56"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Geometric Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 1$ follows the **Geometric distribution** $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$ if it represents the number of trials required to obtain the *first success* in a sequence of independent [[2.2b.3 Bernoulli Distribution|Bernoulli trials]]. Formally, the Geometric distribution of a random variable is given by the PMF,
>$$p_{X}(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p,$$
>where each trial has a probability $p$ of success.
>
>The geometric distribution is the only discrete distribution that is **memoryless**, meaning that the probability of needing more than $m$ additional trials to get the first success is independent of the $k$ trials that have already been conducted. Formally,
>$$\mathbb{P}[X > k + m \mid X > k] = \mathbb{P}[X > m],$$
>showing that whether or not you start fresh or you have already had $k$ failures, the chance of needing more than $m$ additional trials remains the same.

# Intuition
I honestly cannot help you if you don't understand the PMF for the geometric distribution. There is a $p^1$ factor, which indicates that there is only a single success. It is self-descriptive.

However, when I first learned about the memoryless property (i.e. right now), I was confused. So let's get through it together. We have $k$ as the number of initial (failed) trials, and $m$ as the sequential number of trials to get a single success. Then,
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[X > k+m \mid X > k] &= \frac{\mathbb{P}[X > k+m \cap X > k]}{\mathbb{P}[X > k]} \\ 
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}[X > k+m]}{\mathbb{P}[X > k]} \\
&= \frac{(1-p)^{k+m}}{(1-p)^k} \\
&= (1-p)^m \\
&= \mathbb{P}[X > m].
\end{align}$$
where the tail probability of the Geometric random variable is given by $\mathbb{P}[X > x]=(1-p)^x$.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Geom}(p)]=\frac{1}{p}$.
We start by setting up our equation for solving the expectation using the [[2.6b.2 Tail Sum Formula|tail sum formula]] by saying that
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] &= \sum^{\infty}_{j=i}\mathbb{P}[X=j] \\
&=\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}p(1-p)^{j-1} \\
&=\frac{p}{1-p}\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}(1-p)^{j} \\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Using the definition of the infinite geometric sum $S_n=\sum^{\infty}_{i=0}a_ir^i=\frac{a_1}{1-r}$ with $a_1=(1-p)^i$ and $r=1-p$ (a is not $1$ since geometric series start at $j=1$, and it is not $1-p$ since $j=i$, we are led to,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] &= \frac{p}{1-p}\sum^{\infty}_{j=i}(1-p)^{j} \\
&= \frac{p}{1-p}\frac{(1-p)^i}{1-(1-p)} \\
&= (1-p)^{i-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
This means that for large $n$, the probability that we need $i$ trials or more before the first success is determined by $\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] = (1-p)^{i-1}$. Then the probability that we will get a success in less than $i$ trials is $\mathbb{P}[X < i] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[X \geq i]$. 

Let's put this in perspective using a biased coin with a probability of heads $p=\frac{1}{3}$. The probability that we need 1 toss or more before the first success is 1. That we will need 2 or more is $1-p=\frac{2}{3}$. The probability that we will need 3 or more tosses before a success is $(1-p)^2=\frac{4}{9}$. The probability that we will get a successful trial before 3 tosses (so in the first 2 tosses) is $1-\frac{4}{9}=\frac{5}{9}$. Looking at the outcome space for 3 trials or success, we can see why:
$$\Upomega=\set{TTT, TTH, TH, H}$$
Here, $\mathbb{P}[X=3]=\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{3})^2=\frac{4}{27}$. This is confirmed by $\mathbb{P}[X=3]=\mathbb{P}[TTH]$. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[X < 3]=\mathbb{P}[TH]+\mathbb{P}[H]=\frac{1}{3}\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{5}{9}$, which is equal to $1 - (1-p)^2=\frac{5}{9}$.

We now calculate the expectation of the geometric distribution using the [[2.6b.2 Tail Sum Formula|tail sum formula]] and the previously introduced infinite geometric sum as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[X \geq i] \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}(1-p)^{i-1} \\
&= \frac{(1-p)^{1-1}}{1-(1-p)} \\
&= \frac{1}{p}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Therefore, $\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}$ for a geometric distribution.

#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}[X \sim \text{Geom}(x)]=\frac{1-p}{p^2}$
We already know that $\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}$. Therefore, using $Var[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-E[X]^2$, we only need to find $E[X^2]$. We proceed as follows:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X^2] &= \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
# Examples
>[!example] Class Enrollment

>[!example]  Laundry Time
>To avoid doing laundry too often, Marcus creates a system. Each night, he labels one of his shirts as the "dirtiest." In the morning, he randomly picks one of his clean shirts to wear. If he happens to wear the dirtiest one, he throws it in the dirty pile at the end of the day (shirts in the dirty pile aren’t reused). Once all his shirts end up dirty, Marcus does laundry. That night, he again designates one shirt as the dirtiest, and the cycle begins anew.
>
>>[!example]- If Marcus has $n$ shirts, what is the expected number of days that transpire between laundry events?
>>Observe that the cycle can be broken into $n$ phases. During phase $i$:
>>1. Marcus labels one of the remaining $n-i+1$ shirts as the dirtiest.
>>2. In the morning, he picks one of those $n-i+1$ shirts.
>>3. 
>>The number of days it takes for Marcus to throw each shirt in the dirty pile can be expressed as the sum $D=\sum^{n}_{i=1}S_{i}$, where $S_{i} \sim \text{Geom}\left( \dfrac{1}{n-i+1} \right)$. This probability works solely because once Marcus labels a shirt as the "dirtiest," no other shirt can claim this position before the "dirtiest" is thrown in the dirty pile.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.7 Hypergeometric Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:50:13","modified":"2025/06/06 17:16:03"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Hypergeometric Distribution
>A discrete random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Hypergeometric distribution** $X \sim \text{Hypergeom}(N, K, n)$ if it represents the number of successes in a sample of size $n$ drawn without replacement from a finite population of $N$ items that contains $K$ successes. Formally, the Hypergeometric distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=\frac{\binom{K}{x}\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}}=\frac{\frac{K!}{(K-x)!}\frac{(N-K)!}{(N-K-(n-x))!}}{\frac{N!}{(N-n)!}},$$
>where $x$ is the number of successes in the sample and satisfies $\max(0, n)-(N-K) \leq x \leq \min(N, k)$.
# Intuition
We want to draw $n$ balls from a box of $N=B+W$ balls without replacement. Consider a case of a sequence $\upomega$ of n draws where the first $k$ balls are black and the next $n-k$ balls are white. Then, the probability of this particular sequence will be:
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[\upomega] &= \frac{B}{N} \times \frac{B-1}{N-1} \times...\times \frac{B-k+1}{N-k+1} \times \frac{W}{N-k} \times \frac{W-1}{N-k-1} \times...\times \frac{W-(n-k)+1}{N-n+1} \\ &= \frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{W!}{(W-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}} \\ &= \frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{(N-B)!}{(N-B-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Because of this, each sample point of a Hypergeometric [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|distribution]] can be viewed as binomial without repetition.

Now, in order to find all distinct sequences with $n$ draws of $k$ black balls and $n-k$ white balls, we need to multiply by $\binom{n}{k}$, leading to:
$$\mathbb{P}[X=k]=\binom{n}{k}\frac{\frac{B!}{(B-k)!}\frac{(N-B)!}{(N-B-(n-k))!}}{\frac{N}{(N-n)!}}=\frac{\binom{B}{k}\binom{N-B}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}$$
If we had white, black and orange balls, then we need another variable, say $j$, for the number of draws of white balls, and the rest would go to orange.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \operatorname{Hypergeom}(N, K, n)]=\frac{nK}{N}$
#### (*Variance*) $\operatorname{Var}(X \sim \operatorname{Hypergeom}(N, K, n))=\frac{nK(N-K)(N-n)}{N^2(N-1)}.$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2b.8 Poisson Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/03 18:56:26","modified":"2025/06/06 17:15:35"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Poisson Distribution
>A discrete random variable follows the **Poisson distribution** $X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)$ if it represents the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, given that these events occur independently and at a constant average rate $\lambda$. Formally, the Poisson distribution of a random variable is given by the [[2.2b.1 Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]],
>$$p_{X}(x)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!},$$
>where if $\lambda < 1$, the PMF is monotonically decreasing, and if $\lambda > 1$, the PMF first increases then decreases as $x \to \infty$.
# Intuition
The Poisson distribution is used in "rare" events such as in phone call disconnections, radioactive emissions, crossovers in chromosomes, and calculating the number of cases of a disease. This model is appropriate when some event can be assumed to happen randomly with a constant density in a continuous region (of time or space), such that occurrences in disjoint subregions are independent (each event is considered a separate occurrence). 
# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)]=\lambda$.
We calculate the expectation of a poisson random variable using the Taylor series expansion $e^x=\sum^{\infty}_{n=0}\frac{x^n}{n!}$,
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=0}i \times \mathbb{P}[X=i] \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{i=1}i\frac{\uplambda^i}{i!}e^{-\uplambda} \\
&= \lambda e^{-\uplambda}\sum^{\infty}_{i=1}\frac{\uplambda^{i-1}}{(i-1)!} \\
&= \lambda e^{-\uplambda}e^\uplambda \\
&= \lambda
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Note that we omit the 0th term due to it being equal to 0.
#### (*Variance*) $Var[X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)]=\lambda$.
We already know that $\mathbb{E}[X]=\uplambda$. Therefore we need to calculate $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]$ (0 is again trivial in the summation, as well as 1 this time):
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] &= \sum^{\infty}_{i=2}i(i-1)\frac{\lambda^i}{i!}e^{-\lambda} \\
&= \lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum^{\infty}_{i=2}\frac{\lambda^{i-2}}{(i-2)!} \\
&= \lambda^2
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
Knowing this, we can calculate the variance from the expansion $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]$
$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
Var(X)&=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2 \\
&= \uplambda^2+\uplambda-\uplambda^2 \\
&= \uplambda
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
$$
#### (*Sum*) If $X \sim \operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ and $Y \sim \operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$, then $X+Y=\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda + \mu)$.

#### (*Binomial Approximation*)
# Examples
>[!example] Probability of Typos on a Page
>Suppose we are writing an article and make on average 1 typo per page. We can then model a Poisson distribution with $\lambda=1$. So the probability that we make 5 typos on a page is
>$$\mathbb{P}[X=5]=\frac{1^5}{5!}e^{-1}=\frac{1}{120e} \approx 0.003.$$
>Now suppose the article has 200 pages. If the number of typos on each page is independent, then the probability that there is at least one page with exactly 5 typos is
>$$
>\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
>\mathbb{P}[\exists \text{a page with exactly 5 typos}] &= 1 - \mathbb{P}[\text{every page has } \neq 5 \text{ typos}] \\
>&= 1-\prod^{200}_{i=1}\mathbb{P}[\text{page i has } \neq 5 \text{ typos}] \\
>&= 1-\prod^{200}_{i=1}(1 - \mathbb{P}[X=5]) \\
>&= 1-\left(1 - \frac{1}{120e}\right)^{200} \approx 0.46
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
>$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c LTI Impulse Response]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/09/24 15:30:14","modified":"2024/12/14 23:02:06"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] LTI Impulse Response
>The response of a discrete-time[[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] to a [[2.1a.1 Kronecker Delta|unit impulse]] $x(n) = \delta(n)$ is used to find its filter, $h(n)$. Mathematically, the solution $y(n)$ to any input $x(n)$ of the discrete-time LTI can be expressed as the [[2.2b LTI Convolution|convolution]]
>$$y(n) = (\delta * h)(n) = h(n).$$
>
>Similarly, the solution $y(t)$ to any input $x(t)$ of the continuous-time LTI can be expressed as the convolution of its
>$$y(t) = ()$$

# Proof
We proceed by a simple proof, taking $x(n)=\delta(n)$ and a filter $h(n)$:
$$\begin{align}
y(n) &= (x \textasteriskcentered h)(n) \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}x(k)h(n-k) \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(k)h(n-k) \\
&= h(n),
\end{align}$$
since $\delta(k) \neq 0 \iff k = 0$.

# Examples
>[!example] (Discrete-Time) Impulse Response of a Recursive Filter
>A causal, discrete-time LTI system $H$ is characterized by the recursive difference equation $y(n) = \alpha y(n-N)+x(n)$. We can determine its impulse response by observing that for $x(n)=\delta(n)$,
>$$\begin{align}
>h(n) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\delta(n-k)[\alpha h(n-N)+\delta(n)] \\ \\
>&= \alpha h(n-N) + \delta(n).
>\end{align}$$
>We quickly see that since $H$ is causal, then $h(n) = 0$ for all $n < 0$. Therefore, $h(0) = \delta(0)=1$. By observation, we find $h(N) = \alpha$, $h(2N) = \alpha^2$, and so on. Therefore, we can establish that
>$$h(n) = \begin{cases}\alpha^{\frac{n}{N}} \text{ if } n \mod{N} \equiv 0 \\ 0 \text{ otherwise}\end{cases}.$$
>Using the Kronecker delta, we can get rid of this piecewise nature so that
>$$h(n) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}\alpha^n \delta(n - kN).$$
>This is because the delta is nonzero only for $n=kN$, (i.e. a multiple of $N$).

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c Nash Equilibrium]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/30 07:44:09","modified":"2024/07/01 07:36:05"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Nash Equilibrium
>The **Nash equilibrium** of a game is the strategy profile $s^* = (s_i^*, s_{-i}^*)$ which illustrates all players in a game using their [[2.2a Best Response|best response]], such that for all strategies $s_i \in S_i$ of *all* players $i \in N$,
>$$u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \geq u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*).$$
>The payoff that occurs when each player adheres to $s^*$ is the **Nash equilibrium outcome**. 
# Intuition
In a Nash equilibrium outcome, all players know (and expect) the strategy of every other player in the game. In a way, a Nash equilibrium is a stable prescription for play where a single player does not have a positive *unilateral* incentive to deviate from the equilibrium, although they might have an *indifferent* incentive (since we use greater than or equal to '$\geq$' instead of strictly greater than '$>$'). By deviating from the Nash equilibrium, a single player would simply lower their own payoffs if they think the other players will not deviate from their respective strategies, and this is inconsistent with rational play.

Something else to consider is the Nash equilibrium as a *focal point* for players. Since a Nash equilibrium utilizes each player's most rational response, a player could ask themselves what they expect as the outcome of the game by accounting for unreasonable plays (mistakes) by other players. If they expect everyone to play rationally (or coordinate on a Nash equilibrium by pre-play communication), then they are expecting a Nash equilibrium. If mistakes do happen from players, they could be corrected by changes in strategy with trial and error until a Nash equilibrium is reached.

Finally, we can find a Nash equilibrium by identifying the best response $s_i^*$ of player $i$ $S_{-i}$ of $-i$. Then, if $i$'s best response to $-i$ is the best response of $-i$ to $i$, this is a Nash equilibrium. Note that there may be more than one Nash equilibria in a game.

Essentially, when looking for Nash equilibria, ask yourself whether any of the players $i \in N$ have an incentive to deviate from the current strategy profile (change their choice). 
# Properties
##### *(Nash's Theorem)* In a *finite* strategic form game, there is always at least one Nash equilibrium.
We can prove this using [[2.5a Mixed Strategies|mixed strategies]].

##### *(Dominance Subsumption)* Any game with a dominant strategy also has a unique Nash equilibrium.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2c Swaps]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/13 14:52:08","modified":"2025/05/13 17:29:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Swaps
>A swap is an OTC derivative in which two parties agree to exchange a stream of cash flows over multiple future dates. It can be interpreted as a series of [[2.2a Forward Contracts|forward contracts]] for each cash flow leg that are calculated differently and netted,  so that only the difference changes hands on each settlement date.
>
>There are many types of swaps, including uncommon (exotic) swaps. Popular swaps include:
>- **Interest-Rate Swaps,** in which two parties exchange a series of fixed‑rate and floating‑rate interest payments on a notional principal over a specified term.
>- **Credit Default Swaps**, where one party pays a periodic fee in exchange for protection ("insurance") against the default of a specified borrower or bond.
>- **Currency Swaps**, where parties exchange principal and interest payments in different currencies over a set period.
>- **Commodity swaps**, where parties exchange cash flows based on the price of a specified commodity over a set period.
>
>In all swaps, one party typically pays the spot (floating) rate, whereas another pays a rate fixed by the swap contract. However, total floating swaps or fixed swaps are common currency swaps.

# Examples
>[!example] I. Interest Rate Swaps and Comparative Advantage
>Suppose AAACorp and BBBCorp are able to obtain the following borrowing rates for 5-year $100M loans from their respective bankers: 
>
>|      | Fixed Rate |      Floating Rate       |
| :--: | :--------: | :----------------------: |
| AAA  |  $4.00\%$  | $\text{Floating}-0.1\%$ |
| BBBB |  $5.20\%$  | $\text{Floating}+0.6\%$  |
>
>The table above shows that AAA has a comparative advantage in fixed rate borrowing, whereas BBB has a comparative advantage in floating rate borrowing.
>
>Suppose further that AAACorp would prefer to pay a floating rate, whereas BBBCorp would prefer to pay a fixed rate. A banker with relationships with both companies notices this, and contemplates the flowing Interest Rate Swap:
>$$\xleftarrow{4\%}\boxed{\text{AAA}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}^{\xleftarrow{4.35\%}}\boxed{\text{BBB}}\xrightarrow{\text{Floating + 0.6\%}}$$
>
>**A)** What would the net effect of the cash flows be for AAACorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- A) Solution.
>>Since AAA borrows at $4\%$ and is paid at $4.35\%$, AAA's net gain is $0.35\%$. It pays BBB the floating rate, which means that it net pays $\text{Floating}-0.35\%$, which is 25 basis points better than the direct-market price.
>
>**B)** What would the net effect of the cash flows be for BBBCorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for fixed-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- B) Solution.
>>Since BBB directly borrows at $\text{Floating}+0.6\%$ and is paid the floating rate by AAA, its net interest is $0.6\%$. Since BBB also pays AAA $4.35\%$, this means that it pays $4.35\%+0.6\%=4.95\%$ in total fixed rate, which is 25bp less than the market fixed rate.
>
>Suppose the banker instead envisions this arrangement:
>$$\xleftarrow{4\%}\boxed{\text{AAA}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}^{\xleftarrow{4.33\%}}\boxed{\text{Financial Inst.}}^{\xleftarrow{4.37\%}}_{\xrightarrow{\text{Floating}}}\boxed{BBB}\xrightarrow{\text{Floating + 0.6\%}}$$
>
>**C)** What is the new net effect of the cash flows for AAACorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- C) Solution.
>>AAA's  outflow is $\text{Floating}+4\%$, whereas its inflow is $4.33\%$. This equates to a net outflow of
>>$$\text{Floating}+4\%-4.33\%=\text{Floating}-0.33\%,$$
>>which is $23$bp better than their market floating rate.
>
>**D)** What is the new net effect of the cash flows for BBBCorp, and how does this compare to its direct marketplace opportunity for floating-rate borrowing?
>>[!example]- D) Solution.
>>BBB's outflow under this scheme is $\text{Floating}+4.97\%$, whereas its inflow is the floating rate. Therefore, its net outflow is $4.97\%$, which is $5.20\%-4.97\%=0.23\%$ (or 23bp) better than their fixed market rate.
>
>**E)** What is the annual fee (in dollars) effectively earned by the banker under this arrangement?
>>[!example]- E) Solution
>>The banker's outflow is $\text{Floating}+4.33\%$, and their inflow is $\text{Floating}+4.37\%$, which means that their net inflow is $(\text{Floating}+4.37\%)-(\text{Floating}+4.33\%)=0.04\%$ or 4bp.
>>
>>Since the loans are both for $\$100\text{M}$, this means that the banker earns $\$40,000$ per year for 5 years with this scheme.

>[!note] Probability Density Function (PDF)
>The probability [[2.2a Probability Distribution|distribution]] of a continuous random variable $X$ is fully described by a non-negative **probability density function (PDF)** $f_{X}: \mathcal{X} \to [0,\infty)$, which illustrates the density around each value $x \in \mathcal{X}$. In particular, the probability that the value of $X$ falls within an interval $[a, b]$ over the real line is given as
>$$\mathbb{P}(a \leq X \leq b)=\int^{b}_{a}f_{X}(x)dx,$$
>and can be interpreted as the area under the graph of the PDF.
>
>The cumulative probability that $X$ takes on a value less than or equal to $x$ in the PDF is given by the non-decreasing **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** $F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ , formally defined as
>$$F_{X}(x)=\mathbb{P}(X \leq x)=\int^{x}_{-\infty}f_{X}(t)dt,$$
>implying that the PDF is the rate of change of the CDF, $f_{X}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}F_{X}(x)$.
>
>>[!warning] PDFs Measure Density
>>For an individual point $x$, $\mathbb{P}(X = x) = \int^{x}_{x}f_{X}(x)dx = 0$. However, an alternative to this is to select the interval $[x, x + \delta]$ for a very small length $\delta$, and compute
>>$$\int^{x+\delta}_{x}f_{X}(x)dx \approx f_{X}(x) \cdot \delta.$$

# Properties
#### (*Event Conditioning*) If $A \in \mathcal{F} \text{ s.t. } \mathbb{P}(X \in A) > 0$, then $f_{X \mid A}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{f_{X}(x)}{\mathbb{P}(X \in A)} & x \in A, \\ 0 & \text{o.w.}\end{cases}$
#### (R.V. Conditioning) $f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=$
#### (*Joint PDFs*) $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{Y}(y)f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)$.
#### (*Marginality*) $f_{X}(x)=\displaystyle\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}f_{Y}(y)f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)dy$.

#### (*Continuous Bayes'*) $f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\displaystyle\frac{f_{X}(x)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)}{f_{Y}(y)}=\frac{f_{X}(x)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)}{\displaystyle\int f_{X}(t)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid t)dt}.$
#### (*Independence*) R.V.'s $X,Y$ are independent iff $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X}(x) \cdot y_{Y}(y)$ $\forall x,y$.

#### (*Joint CDFs*)

#### (*Sum Convolution*) If $W=X+Y$, $f_{W}(w)=\large\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}f_{X}(x)f_{Y}(w-x)dx$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/23 15:27:36","modified":"2025/06/06 15:31:43"}

>[!note] Continuous Uniform Distribution
>A continuous random variable $X$ with $a<b$ follows the **Uniform distribution** $X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ if it is equally likely to take any value in the interval $[a,b]$.  Formally, the Uniform distribution of a random variable is given by the PDF
>$$f_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a} & \text{if } x \in [a, b], \\
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}$$
>so that every subinterval of $[a,b]$ of the same length has the same probability.
>
>Then, the CDF of $X$ is given by
>$$F_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}
0 & x \leq a, \\
\dfrac{x-a}{b-a} & x \in (a, b), \\
1 & x \geq b.
\end{cases}$$

>[!note] Exponential Distribution
>A non-negative continuous random variable $X \geq 0$ follows the **Exponential distribution** $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ with parameter $\lambda > 0$, defined by the [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|probability density function]]
>$$f_{X}(x)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda x} &\text{if} \enspace  x \geq 0 \\ 0 &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
>The CDF for the Exponential distribution is $F_{X}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$.
>
>The Exponential distribution represents the waiting time until the first occurrence of an event in a process where events occur continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate $\lambda$.
>
>Additionally, akin to the discrete [[2.2b.5 Geometric Distribution|Geometric distribution]], the exponential distribution is the only continuous PDF that has the **memoryless property**, which states that the probability of needing more than $m$ additional trials to get the first success is independent of the $k$ trials that have already been conducted, such that
>$$\mathbb{P}[X > k + m \mid X > k] = \mathbb{P}[X > m],$$
>showing that whether or not you start fresh or you have already had $k$ failures, the chance of needing more than $m$ additional trials remains the same.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}(X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda))= \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
#### (*Variance*) $\text{Var}(X \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda))=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}$.
#### (*Discretization*) If $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$, $\lfloor X \rfloor + 1 \sim \operatorname{Geom}(1-e^{-\lambda})$.
We know that the CDF of $W$ is $F_{W}(w)=1-e^{-\lambda w}$. Then, $F_{X}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \in \mathbb{N}$. We are trying to find the probability of W falling in the interval $[x, x+1)$ (since this continuous interval represents the floor of values of $x$). As such,
$$\begin{align}
f_{X}(x)&=F_{X}(x+1)-F_{X}(x) \\
&=1-e^{-\lambda(x+1)}-1+e^{-\lambda x} \\
&=e^{-\lambda x}(1-e^{-\lambda})\\
&=(e^{-\lambda})^x(1-e^{-\lambda}),
\end{align}$$
which represents a geometric distribution with $p=1-e^{-\lambda}$ by definition.

# Examples
>[!example] Exponential Order Statistics
>Let $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n} \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{i})$ be mutually independent. 
>>[!example]- What is the distribution of $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$?
>>Observe that since each variable $X_{i}$ denotes the time at which the $i$-th event occurs, then $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$ denotes the time until an event occurs. As such, the minimum will be much smaller than just a single $X_{i}$.
>>
>>Think about this in survival time terms. The survival time of $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})$ is
>>$$\begin{align}
>>P(\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) > t) &= P(X_{1} > t, \ldots, X_{n} > t) \\
>>&= P(X_{1}>t) \times \ldots \times P(X_{n} > t) \\
>>&= \prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\lambda_{i} t} \\
>>&= e^{-t \sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}},
>>\end{align}$$
>>and therefore $\min(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) \sim \operatorname{Exp}\left( \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} \right)$.
>>
>>Think of it like $n$ independent phone lines, each getting random calls at their own rate $\lambda_i$. The time until the very first phone rings is faster because all the lines are “competing”–together, they get calls at the combined rate $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_n$.
>
>Now let $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3} \sim_{\text{iid}} \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ be mutually independent.
>>[!example]- Given that $\min(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}) = m$, what is the probability that the difference between the median and the smallest is at least $s$?

>[!note] Gaussian Distribution
>A continuous random variable $X \in \mathbb{R}$ follows the **Gaussian distribution** $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with parameters $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, defined by the [[2.2c.1 Probability Density Function|probability density function]]
>$$f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}.$$
>
>The Gaussian distribution is used to model real-valued data that tend to cluster around a central value (mean) $\mu$ with symmetric dispersion $\sigma$.
>
>Moreover, if $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, then $X$ is a **standard normal random variable**. Its probability density function simplifies to $f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$, which leads to its cumulative distribution function,
>$$\Phi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2 \pi }}\int^{x}_{-\infty}e^{-x^2/2}dx.$$
>
>A key characteristic of the normal distribution is the **empirical rule (68-95-99 rule)**, which states that around $68\%$, $95\%$, and $99\%$ of the data falls within $1\sigma$, $2\sigma$, and $3\sigma$ of the mean.
>>[!warning] Standardization
>>Any Gaussian random variable can be standardized into the Normal distribution using the transformation $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$.

# Properties
#### (*Mean*) $\mathbb{E}[X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)]=\mu$.

#### (*Variance*) $Var[X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)] = \sigma^2$.

#### (*Sum*) If $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_{X}^2)$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\eta, \sigma_{Y}^2)$, then $X+Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu+\eta, \sigma_{X}^2+\sigma_{Y}^2)$.
#### (*Rotational Symmetry*)
#### (Positive Gaussian) $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X>0] = \sigma \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X+Y > 0]$.
Since we know that $f_{X \mid A}(x)=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(X \in A)}$, we proceed as follows:
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}[X \mid X > 0] &= \int^{\infty}_{0} xf_{X \mid X >0}(x)dx \\
&= \frac{\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xf_{X}(x)dx}{\mathbb{P}(X>0)} \\
&= \frac{\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xf_{X}(x)dx}{0.5} \\
&= \frac{2}{\sigma\sqrt{ 2\pi }}\int^{\infty}_{ 0 }xe^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}dx \\
&= -\sigma^2\sqrt{ \frac{2}{\pi\sigma^2} } e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} \bigg|^{\infty}_{x=0} \\
&= \sigma \sqrt{ \frac{2}{\pi} }
\end{align}$$

>[!note] LTI Frequency Response
>The $2\pi$-periodic continuous frequency response of a discrete-time [[2.2a LTI System|LTI system]] can be expressed by convolving its filter $h(n)$ with an eigenfunction input $x(n) = e^{j\omega n}$, such that
>$$\begin{align}
>y(n) &= e^{j\omega n}\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} h(k)e^{-j\omega k} \\
&=H(\omega)e^{j \omega n},
\end{align}$$
>where $H(\omega) = \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty} h(k)e^{-j\omega k}$ is the frequency response of the system, while $\omega$ ($\text{rad}/\text{sample}$) is the fundamental period of the eigenfunction.
>
>Similarly, in continuous-time, the non-periodic continuous frequency response of an LTI system can be expressed by convolving its filter $h(t)$ with an eigenfunction input $x(t) = e^{j\omega t}$, such that
>$$\begin{align}
>y(t) &= e^{j\omega t}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}h(\tau)e^{-j\omega \tau}d\tau \\
>&= H(\omega)e^{j \omega t},
\end{align}$$
>where $H(\omega) = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}h(\tau)e^{-j\omega \tau}d\tau$ is the frequency response of the system.
>>[!warning] Note (New Frequencies)
>>If the output $y$ of a system contains frequencies that are not in its input $x$, then that system cannot be an LTI system; no new frequencies can be created in the output of an LTI system.

# Intuition
9/30 lecture around 40 min to 1:10

# Properties
#### (Standard Conversion) $h(t) = \alpha e^{-\alpha t} \iff H(\omega) = \frac{\beta}{\alpha + j\omega}$.

#### (D-T Eigenfunction Periodicity) $e^{j\omega n}$ is $2\pi$-periodic in $\omega$ and is only periodic in $n$ if $\omega$ is a rational multiple of $\pi$.
We need to decompose this problem into two sub-problems:
1. We begin by equating $e^{j(\omega + W)n}=e^{j\omega n}$, which simplifies into $e^{jWn} = 1$ and into $Wn = 2\pi$. This means that $n=\frac{2\pi}{W} = \omega$.

#### (D-T $2\pi$-periodicity) $H(\omega + 2\pi) = H(\omega)$
We can prove by taking the following:
$$H(\omega + 2\pi)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k}e^{-j2\pi k}.$$
Since for any integer $k$, $e^{j2k\pi}=e^{j2\pi}=1$ due to $2\pi$-periodicity of complex exponentials,
$$\begin{align}
H(\omega + 2\pi) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k}e^{-j2\pi k} \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{-j\omega k} \times 1 \\
&= H(\omega).
\end{align}$$
#### (Real Conjugate) If $h(n)=h\textasteriskcentered(n)$ or $h(t) = h\textasteriskcentered(t)$, then $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$.
Saying that a function is equal to its complex conjugate simply means that it is real. We proceed with a simple proof, where
$$\begin{align}
H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) &= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h\textasteriskcentered(k)e^{-j\omega k} \\
&= \sum^{\infty}_{k=-\infty}h(k)e^{j(-\omega) k} \\
&= H(-\omega).
\end{align}$$
#### (Even Magnitude) If $H\textasteriskcentered(\omega) = H(-\omega)$, then $|H(\omega)| = |H(-\omega)|$.
The LHS implies that $H$ is real.

>[!note] Mesh-Current Method
>The **Mesh-Current Method** is a technique used to find the current flowing in each loop (or mesh) of a circuit. A **mesh** is defined as a loop that does not enclose any other loops. This method simplifies the process of solving for unknown currents in planar circuits by applying [[2.2c KVL|Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law]] to each independent loop.

```tikz
\usepackage{circuitikz}
\begin{document}

\begin{circuitikz} \draw
    % Mesh 1
    (0,0) to[V, v=$V_1$] (0,3) 
    to[R=$R_1$, i=$I_1$] (3,3)
    to[R=$R_3$, i_=$I_1 - I_2$] (6,3) 
    -- (6,0) to[short] (0,0)
    
    % Mesh 2
    (6,0) to[V, v=$V_2$, invert] (6,-3)
    to[R=$R_2$, i=$I_2$] (3,-3)
    -- (0,-3) to[short] (0,0)
    
    % Closing loop for mesh 2
    (3,-3) to[R=$R_3$, i_=$I_2 - I_1$] (3,0)
    ;
    
    % Labels for the mesh currents
    \node at (1.5, 1.5) {$I_1$};
    \node at (4.5, -1.5) {$I_2$};

    % Loops around each mesh
    \draw[dashed, thick, blue] (1.5,0) circle(2);
    \node[blue] at (1.5,4) {Mesh 1: $V_1 = I_1R_1 + (I_1 - I_2)R_3$};
    
    \draw[dashed, thick, red] (4.5,0) circle(2);
    \node[red] at (7.5,-3) {Mesh 2: $V_2 = I_2R_2 + (I_2 - I_1)R_3$};

\end{circuitikz}

\end{document}
```

>[!note] Options
>An **option** is a financial instrument (traded both OTC and on exchanges) that gives the holder **the right, but not the obligation**, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed predetermined price called the **strike price** (or **exercise price**) on or before a future maturity date, after which the option is invalidated:
>- A **call option** gives the holder the right to buy the underlier, whereas a **put option** gives the holder the right to sell the underlier.
>- **American options** can be executed before or on the maturity date, whereas **European options** (common form for non-US options) can only be executed on the maturity date.
>
>
>The price (or premium) of an option at time $t \geq 0$ can be decomposed into two components–its **intrinsic value** (payoff), and its **time value**–such that
>$$P_{t} = \text{IV}_{t} + \text{TV}_{t}.$$
>Here the intrinsic value (payoff) is the value the option would have if the TTM was zero:
>$$\text{IV}_{t}=\begin{cases}
\max(S_{t}-F_{0}, 0) & \text{call option}, \\
\max(F_{0}-S_{t}, 0) & \text{put option},
\end{cases}$$
>where $S_{t}$ is the spot at time $t$, and $F_{0}$ is the strike.
>
>Thus, if $P_{t} > \text{IV}_{t}$ (or equivalently, $\text{TV}_{t}>0$), then one should either sell the option or hold it rather than exercise it. Note that as the option approaches maturity (i.e., $t \to T$), $\text{TV}_{t} \to 0$ and $\text{IV}_{t} \to P_{t}$.
>
>The more volatile that the underlying asset is, the higher the probability that it will be in-the-money at expiration. Given the uncertainty of options pricing, complex methods can be utilized to estimate the price of an option at a given time–one of which is the [[2.2d.2i Black-Scholes Options Pricing|Black-Scholes equation]].

>[!note] LTI Linear Constant Coefficient Difference Equation (LCCDE) Representation
>A **linear constant coefficient difference equation** is a mathematical expression that describes the relationship between the input and output of an [[2.2 LTI Systems|LTI system]]. In discrete-time, is defined as the relationship
>$$\sum^{N}_{k = 0}a_{k}y(n-k) = \sum^{M}_{m = 0}b_{m}x(n-m),$$
>where $N$ is the order of the equation, and $M$ is the delay of the input terms.
>
>Similarly, in continuous-time, 

# Properties
#### (Transfer Function) $H(\omega) = \frac{\sum^{M}_{m=0}b_{m}e^{-j\omega m}}{\sum^{N}_{k=0}a_{k}e^{-j\omega k}}.$

# Example
>[!example] (Discrete-Time) Finding the Transfer Function Using the LCCDE
>In 2.2d, we found that the system with a recursive LCCDE $y(n)=\alpha y(n-N) + x(n)$ has a frequency response of $H(\omega) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha e^{-j\omega N}}$. However, there is a simpler way to find this. The LCCDE for an eigenfunction input $x(n)=e^{j\omega n}$ becomes
>$$H(\omega)e^{j\omega n} = \alpha H(\omega)e^{j\omega(n-N)}+e^{j\omega n}.$$
>Dividing both sides by $e^{j\omega n}$ and factoring out $H(\omega)$, we get
>$$H(\omega) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha e^{-j\omega N}}.$$
>It's as simple as that.

>[!note] Second-Order Circuits
>Second-order circuits are electrical circuits whose behavior is described by a second-order differential equation. These circuits contain both [[2.1i Inductor|inductors]] and [[2.1g Capacitor|capacitors]]. Second-order circuits follow the general equation
>$$\frac{d^2}{dt^2}x(t) + 2\alpha\frac{d}{dt}x(t) + \omega_0^2x(t) = f(t),$$
>where $\alpha$ is the damping coefficient, and $\omega_0$ is the resonant frequency of the circuit at which the impedance is purely real.
>
>The solutions to the second-order differential circuits can be split into 3 cases:
>1. Overdamped Response ($\alpha > \omega_0$):
>$$x(t) = A_1e^{s_1t}+A_2e^{s_2t}+x(\infty),$$
>where $s=-\alpha \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \omega_0^2}$ and the coefficients $A_k =$
>
>2. Critically Damped Response ($\alpha = \omega_0$)
>3. Underdamped Response ($\alpha < \omega_0$)

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:07:32","modified":"2024/11/06 02:18:39"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Sinusoidal Signals
>A **sinusoidal signal** is a type of continuous wave that oscillates smoothly and periodically over time, following the mathematical form of a sine or cosine function. Sinusoidal signals are the core of AC analysis. A sinusoidal signal can be represented of the form
>$$x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi),$$
>where $A$ is the signal's magnitude, $\omega=2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ is its angular frequency, and $\phi$ is its phase angle (the amount by which it is shifted from the standard cosine waveform).

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.2 Phasor]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 01:23:33","modified":"2024/11/06 02:12:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Phasor
>A **phasor** is a [[7.2a Complex Exponentials|complex number representation]] of a sinusoidal function that helps simplify the analysis of sinusoidal steady-state behavior in electrical circuits. It represents both the amplitude and the phase of a sinusoidal wave. In mathematical terms, a phasor can be expressed as:
>$$X = |X|e^{j\phi} \iff X = |X| \angle \phi,$$
>where $|X|$ is the phasor's peak amplitude, and $\phi$ is its phase angle.
>
>Using [[7.2b Euler's Theorem|Euler's theorem]], any [[2.2j.1 Sinusoidal Signals|time-varying sinusoidal signal]] $x(t)$ can be expressed in the form
>$$x(t) = \mathscr{Re}\{X e^{j\omega t} \},$$
>where $x(t) = \mathscr{Re}\{|X|e^{j\phi}e^{j\omega t}\} = \cos(\omega t + \phi).$ Only the real part of its phasor is taken, as its imaginary part does not have any physical-world implications.
>
>To gain some intuition, provided is a table of some standard time-variant functions and their phasor representations:
>
>|                  $x(t)$                  |              $X$               |
| :--------------------------------------: | :----------------------------: |
|            $A \cos (\omega t)$             |              $A$               |
|        $A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$         |          $Ae^{j\phi}$          |
|        $-A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$        |     $Ae^{j(\phi \pm \pi)}$     |
|            $A \sin \omega t$             |      $Ae^{-j\pi/2} = -jA$      |
|        $A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$         |     $Ae^{j(\phi - \pi/2)}$     |
|        $-A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$        |     $Ae^{j(\phi + \pi/2)}$     |
|          $\frac{d}{dt} x(t)$           |          $j\omega X$           |
| $\frac{d}{dt} [A \cos(\omega t + \phi)]$ |      $j\omega Ae^{j\phi}$      |
|            $\int x(t) \, dt$             |     $\frac{1}{j\omega} X$      |
|   $\int A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \, dt$   | $\frac{1}{j\omega} Ae^{j\phi}$ |
>>[!warning] Note!
>>Differentiation of a time function $x(t)$ in the time domain is equivalent to multiplication of its phasor counterpart $X$ by $j\omega$ in the phasor domain. Similarly, integration of $x(t)$ in the time domain is equivalent to dividing its phasor $X$ by $j\omega$ in the phasor domain.

# Intuition
The phasor (frequency) domain is generally used for simplification of mathematical derivations. In the phasor domain, as seen above, operations such as differentiation and integration become straightforward.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.4 Transfer Functions]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:12:37","modified":"2024/11/20 21:03:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Transfer Function
>A **transfer function** is a mathematical representation that describes the input-output relationship of a system in the frequency domain, providing its frequency response. For a system $X(j\omega)$, 
>$$H(j\omega) = \frac{X_\text{out}(j\omega)}{X_\text{in}(j\omega)} = |H(j\omega)|e^{j\omega \phi},$$
>where by definition $|H(j\omega)|$ is the system's gain (or magnitude), and $\phi(j\omega) = \tan^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{Im}\{H(\omega)\}}{\mathrm{Re}\{H(\omega)\}}$ is the system's phase response.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.2j.5 Bode Plots]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/11/06 02:12:26","modified":"2024/11/30 17:06:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bode Plot
>A **bode plot** are graphical representations of the [[2.2j.4 Transfer Functions|frequency response]] of a system. It consists of two separate plots that display how the system's **magnitude** and **phase** responds to different values of $\omega$ on the logarithmic scale.
>
>The magnitude of a transfer function $H(j\omega)$ in decibels (SI: dB) is given by
>$$20\log_{10}|H(j\omega)|,$$
>and the phase of a transfer function is given by
>$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{Im}\{H(j\omega)\}}{\mathrm{Re}\{H(j\omega)\}}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3 Calling Convention]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/06 13:57:21","modified":"2024/07/08 12:43:17"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] RISC-V Calling Convention
>In RISC-V, there are some rules which the programmer is advised to follow. The following are rules for callee-saved registers (registers saved by the function being called):
>1. The register `x2` is reserved as a "stack pointer" (sp), and points to the bottom of the stack. Data above `x2` is (technically) immutable, and `x2` can be decremented during a function call to allocate more space on the stack if its value is returned back to its pre-function call value after the call.
>2. The registers `s0` to `s11` are "saved" registers, meaning that just as `x2`, they need to be restored at the end of the function call. We can do so using `sw s0 0(sp)` in the beginning of the function, and `lw s0 0(sp)` towards the end.
>
>
>The following are caller-saved registers (saved and restored by the function that is calling):
>1. The register `x1` (aka `ra`) is reserved as the register to store return addresses in . There are two pseudoinstructions, `jal label` and `ret` (`ja label`), which assume `x1` as the return address.
>2. The registers `a0` to `a7` are registers used for function arguments, and `a0` and `a1` can alsobe used for return values.
>3. If a function needs more than 8 arguments, the temporary registers `t0` to `t6` can be used as addresses.
>
>The following are miscellaneous registers:
>1. The register `x0` always stores 0/0x0.
>8. The register `x3` is the "global pointer", used to store a reference on the heap.
>9. The register `x4` is the "thread pointer," used to separate stacks for threads.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3 Convex Conjugates]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/29 22:36:19","modified":"2025/05/15 13:51:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Convex Conjugate
>The **convex (Fenchel) conjugate** $f^*: X^* \to \mathbb{R}$ of a function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ is used to represent $f$ as a set of supporting hyperplanes with slopes $x^*$, such that the parameters of each $x^*$ are encoded in $f^*$. Then, $f^*(x^*)$ is the intercept at which the line $\langle x^*, x \rangle$ becomes a tangent of $f$.  Formally,
>$$f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x \in X} \{ \langle x^*, x \rangle - f(x)\},$$
>such that $t(x) = \langle x^*, x \rangle - f^*(x^*)$.
>
>>[!warning] Preservation of Convexity
>>The convex conjugate of any function is always a convex function.

# Properties
#### (*Fenchel's Inequality*) Any conjugate pair $f, f^*$ satisfies $\langle x^*, x \rangle \leq f(x) + f^*(x^*)$.
#### (*Weak Duality of Biconjugation*) For any $f$, it follows that $f^{* *} \leq f$, such that $f^{**}=f$ if and only if $f$ is convex and l.s.c.
#### (*Affine Conjugate*) Any $a(x)=\langle x^*_{a}, x \rangle + b$ has $a^*(x^*)=\begin{dcases}-b & x^*=x_{a}^* \\ + \infty & x^* \neq x_{a}^*\end{dcases}$, and $a^{**}(x)=a(x)$.


# Examples
>[!example] Economic Interpretation
>Let $x$ be the quantity of some goods you are trying to sell (i.e., laptops, tablets, phones, etc.). Then $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ can be defined as the total cost of producing the goods (i.e., the dot product between $x$ and the respective cost of producing 1 unit of each good). Take the Fenchel conjugate of $f(x)$:
>$$\underbrace{f^*(x^*)}_{\text{Profit}}=\sup_{x \in X}\{ \underbrace{\langle x^*, x \rangle}_{\text{Revenue}} - \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{Cost}} \}.$$
>Then, $f^*: X^* \to \mathbb{R}$ represents the optimal profit given the goods are sold at some prices $x^*$ per 1 unit of goods.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.1 Private Equity]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:32:35","modified":"2025/05/12 22:51:22"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Private Equity
>**Private equity firms** are investment management companies that raise capital from institutional and high-net-worth investors to acquire controlling ownership stakes in established but failing privately held or publicly traded companies. 
>
>The goal of PE is to increase the value of these businesses through operational improvements, strategic guidance, and financial restructuring, often using significant leverage (debt financing), before exiting through a sale or IPO.
>
>As with VCs and hedge funds, private equity firms earn profit based on the **2 and 20 model**, which utilizes a 2% management fee (based on AUM), plus 20% of all profits.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2i Venture Capital]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:32:44","modified":"2025/05/12 21:21:54"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Venture Capital
>**Venture capital firms** provide funding to early-stage, high-growth potential startups in exchange for equity ownership. Unlike private equity firms, they typically do not utilize debt financing (leverage), do not hold a majority stake in their investments, and instead take on higher risk in pursuit of outsized returns. 
>
>The goal of VCs is to help startups scale rapidly and eventually exit through an acquisition or IPO, realizing significant gains on their equity stake.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2iii Convertible Securities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 20:36:19","modified":"2025/05/12 23:29:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!notes] Convertible Securities
>**Convertible securities** are financial instruments commonly used in startup financing that begin as debt or contract-based investments and convert into preferred stock upon a specified future event, such as a valuation cap or discount (i.e., shares are priced lower than for new investors at subsequent raises). They allow early-stage startups to delay valuation negotiations while raising initial capital.
>
>There are two major types of convertible securities:
>- **Simple Agreement for Future Equity (SAFEs)** are contractual agreements created by Y Combinator (the largest accelerator in the world) that provide the right to obtain equity in the future without being a loan or having a maturity date.
>	- SAFEs do not have an interest or a maturity date.
>- **Convertible notes** are a short-term debt instrument that converts into equity in a future financing round.
>	- Since convertible notes are debt, they have an interest (usually $4\% - 8\%$ per year) and a fixed maturity date ($12-24$ months). If no conversion event occurs, the debt is due at maturity. Convertible notes work in favor of the investor, who is protected in case of downturn.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.2iv Stock Options]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 23:14:01","modified":"2025/05/13 00:04:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Stock Options
>**Employee Stock Options** are a form of equity compensation that give employees the right–but not the obligation–to purchase a specified number of company shares at a fixed price (called the **strike price**) after meeting certain conditions, such as vesting. 
>
>The **strike price** is usually set at the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the company at the time the option is granted, as determined by a third-party valuation firm (e.g., through a 409A valuation in the U.S.).
>
>ESOs are typically given with a vesting schedule–typically 4 years with a **1-year cliff** (meaning the first 25% vests after one year, and the rest vests monthly or quarterly thereafter). They can be exercised after they vest and within a **fixed post-termination window** (often 90 days after leaving the company).

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3a.3 Hedge Funds]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:38:45","modified":"2025/05/12 20:47:40"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Hedge Funds
>**Hedge funds** are pooled investment vehicles that employ a wide range of strategies–such as long/short equity, global macro, event-driven, and arbitrage–primarily in public markets.
>
>They aim to generate high absolute returns regardless of market direction, often using debt financing (leverage), derivatives, and short selling to amplify gains and hedge risks. 
>
>Managed by professional investment advisors, hedge funds typically cater to institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals, operating with fewer regulatory constraints than mutual funds.

NOTE TITLE: [[2.3c ETFs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/05/12 19:30:14","modified":"2025/05/12 21:00:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Exchange-Traded Funds
>An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** is an investment fund that holds a diversified portfolio of underlying assets, and can be bought and sold on stock exchanges (secondary markets), just like individual equities (stocks).
>
>ETFs can be structured to track anything from the price of a commodity to a large and diverse collection of stocks, which may be done either using passive or active investment strategies. **Leveraged ETFs** seek to deliver multiples of daily index returns by leveraging derivatives and shorting. However, leveraged ETFs typically underperform relative to objectives in the long run.
>
>As with [[2.3b Mutual Funds|mutual funds]], dividends, interest, and capital gains (although rare for ETFs) from the pool are distributed to ETF shareholders. However, since ETFs trade intraday, the supply of shares is regulated through a **creation and redemption** mechanism, which keeps market price close to the **Net Asset Value (NAV)** to prevent inefficiencies that create arbitrage opportunities. It involves a two-step process:
>1. When an ETF manager wants to issue more shares, an authorized participant (AP) buys shares of the assets associated with the ETF.
>2. Then, the AP sells or exchanges the assets to the ETF for new shares of the ETF at equal value. 
>
>In turn, the AP sells the ETF shares in the market for a profit if the selling price is greater than the ETF's NAV, creating an arbitrage opportunity.
>
>The top 3 ETFs based on Assets under Management (AUM) are the **SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY)**, the iShares S&5 500 ETF (IVY), and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO).

>[!note] Divide-and-Conquer
>**Divide-and-conquer** is a problem-solving technique that breaks a complex problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems, solves each subproblem recursively until it bottoms out (i.e. reaches the recursive base case), and then combines their solutions to solve the original problem. It consists of three steps:
>1. **Divide** the problem into subproblems that are smaller instances of the same problem.
>2. **Conquer** the subproblems by solving them recursively.
>3. **Combine** the subproblem solutions to form a solution to the original problem.
>
>Divide-and-conquer problems are analyzed using **recurrences** $T(n)$ that describe the overall running time of an algorithm in terms of the running time of its subproblems. There are a few methods for solving recurrences. Namely, these are:
>- The **master method**, which provides bounds for recurrences of the form $T(n) = aT(n / b) + f(n)$, given constants $a>0$, $b>1$ and a driving function $f(n)$.
>- The **substitution method**, 
>- The **recursion-tree method,**
>- The **Akra-Bazzi method**,

>There are numerous ways to compute the product of two matrices. One way to do so is using a simple divide-and-conquer algorithm with two input matrices $A$ and $B$, and one zero-initialized output matrix $C$. In the algorithm: 
>1. We will partition each $n \times n$ matrix into four $\frac{n}{2} \times \frac{n}{2}$ sub-matrices.
>2. We will recursively call the function for each of the eight pairs of submatrices.
>3. At the base case, each recursive call adds the product of the scalars $A$ and $B$ to the designated element of $C$.
