NOTE TITLE: [[3. Typical Sets]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/27 20:01:58","modified":"2025/03/03 20:26:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Typical Sets
>A **typical set** is an exponentially smaller subset of the space of all $n$-length sequences $\mathcal{X}^n$ (where $|\mathcal{X}^n|=2^{n\log_{2}|\mathcal{X}|}$), which captures most of the probability mass of the source as $n$ grows large. Formally, the $\epsilon$-typical set $A_{\epsilon}^{(n)} \subset \mathcal{X}^n$ is the set of $n$-length sequences $X^{n} = X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$, such that each sequence has a uniform probability of approximately $2^{\mathbb{E}[\log_{2}p_{X}(X^n)]}=2^{-nH(x)}$:
>$$A_{\epsilon}^{(n)} = \{ X^{n} \in \mathcal{X}^n : 2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)} \leq p_{X^n}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) \leq 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)} \},$$
>where $|A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}| \approx 2^{nH(X)}$.
>
>As $n$ grows large, sequences in the (much smaller) typical set $A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}$ contain virtually all the probability mass of $\mathcal{X}^n$. Mathematically, this means that $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}(A_{\epsilon}^{(n)}) = 1$. This property of typical sets is known as **asymptotic equipartition**, and is the LLN-equivalent analogue in information theory. Mathematically,
>$$-\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}p_{X^n}(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}) \to H(X) \quad \text{in probability},$$
>meaning that the per-symbol self-information of a sequence converges to the entropy.
# Properties



# Examples

>[!example] Biased Coin Flips
>You flip $100$ coins with probability $1/4$ of coming up heads.
>>[!example]-  What is the size of the sample space? 
>>We know that each coin can either land on $H$ or $T$. For 100 coins, this becomes $|\Omega| = 2^{100}$.
>
>>[!example]- What is the size of the typical set, and how do the two sizes compare?
>>We can calculate the entropy of each coin as $$H(X) = 0.25 \log 4+0.75\log\frac{4}{3}=0.811 \text{ bits per coinflip.}$$
>>Therefore, the size of the typical set is $\approx 2^{81}$, or $\frac{2^{81}}{2^{100}} = \frac{1}{2^{19}}$ of the size of the sample space.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.1 Concentration Inequalities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/08/07 14:26:17","modified":"2025/08/08 20:52:26"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Concentration Inequalities
>**Concentration inequalities** provide probabilistic bounds on how far a random variable is likely to be from some central value without requiring full knowledge of the distribution:
>- The **Markov inequality** provides a bound on the probability that a nonnegative random variable takes a value significantly larger than its mean. Let $X \ge 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[X] < \infty$. Then for any $c > 0$,
>$$P(X \ge c) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{c}.$$
>
>- The **Chebyshev inequality** strengthens this by incorporating variance, yielding a bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean from above or below by more than a specified amount. For any $X$ with $\mathbb{E}[X] < \infty$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) < \infty$, it follows that
>$$P(|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \ge c) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.$$
>By applying Markov’s Inequality to the nonnegative random variable $(X-\mu)^2$, Chebyshev’s bound follows immediately.
>‎ 
>- Finally, the **Chernoff bound** provides an exponentially decreasing bound on the tail probabilities of a random variable using its [[Mathematics/2. Probability/2. Random Variables/2.3 Functions of Random Variables/2.5c Moment Generating Functions.md|moment generating function]]. For any $X$ with $M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] < \infty$, and for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$, it directly follows from the Markov inequality that
>$$\mathbb{P}(X \ge c) \le \inf_{t \ge 0} \left\{ \frac{M_{X}(t)}{e^{tc}} \right\}.$$

# Intuition
The proof for Markov's Inequality is derived directly from the definition of expectation:
$$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum^{}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}x \cdot \mathbb{P}(X=x) \\
&\ge \sum^{}_{x \ge c}x \cdot \mathbb{P}(X=x) \\
&\ge \sum^{}_{x \ge c}c \cdot \mathbb{P}(X = x) \\
&= c \sum^{}_{x \ge c} \mathbb{P}(X = x) \\
&= c \cdot \mathbb{P}(X \ge c),
\end{align}$$
where the second line follows from the fact that $X$ is nonnegative.

As previously mentioned, Chebyshev's Inequality is a direct consequence of centering $X$ around its mean. Define $Y=(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2$. Then,
$$\begin{align}
P((X-E[X])^2 \ge c^2)&=P(| X-E[X] | \ge c) \\
&\ge \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]}{c^2} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.
\end{align}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[3.1b CAGR]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/24 18:18:19","modified":"2025/03/18 12:57:47"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Compound Annual Growth Rate
>**Compound Annual Growth Rate** (also called compound return) is the cumulative growth of an investment over multiple periods, where the net simple return $R_{t}$ from each period $t$ is reinvested and earns returns in subsequent periods. Formally, the CAGR between time $t_0$ and $t$, given $n$-period returns, is given as
>$$1+R_{t_{0}, t}=\left[\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+R_{t_{0}+i})\right]^{\frac{1}{nt}}.$$
>
>The compounded return over $T$ years, paid $n$ times per year and given an APR $r$ can generally be calculated as
>$$1+R_{T} = \left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nT}.$$
>
>Letting $n \to \infty$ yields continuous returns, such that
>$$1+R_{T} = \lim_{ n \to \infty }\left[\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\right]=e^{rT},$$
>which yields the **log return** $\ln(1+R_{T})=rT$.
>
>>[!warning] Compound Return Excludes the Initial Period $t$
>>Period $t$ isn’t included in the compound return formula because it’s the the subsequent returns that measure the growth or changes in value over the previous period, not the initial period itself.

>[!note] Average Return
>**Average return** is a measure of the central tendency of returns over a period of time, representing the typical or mean performance of an investment or asset. For returns $R_{t}, R_{t+1}, \ldots, R_{t+n}$, the ***arithmetic average return*** is given as
>$$\bar{R}_{\text{A}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=0}R_{t+i},$$
>whereas the ***geometric average return*** is given as
>$$\bar{R}_{\text{G}}=\left(1+\prod^{n}_{i=1}R_{t+i}\right)^\frac{1}{n}.$$

NOTE TITLE: [[3.2 Laws of Large Numbers]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/08 05:55:31","modified":"2025/08/07 15:44:46"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Laws of Large Numbers
>**The Weak Law of Large Numbers** is a direct consequence of [[3.1 Concentration Inequalities|Chebyshev’s inequality]] and describes the convergence of sample averages to the expected value. Formally, if $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$, then for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$P\left(\left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i - \mu\right| \ge \varepsilon\right) \to 0 \quad \text{as} \quad n \to \infty.$$
Since the variance of the sample mean is $\sigma^2/n$, Chebyshev’s inequality shows that the probability of a deviation of size $\varepsilon \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, establishing convergence in probability.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.2b Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/11 12:09:24","modified":"2024/08/09 00:30:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium
>A strategy profile $s^*$ constitutes a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium if for every [[3.2a Subgame|subgame]] $G_E^d$ with root note $d$  in $G_E$, $s^*$ constitutes a [[2.2c Nash Equilibrium|Nash equilibrium]] within $G_E^d$.
>
>Equivalently, a strategy profile $s^*$ constitutes an SPNE if $\forall s_i \in s^*$, every $s_i$ is [[3.2 Sequential Rationality|sequentially rational]] at the root node.
>
>The path of play in a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium is known as the **equilibrium path**.
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The SPNE can never involve mixing in extensive form games of perfect information, since every player's action is observable.
# Intuition
What is the difference between NE and SPNE? Well:
- Nash equilibrium requires rational behavior (best response) only on the path of play.
- SPNE requires rational behavior **ON AND OFF** the path of play.
	- Done to add credibility to threats; if a strategy is not rational, then threatening with it will be irrational.

How do we find SPNEs? Using backward induction. Start at the last non-terminal node. Check the best response of the player at that node. Do so for all nodes on that level. Go back one level, and do the same for the other player. More on this in the future!

# Properties
#### *(Existence)* At least one SPNE exists in any finite extensive form game.
#### (*Uniqueness)* If no players are indifferent between terminal nodes, there is a unique SPNE.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.3 Central Limit Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/21 15:42:11","modified":"2025/08/09 15:00:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Central Limit Theorem
>The **Central Limit Theorem** states that, under certain conditions, the distribution of the **standardized sum** (or average) of a large number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables approaches a [[2.2c.5 Gaussian Distribution|normal distribution]], regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.
>
>Formally, let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and define the sum $S_{n}=\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}X_{i}$. Then, it follows that
>$$\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \frac{S_{n} - \mathbb{E}[S_{n}]}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(S_{n}) }} \leq x \right) = \lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \frac{S_{n} - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{ n }} \leq x \right) = \Phi(x),$$ 
>where $\Phi(x)$ is the CDF of the normal distribution.

# Proof




# Examples
>[!example] Binomial Concentration
>Here, we will prove that the binomial distribution is concentrated about its mean as the number of trials tends to $\infty$. Suppose we have i.i.d. trials, each with a probability of success $1/2$. Let $S_{n}$ be the number of successes in the first $n$ trials.
>>[!example]- Compute the mean and variance of $S_{n}$.
>>Since $S_{n} \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$, it follows that $\mathbb{E}(S_{n}) = n/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_{n})=n/4$.
>
>>[!example]- Define $Z_{n}$ in terms of $S_{n}$ such that $Z_{n}$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$.
>>To normalize the sum, let $Z_{n} = \frac{S_{n} - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{ n }}$. Since $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ should be the mean and variance of a single trial $X_i$, then in terms of $S_{n}$,
>>$$Z_{n} = \frac{S_{n} - \mathbb{E}(S_{n})}{\sqrt{ \operatorname{Var}(X) }} = \frac{S_{n} - n/2}{\sqrt{ n } / 2}.$$
>
>>[!example]- What is the distribution of $Z_{n}$ as $n \to \infty$?
>>Per CLT, we have that $\lim\limits_{ n \to \infty } f_{Z}(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ 2\pi }}e^{-z^2 / 2}$, and therefore $Z_n \to \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ in the discrete realm.
>
>>[!example]- Use the bound $P(Z > z) \le (z\sqrt{ 2\pi })^{-1} e^{−z^2/2}$ (where $Z$ is a standard normal) to approximately bound $P(S_{n}/n > 1/2 + \delta)$, where $\delta > 0$.
>>It follows that
>>$$\begin{align}\mathbb{P}(S_{n} / n > 1 / 2 + \delta) &= \mathbb{P}((\sqrt{ n } / 2) Z_{n}) + n / 2 > n / 2 + \delta n) \\ &= \mathbb{P}(Z_{n} > 2\delta \sqrt{ n })  \leq \frac{1}{2\delta\sqrt{ 2\pi n }}\exp(-2\delta^2n).\end{align}$$

>[!example] Packet Erasures & Inverse CDFs
>Alice is sending $1\;000$ bits to Bob. The probability that a bit gets erased is $p$, and the erasure of each bit is independent of the others.
>
>Alice is using a scheme that can tolerate up to one-fifth of the bits being erased. That is, as long as Bob receives at least 801 of the 1000 bits correctly, he can decode Alice’s message. The probability of more than $1 / 5$ of the bits being erased should be at most $10^{-6}$.
>
>>[!example]- Use Chebyshev’s inequality to upper bound $p$ such that the probability of a communications breakdown is at most $10^{-6}$.
>>Express the number of erased bits as $N \sim \text{Bin}(1000, p)$. Then,
>>$$\begin{align}
P(N \ge 200) &= P(N - 1000p \ge 200-1000p)  \\
&\leq \frac{1000p(1-p)}{(200-1000p)^2} \\
&= \frac{p(1-p)}{40(1-5p)^2} \leq 10^{-6}
\end{align}$$
>>which yields $p \le 3.9986 \times 10^{-5}$.
>
>>[!example]- Use CLT to find an approximate bound for p such that the probability of a communications breakdown is at most $10^{-6}$. Note that $\Phi^{-1}(1-10^{-6}) \approx 4.753$.
>>Let $N \sim \operatorname{Bin}(1000, p)$ be again the number of erasures. Then, $Z=\dfrac{N-1000p}{10\sqrt{ p(1-p) }}$. As such, it holds that
>>$$\begin{alignat}{0}
>>\begin{aligned}
>>P(N \ge 200) &= P\left( Z \ge \frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} \right) \\ &= 1- \Phi\left( \frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} \right) \le 10^{-6} \\
>>\end{aligned} \\ \\
>>\Big\Updownarrow \\ \\
>>\begin{aligned}
>>\frac{200-1000p}{\sqrt{ 1000p(1-p) }} &\ge \Phi^{-1}(1-10^{-6}) = 4.753.
>>\end{aligned}
>>\end{alignat}
>>$$
>>This yields $p \le 0.1468$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.3a Population Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:47:25","modified":"2023/12/13 09:56:43"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Population Distribution
>The population distribution consists of all the members in a population. It is tough to collect data for every member of the population (called a census), so other methods are needed to summarize data.

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>If we want to eat somewhere in San Francisco, but we want to look at the restaurants' Yelp ratings first, then the ratings of each of all the restaurants in the city will make up the population distribution. Let's say restaurants are rated on a 5-star basis. Then the count of all restaurants in San Francisco on Yelp, separated by the number of stars they have, will make up the population distribution:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15))
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows)
>p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar()
>plot(p)
>```
>From the plot above, we can conclude that the mean and standard deviation of the distribution are $\upmu = 3.3$ and $\upsigma = 1.1$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.3b Empirical Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:53:11","modified":"2023/12/13 19:10:24"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Empirical Distribution
>The empirical distribution is a distribution derived from a single sample of the population that is significantly smaller than the population distribution.

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's say we look at the Yelp pages of 100 restaurants and sample them by recording their 5-star ratings. Then the count of the 100 samples filtered by their number of stars is the empirical distribution:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15))
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows)
>sampl_1 <- sample_n(df, size = 10, rep = T)
>sampl_2 <- sample_n(df, size = 50, rep = T)
>p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Population \n Distribution")
>s_1 <- ggplot(sampl_1, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Empirical Distribution 1 \n (n = 10)")
>s_2 <- ggplot(sampl_2, aes(x = stars, y = after_stat(prop))) + geom_bar() + labs(title = paste("Empirical Distribution 2 \n (n = 50)"))
>plot(p + s_1 + s_2)
>```
>As we can see after running the code above, the bigger the sample size, the more the empirical distribution resembles the population distribution. After some calculations we find out that sample one (with n = 10) has a mean and standard deviation of $\bar{x}_1 = 3.90$, $s_1 = 1.29$, whereas sample two (with n = 50) has the statistics $\bar{x}_2 = 3.06$, $s_2 = 1.08$. Therefore sample two comes closer to the population mean and s.d. of $\upmu = 3.28$ and $\upsigma = 1.08$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.3c Sampling Distribution]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 06:56:57","modified":"2023/12/13 23:17:54"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Sampling Distribution
>The sampling distribution is a probability distribution of a statistic (a mean or a median) based on many samples of equal size from the population .

>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's say we sample 100 restaurants at a time, calculate their average rating, and repeat the process 500 times (in STAT 20 this is usually the standard repetition number). We can then make a good inference about the whole population based on our sample. Check this out:
>```R
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) 
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows) 
sampl_1 <- data.frame(avg_stars = replicate(500, mean(sample_n(df, size = 10, rep = T)$stars)))
sampl_2 <- data.frame(avg_stars = replicate(500, mean(sample_n(df, size = 100, rep = T)$stars)))
s_1 <- ggplot(sampl_1, aes(x = avg_stars)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "Sampling Distribution 1 \n (n = 10 per sample)") 
s_2 <- ggplot(sampl_2, aes(x = avg_stars)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "Sampling Distribution 2 \n (n = 100 per sample)") 
>plot(s_1 + s_2)
>```

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Inner Product]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/10/28 15:27:05","modified":"2025/03/08 00:59:18"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Inner Product
>The **inner product** is a function that takes two vectors and returns a real scalar quantifying how much the vectors align in direction. 
>
>For a vector space on $\mathbb{R}$, the inner product of vectors $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\vec{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is also called the **dot product**:
>$$\langle \vec{x}, \vec{y} \rangle = \vec{x} \cdot \vec{y} = \vec{x}^T\vec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i.$$
>Furthermore, the dot product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be given by the geometric definition,
>$$\vec{x}^T\vec{y} = \|\vec{x}\|\|\vec{y}\|\cos\theta,$$
>where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors.
>
>However, for vector spaces on $\mathbb{C}$, the inner product introduces the [[7.3 Complex Conjugate|complex conjugate]], which keeps the output scalar on the real line. Therefore, for two complex vectors  $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n$  and  $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the inner product is defined as
>$$\langle \vec{x}, \vec{y} \rangle = \vec{x}^T\vec{y}\textasteriskcentered =\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i\textasteriskcentered.$$


# Properties
#### (*Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality*) $|\vec{x}^T\vec{y}| \leq \|\vec{x}\|\|\vec{y}\|$.
This follows from the fact that $\cos\theta \leq 1$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Standard Error]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 10:04:18","modified":"2023/12/14 04:18:36"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

> [!note] Standard Error of the Mean
> For a population distribution with a standard deviation $\upsigma$ or an empirical distribution with a standard deviation $s$, and a sample size $n$,
> $$SE(\bar{x}) \approx \frac{\upsigma}{\sqrt{n}} \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
> is the standard error of the sampling distribution.
> 
> When $\frac{n}{N}$ (sampling fraction) is big,
> $$SE(\bar{x}) \approx \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\frac{\upsigma}{\sqrt{n}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
> is the standard error of the sampling distribution, where $\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$ is the finite population correction (FPC) factor.
### Intuition
Standard error suggests how much the values of a sampling distribution deviate from the population parameter. When we don't have access to the population distribution, an estimate can be made using an empirical distribution. From the equation above, we can see that as $n$ increases, $SE(\bar{x})$ decreases. This is because as we increase the number of samples $n$, the distribution becomes more condensed around the mean (check [[3.3c Sampling Distribution|3.3c]] for an example of this.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4a Vector Spaces]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/06 15:29:07","modified":"2025/05/14 00:44:39"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Vector Spaces
>A **vector space** $\mathcal{X}$ is a set of [[3.1 Vector|vectors]] that is **closed under addition** and **scalar multiplication**, such that it remains unchanged when those operations are performed. Formally, for any $u,v \in \mathcal{X}$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$, 
>$$\alpha u+ \beta v \in \mathcal{X}.$$
>
>A nonempty subset $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ of the vector space is called a **subspace** of $\mathcal{X}$ if it is also closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
>
>An **affine subspace** is a subspace shifted away from the origin) $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{V}$, where every elements satisfies
>$$\mathcal{A}=\{ \alpha \vec{x} + (1-\alpha)\vec{y} : \vec{x},\vec{y} \in \mathcal{V}, \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \}.$$
>
>>[!warning] Zero Vector
>>Both vector spaces and subspaces **always contain the zero vector** (confirmed by setting $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 0$).

# Properties
#### (*Sum of Subspaces*) For all subspaces $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, their sum $\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{W}$ is also a subspace.

#### (*Direct Sum*) For all subspaces $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, if $\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}=\{ 0 \}$, then $\mathcal{U} \oplus \mathcal{V}=\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{W}$ and every vector in $\mathcal{W}$ can be uniquely represented as $w=u+v$.

#### (Dimension of Direct Sum) For any $\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}$, $\dim(\mathcal{U}+\mathcal{V})=\dim\mathcal{U}+\dim\mathcal{V}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4b Confidence Intervals]] METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 19:30:05","modified":"2023/12/14 04:18:42"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!note] Confidence Interval >A confidence interval with z-score $z$ is a range of values, >$$[\bar{x} - z \times SE, \bar{x} + z \times SE],$$ > derived from the sampling distribution and believed to contain the true value of the population parameter recorded by the sampling distribution with a certain confidence. ### Intuition Suppose we have a standard normal distribution $X \space \textasciitilde \space N(0, 1)$. We can calculate the probability of a number or interval as a part of the whole distribution by looking at the area under the curve: We can see that instead of the observed values, the x-axis records the number of standard deviations each point is from the mean. For example, it turns out that 68% of data falls within -1 and 1 standard deviations from the mean. We see all major intervals below: - $[-\upsigma, \upsigma] = 0.68$ - $[-1.96\upsigma, 1.96\upsigma] = 0.95$ - $[-2.58\upsigma, 2.58\upsigma] = 0.99$ The multiplicative constant before the standard deviation is known as the z-score. We have already implicitly defined the confidence interval; it is simply a generalization of the intervals above. We can finally denote for any z-score $z$, $\bar{x}$ standard error $SE(\bar{x})$ of a sampling distribution, $[\bar{x}-z \times SE, \bar{x}+z \times SE]$. #### Example >[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco >Consider our sampling distribution of the average rating of restaurants in San Francisco when sampling 100 restaurants per sample. We can now plot a confidence interval on our plot! >```R ># Ignore this. Basically creating the population and drawing a sample. >set.seed(123) >rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) >df <- data.frame(stars = rows) >df %>% specify(response = stars) %>% generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") %>% calculate(stat = "mean") %>% get_ci(level = .95) >``` >Running the example above, we can say with 95% confidence that the population parameter falls between 3.22 and 3.35. This means that 5% of the time a sample from the population will generate a confidence interval which does not contain the population parameter, not that 95% of the time the population parameter falls in that range: think about the population parameter as a constant, and the confidence interval as a variable. Therefore, 5% of all generated confidence intervals from all samples of the population do not contain the population parameter.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4b Span]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/04/04 00:30:56","modified":"2025/05/14 00:35:21"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Span
>The **span** of a set of vectors $\mathcal{P}=\left\{\vec{v}_1, \dots, \vec{v}_n\right\} \subseteq \mathcal{R}^n$ is the set of all vectors that can be built using the vectors in $\mathcal{P}$ by scaling and adding them together (i.e., the linear combinations of vectors in $\mathcal{P}$). Formally,
>$$\mathrm{span}(\mathcal{P})=\left\{\sum^{n}_{i=1}\alpha_i \vec{v}_i : \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}\right\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n,$$
>where $\alpha_{i}$ is the scaling factor (or weight) of each vector in $\mathcal{P}$.
>
>If $\mathcal{P}$ contains $k$ linearly independent vectors, then the dimension $d$ of its span is $n \geq d \geq k$. Note that the maximum amount of linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $n$.
>>[!warning] Infinite Property
>>All nonzero vectors in an infinite vector space have an infinitely extending span.

# Intuition
The span is not too hard of a concept.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.4c Bootstrapping]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/13 23:29:17","modified":"2023/12/20 04:30:14"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bootstrapping
>Bootstrapping is a method of estimating a sampling distribution using an empirical distribution by (1) turning it into the **Bootstrap population**, (2) sampling the same number of rows from it with replacement, and (3) calculating a sample statistic until enough statistics (usually 10,000 reps) are gathered to form the **Bootstrap sampling distribution**.
2
>[!example] Restaurants in San Francisco
>Let's go through the process of Bootstrapping step by step. Let's say Yelp is down and we only remember 100 restaurants' 5-star ratings. We want to devise an average rating for all SF restaurants on Yelp. We can write down the ratings we do remember, randomly resample them with replacement and calculate the average rating of each sample. Then, we plot the Bootstrap sampling distribution:
>```R
># Create population (usually we won't be able to do this)
>set.seed(123)
>rows <- sample(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), size = 1000, rep = T, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)) 
>df <- data.frame(stars = rows) 
>
># Sample from population to create empirical distribution (usually your data set, in this case the 100 restaurants you remember)
>sampl <- data.frame(sample_n(df, size = 100, rep = T))
>
># Utilize the Bootstrapping pipeline (resample and record the average rating of restaurants for each sample)
>bs <- sampl %>% specify(response = stars) %>% generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") %>% calculate(stat = "mean")
>
># Plot!
>bs_sd <- bs %>% ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + geom_histogram()
>plot(bs_sd)
>```

>[!note] Vector Norm
>A **vector norm** is a function $\|\cdot\|: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ that provides a way to measure the magnitude of [[3.1 Vector|vectors]] in a vector space. It satisfies the following three properties for all vectors $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in \mathcal{X}$ and scalars $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$:
>1. (*Positive-Definiteness*) $\|\vec{x}\| \geq 0$, where $\|\vec{x}\|=0 \iff \vec{x}=\vec{0}$.
>2. (*Triangle Inequality*) $\|\vec{x}+\vec{y}\|\leq\|\vec{x}\|+\|\vec{y}\|$.
>3. (Positive Homogeneity) $\|\alpha \cdot \vec{x}\|=|\alpha|\cdot\|\vec{x}\|$.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.5b Bipartite Graphs]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/20 22:06:19","modified":"2025/07/21 19:10:25"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Bipartite Graphs
>A **bipartite graph** is a graph whose vertex set $V = U \cup W$ can be divided into two disjoint subsets $U$ and $W$, such that every edge connects a vertex in $U$ to a vertex in $W$, and vice-versa. That is, *no edge connects two vertices within the same subset*, so that $E \subseteq U \times W$. As such, a graph can only be bipartite if it contains no cycles of odd length.
>
>Complete bipartite graphs are denoted as $K_{|U|, |W|}$.
# Intuition
Although we can't prove bipartition, we can think about as to why the sets $V$ and $E$ can be expressed using the two bipartite sets $L$ and $R$:
- The first fact is simply a union of the two groups of nodes, $L$ and $R$. 
- The second fact states that $E$ is equal to or a subset of all possible combinations of edges between the two groups. **A graph where $E = L \times R$ (every vertex from one group connects to all of the vertices from the other) be expressed as $K_{|L|,|R|}$.

>[!note] Null Distribution
>The null distribution is the sampling distribution of a null hypothesis, and is made up of a test statistic. Test statistics may include finding the mean, a difference in proportions, the chi-squared statistic, and others.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.5c The P-Value]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/14 01:17:28","modified":"2023/12/14 07:31:12"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] P-Value
>The p-value is the probability of a test statistic as extreme (or more extreme) than the one observed under the null hypothesis. If the p-value is high, it is consistent with the null hypothesis. If it is very low, it is very unlikely in a real-world scenario, so the null hypothesis can be rejected.

>[!example] USA v. Gilbert
>Before we shuffled the data, the difference in proportion of deaths was $p_{Gilbert} - p_{\text{No Gilbert}} = \frac{40}{257}-\frac{34}{1384}=0.131$. This is a pretty big discrepancy, but we still need to compare it to the null distribution:
>```R
># Load the Data Frame
>code_blue <- read_csv("https://www.dropbox.com/s/yj3grtilupyj9pv/code_blue.csv?dl=1") %>% slice_sample(prop = 1)
>
># Shuffle the response and explanatory variables 5000 times and calculate the null distribution of the difference in proportions between deaths on and off Gilbert's shift 
>null <- code_blue %>% specify(explanatory = staff, response = death, success = "yes") %>% hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% generate(reps = 5000, type = "permute") %>% calculate(stat = "diff in props")
>
># Plot!
>plot(null %>% ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + geom_histogram(bins = 23) + annotate("segment", x = .131, xend = .131, y = 0, yend = 600, color = "tomato"))
>```
>The difference, highlighted in red on the plot, is nowhere near the null distribution. This means that the p-value is 0, since there are no values larger than 0.131.

NOTE TITLE: [[3.5c Trees]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/05/26 21:49:07","modified":"2025/07/21 19:10:49"}

>[!note] Tree (Connected and Acyclic Graph)
>A tree is a [[3.5b Bipartite Graphs|bipartite graph]] that is both *connected* and *acyclic* (contains no cycles) (i.e., when one node is disconnected, the graph becomes disconnected). A graph that is *not connected* and *acyclic* is called a forest, and consist of more than one tree. Trees consist of a root, internal nodes, and leaf nodes. The following are all equivalent definitions of a tree $G=(V, E)$:
>1. $G$ is connected and contains no cycles.
>2. $G$ is connected and has exactly $|V|-1$ edges.
>3. $G$ is connected and the removal of any edge disconnects $G$.
>4. $G$ is acyclic and the addition of any edge creates a cycle in $G$.

# Properties
#### $G$ has exactly $|V| - 1$ edges.
*Backward direction. Proceed by contradiction.*
- If $G$ is connected and has $n-1$ edges, then it is acyclic.
- However, if $G$ had $n-1$ edges and contained a cycle, then removing one of the cycle's edges does not disconnect the graph. Therefore, we can create a tree with $n-2$ edges. However, a graph that contains less than $n-1$ edges is always disconnected (see 3.1).
#### All trees are [[3.3 Bipartition|bipartite]].

#### For all trees, $f=1$.
Since trees are acyclic by definition, it only follows that the plane will not be subdivided into extra faces.

>An $n$-dimensional hypercube can be represented as a graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{0, 1\}^n$ vertices, where $V$ is the set of all $n$-bit strings. Two vertices of a hypercube are connected by an edge if and only if the two vertices differ in exactly one bit position.
>
>Recursively, an $n$-dimensional hypercube is the result of joining two $(n-1)$-dimensional hypercubes with vertices $0x$ and $1x$ where $x \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$.
# Properties
##### (Hypercube Vertices) For an n-dimensional hypercube, $v=2^n$.
1. *Base Case:* A 0-dimensional hypercube has $2^0=1$ vertex by inspection.

3. *Inductive Step:* We see that for $n+1$, $v=2(2^n)$, and therefore the theorem holds for all $n$.
##### (Hypercube Edges) For an n-dimensional hypercube, $e=n2^{n-1}$.
We observe that the degree of each vertex of an $n$-dimensional hypercube is exactly $n$. Simultaneously, we observe that each edge is counted twice. Therefore, $e=\frac{n2^n}{2}=n2^{n-1}$.

>A **compiler** is a specialized software tool in the build process that translates code written in a high-level programming language (such as C, C++, or Java) into assembly language.

# Understanding
The compiler is essentially the first step in the high-level programming build pipeline. Code such as `for` and `while` loops (that you jump back to), and functions, are translated to labels.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/04/15 17:13:17","modified":"2025/04/23 13:23:16"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Duality
>**Duality** in optimization is the framework that associates every optimization problem, known as the **primal problem**, with another similar problem on the dual space called the **dual problem**. Let $F: X \times Y \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{ +\infty \}$ be a **perturbation function** (i.e., $F(x, 0) = f(x)$), and $p^*$ be the solution to the primal problem
>$$p^* = \inf_{x \in X} f(x).$$
>Then, $p^*$ can be associated with an **always convex** dual optimization problem on the dual space $Y^*$, such that
>$$d^* = \sup_{y^* \in Y^*} \{ -F^*(0, y^*) \}.$$
>The values between these problems are always related via the **weak duality principle**, such that $$p^* \geq d^*.$$
>Moreover, **strong duality** holds (i.e., $p^* = d^*$) if certain constraint qualifications are met.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.1 Modular Arithmetic]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/06 05:53:23","modified":"2025/07/27 20:50:23"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Modular Arithmetic
>For any integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and any positive integer $m \in \mathbb{N}$, known as the **modulus**, the **division algorithm** guarantees that there exist unique integers $q$ (the **quotient**) and $0 \leq r \leq m-1$ (the **remainder**), such that 
>$$x = qm + r.$$
>The remainder, written as $r = x \pmod{m}$, is the **unique value** in the set $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ that is **congruent** to $x$ modulo $m$.
>
>In general, two integers $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$ are said to be **congruent** modulo $m$, written $x \equiv y \pmod{m}$, if they leave the same remainder when divided by $m$. Equivalently, $x \equiv y \pmod{m}$ means that $m \mid (x - y)$ (i.e., the difference $x - y$ is divisible by $m$).
>
>We now define arithmetic operations. Suppose $a \equiv c \pmod{m}$ and $b \equiv d \pmod{m}$: 
>1. **Addition:** $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{m}$.
>2. **Multiplication:** $a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod{m}$.
>3. **Exponentiation:** $a^k \equiv c^k \pmod{m}$ and $b^k \equiv d^k \pmod{m}$. Note that modular arithmetic does not preserve congruence in the exponent.
# Intuition & Proof
Floor division and the modulus are complementary operations: floor division gives the integer part of $x$ divided by $m$, while modulo gives the remainder $r$. Any $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ can be decomposed into these parts using the equation $x=\lfloor \frac{x}{m} \rfloor m+(x \pmod{m})$. Here, $q=\lfloor \frac{x}{m} \rfloor$ is the quotient, and $r=x \pmod{m}$ is the remainder. We now proceed with proving our arithmetic operations.
- **Addition.** We know that $c = a + \alpha m$ and $d = b + \beta m$ for some $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore, $c+d=a+b+m(\alpha+\beta)$. By definition, $q=\alpha + \beta$ and $r=a+b$, so $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{m}$.
- **Multiplication.** Just as above, we substitute for $c,d$ such that $cd=(a+\alpha m)(b+ \beta m)$. This results in $cd=ab+m(\alpha b + \beta a + \alpha \beta m)$. Then, $q=\alpha b + \beta a + \alpha \beta m$ and $r=ab$, so $a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod{m}$.
- **Exponentiation.** We already proved multiplication, so exponentiation is simply an extension of this.

# Properties
#### (*Canonical Representation*) For any modulus $m$, the set of all integers $\mathbb{Z}$ can be divided into exactly $m$ non-overlapping infinite sets, where each set contains all integers that leave the same remainder when divided by $m$.

#### (*Prime Modulus*) For any prime modulus $p$, all numbers in $\{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$ have a modular inverse.
This is trivially true, since $\gcd(i, p)=1$ for all $i=1,\ldots,p-1$.

#### (*Wilson's Theorem*) It holds that $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ if and only if $p$ is prime.
Note that $-1 \equiv p-1 \pmod{p}$. We now prove this theorem.
- Sufficiency ($\implies$): in the previous point, we observed that all numbers in $\{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$ have a modular inverse. Since all prime numbers are odd (for the exception of $2$, which has a single element in the set of nonzero residues), this means that their set of residues are even, and therefore all elements can be matched with their inverse. Since the only two numbers that are their own inverses and cannot be matched are $1$ and $p-1$, this means that
$$(p-1)! \equiv (p-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 1 \equiv p-1 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}.$$
- Necessity ($\impliedby$): consider a composite number $n>3$. Then there exist numbers $k,m \in \{ 1, \ldots, n-1 \}$ for which $km=n$, and therefore $km \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$, which is equivalent to saying that $km \mid (n-1)!$ As such, $$(n-1)! \equiv (n-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot m \cdot \ldots \cdot 1 \equiv (n-1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 0 \cdot 1 \equiv 0 \not\equiv -1 \pmod{n}.$$
Therefore Wilson's Theorem only holds if $\gcd(i, n)=1$ for all $i \in \{ 1, \ldots, n-1 \}$, which is only true for prime numbers.

#### (*Fermat's Little Theorem*) For any prime modulus $p$ and any $a \in \{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$, it holds that $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.


# Examples
>[!example] Party Tricks
>You are at a party celebrating your completion of the CS 70 midterm. Show off your modular arithmetic skills and impress your friends by quickly figuring out the last digit(s) of each of the following numbers:
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $11^{3142}$.
>>We find that $11^{3142} \equiv 1^{3142} \pmod{10}$, and so the last digit is $1$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $9^{9999}$.
>We simplify, such that $9^{9999} \equiv 9 \cdot 9^{2(4999)} \equiv 9 \cdot 81^{4999} \equiv 9 \cdot 1^{4999} \equiv 9 \pmod{10}$, so the last digit is $9$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the last digit of $3^{641}$.
>>We proceed as before, so $3^{641} \equiv 3 \cdot 3^{4(160)} \equiv 3 \cdot 81^{160} \equiv 3 \cdot 1^{160} \equiv 3$, so the last digit is $3$.

>[!note] Portfolio Weighting
>Portfolio weighting is the process of determining what percentage of the total portfolio value $V$ that each asset should represent, such that each asset's value is equal to $V_{i}=w_{i}V$. A portfolio of $n$ assets can be
>- **Equal-weighted**: all assets have a uniform weight of $w_{i}=\frac{1}{n}$.
>- **Price-weighted**: the $i$-th asset has a weight of $w_{i}=\dfrac{P_{i}}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}P_{i}}$ for a share price $P_{i}$.
>- **Value-weighted (cap-weighted)**: the $i$-th asset has a weight of $w_{i}=\dfrac{P_{i} \cdot S_{i}}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}P_{i} \cdot S_{i}}$ for a share price $P_{i}$ and $S_{i}$ total outstanding shares.

>[!note] Shannon's Source Coding Theorem
>**Source coding** is the process of encoding *purely random* information from the symbols $x \in \mathcal{X}$ into a bit string representation that uses the most compressed sequence of bits for which it is possible to recover the symbols.
>
>Source coding is governed by the **Source Coding Theorem**, which states that any source coding scheme must use, on average, at least as many bits per symbol as the [[1. Shannon Entropy|entropy]] of the source, ensuring that the encoded message retains all the original information. 
>
>Mathematically, for a sequence of symbols $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}$ with a random binary length $l(X)$, and an arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0$, there is a source coding scheme from which the sequence can be recovered with high probability (i.e. $p > 1-\epsilon$), such that
>$$H(X) \leq \lim_{ n \to \infty }\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{l(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})}{n} \right] \leq H(X) + \epsilon,$$
>where $\frac{l(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n})}{n}$ represents the average bits per symbol of the sequence.
# Intuition

NOTE TITLE: [[4.1a Residual Sum of Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/20 03:45:21","modified":"2023/12/14 04:15:11"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] RSS & Least Squares
>The residual sum of squares formula is,
$${RSS} = \sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2,$$
>for a value $y_i$ and its fitted value on a regression line $\hat{y}_i = b_1x_i + b_0$, in a set of $n$ observations
### Intuition
The residual sum of squares formula calculates all the squared residuals within $n$ between the actual y-value ($y_i$) and the y-value predicted by the linear model ($\hat{y}_i$). It essentially is a measure of the model error, since the larger the residuals between each $i \to n$, the larger the RSS.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.1b Least Squares]]

METADATA:{"created":"2023/12/14 03:06:47","modified":"2023/12/14 04:26:37"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Optimization
>The least (minimized) squares equations for $b_0$ and $b_1$ are:
>- $$\text{Slope: } b_1=\frac{s_y}{s_x}r$$
>Where $s_i$ is the standard deviation for variable $i$, and $r$ is the correlation coefficient of the variables.
>- $$\text{Intercept: } b_0=\bar{y}-b_1\bar{x}$$
>Where $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ is the mean (mid) point in the scatter plot since the least squares line has to pass through it.

### Intuition
We can express the RSS formula as a function of the slope ($b_1$) and the y-intercept ($b_0$) of the linear model using $\hat{y}_i = b_0+b_1x_i$:
$${RSS}(b_0,b_1)=\sum^{n}_{i=1}[y_i-(b_0+b_1x_i)]^2$$
We must minimize this model for $b_0$ and $b_1$ in order to find the linear model. Two ways to do this is using the newer **Gradient Descent** (which also fits deep-learning models), or the older **Nelder-Mead Algorithm** which works by taking the smallest midpoint on a n-dimensional simplex (a 2D triangle or a 3D pyramid), and transforming it to the most optimal (downhill) point. When optimized, we get the least squares solution.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.1c Explanatory Power]] METADATA:{"created":"2023/11/20 04:50:14","modified":"2023/12/14 05:18:58"} NOTE BLOCK CONTENT: >[!Theorem] >We can define explanatory power as >$$R^2=\frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}.$$ >$0 \leq R^2 \leq 1$: a lower $R^2$ means predictions are less accurate. ### Intuition Before we construct a linear prediction model, we need to make a naive prediction using another type of summary. Usually this is the mean, denoted by $\bar{y}$. We then must measure the degree to which this naive prediction $\bar{y}$ explains away variability in $y_i$. We must first define two more expressions, the **Sum of Squares Due to Regression**, and the **Total Sum of Squares**. $$SSR=\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2$$ The s**um of squares due to regression** explains how much variance was removed due to the regression model. It makes sense: it is the squared sum of residual between each of the points on the linear model and the mean. $$TSS = \sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2$$ The total sum of squares represents the total variability of the data from the mean. It is basically variance without the normalization (division by $\frac{1}{n-1}$). Here is a chart representing all 3 of the statistics (the third one is the Residual Sum of Squares). Because $TSS$ is the total sum, and $SSR$ is the sum due to regression, we can find $SSR$ as a proportion of $TSS$: $$R^2= \frac{SSR}{TSS}=\frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$$ ["Of all the variability in your y-variables, what proportion is explained using the linear model?"] Since SSR is the opposite of the RSS, and SSR+RSS make up TSS, we can find $R^2$ using RSS: $$R^2=1-\frac{RSS}{TSS} = \frac{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2 Assembler]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/07/09 01:21:30","modified":"2024/07/09 04:40:27"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Assembler
>An **assembler** is a specialized software tool in the build process that translates assembly language generated by the [[4.1 Compiler|compiler]] into machine code, which is directly executable by a computer's processor. The RISC-V assembler translates each source RISC-V `*.s` file into a `*.o` object file.
# Understanding
The assembler is the second step of the programming build pipeline. As mentioned, the RISC-V assembler translates all (pseudo)instructions and outputs the `.o` file, which contains:
1. A **file header**, which indicates the size and position of the components mentioned below.
2. A **text segment**, which contains the machine code (stored in `.text`).
3. A **data segment**, containing binary representations of all static data (in `.data`).
4. A **symbol table** that keeps track of the addresses of labels, as well as static and global `.data` variables referenced within that file and other files. 
	- By the native file, used to store symbols and replace their references when not yet defined in the code (forward references).
	- By other files, used to replace their external references to labels and variables in that file.
5. A **relocation table** keeping track of the locations that need to be updated with actual addresses during linking, internally or externally.
	- Internally, used by absolute jumps (`jal`, `jalr`).
	- Externally, used by all 

# Examples
>[!example] Two-Pass RISC-V Assembler
>Consider the following simple RISC-V file, `file_a.s`:
>```
 1	func_name:
 2		addi sp sp -4
 3		beq a0 x0 loop
 4		# [8 instructions here]
12		jal ra malloc
13
14	loop:
15		bneq t0 x0 done
16		# [3 instructions here]
19		j loop
20
21	done:
22		ret
>```
>>[!example]+ First Pass
>>Assume that the function `func_name` starts at some address `fa_start`, which is the line that indicates the start of `file_a.s`. The assembler places this in the file's *symbol table*. 
>>
>>Going down, the assembler recognizes that line 3 references `loop`. However, it has no collection of `loop`'s address in the *symbol table*. As such, `loop` is placed in the *relocation table* for the second pass. 
>>
>>At line 12, the same is done for `malloc`.
>>
>>At line 14, the assembler recognizes the `loop` label, and places the address of `loop` into the *symbol table* as `fa_start + (13 * 4)`, since the first instruction of `loop` is $15-2=13$ lines/instructions away from `fa_start` and each instruction is 4 bytes in size. 
>>
>>At line 15, it stores the reference of `done` in the *relocation table* for the second pass. 
>>
>>At line 19, since it already has the address of `loop` in the *symbol table*, the reference to `loop` is replaced with the address `fa_start + 52`. Since this reference is resolved in the first pass, there is no need to store it in the *relocation table*.
>>
>>At line 21, the assembler recognizes `done`, saving it in the *symbol table* as `fa_start + (20 * 4)` using the same reasoning as before. This concludes our first pass of the assembler.
>
>>[!example]+ Second Pass
>>There are 3 references which need relocation in the second pass. This includes `loop` (3), `malloc` (12), and `done` (15). The assembler proceeds through the code again, setting the address of `loop` (3) to `fa_start + 52`.
>>
>>However, it cannot recognize `malloc` anywhere in the *symbol table*. As such, it skips the reference as it is external. External references are resolved in the linking stage.
>>
>>It then sets the address of `done` (15) to `fa_start + 80`.
>>
>>The second pass is now complete.

# Proof
Consider the perturbation function $F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Ax-y)$. Then, the primal problem is given on the function $F(x,0)$. Taking the convex conjugate of $F(x,0)$, we get:
$$F^*(x^*, 0)=\sup_{x \in X}\{ \langle x^*, x \rangle - F(x^*, x) \}$$

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2 Modular Inverse]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/07/22 20:03:59","modified":"2025/08/10 12:25:58"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Modular Inverse
>In [[4.1 Modular Arithmetic|modular arithmetic]], a **modular inverse** $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ exists for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, such that $a \cdot x \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$, if and only if $\gcd(x, m)=1$ (i.e., $x$ and $m$ must be coprime). The easiest way to find the greatest common divisor of two integers is using **Euclid's Algorithm**, which recursively divides the integers based on the identity
>$$\gcd(x, m) = \gcd(m, x) = \gcd(m, x \bmod m),$$
>and terminates when the remainder becomes zero. 
>
>The **Extended Euclidean Algorithm** not only computes $\gcd(x, m)$, but also performs a backward pass to find (not necessarily distinct) integers $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, which satisfy **Bezout's identity**,
>$$ax + bm = \gcd(x, m).$$
>It is executed as follows:
>1. Set the starting pair $\alpha_{1} = x$ and $\beta_{1} = m$.
>2. While $\beta_{i} \neq 0$ (forward pass / standard Euclid): 
>	1. Let $\alpha_{i+1} = \beta_{i}$ and $\beta_{i+1}=\alpha_{i} \pmod{\beta_{i}}$.
>3. Now set $a_{n} = 1$ and $b_{n}=0$.
>4. Then, for $j = n-1, \ldots, 2, 1$ (backward pass):
>	1. Let $a_{j}=b_{j+1}$ and $b_{j}=a_{j+1}-\lfloor \alpha_{j} / \beta_{j} \rfloor \cdot b_{j+1}$.
>5. When you are done, you will have the coefficients and factor that solve $ax+bm=d$.
# Proof & Intuition
### Inversion
Here is where modular arithmetic gets a little tricky. We will go ahead and prove necessity and sufficiency for inversion:
1. **Sufficiency ($\implies$):** Since $x$ and $m$ are coprime, neither can divide the other. Enter Bezout's Identity, which states that $ax+bm=1$. We take both sides modulo $m$, and obtain $$a \cdot x \equiv 1 \pmod{m}.$$As such, we find that $a$ is the inverse of $x$. You can think of $b$ as the "correction term" for the linear Diophantine, although it has no modular meaning unless we rearrange $m$ and $x$, such that $b$ is the inverse of $m \pmod{x}$.
2. **Necessity ($\impliedby$)** We have that $a \cdot x \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$. Then by definition of modular congruence, there exists an integer (quotient) $q$ such that: $ax=qm+1$. Rearranging, $ax-qm=1=\gcd(x, m)$ per Bezout's identity.

Intuitively, why is $\gcd(x, m)$ the condition for modular inversion? Think about it this way: if $x$ and $m$ shared a common factor $d > 1$, then that $d$ must be able to divide any linear combination of $x$ and $m$. 

### Euclid's Algorithm
The statement above will help us prove the fact that $\gcd(x, m)=\gcd(m \bmod{x})$. In order to see it, express $x=qm+r$. Then, if $d$ divides $x$ and $m$, then $d$ also divides $qm$, as well as $r=x-qm$ when rearranging. Now plug $x=16$ and $m=10$ and try it yourself.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2 Poisson Processes]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/03/23 17:56:55","modified":"2025/08/06 12:53:32"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

(cont'd) #### (*Random Incidence Paradox*) $\mathbb{E}[(T_{n+1}-t^*)+(t^*-T_{n})]=\dfrac{2}{\lambda}$.
Consider some random arrival time $t^*$ dividing the inter-arrival time $S_{n+1}=T_{n+1}-T_{n}$ into two distinct intervals, $L=t^*-T_{n}$ and $M=T_{n+1}-t^*$. Then, because inter-arrival times are memoryless, $L \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $M \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, and $L,M$ are independent of one another. By the linearity of expectation, 
$$\mathbb{E}[L]+\mathbb{E}[M]=1/\lambda+1/\lambda=2/\lambda.$$
This is a paradox for a reason: wouldn't $\mathbb{E}[T_{n+1}-T_{n}]=1/\lambda$? The answer is also yes! We can make the following rationale:
1. $\mathbb{E}[T_{n+1}-T_{n}]=1/\lambda$ is the expected inter-arrival time in a Poisson process.
2. $\mathbb{E}[(T_{n+1}-t^*)+(t^*-T_{n})]=2/\lambda$ is the expected inter-arrival time in the interval which some random $t^*$ falls into.

It turns out that this result leads us to the conclusion that since we are choosing our time $t^*$ randomly, it’s more likely it lands in a longer interval than a short one regardless of its distribution. Longer intervals have a better chance to be chosen, while shorter intervals have a lower chance. Think about that the next time you are trying to catch the next bus!
# Examples
>[!example] Bus Station
>You are waiting for a bus at a bus station. A-line buses arrive at the station according to a Poisson process with an average arrival time of 10 minutes. 
>>[!example]- If the A-line has been running for a long time and you arrive at the bus station at a random time, what is your expected waiting time?
>>The expected time of the Poisson Process $\text{PP}(0.1)$ is $1/0.1=10$ minutes. Therefore, on average, you will have to wait 10 minutes for the next bus.
>
>>[!example]- On average, how many minutes ago did the last A-line bus leave?
>>The memoryless property still applies backwards in time, so on average, the last bus arrived 10 minutes ago as well.
>
>The bus station you are waiting at also services B- and C-line buses, and you can use the C-line to reach your destination. There is a 95% chance that the next C-line bus will arrive within 26 minutes.
>
>>[!example]- You are in a rush to make it to your probability class–what is the chance that the next C-line bus will arrive within 6 minutes?
>>We start by observing that $F_{T}(x=26)=1-e^{-26\lambda}=0.95$. Solving, we obtain $\lambda \approx 0.115$ (i.e., 8.7 minutes on average per bus). We then plug in $F_{T}(x=6)=1-e^{-6 \cdot 0.115} \approx 0.5$.
>
>The B-line buses arrive every 5 minutes on average. However, B-line buses take you on a completely different route, and are not useful.
>>[!example]- What is the chance that an A-line or C-line bus will arrive before a B-line bus?
>>Assume all three lines are independent Poisson processes, so the time until the next bus on each line is exponential with rates $\lambda_{A}=1/10$, $\lambda_{B}=23/200$, $\lambda_{C}=1/5$. We merge these 3 processes and look at the result:
>>$$\mathbb{P}(\min(T_{A}, T_{C}) < T_{B})=\frac{\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}}{\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{B}+\lambda_{C}} \approx 0.52.$$

>[!example] Spam/Ham (Poisson Merging)
>Emails to Bob gets automatically classified, and those considered to be Spam are routed to a Spam folder. Emails not classified as spam are routed to Bob's Inbox. Regular email arrives as a Poisson Process with rate **10 msgs/hr** and Spam arrives at a rate of **20 msgs/hr**. A regular email is classified as **spam with probability 0.05** and a spam email is classified as **regular mail with probability 0.01**. 
>>[!example]- Bob checks his Inbox after a long time and selects the most recent message. What is the probability it is spam?
>>Genuine mails that pass the spam filter arrive at $\lambda_{\text{regular}}=10 \cdot (1-0.05)=9.5$ msgs/hr. Spam mails that pass the spam filter arrive at $\lambda_{\text{spam}}=20 \cdot 0.01=0.2$ msgs/hr.
>>
>>As such, the probability of spam mail in Bob's Inbox is $\dfrac{0.2}{9.5+0.2}=0.0206$.
>
>>[!example]- What’s the probability that the top email in his spam mail is regular mail?
>>We use the logic from the previous problem: genuine mail gets rejected by the spam filter at a rate of $\lambda_{\text{reg, rej}}=10 \cdot 0.05=0.5$ msgs/hr, whereas spam gets rejected at a rate of $\lambda_{\text{spam, rej}}=20 \cdot (1-0.01)=19.8$ msgs/hr.
>>
>>As such, the probability of regular mail in Bob's spam mail is $\dfrac{0.5}{19.8+0.5}=0.0246$.

>[!note] History
>The history $h_t$ of a [[4.1 Infinitely Repeated Game|repeated game]] at period $t$ is the set of all possible actions taken by all players at times $\tau < t$. Formally, the history of a repeated game at time $t$ given the strategy profile of every stage game at $\tau < t$ can be expressed as
>$$h_t = s_2 \times s_3 \times \ldots \times s_{t-1}$$
>>[!warning] Note!
>>The history of period $1$ is simply $h_1=\emptyset$, since there is nothing occurring before stage $1$ of the game.
# Properties
##### At period $t \geq 2$, the set $h_t$  specifies $n^{t-1}$ actions.

# Example
>[!example] Infinitely Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
>Consider again the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma of two players. At $t=1$, there is no history, so $h_1=\emptyset$. However, at $t=1$, players can play the strategies $s_i=\{D, C\}$. As such, the history at $t=2$ is $h_2=\{(D, D), (D, C), (C, D), (C, C)\}$. Then, at $t=3$, players can again play the strategies $s_i\{D, C\}$. This leads to 
>$$h_3=\{\{(D, D), (D, D)\}, \{(D, D), (D, C)\}, \ldots, \{(C, C), (C, D)\}, \{(C, C), (C, C)\}\},$$
>specifying a complete history of all possible paths of play up to $t-1$.

METADATA:{"created":"2025/09/10 15:19:51","modified":"2025/09/10 16:06:45"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Heuristics
>**Heuristics** are functions $h(n)$ that estimate the cost from a state $n$ to a goal state. They guide informed search algorithms by “preferring” nodes believed to be closer to a goal. Good heuristics often come from solving _relaxed versions_ of the original problem, where constraints are removed so that the solution is easier to compute. Common heuristics for grid problems include Manhattan distance ($\ell^1$ norm)  and Euclidean distance ($\ell^2$ norm).
>
>Heuristics are crucial because they can dramatically reduce the number of expanded nodes compared to uninformed search, though their effectiveness depends on how well they approximate the true cost.

# Properties
#### (*Admissibility*) For any node $n$, $0 \leq h(n) \le h^*(n)$, where $h^*(n)$ is the actual minimal cost from $n$ to a goal.

#### (*Consistency*) A heuristic is consistent if, for every node $n$, successor $n’$, and step cost $c(n,a,n’)$, it holds that $h(n) \leq c(n,a,n’) + h(n’)$.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2b.2 Arrow-Debreu Securities]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/02/25 15:55:57","modified":"2025/03/29 02:22:44"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Arrow-Debreu Securities
>An **Arrow-Debreu security** is a contract that pays exactly one unit of currency *if a specific future state occurs*, and nothing otherwise.
>
>In an [[4.2b Arbitrage|arbitrage-free]] market with $N$ assets and $s$ possible future states, every asset’s price can be expressed as a linear combination of exactly $s$ Arrow-Debreu securities, with *no two securities paying in the same state*. The price of an Arrow–Debreu security is called the **state price** $q_i$ for state $i \in \{ 1, \ldots, N \}$. For a payoff matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times N}$ ($N \geq s$) and a state price vector $q \in \mathbb{R}^s$, the vector of today's asset prices $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is expressed as
>$$p=X^Tq.$$
>
>The existence of a distinct Arrow–Debreu security for every possible state implies that the **market is complete**. In other words, the market is complete if $\operatorname{Rank}(X) = s$. This means the $s$-dimensional space of all possible state payoffs is fully spanned by the assets, so every contingent claim can be replicated as a linear combination of these Arrow–Debreu securities.

# Properties
#### (*State Price Decomposition*) $q=\begin{dcases}(X^T)^{-1}p & \text{if } N=s, \\ (XX^T)^{-1}Xp & \text{if } N \ge s, \\ \varnothing & \text{otherwise.}\end{dcases}$
#### (*Uniqueness of State Price*) If LOOP holds and market is complete, then $q$ exists and is unique.

#### (*Market Completeness*) If $\min(q) > 0$, the market is complete.
# Examples
>[!example] Asset Pricing With Sate Prices
>We can describe a 3-state, 3-asset *complete* market as follows:
>
>|     **State/Asset**    |  $\textbf{AD}_{1}$  |  $\textbf{AD}_{2}$  |  $\textbf{AD}_{3}$  | $\textbf{A}_{1}$ | $\textbf{A}_2$ |
|:-------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------:|:-------:|
| $S_{1}$ |   1   |   0   |   0   |    3    |   $u_{1}$    |
| $S_{2}$ |   0   |   1   |   0   |    2    |   $u_{2}$   |
| $S_{3}$ |   0   |   0   |   1   |    1    |   $u_{3}$    |
| **Price**   |  $q_{1}$   |  $q_{2}$   |  $q_{3}$   |         |         |
>Then, the price of asset 1 can be expressed as the linear combination $q_{\text{A}_{1}}=3q_{1}+2q_{2}+q_{3}$. Similarly, the price of asset 2 is $q_{\text{A}_{2}} = u_{1}q_{1}+u_{2}q_{2}+u_{3}q_{3}$.

>[!note] Constant + MSE Solution
>The solution to the [[4.2b.1 Constant Model|constant model]] fitted with [[6.6a.2 MSE (L2 Loss)|L2 Loss]] is
>$$\hat{\theta}_0 = \bar{y}.$$
# Proof
First we differentiate MSE with respect to $\theta_0$:
$$\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MSE=\frac{-2}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\theta_0)$$
Then, we set $\frac{d}{d \theta_0}MSE=0$:
$$0 =\frac{-2}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i-\hat{\theta}_0) \iff \sum^{n}_{i=1}y_i=n \hat{\theta}_0$$
Therefore, we find that
$$\hat{\theta}_0=\frac{1}{n}\sum y_i=\bar{y}.$$

>[!note] A* Search
>**A* Search** is a search algorithm that expands the frontier node with the lowest estimated total cost, where $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$. Here, $g(n)$ is the actual path cost from the start to $n$ as used in [[[4.2a.3 Uniform Cost Search|UCS]], and $h(n)$ is the estimated cost from $n$ to a goal. Like Greedy and UCS, it uses a priority queue, but its ordering is by $f(n)$. 
>
>A* is both complete and optimal when the heuristic is **admissible** and **consistent**, where
>- **Admissibility** ensures that the algorithm never overestimates the true cost to the goal, such that for any node $n$, it holds that$0 \le h(n) \le h^*(n)$, where $h^*(n)$ is the true minimal cost from $n$ to the goal.
>- Consistency ensures that $f(n)$ is nondecreasing along paths, such that for every transition $n \xrightarrow{a} n’$ with step cost $c(n,a,n’)$, it holds that $h(n) \le c(n,a,n’) + h(n’)$, where $n'$ is the next node after action $a$ has been applied to it. 
>
> A*'s worst-case time and space complexity are exponential in the depth of the solution, but in practice, a good heuristic can dramatically reduce the number of expanded nodes. It is one of the most widely used search algorithms in AI because it combines the efficiency of heuristic guidance with the guarantees of UCS.

>[!note] Multiple Linear Regression (SLR)
>The multiple regression line is the unique straight line that minimizes the mean squared error across a dataset using multiple features given by the equation
>$$
>\hat{\mathbb{Y}} = \mathbb{X}\theta \iff
>\begin{bmatrix} \hat{y}_1 \\ \hat{y}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_n \end{bmatrix} =
>\begin{bmatrix}
>1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_1p \\
>1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_2p \\
>\vdots &   & \ddots &   & \vdots \\
>1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_np \\
>\end{bmatrix}
>\begin{bmatrix} \theta_0 \\ \theta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta_p \end{bmatrix}
>$$
>where $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the prediction vector, $\mathbb{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (p+1)}$ is the design matrix containing $x_{ij}$ for the $i$th observation and $j$th feature, and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+1)}$ is the parameter vector.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2c.2 MLR + MSE]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/03/07 00:45:05","modified":"2025/01/21 17:38:28"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Least Squares Estimate
>When fitted using [[6.6a.2 MSE (L2 Loss)|L2 loss]], the general solution to [[4.2c.1 Multiple Linear Regression|multiple linear regression]] is of the form
>$$\hat{\theta} = (\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{Y}$$
>for an invertible $\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X}$ only possible when $\mathbb{X}$ is in full column rank.
# Proof
We first take the original definition of MSE and massage it into vector form using the L2 norm:
$$MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2=\frac{1}{n}(||\mathbb{Y} - \hat{\mathbb{Y}}||_2)^2=\frac{1}{n}(||\mathbb{Y} - \mathbb{X}\theta||_2)^2$$
Since $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} = \mathbb{X}\theta$ is a linear combination of $\mathbb{X}$, $\hat{\mathbb{Y}} \in \mathrm{span}(\mathbb{X})$. To minimize the MSE we need that $\hat{\mathbb{Y}}$ which is closest to $\mathbb{Y}$. It turns out that the closest vector to $\mathbb{Y}$ in $\mathrm{span}(\mathbb{X})$ is the one right below $\mathbb{Y}$. Therefore, $\hat{\mathbb{Y}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{Y}$ onto $Span(\mathbb{X})$. However, the formula for orthogonality (perpendicularity) requires the dot product of two vectors to be equal to zero, or similarly $M^T \vec{v}=\vec{0}$. We can substitute $M$ with the design matrix, and $\vec{v}$ with the residual vector $\vec{e}$ to find $\theta$:
$$\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbb{Y}-\hat{\mathbb{Y}})=\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbb{Y}-\mathbb{X}\theta)=\vec{0} \iff \mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{Y}=\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X}\theta$$
Therefore,
$$\theta=(\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T \mathbb{Y}.$$
Note that $\vec{e} \perp Span(\mathbb{X})$, which includes $\mathbb{X}, \hat{\mathbb{Y}}$, their columns and any other vector/matrix $\in Span(\mathbb{X)}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.2c.3 MLR + Batch Gradient Descent]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/05/08 23:46:02","modified":"2024/05/22 03:21:59"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Gradient Descent and The Gradient Vector
>We may use an iterative algorithm, known as gradient descent, to numerically compute the optimal value of $\theta$ where the loss of a [[4.2c.1 Multiple Linear Regression|linear regression]] model is minimized by guesstimating the minimum until we converge to the real minimum value such that
>$$\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t - \alpha\frac{d}{d\theta}L(\theta_t),$$
>where $\alpha$ is the learning rate (or the magnitude of the steps).
>
>
>In doing so for multivariate models, we may generalize the gradient descent process for $n$ minimum theta values $\vec{\theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\theta}_0 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{\theta}_n\end{bmatrix}$ as
>$$\vec{\theta}_{t+1}=\vec{\theta}_t-\nabla_\vec{\theta}L(\theta_t),$$
>where $\nabla_\vec{\theta}L(\theta_t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_0} \\ \dots \\ \partial\theta_n\end{bmatrix}$ is the gradient vector.
>>[!warning] Convexity of the Loss Function
>>If our loss function is not convex (has more than one local minimum), choosing the wrong $\theta_G$ may lead to convergence to the wrong minimum.

# Intuition
Suppose we start at an optimal value of $\theta_G=\theta_0$. Since our guess $\theta_0 \neq \hat{\theta}$, we can split our guess into two cases:
1. The guess $\theta_0$ "undershoots" $\hat{\theta}$ ($\theta_G < \hat{\theta}$).
	- The derivative of our loss function will be **negative**, so we must **increase** our guess by moving in the positive direction of $\theta$ until $\theta_G \to \hat{\theta}$.
2. The guess $\theta_0$ "overshoots" $\hat{\theta}$ ($\theta_G > \hat{\theta}$).
	- The derivative of our loss function will be **positive**, so we must **decrease** our guess until $\theta_G \to \hat{\theta}$.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.3 Chinese Remainder Theorem]]

METADATA:{"created":"2024/06/12 09:51:39","modified":"2025/08/10 11:14:38"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Chinese Remainder Theorem
>Given pair-wise **coprime moduli**  $n_{1},\dots ,n_{k}$ and their product $N=\prod_{i=1}^{k}n_{i}$, the **Chinese Remainder Theorem** states that there exists a **unique integer** $0 \leq x \leq N - 1$ that simultaneously satisfies $x\equiv a_{i}\pmod{n_{i}}$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, n$. 
>
>Moreover, writing $N_{i}=N/n_{i}$ and letting $N_{i}^{-1}$ denote the [[4.2 Modular Inverse|modular inverse]] of $N_{i} \pmod{n_{i}}$, the unique solution for $x$ can be explicitly constructed as
>$$x\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\,\bigl(N_{i}\,N_{i}^{-1}\bigr)\pmod{N},$$
>where $N_{i}N_{i}^{-1}$ are the **basis residues**, such that $N_{i}N_{i}^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n_{i}}$ and $N_{i}N_{i}^{-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{n_{j}}$ for all $n_{j} \neq n_{i}$.

# Intuition
Although difficult in theory, the CRT is based on the following claim:
- For $m, n$ with $\gcd(m, n) = 1$ that there is exactly one $x \pmod{mn}$ that satisfies the equations $x \equiv a \pmod{n}$ and $x \equiv b \pmod{m}$.

The proof for this claim is as follows. Let $u \equiv m(m^{-1} \pmod{n})$ and $v \equiv n(n^{-1} \pmod{m})$. Then, $u \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ and $u \equiv 0 \pmod{m}$, whereas $v \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ and $v \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$. This means that $x = ua+vb \equiv (1)a+(0)b \equiv a \pmod{n}$, and similarly $x \equiv b \pmod{m}$, meaning we have an $x$ satisfying the equation.
# Examples
>[!example] How Many Solutions?
>Consider the equation $ax \equiv b \pmod{pq}$ for distinct primes $p, q$. In the below three parts, all values $a, b, x$ are defined as values in in the range $\{ 0, 1, \ldots, pq-1 \}$.
>>[!example]- If $\gcd(a, pq) = p$, show that there exists a solution if and only if $b = 0 \pmod{p}$.
>>We proceed in the following way:
>>- **Sufficiency ($\implies$):** Since $b = 0 \pmod{p}$, this means that $b$ is also a multiple of $p$. As such, we can express $\frac{a}{p}x=\frac{b}{p} + kq$, which reduces to $\frac{a}{p}x \equiv \frac{b}{p}+mpq \equiv \frac{b}{p} \pmod{q}$. This congruence has a solution as long as $\gcd(a/p, q)=1$ (i.e., $a/p$ is invertible). We know that this requirement is satisfied since $\gcd(a, pq)=p$, meaning that $p \mid a$, but $q \not\mid a$.
>>- **Necessity ($\impliedby$):** Let $ax=b+kpq$. Since $\gcd(a, pq)=p$, then $0 \equiv b + 0 \pmod{p}$.
>
>>[!example]- If $\gcd(a, pq) = p$, and there is a solution $x$, show that there are exactly $p$ solutions.
>>a

Since $\gcd(a, pq) = p$, $a \equiv b \equiv 0$ as shown in the last step. We know that all solutions are of the form $\frac{a}{p}x=\frac{b}{p}+kq$. Therefore, it must be that $q \mid \left( \frac{a}{p}x-\frac{b}{p} \right)$. Since $\gcd(a, q)=1$, then $a/p$ is invertible, and we get $x \equiv (a/p)^{-1}b$. We lift to modulo $pq$, where we get In the set $\{ 0, 1, \ldots, pq-1 \}$ there are exactly $p$ multiples of $q$ (including $0$) that satisfy this condition given the right values of $a,b$.

NOTE TITLE: [[4.3a Markov Chains]]

METADATA:{"created":"2025/06/10 18:43:58","modified":"2025/06/10 19:50:41"}

NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:

>[!note] Markov Chain
>A **discrete-time Markov chain** is a sequence of random variables $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where the future only depends on the current state. Formally, $(X_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a Markov chain if and only if it satisfies the Markov property,
$$\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n}, \ldots, X_{0} = x_{0}) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = x_{n+1} \mid X_{n} = x_{n})=P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}).$$
>
>When $\mathcal{X}$ is finite, the set of one-step transition probabilities $\{ P(x_{n}, x_{n+1}) : x_{n},x_{n+1} \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}\}$ can be organized into a **transition probability matrix** $P \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}| \times |\mathcal{X}|}$, such that its rows sum to one. Then, the $k$-step transition equation is given as $$P_{k}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X_{k}=y \mid X_{0} = x) = P^k(x,y).$$
>
>Similarly, a sequence of random variables $(X_{t})_{{t \in \mathbb{R_{+}}}}$ is a **continuous-time Markov chain** on $\mathcal{X}$ if it satisfies the continuous-time Markov property,
>$$\mathbb{P}(X_{t+\delta t} = x_{t+\delta t} \mid X_{t} = x_{t}, \ldots, X_{0} = x_{0}) = \mathbb{P}(X_{t+\delta t} = x_{t+\delta t} \mid X_{t} = x_{t}).$$
>
>Different from DTMCs, CTMCs employ a **rate matrix** 
>
>>[!warning] Dependence on Past States
>>The fact that knowledge of the current state $X_{n}$ fully determines the distribution of the next state $X_{n+1}$ does not imply that $X_{n+1}$ is independent of all $X_{n-k}$ for $k \geq 1$. In general, the random variables in a Markov chain are *not independent*.

>[!note] Discounting
>Discounting is the process of reducing the value of payoffs in future stages of an [[4.1 Infinitely Repeated Game|infinitely repeated game]] to account for the preference for immediate rewards over delayed ones. This is represented by a discount factor $\delta \in (0,1)$, applied to future payoffs to compute their present value. A player $i$'s discounted payoff, provided that $i$ plays a strategy $s_i \in S_i$, is then given as
>$$\sum^{}_{i=1}\delta^{i-1}u_i(s_i)=\frac{u_i(s_i)}{1-\delta},$$
>where $u_i$ is the payoff function of player $i$.

>[!note] Risk
>Risk refers to the uncertainty (volatility) or potential for financial loss in an investment or business decision. It reflects the variability in returns due to external and internal factors. The risk of an asset can be quantified in a variety of ways, including the standard deviation of its price.
>
>Furthermore, risk can be broadly categorized into **systematic risk** and **idiosyncratic risk**:
>- **Systematic (market) risk** affects the entire market or economy. It cannot be eliminated through diversification.
>- **Idiosyncratic risk** affects a specific company, industry, or asset. It can be reduced through diversification.

>[!note] Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
>Two [[4.3 Matrix Multiplication|matrices]] $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ can be multiplied to create a matrix $A \times B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$, such that
>$$
>AB=
>\begin{bmatrix}  
>----\vec{a}_1^T---- \\  
>----\vec{a}_2^T---- \\
>\vdots \\  
>----\vec{a}_m^T----
>\end{bmatrix}
>\begin{bmatrix}  
>| & | &  & | \\  
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & | \\
>\vec{b}_1 & \vec{b}_2 & \cdots & \vec{b}_p \\ 
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & | \\
>| & | &  & |
>\end{bmatrix}
>=
>\begin{bmatrix}
>\vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_1^T\vec{b}_p\\
>\vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_2^T\vec{b}_p\\
>\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
>\vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_1 & \vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{a}_m^T\vec{b}_p
>\end{bmatrix},
>$$
>where each element of the resulting matrix $D_{ij} = \vec{a}_i^T\vec{b}_j$ equals the [[3.9a Dot Product|inner product]] of the left ($A$) matrix's $i$th row vector and the right ($B$) matrix's $j$th column vector.
>
>>[!warning] Non-Commutativity
>>The matrix product is non-commutative, meaning that, in general, $AB \neq BA$.
